title: French B2
description: The fourth step in French, from B1 to CEFR level B2, the level of the DELF B2. Lessons cover reading literary narrative in the passé simple and the passé antérieur, time relations such as à peine … que and en attendant que, past participle agreement in hard cases, the futur antérieur and the future in the past, the subjonctif passé, the subjunctive in relative clauses and after superlatives, fine choices between the subjunctive and the indicative, concession with quel que soit, si … que and quand bien même, conditions without si, every use of the conditionnel, modal verbs of probability, comparison and proportion, complex relatives, nominalisation, alternatives to the passive, the pronouns le, en and y in depth, cause, consequence, purpose and opposition, reported speech with free indirect speech, emphasis and inversion, the argued essay, the formal letter, defending a point of view aloud, and the DELF B2. About 580 new words build on the roughly 1,900 core words of French A1 to B1 for about 2,500 in all. Conjugation drills carry the A1 to B1 forms, optional honors lessons explore French and francophone literature, the Enlightenment and a capstone press dossier, and a reading list suggests graded readers, novels and free resources for this level. The standard is the French of France; Belgian, Swiss and Québec usage is noted where it differs. Unlocks when French B1 is complete.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Il était une fois un crime: the passé simple and the passé antérieur
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Open almost any French novel, tale or history book and the past is not told in the passé composé
you have used since A1. It is told in the **[[passé simple]]**: *il entra, elle vit, ils
s'enfuirent*. You won't need to write it, but at B2 you must read it without stopping, because
literature, history and some press articles are full of it.

This lesson teaches you to recognise the forms you'll meet, and one skill you will use: retelling
a passé simple story in the passé composé. The theme is the detective novel, *le roman policier*:
an original mystery set in Normandy, with an inspector, a body and three suspects.

## Two pasts for two worlds

French has two tenses for a completed past event:

- the passé composé (*elle est entrée*) for speech, letters, e-mails, most journalism and
  anything linked to the present;
- the **[[passé simple]]** (*elle entra*) for written narrative cut off from the present: novels,
  tales, history books, some biographies.

The passé simple is a **[[narrative tense]]**: it tells the events of a story. It is also a
**[[literary tense]]**, one that belongs to writing rather than speech. In conversation, *Hier, je
mangeai une pizza* would sound like a parody of a novel. But a novelist who writes *Il
ouvrit la porte* is writing perfectly normal French.

The passé simple does exactly the job the passé composé does in speech, and the imparfait keeps
its job: background and habits stay in the imparfait; the events that move the story forward go
in the passé simple.

![Two columns of sentences. Left, headed Written narrative (imparfait + passé simple): Il pleuvait sur la ville. L'inspectrice entra. Elle vit le cadavre. Dès qu'elle eut fini, elle sortit. Les témoins s'enfuirent. Right, headed Speech, letters, e-mails (imparfait + passé composé), the same sentences: Il pleuvait sur la ville. L'inspectrice est entrée. Elle a vu le cadavre. Dès qu'elle a fini, elle est sortie. Les témoins se sont enfuis. The first row, in the imparfait, is shaded because it doesn't change. A footnote gives the spoken alternative Après avoir fini, elle est sortie.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Recognising the passé simple

### The four ending sets

Every passé simple belongs to one of four sets. The third persons (*il / elle* and *ils /
elles*) are the forms you'll meet most, because most stories are about other people. Learn to
spot them first.

| | -er verbs: parler | -i- set: finir | -u- set: vouloir | -in- set: venir |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| je | parlai | finis | voulus | vins |
| tu | parlas | finis | voulus | vins |
| il / elle | parla | finit | voulut | vint |
| nous | parlâmes | finîmes | voulûmes | vînmes |
| vous | parlâtes | finîtes | voulûtes | vîntes |
| ils / elles | parlèrent | finirent | voulurent | vinrent |

- **-er verbs** (all of them, including *aller*: *il alla*) take *-a* in the third person
  singular and *-èrent* in the plural. Verbs in *-ger* and *-cer* keep their soft sound before *a*:
  *il mangea, il commença* (but *ils mangèrent, ils commencèrent*, with no extra letter before *è*).
- **The -i- set**: regular *-ir* verbs (*il finit, ils finirent*), *-re* verbs like *vendre* (*il
  vendit*), and many irregular verbs (*il prit, il mit, il dit, il fit, il vit*).
- **The -u- set**: *être, avoir* and many verbs in *-oir* (*il fut, il eut, il voulut, il
  put, il sut, il dut, il reçut*), and some others (*il connut, il vécut, il mourut, il lut*).
- **The -in- set**: *venir, tenir* and their compounds (*il revint, il devint, il obtint*).

![Four cards. Blue card, -er verbs: parler, with je parlai, tu parlas, il parla, nous parlâmes, vous parlâtes, ils parlèrent, and the note also il mangea, il commença. Green card, -i- set: finir, prendre, with je finis to ils finirent, and the note prendre: il prit, ils prirent. Yellow card, -u- set: vouloir, être, with je voulus to ils voulurent, and the note être: il fut, ils furent. Pink card, -in- set: venir, tenir, with je vins to ils vinrent, and the note tenir: il tint, ils tinrent. The il and ils forms are in bold.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two tricks help you read:

- The *nous* and *vous* forms carry a circumflex (*-âmes, -âtes*) and are rare: don't spend time
  on them.
- Some singular forms look exactly like the present: *il finit, il dit, il s'enfuit* can be
  either. Context decides. If the verbs around it are in the passé simple (*il se leva, il dit
  au revoir et il sortit*), so is this one.

### The irregular stems you'll meet most

Many irregular verbs build their passé simple on a stem that looks like the past participle
(*pris → il prit, voulu → il voulut, lu → il lut*). The ones below are worth knowing on sight,
because they are everywhere:

| infinitive | il / elle | ils / elles | infinitive | il / elle | ils / elles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| être | fut | furent | vouloir | voulut | voulurent |
| avoir | eut | eurent | savoir | sut | surent |
| faire | fit | firent | devoir | dut | durent |
| voir | vit | virent | venir | vint | vinrent |
| prendre | prit | prirent | naître | naquit | naquirent |
| mettre | mit | mirent | mourir | mourut | moururent |
| dire | dit | dirent | vivre | vécut | vécurent |
| pouvoir | put | purent | écrire | écrivit | écrivirent |
| conduire | conduisit | conduisirent | craindre | craignit | craignirent |
| recevoir | reçut | reçurent | connaître | connut | connurent |

Watch three false friends: *il fut* is *être* (not *faire*: that is *il fit*); *il vit* is
*voir* (not *vivre*: that is *il vécut*); and *il eut* (from *avoir*, pronounced like *u*) appears
in the passé antérieur below. This lesson's two irregular verbs follow the same patterns:
*résoudre* gives *il résolut* (-u- set), *s'enfuir* gives *il s'enfuit, ils s'enfuirent* (-i- set).

## The passé antérieur

The **[[passé antérieur]]** is the passé simple of *avoir* or *être* + a past participle: *il eut
fini, elle fut partie, ils se furent enfuis*. It has the same auxiliary and the same agreement as
the passé composé.

You'll meet it in passé simple narration, usually after a time word, for an action
finished just before the next event:

- *Dès qu'elle eut terminé, elle fit venir les suspects.* — As soon as she had finished, she
  sent for the suspects.
- *Quand les gendarmes furent partis, la maison redevint silencieuse.* — When the police had
  gone, the house fell silent again. (*Le gendarme*: a police officer of the gendarmerie.)
- *À peine eut-il prononcé ces mots qu'on frappa à la porte.* — Hardly had he spoken those words
  when someone knocked at the door.

The time words are *quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, après que, une fois que* and *à peine
… que* (lesson 02 looks at *à peine* closely). In everyday French a plain passé composé
replaces it (*Dès qu'elle a terminé, elle a fait venir les suspects*), or *après* + a past
infinitive (*Après avoir terminé, elle a fait venir les suspects*).

## Reading: Le mystère de la villa des Tilleuls

Read the story once for the plot, then again for the verbs: background in the imparfait, events
in the passé simple, earlier events in the plus-que-parfait, and two passé antérieurs.

> Ce soir-là, une pluie fine tombait sur Honfleur. Vers minuit, la cuisinière de la villa des
> Tilleuls découvrit le cadavre de Victor Ledru dans sa bibliothèque. La porte était fermée à clé
> de l'intérieur ; on dut la forcer. Personne, semblait-il, n'avait pu entrer ni sortir. C'était
> une véritable énigme.
>
> L'inspectrice Claire Morel arriva à l'aube. Elle examina la pièce pendant une heure sans dire un
> mot. Sur le bureau, elle remarqua une carafe de cognac, un verre vide et un agenda dont on avait
> arraché une page. Dès qu'elle eut terminé, elle fit venir les trois personnes qui avaient dîné
> avec la victime : son neveu Julien, sa secrétaire, Mme Aubry, et son vieil ami, le docteur Fabre.
>
> Les interrogatoires durèrent toute la matinée. Chacun avait un alibi : Julien et le docteur
> avaient joué aux cartes au salon de neuf heures à onze heures, et Mme Aubry affirma qu'elle
> s'était couchée vers dix heures. Mais chacun avait aussi un mobile. Julien attendait l'héritage,
> la secrétaire allait perdre sa place, et le docteur devait vingt mille francs à Ledru.
>
> L'enquêtrice suivit d'abord une fausse piste : la fenêtre. Puis deux détails l'arrêtèrent. La
> cuisinière jura que la carafe était à moitié vide la veille au soir ; or, elle était pleine. Et
> Julien se souvint soudain que le docteur avait quitté la table pendant dix minutes, vers dix
> heures, « pour téléphoner ». Ledru, comme chaque soir, s'était enfermé à onze heures et demie
> pour boire son cognac. Claire Morel comprit alors la vérité et l'annonça aux trois suspects : le
> meurtrier n'était jamais entré dans la bibliothèque fermée ; le poison l'attendait dans la carafe.
>
> À peine eut-elle prononcé ces mots que Mme Aubry se leva et s'enfuit vers le jardin. On la
> rattrapa au portail. Elle passa aussitôt aux aveux : elle avait fait le guet dans le couloir
> pendant que le docteur remplissait la carafe, contre la promesse d'une grosse somme. Le soir même,
> on procéda à l'arrestation du médecin. Dans la poche de son manteau, on retrouva la page de
> l'agenda : Ledru y avait noté la date à laquelle Fabre devait le rembourser.

*That evening, a fine rain was falling on Honfleur. At about midnight, the cook at the Villa des
Tilleuls discovered Victor Ledru's body in his library. The door was locked from the inside; it
had to be forced. Nobody, it seemed, could have got in or out. It was a real puzzle.*

*Inspector Claire Morel arrived at dawn. She examined the room for an hour without saying a
word. On the desk she noticed a decanter of cognac, an empty glass and a diary from which a page
had been torn out. As soon as she had finished, she sent for the three people who had dined with
the victim: his nephew Julien, his secretary, Mrs Aubry, and his old friend, Dr Fabre.*

*The questioning lasted all morning. Each of them had an alibi: Julien and the doctor had played
cards in the drawing room from nine to eleven, and Mrs Aubry stated that she had gone to bed at
about ten. But each of them also had a motive. Julien was waiting for the inheritance, the
secretary was about to lose her job, and the doctor owed Ledru twenty thousand francs.*

*The investigator first followed a false lead: the window. Then two details stopped her. The
cook swore that the decanter had been half empty the evening before; yet it was full. And Julien
suddenly remembered that the doctor had left the table for ten minutes, at about ten, "to make a
phone call". Ledru, as every evening, had shut himself in at half past eleven to drink his
cognac. Claire Morel then understood the truth and announced it to the three suspects: the
murderer had never entered the locked library; the poison had been waiting for him in the
decanter.*

*Hardly had she said these words when Mrs Aubry stood up and ran off towards the garden. She was
caught at the gate. She confessed at once: she had kept watch in the corridor while the doctor
filled the decanter, in exchange for the promise of a large sum. That same evening, the doctor
was arrested. In his coat pocket they found the page from the diary: Ledru had written on it
the date by which Fabre had to pay him back.*

Notice:

- *on dut la forcer* (*devoir*, -u- set), *il fit venir* (*faire*), *elle comprit* (*comprendre*,
  like *prendre*), *elle se leva … et s'enfuit*: each moves the story on.
- *tombait, était, avait, devait, attendait* set the scene: imparfait, as in speech.
- *avaient dîné, s'était couchée, avait quitté*: earlier events, plus-que-parfait, as in speech.
- *Dès qu'elle eut terminé* and *À peine eut-elle prononcé*: the two passés antérieurs.

## Retelling the story aloud: the passé composé

When you tell a story you've read, you switch to the passé composé. This is the productive skill
of the lesson. Here the inspector sums up the case for a local journalist.

```dialogue
# L'inspectrice raconte
Journaliste: Alors, inspectrice, comment avez-vous résolu cette énigme ?
= So, Inspector, how did you solve this puzzle?
Claire Morel: D'abord, j'ai suivi une fausse piste : la fenêtre. Ensuite, la cuisinière m'a parlé de la carafe.
= First, I followed a false lead: the window. Then the cook told me about the decanter.
Journaliste: Et vous avez compris que le meurtrier n'était jamais entré dans la pièce ?
= And you understood that the murderer had never been in the room?
Claire Morel: Exactement. Dès que j'ai dit le mot « poison », la secrétaire s'est levée et elle s'est enfuie.
= Exactly. As soon as I said the word "poison", the secretary stood up and ran off.
Journaliste: C'était la complice ?
= Was she the accomplice?
Claire Morel: Oui. Elle a fait le guet pendant que le docteur remplissait la carafe. Elle est passée aux aveux tout de suite.
= Yes. She kept watch while the doctor filled the decanter. She confessed straight away.
Journaliste: Et le mobile du docteur ?
= And the doctor's motive?
Claire Morel: Une dette. La page arrachée de l'agenda était dans sa poche. Nous l'avons arrêté le soir même.
= A debt. The page torn out of the diary was in his pocket. We arrested him that same evening.
```

### Example 1: converting a passage

*Task.* Put this passage into spoken French: *Elle entra, vit le corps et s'évanouit presque.
Quand elle eut repris ses esprits, elle appela la police.*

1. Find the passé simple verbs: *entra* (*entrer*), *vit* (*voir*), *s'évanouit* (*s'évanouir*,
   lesson 03). Each becomes a passé composé with its usual auxiliary: *elle est entrée, elle a
   vu, elle s'est presque évanouie*. The adverb *presque* goes between the auxiliary and the
   participle.
2. Find the passé antérieur: *eut repris*. In speech, use a plain passé composé (*Quand elle a
   repris ses esprits*) or *après* + a past infinitive (*Après avoir repris ses esprits*).
3. Check agreement with *être*: she is a woman, so *entrée, évanouie*.

Result: *Elle est entrée, elle a vu le corps et elle s'est presque évanouie. Quand elle a repris
ses esprits, elle a appelé la police.* (*Reprendre ses esprits*: to come round.)

### Example 2: which verb is which?

*Task.* Give the infinitive of *ils firent, elle fut, il vit, ils vécurent, il mit, elle naquit*.

*Faire, être, voir, vivre, mettre, naître.* The first three are the classic traps: *fit* (faire)
/ *fut* (être), and *vit* (voir) / *vécut* (vivre).

## Where else you meet the passé simple

- **Tales**: *Il était une fois une princesse … Un jour, elle partit …* (the opening, "once upon a
  time", is imparfait; the events are passé simple).
- **History books**: *Louis XIV naquit en 1638 et mourut en 1715.*
- **Some press narratives**, such as sports reports and history features: *À la 89e minute, le
  capitaine reprit le ballon et marqua.*

## The words of the detective novel

A detective novel follows a pattern. There is *un crime*, usually *un meurtre*: someone finds *le
cadavre*. The police send *un inspecteur* or *une inspectrice*, or *un enquêteur* / *une
enquêtrice*. They hold *des interrogatoires*, check each suspect's *alibi*, look for *le mobile*
and collect *des indices*. They follow *une piste*, sometimes *une fausse piste*. *Le mystère*
deepens; some puzzles, like a body in a room locked from the inside, are real *énigmes*. In the
end the detective *résout l'énigme* or *élucide l'affaire*, *l'assassin* or *le meurtrier* tries
to *s'enfuir*, *le complice* passes *aux aveux*, and *l'arrestation* closes the book. That last
part is *le dénouement*. A *mystérieux* stranger is almost compulsory, and *le narrateur* is often
the detective's friend.

![A detective's cork board with red strings joining four pinned items to a central photo of a man marked Dr F. Top left: a photo of a decanter under a magnifying glass, labelled l'indice. Top right: a card with a clock, two playing cards and the times 21 h – 23 h, labelled l'alibi. Bottom left: a card with banknotes and the words dette : 20 000 F, labelled le mobile. Bottom right: a photo of a woman marked Mme A., labelled la complice.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- **Writing the passé simple in your own letters or essays.** At B2, write the passé composé;
  keep the passé simple for reading. In a DELF letter, *je reçus votre courrier* would sound
  wrong.
- **Reading *il fut* as *faire* or *il vit* as *vivre*.** *Fut* is *être*, *vit* is *voir*.
- **Translating every imparfait as "was …-ing".** *Il pleuvait* can be "it was raining" or "it
  rained": what matters is that it is background.
- **Mistaking a passé antérieur for a plus-que-parfait.** *Il eut fini* is a single event just
  before the next one (*dès qu'il eut fini, il partit*); *il avait fini* is any earlier event.
  Both translate as "he had finished".
- **Forgetting that direct speech in a novel stays spoken:** *J'ai vu le meurtrier*, not *Je vis
  le meurtrier*.

## Key points

- The passé simple is the written narrative tense of novels, tales and history; the passé
  composé does the same job in speech and everyday writing. The imparfait is the same in both.
- Four ending sets: *-a / -èrent* (all -er verbs), *-it / -irent*, *-ut / -urent*, *-int /
  -inrent*. Learn the third persons first.
- Traps: *fut* (être) / *fit* (faire); *vit* (voir) / *vécut* (vivre); *il finit, il dit, il
  s'enfuit* can be present or passé simple.
- The passé antérieur (*il eut fini, elle fut partie*) follows *quand, dès que, à peine … que*
  in passé simple narration for an event finished just before the next one.
- Retell a passé simple story with the passé composé, the imparfait and the plus-que-parfait.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: À peine arrivée, elle repartit: time relations at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 gave you the tenses of written narrative. This lesson is about how events relate to
one another in time: what came first, what happened at the same moment, what was still to come.
At B1 you used *quand, dès que, avant que, jusqu'à ce que* and the futur antérieur after *dès
que*. B2 adds the precise, often formal tools: *à peine … que* with inversion, *sitôt*, *en
attendant que, le temps que, d'ici à ce que*, the *ça fait … que* family, and the adverbs that
mark a turning point (*désormais, dorénavant, dès lors*).

The theme is history and memory: the First World War, the 11 November commemorations, and a
family that goes looking for its past in the archives.

## Before, at the same time, after: one chart

In a sentence with a time clause, ask one question: when does the event in the time clause
happen compared with the main event?

- **[[Anteriority]]**: the time-clause event comes first. *Dès qu'elle eut fini, elle partit.*
- **[[Simultaneity]]**: the two happen at the same time. *Quand il est arrivé, il pleuvait.*
- **[[Posteriority]]**: the time-clause event comes later, or hasn't happened yet when the main
  event takes place. *Il est parti avant que je (ne) le voie.*

![A time arrow with a dark box labelled main-clause event in the middle. Three columns hang from the arrow. Left, blue, BEFORE it, anteriority: après que; dès que, aussitôt que; une fois que; sitôt que (literary); à peine … que; + indicative. Middle, green, AT THE SAME TIME, simultaneity: quand, lorsque; pendant que; au moment où; tant que; alors que, tandis que; + indicative. Right, pink, AFTER it (not yet), posteriority: avant que; jusqu'à ce que; en attendant que; le temps que; d'ici à ce que; + subjunctive. A note says quand and lorsque + a compound tense also mark anteriority.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The mood follows from the meaning. A time clause whose event has happened, or is presented as
certain, takes the indicative. A time clause whose event is still to come, from the point of view
of the main verb, takes the subjunctive: that is why *avant que* and *jusqu'à ce que* (B1) and
this lesson's *en attendant que, le temps que, d'ici à ce que* all take it. (*Après que* takes the
indicative in careful French, though the subjunctive is very common, as you saw at B1.)

The tenses also follow the frame of the story:

| frame | anteriority | simultaneity | posteriority |
|---|---|---|---|
| past | *Dès qu'il avait fini, il sortait.* | *Quand je suis arrivé, il pleuvait.* | *Il est parti avant que je le voie.* |
| present | *Dès qu'il a fini, il sort.* (habit) | *Quand il pleut, je lis.* | *Je reste jusqu'à ce qu'il revienne.* |
| future | *Dès qu'il aura fini, il sortira.* | *Quand il arrivera, on mangera.* | *Je resterai jusqu'à ce qu'il revienne.* |

In the future frame, French puts the time clause in the future too (*quand il arrivera*), and in
the futur antérieur for an event finished first (*dès qu'il aura fini*). Lesson 04 builds on this.

## À peine … que: hardly … when

*À peine … que* says that the second event followed the first almost at once. The clause with
*à peine* is the first event; *que* introduces the second.

In writing, when *à peine* opens the sentence, the subject pronoun usually goes after the verb.
This is **[[stylistic inversion]]**: an inversion that marks a formal written style, not a
question. It works like a question's inversion, with a hyphen and a *-t-* where needed:

- *À peine était-elle arrivée qu'on l'appela.* — She had hardly arrived when they called her.
- *À peine eut-il fini qu'il repartit.* (passé antérieur, lesson 01, in a literary text)
- With a noun subject, the noun stays first and a pronoun repeats it: *À peine le train était-il
  parti que l'orage éclata.*

In speech, put *à peine* after the verb (or the auxiliary) and don't invert: *Elle était à peine
arrivée qu'on l'a appelée.* You'll also hear *À peine elle était arrivée que …*: informal,
avoid it in writing.

The tenses pair up like this:

| frame | first event (à peine) | second event (que) |
|---|---|---|
| past, written | plus-que-parfait or passé antérieur | passé simple |
| past, spoken | plus-que-parfait | passé composé |
| present | passé composé | present: *À peine est-il rentré qu'il repart.* |
| future | futur antérieur | futur: *À peine sera-t-il arrivé qu'il voudra repartir.* |

A shorter written form drops the verb altogether: *À peine arrivée, elle repartit.* — She had
hardly arrived when she left again. The participle agrees with the subject, as with *être*.

Without *que*, *à peine* simply means "barely, hardly": *Il avait à peine vingt ans.* — He was
barely twenty. Here it doesn't open the sentence, so there's no inversion.

## Sitôt: immediately after

*Sitôt* + past participle is a compact, slightly literary "as soon as … had": *Sitôt arrivée aux
archives, elle a demandé le registre.* — As soon as she got to the archives, she asked for the
register. A participle on its own refers to the subject of the main verb and agrees with it; with
its own noun it agrees with that noun (*sitôt la cérémonie terminée*). Two set phrases: *sitôt dit, sitôt fait* (no sooner said than done). *Sitôt que* is
a literary *dès que*: *Sitôt qu'il eut reçu la lettre, il partit.*

## Waiting, the time it takes, until: three conjunctions + subjunctive

| conjunction | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *en attendant que* | while waiting for something to happen | *En attendant que la cérémonie commence, les enfants ont répété leur texte.* — While they waited for the ceremony to start, the children rehearsed their lines. |
| *le temps que* | in the time it takes for something to happen | *Le temps que je m'habille, le taxi sera là.* — By the time I'm dressed, the taxi will be here. |
| *d'ici à ce que* | by the time / until (often: that's a long way off) | *D'ici à ce que les archives rouvrent, on aura le temps de vieillir !* — By the time the archives reopen, we'll have grown old! |

All three take the subjunctive. When the subject is the same, use the infinitive: *en attendant
de partir, le temps de m'habiller*. *D'ici à ce que* is also written *d'ici que*.

Keep them apart from the B1 pair:

- *jusqu'à ce que* marks the end point: *Restez jusqu'à ce que le maire arrive* (stay until he
  arrives, then you can go).
- *en attendant que* stresses what you do during the wait: *En attendant que le maire arrive,
  lisez les noms sur le monument* (read the names while you wait).
- *avant que* simply places one event before another: *Partons avant qu'il pleuve.*

## For how long, since when: depuis que, il y a … que, voilà … que, ça fait … que

These four say how long a situation has lasted. Put the present for something still going
on, and the passé composé for something that happened once and whose result is still true,
especially with a negative:

- *Ça fait trois ans qu'il habite à Verdun.* — He's lived in Verdun for three years. (still
  does)
- *Ça fait trois ans qu'il est parti.* — He left three years ago. (and he's still away)
- *Il y a longtemps que je ne l'ai pas vu.* — I haven't seen him for a long time.
- *Voilà vingt ans qu'elle travaille aux archives.* — She has been working at the archives for
  twenty years.
- *Depuis que ma grand-mère est morte, personne n'ouvre plus le grenier.* — Since my
  grandmother died, nobody opens the attic any more.

*Ça fait … que* is spoken; *il y a … que* is neutral; *voilà … que* is slightly emphatic. Don't
confuse *il y a … que* (for, since) with *il y a* alone (ago): *Il est parti il y a trois ans* =
*Ça fait trois ans qu'il est parti.* In a past story, these move to the imparfait: *Ça faisait
cinquante ans que personne n'avait ouvert cette boîte.*

## A turning point: dès lors, désormais, dorénavant

- *Désormais* (from now on, henceforth) looks forward from the moment you're talking about. In
  the present it announces a change: *Désormais, la cérémonie aura lieu à onze heures.* In a past
  story it means "from then on": *Désormais, il ne parla plus de la guerre.*
- *Dorénavant* means the same and is used mostly for the present and future: rules, decisions,
  resolutions. *Dorénavant, les archives seront ouvertes le samedi.*
- *Dès lors* means "from then on", from a point in the past: *Il trouva le carnet ; dès lors, il
  ne pensa plus qu'à son grand-père.* It can also mean "consequently", in argument.
- *Jadis*, the opposite direction, is a literary "long ago": *Jadis, ce champ était un champ de
  bataille.* The everyday word is *autrefois* (A2).

## Formal time words: au préalable, entre-temps, ultérieurement

- *Au préalable* (beforehand, first) in instructions: *Pour consulter les registres, inscrivez-vous
  au préalable.*
- *Entre-temps* (1990 spelling *entretemps*: meanwhile, in the meantime): *Il est parti en 1914
  et n'est rentré qu'en 1919 ; entre-temps, sa fille était née.*
- *Ultérieurement* (later, at a later date) in official writing: *La date sera communiquée
  ultérieurement.* In speech, *plus tard*.

## Reading: Le carnet de Lucien

A woman writes on her family-history blog. Watch for the time words.

> Voilà trois ans que je cherche des traces de mon arrière-grand-père, Lucien, un poilu de la
> Somme. Tout a commencé dans le grenier de ma grand-mère. Ça faisait sans doute cinquante ans que
> personne n'avait ouvert la vieille boîte en fer. À peine l'avais-je ouverte que je suis tombée
> sur son carnet de guerre. Sitôt rentrée chez moi, je l'ai lu d'une traite.
>
> Lucien avait à peine vingt ans en 1914. Il a passé trois hivers dans les tranchées. Dans son
> carnet, il parle du froid, de la boue, des camarades disparus, mais presque jamais de lui. Il a
> été blessé en 1916 ; entre-temps, sa fille, ma grand-mère, était née.
>
> Pour en savoir plus, je suis allée aux archives départementales. Il faut s'inscrire au
> préalable, et le temps qu'on vous apporte les registres, une heure peut passer. En attendant que
> mon dossier arrive, une historienne m'a appris à lire une fiche matricule. Dès lors, je n'ai
> plus arrêté.
>
> Le 11 novembre dernier, j'ai assisté à la commémoration devant le monument aux morts de son
> village ; comme chaque année, on y commémorait l'armistice. Il a été signé vers cinq heures du
> matin, le 11 novembre 1918, dans un wagon, en forêt de
> Compiègne, près de Rethondes, et les combats ont cessé à onze heures. Le 11 Novembre est férié depuis 1922 ; depuis
> 2012, on y rend hommage à tous les morts pour la France. Il y avait des anciens combattants
> d'autres guerres, mais plus aucun de 14-18, évidemment : le dernier poilu, Lazare Ponticelli, est
> mort en 2008. Avec lui, une ère s'est achevée.
>
> Désormais, c'est à nous de faire vivre la mémoire collective. Le devoir de mémoire, pour moi, ce
> n'est pas un discours une fois par an. Jadis, les familles se racontaient ces histoires à table ;
> aujourd'hui, ce sont les archives qui les gardent. Je publierai le carnet de Lucien
> ultérieurement, quand je l'aurai recopié. Et d'ici à ce que mes enfants soient grands, j'espère
> qu'ils auront envie de le lire. Dorénavant, je ne passe plus devant un monument aux morts sans
> lire les noms.

*For three years now I've been looking for traces of my great-grandfather, Lucien, a poilu from
the Somme. It all started in my grandmother's attic. Nobody had opened the old tin box
for probably fifty years. I had hardly opened it when I came across his war notebook. As soon as
I got home, I read it in one go.*

*Lucien was barely twenty in 1914. He spent three winters in the trenches. In his notebook he
talks about the cold, the mud, the comrades who were lost, but hardly ever about himself. He was
wounded in 1916; in the meantime his daughter, my grandmother, had been born.*

*To find out more, I went to the departmental archives. You have to register beforehand, and
by the time they bring you the registers, an hour can go by. While I waited for my file to
arrive, a historian taught me how to read a military service record. From then on, I never
stopped.*

*Last 11 November, I went to the commemoration in front of the war memorial in his village; as every year, the armistice was being commemorated there. It was signed
at about five in the morning on 11 November 1918, in a railway carriage in the forest of
Compiègne, near Rethondes, and the fighting stopped at eleven o'clock. 11 November has been a public holiday since
1922; since 2012, it has honoured everyone who died for France. There were veterans of other wars,
but of course none from 1914–18 any more: the last poilu, Lazare Ponticelli, died in 2008. With
him, an era came to an end.*

*From now on, it's up to us to keep collective memory alive. The duty to remember, for me, isn't
a speech once a year. Long ago, families told each other these stories at the table; today, the
archives keep them. I'll publish Lucien's notebook later, when I've copied it out. And by the
time my children are grown up, I hope they'll want to read it. From now on, I never walk past a
war memorial without reading the names.*

Notice:

- *À peine l'avais-je ouverte que je suis tombée*: written inversion with a spoken passé
  composé, as in a blog. *Ouverte* agrees with *l'* (= *la boîte*), a direct object placed before
  (lesson 03).
- *Ça faisait … que personne n'avait ouvert*: the *ça fait* structure moved into the past.
- *Je publierai … quand je l'aurai recopié*: the futur antérieur for the event finished first.
- *Une fiche matricule* is a soldier's service record; *le poilu* (literally "hairy") was the
  nickname of the French infantryman of 1914–1918.

![A village square on 11 November. In the centre, a stone war memorial with a plaque of names and a statue of a First World War soldier on top, labelled le poilu; a green wreath lies at its foot, and the stone is labelled le monument aux morts. On the left, an old man in a beret with two medals holds a French flag, labelled l'ancien combattant. On the right, a man wearing a blue, white and red sash, labelled le maire, stands near two children, in front of the town hall with its flag.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- **Inverting after *à peine* in the middle of a sentence.** *Il avait à peine vingt ans*, not
  ~~Il avait à peine-il vingt ans~~. Inversion only when *à peine* opens the sentence.
- **Forgetting the subjunctive after *en attendant que, le temps que, d'ici à ce que*.** *En
  attendant qu'il vienne*, not *en attendant qu'il vient*.
- **Using *que* + subjunctive with the same subject.** Say *En attendant de partir, je range*;
  careful French avoids *en attendant que je parte, je range*.
- **Mixing up *il y a … que* and *il y a*.** *Il y a dix ans que j'habite ici* (for ten years,
  still true); *J'ai emménagé il y a dix ans* (ten years ago).
- **Following English "have worked" for a situation that continues.** "I've worked here for ten
  years" (and still do) is *Ça fait dix ans que je travaille ici*, with the present.
- **Using *dorénavant* in a past story.** It usually looks forward from now; in a narrative,
  prefer *désormais* or *dès lors*: *Désormais, il ne sortit plus.*

## Key points

- Anteriority, simultaneity, posteriority: ask when the time-clause event happens. Posteriority
  (*avant que, jusqu'à ce que, en attendant que, le temps que, d'ici à ce que*) takes the
  subjunctive.
- *À peine … que*: in writing, *À peine était-il arrivé qu'on l'appela*; in speech, *Il était à
  peine arrivé qu'on l'a appelé*. Short form: *À peine arrivée, elle repartit.*
- *Sitôt* + participle = as soon as (*sitôt arrivée*: same subject as the main verb); *sitôt
  que* = *dès que* (literary).
- *Ça fait / il y a / voilà … que* and *depuis que*: present for what continues, passé composé
  for a completed event whose result lasts (*Ça fait trois ans qu'il est parti*).
- *Désormais* (from now on, or from then on in a story), *dorénavant* (from now on), *dès lors*
  (from then on), *jadis* (long ago, literary); *au préalable, entre-temps, ultérieurement* in
  formal writing.

lessons.title: Les lettres que j'ai reçues: past participle agreement in hard cases
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since A1 you've known the two basic rules: with *être* the participle agrees with the subject,
with *avoir* it agrees with a direct object placed before it. At B2 you write longer sentences,
with relative clauses, pronouns and infinitives, and that is where the hard cases come up: *les
médicaments qu'il m'a prescrits*, *les heures qu'a duré l'opération*, *elle s'est lavé les
mains*. Most of these endings can't be heard, so they are a written skill, and a mark of careful
writing in an exam.

The theme is health and medicine: a stay in hospital, a GP's advice, public health and
screening.

## The two basic rules in one table

| auxiliary | the participle agrees with | examples |
|---|---|---|
| *être* (including the passive) | the subject | *La patiente est sortie hier. Les résultats ont été envoyés.* |
| *avoir* | a direct object placed before the verb | *J'ai reçu les résultats. Les résultats que j'ai reçus. Je les ai reçus.* |
| *avoir*, no object before | nothing: the participle stays as it is | *Elle a beaucoup toussé. Ils ont opéré ce matin.* |

The second line is the one that causes trouble. A direct object comes before the verb in four
main kinds of sentence. Each of them has a **[[preceding direct object]]**:

- a relative *que*: *Les symptômes que vous avez décrits sont fréquents.* — The symptoms you
  described are common.
- an object pronoun *le, la, les, l', me, te, nous, vous*: *La chirurgienne ? Je l'ai vue ce
  matin.* (*l'* = *la chirurgienne*)
- a question with *quel* or *combien de*: *Quelles analyses vous a-t-il prescrites ? Combien de
  patients avez-vous vus ?*
- *lequel / laquelle* in a question: *De ces deux spécialistes, laquelle as-tu consultée ?*

Ask *what?* or *whom?* after the verb: *J'ai prescrit quoi ? → des analyses.* If the answer is
already behind you in the sentence, agree with it.

## Hard cases with avoir

### En: usually no agreement

*En* is a direct object, but it stands for a quantity, not a definite thing, so the participle
usually stays as it is: *Des symptômes, j'en ai eu beaucoup.* — Symptoms? I had a lot of them.
Some grammars accept *eus* here, and you'll see it in print. Write it without agreement, and
don't mark the other version wrong when you read it.

### Impersonal verbs: never

A verb used impersonally, with *il* meaning "it", never agrees, even after *que*: *les grandes
chaleurs qu'il a fait l'été dernier*; *les trois semaines de soins qu'il a fallu*. The *que* is
not a real direct object of *faire* or *falloir* here.

### Participle + infinitive: who does the action?

When an infinitive follows the participle (*entendu, vu, regardé, senti*), ask who does the
action of the infinitive:

- *Les infirmières que j'ai entendues rire.* — The nurses I heard laughing. The nurses laugh,
  so *que* (the nurses) is the object of *entendre*: agreement.
- *Les chansons que j'ai entendu chanter.* — The songs I heard (someone) sing. The songs don't
  sing; *que* is the object of *chanter*: no agreement.

Two verbs have their own rule:

- ***Fait* + infinitive never agrees**: *La radio ? Je l'ai fait faire hier.* (*La radio* here
  is an X-ray.) *Elle s'est fait
  opérer du genou.* (*se faire* + infinitive: to have something done to you)
- ***Laissé* + infinitive**: under the 1990 spelling recommendations it is invariable, like
  *fait* (*Les visiteurs ? On les a laissé entrer*). The traditional rule treats it like
  *entendu* (*On les a laissés entrer*, since the visitors do the entering). Both are accepted
  today; this course doesn't test the choice.

### An infinitive or clause left out: dû, pu, voulu

After *devoir, pouvoir, vouloir, croire, penser*, the *que* often belongs to an infinitive that
is left out. The participle doesn't agree: *Il a fait tous les efforts qu'il a pu* (= *qu'il a
pu faire*). *Elle a pris tous les médicaments qu'elle a dû* (= *qu'elle a dû prendre*).

### Verbs of measure: coûter, valoir, peser, mesurer, durer, vivre, courir

With a measure (a price, a weight, a length of time), these verbs have no direct object, so no
agreement:

- *les deux heures qu'a duré l'opération* (durer never has a direct object)
- *les soixante-dix kilos que j'ai pesé* — the seventy kilos I weighed (my weight)
- *les dix euros que ce livre m'a coûté*

Several of them have a second, transitive sense, and then they agree like any verb:

- *les bébés que l'infirmière a pesés* — the babies the nurse weighed (she put them on the scales)
- *les efforts que ce traitement m'a coûtés* — the efforts this treatment cost me
- *les dangers qu'il a courus* — the dangers he ran

With *vécu* and *coûté*, grammars don't always agree on where the measure ends and the object
begins, so don't worry about borderline cases; learn the clear pairs above.

## Pronominal verbs

Pronominal verbs take *être*, but they don't simply agree with the subject. The question is what
*se* is.

- An **[[essentially pronominal verb]]** only exists with *se* (*s'évanouir, s'enfuir, s'absenter,
  se méfier, se souvenir*: there is no *évanouir quelqu'un*), or means something else without it
  (*se plaindre*, to complain; *plaindre*, to pity). These agree with the subject: *Elle s'est
  évanouie dans la salle d'attente. Ils se sont enfuis. Elle s'est plainte.*
- A **[[reflexive verb]]** is an ordinary verb whose object is the subject itself: *laver → se
  laver*. A **[[reciprocal verb]]** does the same with "each other": *voir → se voir*. For both,
  agree with *se* only when *se* is the direct object.
  - *Elle s'est lavée.* (She washed whom? Herself → *se* is direct → *lavée*.)
  - *Elle s'est lavé les mains.* (She washed what? Her hands. *Se* means "for herself", an
    indirect object → no agreement with *se*.)
  - *Les mains qu'elle s'est lavées.* (Now the direct object *que* = *les mains* comes first →
    agreement.)
  - *Ils se sont rencontrés* (rencontrer quelqu'un: direct) but *Ils se sont parlé* (parler à
    quelqu'un: indirect).
- So verbs built on an indirect object (*parler à, téléphoner à, succéder à, plaire à, nuire à,
  mentir à, sourire à, ressembler à* someone) don't agree with *se*: *Les médecins se sont succédé à son chevet.
  Elles se sont souri. Ces deux traitements se sont nui.*
- A **[[pronominal passive]]** agrees with the subject: *Ces médicaments se sont très bien
  vendus.*
- *Se rendre compte* never agrees: *Elle s'est rendu compte de son erreur* (*compte* is the
  object).

## A decision chart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Does the past participle agree?
  accDescr: A decision chart. First ask which auxiliary. With être and a verb that is not pronominal, agree with the subject. With a pronominal verb, ask whether the verb is essentially pronominal or a pronominal passive, or whether se is the direct object; if yes, agree with the subject; if se is indirect, agree only with a direct object placed before. With avoir, ask whether the verb is impersonal, is fait plus an infinitive, or has en as its object; if so, no agreement (with en, usually). Otherwise ask whether a direct object comes before the verb: if yes, agree with it; if no, no agreement.
  A["Which auxiliary?"] -->|être| B["Pronominal verb?"]
  B -->|no| C["Agree with the subject: elle est sortie"]
  B -->|yes| D["Essentially pronominal, passive, or se = direct object?"]
  D -->|yes| E["Agree with the subject: elle s'est évanouie"]
  D -->|"no, se is indirect"| F["Agree only with a direct object placed before: elle s'est lavé les mains"]
  A -->|avoir| G["Impersonal, fait + infinitive, or en?"]
  G -->|yes| H["No agreement (en: usually)"]
  G -->|no| I["Direct object before the verb?"]
  I -->|yes| J["Agree with it: les lettres que j'ai reçues"]
  I -->|no| K["No agreement: j'ai reçu les lettres"]
```

### Example 1: working through a sentence

*Task.* Choose the right ending: *Les comprimés que le généraliste m'a prescrit__ m'ont donné
des effets secondaires.*

1. Auxiliary: *avoir* (*m'a prescrit*).
2. Impersonal, *fait*, *en*? No.
3. Direct object: *prescrire quoi ? → que = les comprimés* (masculine plural), placed before.
   *M'* is the indirect object (to me), so it doesn't count.
4. Agree: *prescrits*. You can hear it in the feminine: *les pilules qu'il m'a prescrites*
   [pʁɛskʁit]. (*La pilule*: pill.)

### Example 2: pronominal or not?

*Task.* Complete: *Ma voisine de chambre s'est plaint__ toute la nuit, puis elle s'est
endormi__ ; le matin, les infirmières se sont parl__ dans le couloir.*

- *Se plaindre* (to complain) and *s'endormir* agree with the subject: *plainte, endormie*.
- *Se parler* = *parler à*: indirect, no agreement: *parlé*.

## Health and medicine in context

At the GP's (*chez le généraliste*), the patient (*le patient, la patiente*) describes the
*symptômes*; the doctor makes *un diagnostic* (*diagnostiquer* = to diagnose) and may refer the
patient to *un spécialiste*. For an operation, *le chirurgien* or *la
chirurgienne* operates on you (*on vous opère*) in a hospital department of *chirurgie*. *Le
traitement* may cause *des effets secondaires*; *les soins* continue at home until *la guérison*.
A *malade chronique* lives with a long illness.

Public health, *la santé publique*, is about *la prévention*: *la vaccination*, and *le
dépistage* (screening). In France, two national screening programmes invite people aged 50 to 74
every two years: women for a breast-cancer mammogram, and both sexes for a bowel-cancer test done
at home. Flu is *contagieuse* and causes *une épidémie* most winters; *une pandémie* crosses
continents.

![Two panels. Left, Au cabinet médical: a doctor in a white coat with a stethoscope, labelled le généraliste, sits behind a desk with a sheet of paper on it, labelled l'ordonnance; a person sits on a chair opposite. Right, À l'hôpital: a man in blue scrubs, a cap and a mask, labelled le chirurgien, stands behind a hospital bed where someone lies under a green sheet, labelled le patient; on the right, a woman in a white uniform next to a drip stand, labelled l'infirmière.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: Dix jours à l'hôpital

Inès, 52, writes to a friend after an operation. Watch every participle.

> Chère Agnès,
>
> Je suis enfin rentrée chez moi ! Tu te souviens des douleurs que j'ai eues tout l'automne ? Je
> pensais que c'était le stress. La généraliste que j'ai consultée en novembre m'a tout de suite
> envoyée chez un spécialiste, et le diagnostic qu'il a posé était clair : il fallait opérer.
>
> Les examens qu'il a fallu faire avant l'opération ont pris trois semaines. Le jour J, je me suis
> évanouie dans la salle d'attente, de peur sans doute ! La chirurgienne m'a opérée le lendemain.
> Les deux heures qu'a duré l'opération ont paru bien longues à mon mari.
>
> À l'hôpital, les infirmières se sont succédé jour et nuit ; je les ai trouvées formidables. Ma
> voisine de chambre, une malade chronique, s'est plainte de tout, mais nous nous sommes beaucoup
> parlé et nous nous sommes bien entendues. Des visites, j'en ai eu beaucoup, et les fleurs que
> mes collègues m'ont envoyées ont égayé la chambre.
>
> Les médicaments qu'on m'a prescrits me fatiguent un peu, mais le médecin m'a dit que ces effets
> secondaires disparaîtraient vite. Je me suis rendu compte que j'avais trop attendu avant de
> consulter. Alors, un conseil : le test de dépistage que l'Assurance maladie t'a envoyé, fais-le !
>
> Je t'embrasse,
> Inès

*Dear Agnès,*

*I'm home at last! Do you remember the pains I had all autumn? I thought it was stress. The GP I
saw in November sent me straight to a specialist, and the diagnosis he made was clear: I needed
an operation.*

*The tests that had to be done before the operation took three weeks. On the day itself, I
fainted in the waiting room, from fear, I suppose! The surgeon operated on me the next day. The
two hours the operation lasted seemed very long to my husband.*

*In hospital, the nurses came one after another day and night; I found them wonderful. The woman
in the next bed, who has a chronic illness, complained about everything, but we talked a lot and
we got on well. Visitors? I had lots, and the flowers my colleagues sent me brightened up the
room.*

*The medicines I was prescribed make me a bit tired, but the doctor told me these side effects
would soon go away. I realised that I had waited too long before seeing a doctor. So, some
advice: the screening test the health insurance sent you, do it!*

*Love,*
*Inès*

Notice the reasons for each ending:

- *rentrée, évanouie, plainte*: *être*, or essentially pronominal → agree with *je* / *elle*.
- *eues, consultée, envoyée, posé … opérée, trouvées, envoyées, prescrits*: *avoir* with a
  preceding direct object (*que* or a pronoun) → agree. Inès is a woman, so *m'a envoyée* and *m'a
  opérée* agree with *m'*. *Posé* agrees with *que* = *le diagnostic*, masculine singular, so no
  ending shows.
- *fallu, duré, eu*: impersonal, a measure, *en* → no agreement.
- *se sont succédé, nous nous sommes parlé, je me suis rendu compte*: *se* is indirect, or *se
  rendre compte* → no agreement. *Nous nous sommes entendues* agrees: *entendre quelqu'un* is direct.

## Common mistakes

- **Agreeing with *avoir* when the object comes after.** *Elle a prescrit des antibiotiques*, not
  *prescrits*.
- **Agreeing with an indirect object.** *Les patients à qui j'ai parlé* (*parler à*), not
  *parlés*. *Elle m'a téléphoné*, whoever *m'* is.
- **Agreeing *fait* + infinitive.** *Elle s'est fait opérer*, not *faite*.
- **Making every pronominal verb agree.** *Ils se sont parlé, elles se sont succédé, elle s'est
  rendu compte* stay invariable.
- **Agreeing impersonal *fallu, fait*.** *Les efforts qu'il a fallu*: no *-s*.
- **Forgetting the gender of *je, tu, me, vous*.** A woman writes *je suis rentrée*, *on m'a
  opérée*; to several people, *je vous ai vus*.

## Key points

- *Être*: agree with the subject. *Avoir*: agree only with a direct object placed before (*que*,
  *le / la / les*, *quel*, *combien de*, *lequel*).
- No agreement with *en* (usually), impersonal verbs, *fait* + infinitive, an implied infinitive
  (*tous les efforts qu'il a pu*), or a measure (*les deux heures qu'a duré l'opération*).
- Participle + infinitive: agree if the preceding object does the action (*les infirmières que
  j'ai entendues rire*). *Laissé* + infinitive: both forms accepted.
- Pronominal verbs: essentially pronominal and passive ones agree with the subject; reflexive and
  reciprocal ones agree only if *se* is the direct object (*elle s'est lavée / elle s'est lavé les
  mains*); *se parler, se succéder, se rendre compte* never agree with *se*.

lessons.title: Il aura oublié: the futur antérieur and the future in the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 you used the futur antérieur after *quand* and *dès que* (*Quand tu auras fini, tu
m'appelleras*). At B2 it becomes a full tool with four uses, two of which surprise English
speakers: it can guess about the past (*Il aura oublié* = he must have forgotten) and sum up a
whole period (*On aura tout essayé*). The second half of the lesson looks at the future seen from
the past: *Elle savait qu'elle prendrait sa retraite à 64 ans.*

The theme is demography and the ageing population: retirement, life expectancy, caring for older
relatives and generations living together. The figures in the reading come from INSEE, France's
national statistics office.

## The futur antérieur: forms

The **[[futur antérieur]]** is the futur simple of *avoir* or *être* + the past participle, with the
same auxiliary and the same agreement as the passé composé (lesson 03):

| | cotiser (avoir) | partir (être) | s'installer (pronominal) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je / j' | aurai cotisé | serai parti(e) | me serai installé(e) |
| tu | auras cotisé | seras parti(e) | te seras installé(e) |
| il / elle / on | aura cotisé | sera parti(e) | se sera installé(e) |
| nous | aurons cotisé | serons parti(e)s | nous serons installé(e)s |
| vous | aurez cotisé | serez parti(e)(s) | vous serez installé(e)(s) |
| ils / elles | auront cotisé | seront parti(e)s | se seront installé(e)s |

- With *être*, the participle agrees with the subject: *Mes parents seront partis à la retraite
  avant moi. Elle se sera installée à la campagne.*
- With *avoir*, it agrees with a direct object placed before: *les lettres qu'il aura écrites*.
- The passive has two participles: *La réforme aura été votée avant l'été.*
- Negation goes around the auxiliary: *Il n'aura pas fini. Elle ne sera pas encore rentrée.*

Don't confuse *j'aurai fini* (futur antérieur) with *j'aurais fini* (conditionnel passé): one
letter apart in writing, the same sound for many speakers, different meanings.

## Four uses

### 1. Finished before a point in the future

With *d'ici* + a date, *avant* + a date, *dans* + a length of time, or *à la fin de*, the futur
antérieur says what will be done by then:

- *Dans dix ans, la population aura encore vieilli.* — In ten years, the population will have aged
  further.
- *D'ici 2030, la commune aura ouvert une deuxième maison de retraite.* — By 2030, the town will
  have opened a second care home.
- *À la fin de sa carrière, elle aura cotisé quarante-trois ans.* — By the end of her career, she
  will have paid in for forty-three years.

### 2. After quand, dès que, une fois que (B1 review)

In a time clause about the future, the futur antérieur marks the action finished first: *Quand
nous aurons vendu la maison, nous nous installerons près de nos enfants. Dès que tu auras reçu ta
pension, tu pourras voyager.*

### 3. A guess about the past

The futur antérieur can explain something that has already happened, as a likely guess:

- *Mamie ne répond pas ? Elle aura oublié son portable.* — Grandma isn't answering? She must
  have forgotten her phone.
- *Il n'est pas encore là : son train aura eu du retard.* — He isn't here yet: his train must
  have been late.
- *Les voisins sont partis tôt : ils seront allés voir leur fille.* — The neighbours left early:
  they'll have gone to see their daughter.

It means the same as *a dû* + infinitive (*Elle a dû oublier son portable*), which is more
common in speech; the futur antérieur presents the guess as the obvious explanation, often
with a shrug. Lesson 11 compares it with the other ways of expressing probability.

### 4. Looking back on a whole period

Journalists and speakers use the futur antérieur to sum up something that is ending or will
soon be over, as if looking back from the future:

- *On aura tout essayé.* — We'll have tried everything. (Said when nothing has worked.)
- *Ce siècle aura été celui de la longévité.* — This century will have been the century of
  longevity.
- *Cette année, l'espérance de vie aura encore progressé.* — This year, life expectancy will have
  risen again.
- *J'aurai tout entendu !* — Now I've heard everything! (surprise or indignation)

English often uses a simple past or the present perfect here; French adds a sense of
"when all is said and done".

### Example 1: which use?

*Task.* Say which use each sentence shows.

1. *Le bus ne s'est pas arrêté ? Le chauffeur ne t'aura pas vu.* — A guess about the past (use 3):
   "the driver probably didn't see you".
2. *Quand vous aurez rempli le dossier, envoyez-le à votre caisse de retraite.* — After *quand*,
   the action finished first (use 2).
3. *D'ici la fin du mois, nous aurons trouvé une place pour Papi.* — Finished before a future
   point (use 1).
4. *Sa vie durant, elle aura aidé les autres.* — Looking back on a whole life (use 4).

Careful: *aura* alone is the plain futur of *avoir* (*En 2040, il aura 80 ans*: he will be 80),
and *sera* + participle can be a plain passive futur (*Les travaux seront terminés en mai*: will
be finished in May). Only *avoir / être* in the futur + a participle for a completed action is
a futur antérieur.

## The future in the past

When the point of view moves into the past, the futures move too:

- the futur simple becomes the conditionnel présent: *Elle sait qu'elle prendra sa retraite
  à 64 ans* → *Elle savait qu'elle prendrait sa retraite à 64 ans.* — She knew she would retire at
  64.
- the futur antérieur becomes the **[[conditionnel passé]]**: *Il promet qu'il aura fini avant juin*
  → *Il avait promis qu'il aurait fini avant juin.* — He had promised he would have finished
  before June.

This is the **[[future in the past]]**: the conditionnel used not for a condition or a wish, but for
an event that was still to come from a past point of view. The forms are exactly the
conditionnel you know; only the job is different.

![Two timelines. Top, blue, Centred on now: a bar labelled maintenant (présent: elle sait), then a white dot labelled futur antérieur: elle aura fini, a dashed mark labelled juin, and a white dot labelled futur simple: elle partira. Bottom, yellow, Centred on a past moment: a bar labelled alors (imparfait, passé composé: elle savait), then conditionnel passé: elle aurait fini, the juin mark, and conditionnel présent: elle partirait.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

You meet the future in the past in three places:

- **after a past verb of saying, knowing or promising**: *Le ministre a annoncé que les pensions
  augmenteraient en janvier.* Lesson 19 covers reported speech in full; here, just notice that
  *augmenteront* became *augmenteraient*.
- **in time clauses inside it**: *Il a dit qu'il m'appellerait quand il aurait fini.* The
  futur antérieur after *quand* moves to the conditionnel passé too.
- **in narrative, for what the narrator knows will happen**: *Ce jour-là, elle quitta le village.
  Elle n'y reviendrait que trente ans plus tard.* — She would not come back until thirty years
  later. Novelists use it to look ahead.

### Example 2: moving a sentence into the past

*Task.* Start each sentence with *Elle pensait que …*

1. *Ses enfants s'occuperont d'elle.* → *Elle pensait que ses enfants s'occuperaient d'elle.*
2. *Elle aura remboursé sa maison avant sa retraite.* → *Elle pensait qu'elle aurait remboursé sa
   maison avant sa retraite.*
3. *Quand elle aura soixante-dix ans, elle déménagera.* → *Elle pensait que, quand elle aurait
   soixante-dix ans, elle déménagerait.* Here *aura* is the plain futur of *avoir* (she will be
   seventy), so it becomes the plain conditionnel *aurait*.

## Reading: La France vieillit

> La France vieillit : ce que disent les chiffres
>
> Chaque mois de janvier, l'Insee publie son bilan démographique. Celui de 2026, consacré à
> l'année 2025, a marqué les esprits : pour la première fois depuis la fin de la Seconde Guerre
> mondiale, la France a compté plus de décès (environ 651 000) que de naissances (environ
> 645 000). Le taux de natalité continue de baisser, et la fécondité est tombée à 1,56 enfant par
> femme, son niveau le plus bas depuis la fin de la Première Guerre mondiale.
>
> À l'autre bout de la vie, la longévité progresse. L'espérance de vie à la naissance atteint
> 85,9 ans pour les femmes et 80,3 ans pour les hommes. Au 1er janvier 2026, les 65 ans ou plus
> représentaient 22,2 % de la population, et les 75 ans ou plus, 11,1 %.
>
> Ce vieillissement n'est pas une surprise. Les démographes savaient depuis longtemps que les
> générations nombreuses nées après 1946 arriveraient un jour à l'âge de la retraite, et que la
> tranche d'âge des plus de 75 ans grossirait ensuite.
>
> Les défis sont connus. Il y aura moins d'actifs pour chaque retraité, alors que ce sont les
> cotisations des actifs qui financent l'essentiel des pensions. La dépendance, elle, pèse déjà sur les
> familles : beaucoup d'aidants s'occupent d'un parent tout en travaillant, et une place en maison
> de retraite coûte cher.
>
> Faut-il s'inquiéter ? Pas forcément, disent certains économistes : l'allongement de la vie en
> bonne santé, l'emploi des seniors et les projets intergénérationnels, comme la colocation entre
> étudiants et retraités, peuvent changer la donne. D'autres estiment qu'il faudra cotiser plus
> longtemps ou trouver d'autres financements.
>
> Une chose est sûre : d'ici 2050, selon les projections de l'Insee, la part des seniors aura
> encore augmenté. Les communes qui auront anticipé, avec des logements adaptés, des transports
> et des services à domicile, s'en sortiront mieux que les autres. Et quand on fera le bilan, on
> dira peut-être que ce siècle aura été celui de la longévité.

*Every January, INSEE publishes its demographic report. The 2026 report, on the year 2025,
made an impression: for the first time since the end of the Second World War, France recorded
more deaths (about 651,000) than births (about 645,000). The birth rate keeps falling, and
fertility has dropped to 1.56 children per woman, its lowest level since the end of the First
World War.*

*At the other end of life, longevity is increasing. Life expectancy at birth has reached 85.9
years for women and 80.3 years for men. On 1 January 2026, people aged 65 or over made up 22.2%
of the population, and those aged 75 or over, 11.1%.*

*This ageing is no surprise. Demographers had long known that the large generations born after
1946 would one day reach retirement age, and that the over-75 age group would grow after that.*

*The challenges are well known. There will be fewer working people for each retired person,
while it is working people's contributions that pay for most of the pensions. Loss of autonomy is already a
burden on families: many carers look after a parent while working, and a place in a care home is
expensive.*

*Should we worry? Not necessarily, say some economists: longer healthy lives, employment of older
workers and intergenerational projects, such as flatshares between students and pensioners, can
change things. Others think that people will have to pay in for longer or that other sources of
funding will have to be found.*

*One thing is certain: by 2050, according to INSEE's projections, the share of older people will
have grown further. Towns that have planned ahead, with adapted housing, transport and home
services, will cope better than the others. And when the time comes to take stock, people may
say that this century will have been the century of longevity.*

Notice:

- *savaient … arriveraient … grossirait*: the future in the past after a past verb of knowing.
- *aura encore augmenté* (use 1, by a date), *auront anticipé* (finished before *s'en
  sortiront*), *aura été* (use 4, looking back).
- *Il y aura moins d'actifs*: plain futur; *aura* + participle would be the futur antérieur.

![A simplified population pyramid with invented figures in millions, by ten-year age groups from 0–9 to 90+. Bars for men on the left, labelled les hommes, and for women on the right, labelled les femmes. The 70–79 bars are highlighted, labelled une tranche d'âge. A bracket on the right groups the four top age groups, from 60–69 up, labelled les seniors. The women's bars are longer than the men's at the top of the pyramid.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The words of demography

*La démographie* studies *la natalité* (births), *la mortalité* (deaths: *la mortalité
infantile a fortement reculé au XXe siècle*) and *l'espérance de vie*. A rate is *un taux* (*le
taux de natalité*). *Le vieillissement* of a population comes from *l'allongement* of life and
from falling births: medical progress *a allongé la vie*. People are counted by *tranche d'âge*. *Les
actifs* (people in the labour force) *cotisent*, and their *cotisations* pay *les pensions* of
*les retraités*. In the press, older people are often *les seniors*. When an older person can no
longer live alone, the word is *la dépendance*; a relative who helps is *un aidant*, and some
people move into *une maison de retraite*. *Les projections* (forecasts) help a country
*anticiper*; one answer to *le défi* of ageing is *intergénérationnel* housing.

## Common mistakes

- **Using the passé composé after *quand* for a future action.** In careful French, *Quand j'aurai
  fini, je t'appellerai*, not *Quand j'ai fini, je t'appellerai*. Relaxed speech puts both verbs
  in the present: *Quand j'ai fini, je t'appelle.*
- **Translating "he must have forgotten" word for word.** *Il doit avoir oublié* exists, but *il
  a dû oublier* or *il aura oublié* is what French usually says.
- **Writing *j'aurais* for *j'aurai* (or the reverse).** *Demain, j'aurai fini* (futur antérieur);
  *Il pensait que j'aurais fini* (conditionnel passé, future in the past).
- **Keeping the futur after a past verb.** *Elle a dit qu'elle viendrait*, not *qu'elle
  viendra*, when her coming is seen from the past. (If it is still ahead now, *viendra* is also
  heard; lesson 19.)
- **Forgetting agreement with *être*.** *Ma mère sera rentrée avant nous. Elles se seront
  trompées de route.*

## Key points

- Futur antérieur = *aurai / serai …* + participle, with the passé composé's auxiliary and
  agreement (*elle sera partie, les lettres qu'il aura écrites*).
- Four uses: finished before a future point (*d'ici 2030, …*); after *quand, dès que* for the
  first action; a guess about the past (*Il aura oublié* = *il a dû oublier*); looking back on a
  whole period (*On aura tout essayé*).
- Future in the past: futur → conditionnel présent (*Elle savait qu'elle partirait*); futur
  antérieur → conditionnel passé (*Il avait promis qu'il aurait fini*).
- *J'aurai fini* (futur antérieur) ≠ *j'aurais fini* (conditionnel passé).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Qu'il fût: the literary tenses of the subjunctive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 taught you to read the passé simple. Open a novel written before about 1950, or a
carefully written one since, and you'll meet its partners: *qu'il fût, qu'elle eût, qu'il vînt,
qu'il eût fini, j'eusse aimé*. These are the literary tenses of the subjunctive, and like the
passé simple they are for **reading only**. Nobody expects you to write them, and in a DELF essay
they would look odd. But if you can't recognise them, a sentence like *Il fallait qu'il partît*
stops you dead.

This lesson covers the **[[imperfect subjunctive]]**, the **[[pluperfect subjunctive]]**, the classical
rule that chose between them, and a literary form of the conditionnel passé. All the example
passages are original pastiches written for this course: they imitate the style of older prose
without quoting any real book.

## The imperfect subjunctive

### How it is built

Take the *tu* form of the passé simple, drop the final *-s*, and add *-sse, -sses, -t (with a
circumflex), -ssions, -ssiez, -ssent*:

| | parler (tu parlas) | finir (tu finis) | être (tu fus) | avoir (tu eus) | venir (tu vins) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| que je / j' | parlasse | finisse | fusse | eusse | vinsse |
| que tu | parlasses | finisses | fusses | eusses | vinsses |
| qu'il / elle | parlât | finît | fût | eût | vînt |
| que nous | parlassions | finissions | fussions | eussions | vinssions |
| que vous | parlassiez | finissiez | fussiez | eussiez | vinssiez |
| qu'ils / elles | parlassent | finissent | fussent | eussent | vinssent |

Three things make this easier than it looks:

- **The third person singular is the form you'll really meet.** The others are much rarer:
  their long endings (*que nous parlassions*) sound heavy, and many writers avoided them.
- **The circumflex tells it apart from the passé simple.** *Il fut* (passé simple) / *qu'il
  fût* (subjunctive); *il eut / qu'il eût*; *il parla / qu'il parlât*; *il finit / qu'il finît*.
  The 1990 spelling rules, which drop many circumflexes on *i* and *u*, keep this one.
- **Some forms look like the present subjunctive.** For *finir*, only the *il* form differs
  (*qu'il finisse / qu'il finît*). Context and the tense of the main verb tell you which you're
  reading.

The irregular ones follow the passé simple, so if you know *il fit, il put, il sut, il dut, il
prit*, you can read *qu'il fît, qu'il pût, qu'il sût, qu'il dût, qu'il prît*.

### What it means

The imperfect subjunctive is the subjunctive you would use today, moved into the past by the
classical rules (below). Read it as a present subjunctive: *Il fallait qu'il partît* = *Il
fallait qu'il parte* (He had to leave).

## The pluperfect subjunctive

The **[[pluperfect subjunctive]]** is the imperfect subjunctive of *avoir* or *être* + a past
participle, with the usual auxiliary and agreement: *qu'il eût fini, qu'elle fût partie, qu'ils
se fussent trompés*. Read it as a subjonctif passé: *Je doutais qu'il eût compris* = *Je doutais
qu'il ait compris* (I doubted that he had understood).

## The classical concordance des temps

In modern French, the subjunctive mostly uses two tenses, present and past, whatever the tense of
the main verb. Classical prose followed a stricter rule, the **[[concordance des temps]]** of the
subjunctive: a main verb in a past tense or the conditionnel called for a past-looking
subjunctive.

| main verb | event at the same time or later | event earlier |
|---|---|---|
| present, futur | present subjunctive: *Je veux qu'il vienne.* | past subjunctive: *Je doute qu'il soit venu.* |
| past tense or conditionnel (classical) | imperfect subjunctive: *Je voulais qu'il vînt.* | pluperfect subjunctive: *Je doutais qu'il fût venu.* |
| past tense or conditionnel (today) | present subjunctive: *Je voulais qu'il vienne.* | past subjunctive: *Je doutais qu'il soit venu.* |

![A chart titled Reading a classical subjunctive: translate it into today's form. Three columns: main verb, classical prose, French today. Je veux …: qu'il vienne → qu'il vienne. Je voulais …: qu'il vînt → qu'il vienne. Je doutais …: qu'il fût venu → qu'il soit venu. J'aurais voulu …: qu'il vînt → qu'il vienne. A note says the classical rule puts a past or conditional main verb with the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

So the reading rule is simple: **imperfect subjunctive → present subjunctive; pluperfect
subjunctive → past subjunctive.** Even in its heyday the rule had exceptions, and writers kept the
present subjunctive when the event was still true at the time of writing.

### Example 1: modernising a pastiche

*Task.* Here is an original passage written in the style of a 19th-century novel. Find the
literary forms and rewrite it in today's French.

> Bien qu'il fût tard et que la pluie n'eût pas cessé, le notaire exigea que son clerc partît sur-le-champ.
> Il eût été plus sage d'attendre le matin ; mais le vieil homme craignait que la lettre ne
> parvînt trop tard, et il n'aurait pas supporté qu'on l'accusât de négligence. Le clerc obéit,
> quoiqu'il n'en eût aucune envie.

1. Passé simple: *exigea, obéit* → passé composé *a exigé, a obéi*.
2. Imperfect subjunctive: *fût, partît, parvînt, accusât, eût (aucune envie)* → present
   subjunctive *soit, parte, parvienne, accuse, ait*.
3. Pluperfect subjunctive: *n'eût pas cessé* → past subjunctive *n'ait pas cessé*.
4. *Il eût été plus sage*: not a subjunctive at all here. It's the literary conditionnel passé
   (next section) → *Il aurait été plus sage*.

Result: *Bien qu'il soit tard et que la pluie n'ait pas cessé, le notaire a exigé que son clerc
parte immédiatement. Il aurait été plus sage d'attendre le matin ; mais le vieil homme craignait
que la lettre ne parvienne trop tard, et il n'aurait pas supporté qu'on l'accuse de négligence. Le
clerc a obéi, bien qu'il n'en ait aucune envie.*

Translation: Although it was late and the rain hadn't stopped, the notary insisted that his clerk
leave at once. It would have been wiser to wait until morning; but the old man was afraid the
letter would arrive too late, and he could not have borne being accused of negligence. The clerk
obeyed, although he had no wish to. (*Le clerc*: a solicitor's clerk; *sur-le-champ*: at once.)

## The conditionnel passé deuxième forme

The pluperfect subjunctive had a second job: in literary style it replaces the conditionnel passé.
This is called the **[[conditionnel passé deuxième forme]]** (second form): *j'eusse aimé* = *j'aurais
aimé*, *il eût fallu* = *il aurait fallu*, *elle fût venue* = *elle serait venue*.

It often appears in both halves of a past hypothesis: *S'il eût parlé, on l'eût cru* = *S'il
avait parlé, on l'aurait cru* (If he had spoken, people would have believed him). Read the first
*eût* as a plus-que-parfait and the second as a conditionnel passé.

Inverted, it can mean "even if": *Eût-il été riche, il n'aurait rien changé* = *Même s'il avait
été riche, …* (Even if he had been rich, …).

### Example 2: subjunctive, conditional or passé simple?

*Task.* For each form, say what it is and give today's equivalent.

1. *eut* in *Il eut froid et rentra.* — No circumflex: passé simple of *avoir* → *Il a eu froid et il
   est rentré.*
2. *eût* in *Il fallait qu'il eût terminé avant midi.* — After *il fallait que*: pluperfect
   subjunctive → *Il fallait qu'il ait terminé avant midi.*
3. *eusse* in *J'eusse préféré le silence.* — No *que*, a main clause expressing regret: conditionnel
   passé deuxième forme → *J'aurais préféré le silence.*
4. *fût* in *Elle attendit qu'il fût parti.* — After *attendre que*: pluperfect subjunctive → *Elle a
   attendu qu'il soit parti.*

## Where you still meet these forms

- **Novels** before the mid-20th century, and some later writers who like a classical style.
  Reading an *extrait* from a 19th-century *ouvrage* or a *recueil* of short stories, expect them
  on every page.
- **Formal speeches and essays** that aim for the *soutenu* register, where a single *qu'il fût*
  can signal elegance, or irony.
- **Set phrases** still used today, mostly in careful speech and writing:
  - *fût-ce* (even if it were, even if only): *Il faut le dire, fût-ce au risque de déplaire.* —
    It must be said, even at the risk of giving offence.
  - *ne fût-ce que* (if only, even just): *Passe me voir, ne fût-ce que cinq minutes.* — Come
    and see me, even just for five minutes.
  - *Qui l'eût cru ?* — Who would have thought it?
  - *Il eût fallu* … — It would have been necessary to …, in formal criticism.
- **Pastiche and humour**: writers sometimes use them on purpose to sound *désuet* or
  *archaïque*, the way English might use "thou" or "whom" for effect.

These forms belong to written *prose*, to the *littéraire* side of French. A *tournure* such as
*qu'il fût* has a slightly old-fashioned charm today, and many readers enjoy it. In a novel you
might read *Cette maison, naguère si animée, était devenue silencieuse* (not long ago so lively);
*naguère*, like these tenses, is a word you'll mostly meet in print.

## Common mistakes

- **Reading *qu'il fût* as *il fut*.** The circumflex and the *que* show a subjunctive; *il fut*
  is a passé simple.
- **Taking *il eût fallu* for a subjunctive that needs a *que*.** Without *que*, in a main clause,
  it's almost always the conditionnel passé deuxième forme: *it would have been necessary*.
- **Translating the imperfect subjunctive with a past.** *Je voulais qu'il vînt* is "I wanted him
  to come", not "I wanted that he came". Read it as *qu'il vienne*.
- **Using these forms in your own writing.** At B2 (and in the DELF), write *Je voulais qu'il
  vienne* and *J'aurais aimé*. The one exception is a set phrase like *ne fût-ce que*.

## Key points

- Imperfect subjunctive: *tu* passé simple minus *-s* + *-sse …*; you'll mostly meet the *il*
  form with its circumflex: *qu'il parlât, finît, fût, eût, vînt*. Read it as a present
  subjunctive.
- Pluperfect subjunctive: *qu'il eût fini, qu'elle fût partie*. Read it as a subjonctif passé.
- Classical concordance: a past or conditional main verb took the imperfect or pluperfect
  subjunctive; today the present and past subjunctive do the job.
- Conditionnel passé deuxième forme: *j'eusse aimé* = *j'aurais aimé*; *S'il eût parlé, on l'eût
  cru* = *S'il avait parlé, on l'aurait cru*.
- Still alive in set phrases: *fût-ce, ne fût-ce que, Qui l'eût cru ?*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Saint-Exupéry, aviateur et écrivain
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry is known around the world for one short book, *Le Petit Prince*. In
France he is just as famous as an airmail pilot of the 1920s and 1930s, when flying across the
Sahara or the South Atlantic was an adventure. This lesson tells his life in an original
biography written in the **[[passé simple]]**, the way a reference book or an older school textbook
would tell it (lesson 01), and uses the time relations of lesson 02: *à peine … que, sitôt, dès
que* with a passé antérieur, *jusqu'à ce que*.

You'll read the text, convert part of it into the passé composé, and practise talking about a
book without quoting it, which is what a DELF essay or oral asks you to do anyway. There are no
quotations from his books in this lesson.

## Before you read

- Most verbs are in the third person: *il naquit, il fit, il devint, il partit, il écrivit, il
  mourut*. Check lesson 01's tables if one stops you.
- The background is in the imparfait (*les avions décollaient*), as in speech.
- One passé antérieur: *Dès qu'il eut obtenu …* (as soon as he had obtained).
- Glossed words come after each part.

## Antoine de Saint-Exupéry (1900–1944)

### Part 1: the airmail pilot

> Antoine de Saint-Exupéry naquit à Lyon le 29 juin 1900. Appelé au service militaire en 1921, il
> fut affecté à un régiment d'aviation à Strasbourg, où il prit ses premières leçons de pilotage. Pendant
> quelques années, il chercha sa voie et exerça plusieurs métiers, sans jamais renoncer à voler.
>
> En 1926, il entra dans la compagnie de Pierre Latécoère, qui allait devenir l'Aéropostale. Sitôt
> engagé, il dut, comme tous les débutants, travailler d'abord avec les mécaniciens, avant de
> piloter les avions postaux entre Toulouse, Casablanca et Dakar. À cette époque, les avions
> décollaient et atterrissaient sur des terrains sommaires : chaque décollage et chaque
> atterrissage demandait de l'adresse, et une panne au-dessus du Sahara pouvait obliger le
> pilote à se poser en plein désert.
>
> En 1927, on le nomma chef d'escale à Cap Juby, une petite station au bord du désert, sur la côte
> sud de l'actuel Maroc. Il y passa de longs mois, entre le sable et la mer. C'est là qu'il écrivit son
> premier roman, *Courrier sud*, publié en 1929.

*Summary.* Born in Lyon in 1900, he learned to fly during his military service in Strasbourg. In
1926 he joined the Latécoère company, the future Aéropostale, starting with the mechanics before
flying the mail between Toulouse, Casablanca and Dakar. In 1927 he became station manager at Cap
Juby, on the edge of the desert, where he wrote his first novel.

*Glosses.* *Affecté à*: posted to. *Chercher sa voie*:
to look for one's path in life. *Sitôt engagé*: as soon as he was taken on. *Un terrain
sommaire*: a rough airstrip. *Se poser*: to land (= *atterrir*). *Le chef d'escale*: station
manager.

![A simplified map, not to scale, showing the coasts of south-western Europe, north-west Africa and South America separated by the Atlantic Ocean. A dashed red route runs from Toulouse down to Casablanca, Cap Juby and Dakar on the African coast, then across the ocean to Natal on the Brazilian coast and down to Buenos Aires. The Sahara is marked inland in Africa.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Part 2: South America and the first books

> À peine son livre était-il paru qu'il partit pour l'Amérique du Sud. En 1929, il prit à Buenos
> Aires la direction de l'Aeroposta Argentina, la filiale de l'Aéropostale, et ouvrit de nouvelles
> lignes vers la Patagonie. Le courrier venu de France faisait alors la traversée de l'Atlantique
> Sud entre Dakar et le Brésil, d'abord surtout par bateau. Les vols de nuit, dangereux mais
> indispensables pour gagner du temps sur les trains et les navires, lui inspirèrent son deuxième
> roman, *Vol de nuit*, qui reçut le prix Femina en 1931.
>
> Les années suivantes furent plus difficiles. L'Aéropostale connut de graves problèmes financiers
> et ses lignes furent intégrées à Air France en 1933. Saint-Exupéry devint journaliste et
> conférencier, sans cesser de piloter. Le 30 décembre 1935, alors qu'il tentait de battre le
