> record du trajet Paris–Saïgon avec son mécanicien, André Prévot, leur avion s'écrasa dans le
> désert de Libye. Les deux hommes survécurent, mais ils errèrent plusieurs jours sans eau,
> jusqu'à ce qu'un Bédouin les trouve et les sauve. Saint-Exupéry raconta cet accident, et bien
> d'autres souvenirs de l'aviation, dans *Terre des hommes*, publié en 1939.

*Summary.* In 1929 he went to Buenos Aires to run the company's Argentine branch and open lines
to Patagonia; night flying inspired *Vol de nuit* (prix Femina, 1931). After the Aéropostale was
absorbed into Air France in 1933, he worked as a journalist and speaker. In December 1935 he and
his mechanic crashed in the Libyan desert during a record attempt and were rescued after several
days by a Bedouin, an episode he told in *Terre des hommes* (1939).

*Glosses.* *Paraître* (of a book): to come out. *La filiale*: subsidiary. *Le navire*: ship.
*Le conférencier*: lecturer, speaker. *Errer*: to wander. *Jusqu'à ce qu'un Bédouin les trouve*:
a modern text keeps the present subjunctive here; an older one would write *les trouvât*
(lesson 04h1).

### Part 3: the war, the Little Prince and a mystery

> En 1939, il fut mobilisé dans un groupe de reconnaissance aérienne, le groupe 2/33. Après la
> défaite de 1940, il partit pour les États-Unis. Il y publia *Pilote de guerre* en 1942, puis, en
> 1943, à New York, un conte qu'il avait lui-même illustré de ses aquarelles : *Le Petit Prince*.
> En 1943, il rejoignit son ancien groupe, alors basé en Afrique du Nord. Dès qu'il eut obtenu
> l'autorisation de voler de nouveau, il reprit les missions, malgré son âge et ses anciennes
> blessures.
>
> Le 31 juillet 1944 au matin, il décolla de Borgo, en Corse, à bord d'un P-38 Lightning, pour une
> mission de reconnaissance au-dessus du sud de la France. Il ne revint jamais. Pendant plus de
> cinquante ans, sa disparition resta un mystère.
>
> En septembre 1998, un pêcheur remonta dans ses filets, près de l'île de Riou, au large de
> Marseille, une gourmette en argent qui portait son nom et celui de sa femme, Consuelo. En 2000,
> un plongeur repéra des débris d'avion à environ 70 mètres de fond. L'épave fut remontée en 2003,
> et en 2004 un numéro de série permit de l'identifier : c'était bien l'avion de l'aviateur. On
> ignore encore aujourd'hui ce qui provoqua l'accident.

*Summary.* Mobilised in 1939 in a reconnaissance group, he left for the United States after the
1940 defeat, published *Pilote de guerre* (1942) and, in 1943 in New York, *Le Petit Prince*,
illustrated with his own watercolours. He rejoined his group in North Africa and, on 31 July
1944, took off from Corsica on a reconnaissance flight and never came back. A fisherman found
his silver bracelet in 1998 near Marseille; the wreck, spotted in 2000 and raised in 2003, was
identified in 2004. What caused the crash is still unknown.

*Glosses.* *La reconnaissance aérienne*: aerial reconnaissance (photographing enemy territory).
*L'aquarelle*: watercolour. *Les blessures*: injuries (from his earlier crashes). *La
gourmette*: chain bracelet. *Le filet*: net. *Repérer*: to spot. *Remonter*: to bring up.

## Example 1: a paragraph in the passé composé

*Task.* Retell the first paragraph of Part 2 as you would aloud.

1. Passé simple → passé composé, with the usual auxiliaries: *partit* → *il est parti*; *prit* →
   *il a pris*; *ouvrit* → *il a ouvert*; *inspirèrent* → *ont inspiré*; *reçut* → *a reçu*.
2. The imparfait stays: *faisait*.
3. *À peine son livre était-il paru que* … : in speech, no inversion: *Son livre était à peine
   paru que …* (lesson 02).

Result: *Son livre était à peine paru qu'il est parti pour l'Amérique du Sud. En 1929, il a pris
à Buenos Aires la direction de l'Aeroposta Argentina, la filiale de l'Aéropostale, et il a ouvert
de nouvelles lignes vers la Patagonie. Le courrier venu de France faisait alors la traversée de
l'Atlantique Sud entre Dakar et le Brésil, d'abord surtout par bateau. Les vols de nuit, dangereux
mais indispensables pour gagner du temps sur les trains et les navires, lui ont inspiré son
deuxième roman, Vol de nuit, qui a reçu le prix Femina en 1931.*

## Example 2: the time relations in the text

*Task.* For each phrase, say whether the time-clause event comes before the main event
(anteriority), at the same time (simultaneity) or after it (posteriority).

| phrase | relation | why |
|---|---|---|
| *Sitôt engagé, il dut travailler avec les mécaniciens* | anteriority | he was hired first, then put to work |
| *À peine son livre était-il paru qu'il partit* | anteriority | publication first, departure almost at once |
| *alors qu'il tentait de battre le record, leur avion s'écrasa* | simultaneity | the crash interrupted the attempt |
| *ils errèrent jusqu'à ce qu'un Bédouin les trouve* | posteriority | the rescue came at the end of the wandering (subjunctive) |
| *Dès qu'il eut obtenu l'autorisation, il reprit les missions* | anteriority | passé antérieur: just before the next event |

## Example 3: talking about a book without quoting it

*Task.* Present *Le Petit Prince* in three or four sentences, in the present, as in a DELF oral.

A model: *Le Petit Prince est un conte illustré publié en 1943. Un aviateur, tombé en panne dans
le Sahara, rencontre un petit garçon venu d'une autre planète, qui lui raconte son voyage. Le
livre parle d'amitié, de responsabilité et de ce qui compte vraiment dans la vie. C'est
aujourd'hui l'un des livres les plus traduits au monde.*

Notice what the model does: it gives facts (date, genre), sums up the situation in your own words,
names the themes, and quotes nothing. That's the safe and expected way to talk about any work in an
exam.

## The words of early aviation

*L'aviation* of the 1920s was a young industry, and *l'aviateur* (or *l'aviatrice*) was a hero.
To *piloter* an airmail plane, you had to *décoller* in all weathers and *atterrir* wherever you
could: *le décollage* and *l'atterrissage* were the dangerous moments. Planes sometimes *s'écrasaient*;
an *épave* could be lost for decades. *La traversée* of the Sahara or the South Atlantic was the
great challenge of the line.

## Common mistakes

- **Retelling a biography in the passé simple.** In your own writing or speaking, use the passé
  composé, or the present for a lively summary (*En 1926, il entre chez Latécoère*).
- **Quoting a famous line from memory.** In an exam, describe the idea in your own words; a
  misquotation costs more than it earns.
- **Conjugating *atterrir* like an *-er* verb.** *Atterrir* is like *finir*:
  *nous atterrissons, l'avion a atterri* (not *atterré*, which means "appalled").
- **Mixing up *l'épave* and *les débris*.** *L'épave* is the wreck as a whole; *les débris* are
  pieces.

## Key points

- Saint-Exupéry (Lyon 1900 – lost at sea off Marseille, 1944): airmail pilot for the Aéropostale,
  author of *Courrier sud* (1929), *Vol de nuit* (1931, prix Femina), *Terre des hommes* (1939)
  and *Le Petit Prince* (New York, 1943).
- A biography in the passé simple reads like a reference book; retell it in the passé composé.
- The time relations of lesson 02 organise a life story: *sitôt engagé, à peine … que, alors que,
  jusqu'à ce que, dès qu'il eut obtenu*.
- Talk about a book with facts, a summary and its themes, never a quotation.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Bien qu'elle ait perdu: the subjonctif passé
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 every subjunctive you produced was in the present: *Je suis content que tu viennes.* But a
lot of what we feel, doubt or concede is about something already over: *I'm glad she won. I don't
think he cheated. Although she lost, …* French uses a second subjunctive tense for this, the
**[[subjonctif passé]]**: *Je suis contente qu'elle ait gagné.*

This lesson makes it productive. You will build it for every kind of verb (with *avoir*, with
*être*, pronominal), choose between present and past by looking at time, use it after the
triggers you already know, swap it for a past infinitive when there is only one subject, and meet
the **[[ne explétif]]** again. From the end of this lesson the subjonctif passé joins your
conjugation drills. The theme is sport and competition.

Module 1 gave you two tools you need here: past participle agreement (lesson 03) and the habit of
placing one event before another (lesson 02).

## Building the subjonctif passé

It is built exactly like the passé composé, with the auxiliary in the present subjunctive:

> *avoir* or *être* in the subjonctif présent + past participle

| | remporter (avoir) | arriver (être) | se qualifier (pronominal) |
|---|---|---|---|
| que j' / je | aie remporté | sois arrivé(e) | me sois qualifié(e) |
| que tu | aies remporté | sois arrivé(e) | te sois qualifié(e) |
| qu'il / elle / on | ait remporté | soit arrivé(e) | se soit qualifié(e) |
| que nous | ayons remporté | soyons arrivé(e)s | nous soyons qualifié(e)s |
| que vous | ayez remporté | soyez arrivé(e)(s) | vous soyez qualifié(e)(s) |
| qu'ils / elles | aient remporté | soient arrivé(e)s | se soient qualifié(e)s |

Watch the spelling of *avoir*: *aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient* (no *i* after the *y*). And
watch the elision of *que*: *que j'aie, qu'il ait, qu'elle soit, qu'ils aient, qu'on ait*, but
*que nous ayons, que tu sois*.

Everything you know about the passé composé carries over:

- **The same auxiliary.** The verbs that take *être* in the passé composé (*aller, venir, arriver,
  partir, tomber, naître, mourir* …) and all pronominal verbs take *être*: *que l'équipe soit
  rentrée, qu'ils se soient entraînés*.
- **The same agreement.** With *être*, the participle agrees with the subject: *Je suis
  soulagé que les joueuses soient arrivées.* With *avoir*, it agrees only with a direct object
  placed before it: *Ces médailles, je ne crois pas qu'il les ait volées.*
- **Pronominal verbs follow lesson 03.** Most of them agree with the subject (*bien qu'elle se
  soit blessée*), but not when *se* is an indirect object: *bien qu'ils se soient parlé*
  (they spoke *to* each other).
- **The same position for pronouns and negation.** Object pronouns go before the auxiliary,
  and *ne … pas* goes around it: *Je regrette que tu ne l'aies pas vu.*

## Present or past? Measure from the main verb

The tense of the subjunctive tells you when the action happens **compared with the main verb**,
not compared with today.

![Two timelines, one above the other. On the first, the main verb "je suis content(e)" is in the middle: to its left, in the "before: already done" zone, il a gagné hier gives qu'il ait gagné (subjonctif passé); to its right, in the "same time or later" zone, il gagne, il gagnera demain give qu'il gagne (subjonctif présent). The second timeline has the main verb "j'étais content(e)" and the same two answers: il avait gagné la veille gives qu'il ait gagné, il gagnait or il gagnerait gives qu'il gagne.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- **Subjonctif présent:** the action happens at the same time as the main verb or later. *Je
  suis content qu'il gagne demain.* — I'm glad he's going to win tomorrow.
- **Subjonctif passé:** the action is finished before the main verb. *Je suis content qu'il ait
  gagné hier.* — I'm glad he won yesterday.

Because the measure is the main verb, a main verb in the past changes nothing in modern French:

- *J'étais déçue qu'elle ne soit pas là.* — I was disappointed that she wasn't there (at the
  same time as my disappointment).
- *J'étais déçue qu'elle ne soit pas venue.* — I was disappointed that she hadn't come (before
  it).

Older literary French used the imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive here (*qu'elle vînt, qu'elle
fût venue*); honors lesson 04h1 shows you how to recognise them.

### Done before a point in the future

The subjonctif passé can also look forward, to something that will be **finished** by a certain
time, like the futur antérieur:

- *Il faut que tu aies fini ton échauffement avant 14 heures.* — You must have finished your
  warm-up by 2 pm.
- *Restez sur le terrain jusqu'à ce que l'arbitre ait sifflé la fin.* — Stay on the pitch until
  the referee has blown the final whistle.
- *Je ne partirai pas avant que le classement ait été publié.* — I won't leave before the
  rankings have been published.

In these sentences the present subjunctive is often possible too (*avant que le classement soit
publié*); the past stresses that the action must be complete.

## The triggers you know, now in the past

Every trigger from B1 works with both tenses. Only time decides.

**Feelings:** *être content, ravi, fier, triste, déçu, surpris que; regretter que; avoir peur
que*.

- *Nous sommes fiers que tu aies remporté ce tournoi.* — We're proud that you won this
  tournament.
- *Les supporters regrettent que l'équipe ait été éliminée si tôt.* — The fans are sorry the team
  was knocked out so early.

**Doubt and negative opinion:** *douter que, ne pas être sûr que, ne pas croire / penser que*.

- *Je doute qu'elle se soit vraiment blessée.* — I doubt she really hurt herself.
- *Je ne crois pas qu'il ait triché.* — I don't think he cheated. (*tricher* = to cheat)

In the affirmative, *croire* and *penser* take the indicative: *Je crois qu'il a triché.* A
negative or doubting main verb casts doubt on the action; that is why the subjunctive follows.

**Necessity and possibility:** *il faut que, il est possible que, il se peut que*.

- *Il est possible que l'arbitre se soit trompé.* — The referee may have made a mistake.

**Conjunctions:** *bien que, avant que, à condition que, sans que, jusqu'à ce que, pour que*.

- *Bien qu'elle ait perdu la finale, elle a battu son record personnel.* — Although she lost the
  final, she beat her personal best.
- *Il est parti sans que personne l'ait remarqué.* — He left without anyone having noticed.
- *Tu joueras samedi, à condition que tu te sois bien remis de ta blessure.* — You'll play on
  Saturday, provided you've recovered properly from your injury.

## One subject? Use the past infinitive

As at B1, the subjunctive needs a **new** subject. When the same person feels and acts, use an
infinitive; when the action is over, a past infinitive (*avoir / être* + participle):

| two subjects: subjonctif passé | one subject: past infinitive |
|---|---|
| *Je suis content qu'il ait gagné.* | *Je suis content d'avoir gagné.* |
| *Elle regrette que tu sois parti.* | *Elle regrette d'être partie.* |
| *Il est parti sans que je l'aie vu.* | *Il est parti sans m'avoir vu.* |

~~Je suis content que j'aie gagné~~ is not French. *Bien que* has no everyday partner preposition, so it
keeps the subjunctive with one subject: *Bien qu'elle ait perdu, elle sourit.* (With *bien que*,
the subject and *être* are often dropped: *bien que fatiguée*.)

## The ne explétif

After a few triggers, careful French adds a *ne* that is **not** a negative. This **[[ne explétif]]**
appears mainly after *avant que, à moins que* and verbs of fear (*avoir peur que, craindre que*):

- *Il faut tout vérifier avant que les athlètes ne soient arrivés.* — We must check everything
  before the athletes have arrived.
- *L'entraîneur a peur que sa meilleure joueuse ne se soit blessée.* — The coach is afraid his
  best player has been injured.

Three facts to keep in mind:

- It is optional. *Avant que les athlètes soient arrivés* means the same; the *ne* simply sounds
  more formal.
- It never comes with *pas*. *J'ai peur qu'il ne se soit blessé* = I'm afraid he has hurt
  himself; *J'ai peur qu'il ne se soit pas blessé* would be a real negative (I'm afraid he
  *hasn't*).
- Careful writers avoid it after *sans que*, which already means "without".

## Worked examples

### Example 1: build it step by step

*"The coach is glad that his players have qualified."* (*être content que, se qualifier*)

1. Two subjects (*l'entraîneur*, *ses joueuses*) and a feeling: subjunctive.
2. The qualifying is over before the feeling: subjonctif passé.
3. *Se qualifier* is pronominal: auxiliary *être*, subjunctive for *elles*: *se soient*.
4. *Se* is the direct object here, so the participle agrees with the subject: *qualifiées*.

*L'entraîneur est content que ses joueuses se soient qualifiées.*

### Example 2: present or past?

- *Je suis surpris qu'elle ___ (abandonner) hier soir.* *Hier soir* is before the surprise: *ait
  abandonné*.
- *Il est possible qu'il ___ (pleuvoir) pendant la course demain.* Later than the main verb:
  *pleuve*.
- *Je doute que l'équipe ___ (se qualifier) la semaine dernière.* Before: *se soit qualifiée*
  (*l'équipe* is feminine singular).
- *Il faut que vous ___ (s'échauffer) avant d'entrer sur le terrain.* An instruction for later:
  *vous échauffiez* is the usual form. *vous soyez échauffé(e)s* would stress completion; both are
  correct.

## Reading: une saison pas comme les autres

> Il y a un an, personne n'aurait parié sur Inès Morel. Blessée au genou en mars, la jeune
> athlète lyonnaise avait dû renoncer au championnat de France, et son classement avait chuté.
> Elle a repris l'entraînement dès l'été, bien que son genou la fasse encore souffrir. « Je ne pense pas qu'elle ait jamais
> douté », raconte son entraîneur, Karim Benali. « Il a fallu qu'elle reconstruise son endurance
> pas à pas, sans que nous ayons de certitude. »
>
> Ce dimanche, au meeting de Lille, la spécialiste du 800 mètres a signé la meilleure
> performance de sa carrière, à un centième du record de France. Ses adversaires semblaient
> encore surprises qu'elle les ait toutes dépassées dans les cent derniers mètres. « C'est un
> exploit, mais je regrette qu'on ait tant parlé de ma blessure », a-t-elle confié après la
> course.
>
> Les supporters, eux, sont ravis que leur championne se soit qualifiée pour les Jeux
> olympiques. Il faudra cependant qu'elle ait retrouvé toute sa vitesse avant l'été. Sa
> fédération, elle, se réjouit qu'aucun contrôle antidopage n'ait jamais été positif dans le
> groupe : « Le dopage n'a pas sa place chez nous. » Prochaine étape : remporter une médaille.

**Translation.** A year ago, nobody would have bet on Inès Morel. Injured in the knee in March,
the young athlete from Lyon had had to give up the French championships, and her ranking had
dropped. She went back to training as early as the summer, although her knee still hurt. "I don't think she ever doubted," says her coach,
Karim Benali. "She had to rebuild her endurance step by step, without our being sure of anything."

This Sunday, at the Lille meeting, the 800-metre specialist set the best performance of her
career, one hundredth of a second off the French record. Her opponents still seemed surprised
that she had overtaken them all in the last hundred metres. "It's a real feat, but I'm sorry there
was so much talk about my injury," she said after the race.

The fans, for their part, are delighted that their champion has qualified for the Olympic Games.
But she will need to have got back all her speed before the summer. Her federation, for its part,
is glad that no doping test in the group has ever been positive: "Doping has no place here." Next
step: winning a medal.

**Notice:** *bien que son genou la fasse* (a main verb in the past, but the pain is at the same
time: present subjunctive); *qu'elle les ait toutes dépassées* (*les* = her opponents, feminine plural, placed
before *avoir*: agreement); *qu'elle se soit qualifiée* (pronominal, *être*); *qu'elle ait
retrouvé … avant l'été* (finished before a future point); *aucun … n'ait été* (a negative
subject with *ne*, not a ne explétif).

## Dialogue: après le match

> **Léo:** Tu as vu ? On a été éliminés aux tirs au but. Je n'arrive pas à croire que l'arbitre
> ait refusé ce but.
>
> **Sarah:** Franchement, je ne suis pas sûre qu'il se soit trompé. Il y avait hors-jeu.
>
> **Léo:** Quand même, je suis déçu qu'on n'ait pas mieux joué en première mi-temps.
>
> **Sarah:** Moi, je suis contente qu'on soit allés si loin. Personne ne pensait qu'on
> arriverait en demi-finale.
>
> **Léo:** C'est vrai. Il faudra juste que les joueurs aient récupéré avant le prochain
> tournoi.

**Summary.** Léo and Sarah talk after their team is knocked out on penalties (*aux tirs au but*).
Léo can't believe the referee disallowed a goal; Sarah isn't sure the referee was wrong, because
of offside (*hors-jeu*). Léo is disappointed with the first half (*la première mi-temps*); Sarah
is pleased they got as far as a semi-final, and Léo hopes the players will have recovered before
the next tournament.

## At the stadium

Name the people and things in the picture: *l'athlète* on *le podium* with *la médaille*,
*l'arbitre* with a whistle, *l'entraîneur* at the side of the track and *les supporters* in the
stand.

*Pour un sportif ou une sportive de haut niveau, chaque compétition compte : une qualification
ouvre la porte des grands championnats, une élimination la ferme.* — For a top-level sportsman or
sportswoman, every competition counts: qualifying opens the door to the big championships,
elimination shuts it.

A few facts to talk about: at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games France won 64 medals, 16 of
them gold, its best haul in more than a century; the swimmer Léon Marchand won four individual
titles there.

![A stadium scene: three athletes on a podium, the winner in the middle with a gold medal round her neck; a referee in black with a whistle on the left; a coach in a tracksuit holding a stopwatch on the right; supporters waving flags in the stand at the back.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- **Building it on the indicative.** ~~Je suis content qu'il a gagné~~ → *qu'il ait gagné*. The
  two sound alike (*a / ait*), so check in writing.
- **Wrong spelling of *avoir*.** ~~que nous ayions~~, ~~que vous ayiez~~ → *que nous ayons, que
  vous ayez*.
- **Forgetting agreement with *être*.** ~~Je suis ravi que mes filles soient arrivé~~ →
  *soient arrivées*.
- **Using the subjunctive with one subject.** ~~Je suis fière que j'aie fini~~ → *Je suis fière
  d'avoir fini*.
- **Reading the ne explétif as a negative.** *Avant qu'il ne soit parti* means "before he has
  left", not "before he hasn't left".
- **Choosing the tense from today.** *J'étais contente qu'il vienne* is right when his coming and
  my joy were at the same time, even though both are in the past.

## Key points

- Subjonctif passé = *aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient* or *sois, sois, soit, soyons, soyez,
  soient* + participle, with the passé composé's auxiliary and agreement.
- Present subjunctive: same time or later than the main verb. Past subjunctive: done before it,
  or done before a stated point in the future.
- The main verb's own tense doesn't change the choice in modern French.
- Same subject: past infinitive (*content d'avoir gagné*); *bien que* keeps the subjunctive.
- The ne explétif (*avant qu'il ne soit trop tard*) is optional, formal and not negative.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. The subjonctif passé now appears in your conjugation drills.

lessons.title: Je cherche un appartement qui soit calme: the subjunctive in relative clauses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far the subjunctive has come after a verb (*il faut que, je doute que*) or a conjunction (*bien
que, avant que*). This lesson adds a third place: the **[[relative clause]]**, the clause that starts
with *qui, que, où, dont* or *lequel* and describes a noun. Compare:

- *J'ai trouvé un appartement qui est calme.* — I've found a flat that is quiet.
- *Je cherche un appartement qui soit calme.* — I'm looking for a flat that is (would be) quiet.

The words are almost the same; only the mood changes. The first flat exists and you have found it;
the second is an idea, a flat you hope exists. French marks that difference with the subjunctive.
You'll learn the four situations where it happens, a decision chart, and the cases where both
moods are correct. The theme is housing: buying, renting and the housing crisis.

## The antecedent decides

The noun a relative clause describes is its **[[antecedent]]**: in *un appartement qui soit calme*,
the antecedent is *un appartement*. The mood of the relative clause depends on how the speaker
sees that antecedent:

- **real and identified** (it exists, you know which one): indicative;
- **wished for, denied, or picked out by a superlative**: usually subjunctive.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Indicative or subjunctive in a relative clause?
  accDescr: Start from the antecedent, the noun the relative clause describes. If it is a real, identified person or thing, use the indicative. If it is looked for or wished for and may not exist, use the subjunctive. If it is denied or indefinite, such as personne, rien or aucun, use the subjunctive. If it follows a superlative, le seul, le premier, le dernier or l'unique, the subjunctive is usual and the indicative is also correct when you state a plain fact: both are possible.
  A["The antecedent: the noun before qui / que / où / dont"] --> B{"Real and identified?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Indicative: J'ai trouvé un studio qui est calme."]
  B -- no --> D{"What kind?"}
  D -- "looked for, wished for" --> E["Subjunctive: Je cherche un studio qui soit calme."]
  D -- "denied: personne, rien, aucun" --> F["Subjunctive: Il n'y a aucun studio qui soit libre."]
  D -- "superlative, le seul, le premier" --> G["Both possible: subjunctive usual, indicative for a plain fact"]
```

## 1. Looked for, wished for, required

After verbs and phrases of searching or wanting (*chercher, vouloir, souhaiter, avoir besoin de,
il nous faut, rêver de*) with an indefinite noun, the subjunctive shows that the thing may not
exist:

- *Nous cherchons une maison qui ait un jardin.* — We're looking for a house that has a garden.
- *Il nous faut un appartement qui soit lumineux et bien insonorisé.* — We need a flat that's
  bright and well soundproofed.
- *Elle voudrait un agent immobilier qui connaisse bien le quartier.* — She'd like an estate agent
  who knows the area well.

Change the antecedent to something identified and the indicative comes back:

- *Nous avons visité une maison qui a un jardin.* — We viewed a house that has a garden.
- *Je cherche l'agence immobilière qui est en face de la gare.* — I'm looking for the estate
  agency that's opposite the station. (A definite place that exists: indicative.)

In everyday speech many people use the indicative even for something wished for (*Je cherche un
appart qui est calme*); the subjunctive is the careful choice, and it stresses that you don't yet
know whether such a flat exists.

## 2. Denied or indefinite: personne, rien, aucun

When the antecedent is denied (*personne, rien, aucun, pas un, il n'y a pas de*) or left vague
(*quelqu'un, quelque chose* in a doubtful context), the relative clause describes something that
doesn't exist or may not exist: subjunctive.

- *Il n'y a personne qui puisse nous aider.* — There's nobody who can help us.
- *Je ne connais aucun notaire qui soit libre lundi.* — I don't know any notary who is free on
  Monday.
- *Il n'y a rien dans cette annonce qui me plaise.* — There's nothing in this ad that I like.
- *Dans ce quartier, il n'existe pas un seul logement social qui soit vacant.* — In this area
  there isn't a single social housing flat that's empty.

## 3. Superlatives and le seul, le premier, le dernier

After a **[[superlative]]** (*le plus …, le moins …, le meilleur, le pire*) and after *le seul,
l'unique, le premier, le dernier*, the subjunctive is usual:

- *C'est le plus bel appartement que nous ayons visité.* — It's the most beautiful flat we've
  viewed.
- *C'est la seule agence qui ait répondu à notre message.* — It's the only agency that has
  replied to our message.

Here the **indicative is also correct**. It presents the fact as plain and checkable, while the
subjunctive presents it as the speaker's judgment, with a nuance of "as far as we know":

- *C'est le premier acquéreur qui a fait une offre.* — He's the first buyer who made an offer
  (a fact in the order of events).
- *C'est le meilleur notaire que je connaisse.* — He's the best notary I know (my opinion).

So don't treat this as right or wrong: in careful writing the subjunctive is the more common
choice after a superlative, and the indicative is normal for a dated, factual "first" or "last"
(*le dernier train qui part à minuit*).

## 4. Questions

A question about whether something exists works like case 1: *Connais-tu quelqu'un qui sache
réparer une chaudière ?* — Do you know anyone who can fix a boiler? *Y a-t-il un appartement qui
soit libre en mars ?* The indicative is common in speech here too (*Tu connais quelqu'un qui sait
… ?*).

## Present or past subjunctive in the relative

Lesson 05's time rule applies inside the relative clause:

- *Je cherche un appartement qui soit libre en mars.* — same time or later: present.
- *C'est la plus petite surface habitable que nous ayons jamais vue.* — before the main verb:
  past. *Vue* agrees with *que* (= *la surface*), a direct object placed before *avoir*.
- *Je ne connais personne qui ait acquis un logement sans prêt immobilier.* — I don't know anyone
  who has bought a home without a mortgage.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: choose the mood

*Complete with* être: "Nous cherchons un studio qui ___ près du métro."

1. Antecedent: *un studio*, indefinite, after *chercher*. It may not exist.
2. So: subjunctive, present (the being near is now or later): *soit*.

*Nous cherchons un studio qui soit près du métro.* If you had already found it: *Nous avons
trouvé un studio qui est près du métro.*

### Example 2: three antecedents, three answers

- *Il n'y a aucune pièce qui ___ (avoir) de fenêtre.* Denied antecedent: *ait*.
- *J'ai acheté la maison qui ___ (avoir) des volets bleus.* Real and identified: *a*.
- *C'est l'appartement le moins cher que nous ___ (trouver).* Superlative, finished: *ayons
  trouvé* (usual) or *avons trouvé* (a plain fact). Both are correct; the subjunctive is the
  more common written choice.

## Reading: notre chasse à l'appartement

> Depuis six mois, Julien et moi cherchons un appartement qui soit à la fois lumineux, spacieux et
> pas trop cher à Lyon. Autant dire un rêve. À chaque visite, l'agent immobilier nous promet « un
> bien rare ». Le dernier était un deux-pièces exigu, au rez-de-chaussée, avec une chambre qui
> donnait sur un mur. Pas une seule pièce qui soit vraiment claire !
>
> Le marché de l'immobilier est tendu. Les prix au mètre carré ont beaucoup augmenté, et la banque
> exige un apport d'au moins 10 % pour nous accorder un prêt immobilier. Je ne connais personne de
> notre âge qui ait pu acquérir un logement sans l'aide de ses parents.
>
> Pourtant, samedi, nous avons visité une petite maison mitoyenne, dans un voisinage calme. La
> surface habitable n'est que de 58 m², mais c'est le premier logement qui nous plaise vraiment
> tous les deux. Le mur mitoyen est bien insonorisé, et le notaire nous a confirmé qu'il n'y avait
> pas de copropriété, donc pas de charges. Nous avons fait une offre, mais un autre
> acquéreur en a fait une avant nous : s'il se retire, nous pourrions emménager en juin.

**Translation.** For six months Julien and I have been looking for a flat in Lyon that is bright,
spacious and not too expensive all at once. You might as well say a dream. At every viewing the estate
agent promises us "a rare property". The last one was a cramped two-room flat on the ground floor,
with a bedroom that looked onto a wall. Not one room that was really light!

The property market is tight. Prices per square metre have risen a lot, and the bank requires a
down payment of at least 10% before it will give us a mortgage. I don't know anyone our age who has
managed to buy a home without help from their parents.

Yet on Saturday we viewed a small semi-detached house in a quiet neighbourhood. The living area is
only 58 m², but it's the first home we both really like. The party wall is well soundproofed, and
the notary confirmed to us that there was no co-ownership, so no service charges. We've made an
offer, but another buyer made one before us: if he pulls out, we could move in in June.

**Notice:** *qui soit … lumineux* (wished for); *pas une seule pièce qui soit* (denied); *personne
… qui ait pu* (denied, and past: any such purchase is already over); *le premier logement qui nous
plaise* (after *le premier*: subjunctive as a judgment); *une chambre qui donnait* and *il n'y
avait pas* (real, described facts: indicative).

## The housing crisis in a few lines

*La crise du logement* is a constant topic in French debate. Here is a short summary of the
facts: the law known as the *loi SRU* (13 December 2000) requires communes of more than 3,500
inhabitants in large urban areas to have a minimum share of social housing, 20% or 25% of their
homes depending on the case, and penalises those that fall short. Supporters say it spreads *le
logement social* fairly; critics say the targets are hard to reach where land is scarce.

Two more words you'll read in the press: *le parc immobilier* (the housing stock: *le parc
immobilier ancien est mal isolé*) and *l'expulsion* (eviction). A landlord who wants to *expulser*
a tenant must go through the courts, and in France most evictions are suspended during the
winter months (*la trêve hivernale*).

**Variant:** in French-speaking Switzerland, the firm that manages rented flats for owners is
usually called *une régie* (*la régie immobilière*) rather than *une agence*.

## The plan of the house

The picture is the plan of the house the narrator and Julien have made an offer on. Find *le salon, la cuisine, la
chambre, la salle de bains* (A1), *le mur mitoyen* shared with the next house, and the total
*surface habitable* written in *mètres carrés*.

![A floor plan of a small house with a living room and an open kitchen on one side, a bedroom and a bathroom on the other, a thick wall along the left edge marked as shared with the house next door, a front door at the bottom and a total area of 58 m² written in a box.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- **Subjunctive for a real thing.** ~~J'ai acheté une maison qui ait un jardin~~ → *qui a un
  jardin*: you bought it, it exists.
- **Indicative after a denied antecedent in writing.** *Il n'y a personne qui peut m'aider* is
  heard in casual speech; in careful French write *qui puisse*.
- **Treating the superlative as a trap.** *Le meilleur film que j'aie vu* and *le meilleur film
  que j'ai vu* are both correct. Prefer the subjunctive in an essay.
- **Forgetting agreement in the past.** *La plus belle maison que nous ayons vue*: *que* stands
  for *la maison*, placed before *avoir*.
- **Confusing *emménager* and *déménager*.** *Emménager* = move in; *déménager* = move out (move
  house).

## Key points

- In a relative clause, the antecedent decides the mood.
- Real, identified antecedent: indicative. Looked for or wished for, or denied (*personne, rien,
  aucun*): subjunctive.
- After a superlative, *le seul, le premier, le dernier*: subjunctive usual, indicative for a
  plain fact; both are correct.
- Present or past subjunctive by lesson 05's time rule; past participle agreement as usual.
- Casual speech often keeps the indicative; careful writing uses the subjunctive.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Qu'il ait raison, personne ne le conteste: fine mood choices
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 you learned lists: *il faut que* takes the subjunctive, *je sais que* the indicative. At
B2 the lists stop being enough. Some verbs take either mood, and the mood changes what they mean.
*Dis-lui qu'il vient* reports a fact (tell him he's coming); *Dis-lui qu'il vienne* gives an order
(tell him to come). This lesson shows the verbs and conjunctions where that happens, what a
negative or a question does to verbs of saying and thinking, and why a *que*-clause at the start
of a sentence takes the subjunctive. The theme is school and the French education system.

## Mood: what the choice says

A verb's **[[mood]]** shows how the speaker presents an action. The indicative presents it as a fact
or something taken as real; the subjunctive presents it as something wanted, required, felt,
doubted, or simply *considered* without being asserted. Most of the time the trigger decides for
you. In this lesson the speaker decides, and the choice is part of the meaning.

## Verbs whose mood changes the meaning

![Six cards, each split into an indicative half and a subjunctive half: dire que (statement / order), admettre que (acknowledge / accept), comprendre que (realise / find understandable), supposer que (think / imagine), expliquer que and cela explique que (explain / account for), de sorte que (result / purpose).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**dire, écrire, crier que**: indicative for a statement, subjunctive for an order.

- *Le proviseur dit que les cours reprennent lundi.* — The head says lessons start again on
  Monday.
- *Dites aux élèves qu'ils fassent silence.* — Tell the pupils to be quiet. (Compare *Dites
  aux élèves qu'ils font trop de bruit*: a statement, tell them they're too noisy.)

**admettre que**: indicative = acknowledge a fact; subjunctive = accept something as possible or
allowable.

- *J'admets que le redoublement a coûté cher.* — I admit that repeating the year was expensive.
- *J'admets qu'on puisse ne pas être d'accord.* — I accept that people may disagree.

**comprendre que**: indicative = realise; subjunctive = find it understandable.

- *J'ai compris qu'elle allait redoubler.* — I realised she was going to repeat the year.
- *Je comprends que les parents soient inquiets.* — I can understand parents being worried.

**supposer que**: indicative = think, assume; subjunctive (especially *supposons que*) = imagine
a case.

- *Je suppose que tu as vu le bulletin.* — I suppose you've seen the school report.
- *Supposons que le redoublement soit supprimé : que se passerait-il ?* — Let's suppose repeating
  a year were abolished: what would happen?

**expliquer que / cela explique que**: a person who explains gives a statement (indicative);
a fact that *accounts for* another takes the subjunctive.

- *L'enseignante explique que la classe est trop chargée.* — The teacher explains that the class
  is too big.
- *La distance explique que tant d'élèves soient en retard.* — The distance accounts for so many
  pupils being late.

**entendre que** + subjunctive is formal for "to intend, to require": *La directrice entend que
chacun soit à l'heure.* — The head intends everyone to be on time. (*J'ai entendu dire que* +
indicative is "I've heard that".)

**s'attendre à ce que** + subjunctive: *Personne ne s'attendait à ce que la réforme soit
appliquée si vite.* — Nobody expected the reform to be applied so fast. With a noun or an
infinitive: *s'attendre au pire, s'attendre à réussir*.

## Negated or questioned verbs of saying and thinking

A **[[declarative verb]]** reports a statement or an opinion: *dire, affirmer, déclarer, penser,
croire, être sûr*. In the affirmative it takes the indicative (*Je pense qu'il a raison*). When
it is negated or questioned, the content is no longer asserted, and careful French uses the
subjunctive:

- *Je ne dis pas que le système éducatif soit parfait.* — I'm not saying the education system is
  perfect.
- *Pensez-vous que l'évaluation soit juste ?* — Do you think the assessment is fair? (formal:
  inversion with *penser*; *Vous pensez que l'évaluation est juste ?* is the everyday question)

The indicative after a negated verb is also found, when the speaker still sees the content as a
fact: *Je ne dis pas qu'il a tort* can mean "he may be right, I'm not saying otherwise".

*Ne pas nier que* and *ne pas douter que* are the classic cases where both moods are correct.
*Je ne nie pas qu'il soit compétent* (careful style; in literary French also *qu'il ne soit
compétent*, with a ne explétif) and *Je ne nie pas qu'il est compétent* (presenting it as a fact)
are both good French. You can use either; this course won't test them as one answer.

*Espérer que*, reviewed: affirmative *espérer* takes the indicative, often the future: *J'espère
que tu réussiras ton bac.* Compare *souhaiter que* + subjunctive: *Je souhaite que tu réussisses.*

## A que-clause at the start: subjunctive

When a *que*-clause opens the sentence, before the main verb, it takes the subjunctive, even when
it states a fact. The main clause usually takes it up again with a pronoun (*le, cela*):

- *Qu'il ait raison, personne ne le conteste.* — That he's right, nobody disputes.
- *Que l'échec scolaire commence tôt, beaucoup d'études le montrent.* — That failure at school
  starts early, many studies show.

Put the same clause after the verb and the indicative becomes possible: *Personne ne conteste
qu'il a raison* (or *ait raison*: *contester* is a verb of doubt, and it often keeps the
subjunctive even when negated). The fronted clause is a topic
put up for discussion, not yet asserted: that is why it takes the subjunctive.

**Le fait que** (the fact that) often takes the subjunctive, especially at the start of a
sentence, though the indicative is also found when the fact is stressed: *Le fait que les classes soient (sont) surchargées
explique beaucoup de choses.* Both are correct.

## De sorte que, de façon que, de manière que: result or purpose

These three conjunctions mean "so that", in two senses:

- **[[result]]** (what happened as a consequence), indicative: *Le cours a été déplacé, de sorte que
  la moitié de la classe l'a raté.* — The lesson was moved, so half the class missed it.
- **[[purpose]]** (what you aim at), subjunctive: *L'enseignante parle lentement, de sorte que tout
  le monde comprenne.* — The teacher speaks slowly so that everyone understands.

The mood tells the reader which you mean, so read it carefully in exam texts.

## Seem and appear, reviewed

- *Il paraît que la réforme est reportée.* — Apparently the reform has been postponed
  (hearsay): indicative.
- *Il semble que la réforme soit reportée.* — It seems the reform has been postponed: usually
  subjunctive.
- *Il me semble que la réforme est reportée.* — I think the reform has been postponed (my
  impression): indicative.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: what does the mood say?

*Le principal a écrit aux familles que les élèves ___ (venir) en tenue de sport.*

1. Is *écrire* reporting a fact or giving an instruction? Both are possible, so the mood decides.
2. Fact (the pupils are coming in sportswear): *viennent* in the indicative present. Instruction
   (the pupils are to come in sportswear): *viennent* in the subjunctive, which here looks the
   same.
3. Use a verb where the forms differ to see it: *… que les élèves sont en tenue de sport*
   (statement) / *… que les élèves soient en tenue de sport* (order).

### Example 2: result or purpose?

- *Elle a révisé tous les soirs, de sorte qu'elle ___ (obtenir) son bac avec mention.* A result
  that happened: *a obtenu*.
- *Organisons des groupes de soutien, de manière que personne ne ___ (décrocher).* A goal:
  *décroche* (subjunctive).

## Reading: faut-il en finir avec le redoublement ?

> Longtemps, le redoublement a été un rite de l'école française : un élève qui n'avait pas le
> niveau refaisait l'année. Il est devenu beaucoup plus rare, et le débat revient à chaque
> réforme du système éducatif.
>
> Que le redoublement coûte cher à l'État, personne ne le conteste : une année de scolarité de
> plus, c'est une place en classe, un enseignant, un établissement. Mais le vrai débat porte sur
> son efficacité. Certains chercheurs en pédagogie expliquent qu'un élève qui redouble progresse
> souvent la première année, puis retombe. Beaucoup d'enseignants admettent que la mesure a des
> limites, mais ils comprennent que des parents la réclament pour un enfant en difficulté.
>
> D'autres soulignent les inégalités : ce sont plus souvent les enfants des milieux modestes qui
> redoublent, de sorte que la mesure renforce parfois l'échec scolaire au lieu de le réparer.
> L'absentéisme et le décrochage scolaire touchent plus souvent les élèves qui ont redoublé.
>
> Je ne dis pas que la solution soit simple. Mais si l'on veut l'égalité des chances, il faut que
> chaque élève reçoive de l'aide avant d'avoir accumulé les retards, de manière qu'il n'ait pas à
> refaire toute une année.

**Translation.** For a long time, repeating a year was a ritual of French schooling: a pupil who
wasn't up to standard did the year again. It has become much rarer, and the debate comes back with
every reform of the education system.

That repeating a year costs the state a lot of money, nobody disputes: one more year of schooling
means a place in a class, a teacher, a school. But the real debate is about whether it works.
Some education researchers explain that a pupil who repeats a year often makes progress in the first
year, then falls back. Many teachers admit that the measure has its limits, but they understand
parents asking for it for a child who is struggling.

Others point out the inequalities: it is more often children from modest backgrounds who repeat a
year, so that the measure sometimes reinforces failure at school instead of repairing it.
Absenteeism and dropping out affect pupils who have repeated a year more often.

I'm not saying the solution is simple. But if we want equal opportunities, every pupil must get
help before falling far behind, so that they don't have to do a whole year again.

**Notice:** the fronted *Que le redoublement coûte cher*; *expliquent qu'un élève … progresse*
(statement, indicative); *admettent que la mesure a* (acknowledge) beside *comprennent que des
parents la réclament* (find understandable); *de sorte que la mesure renforce* (result,
indicative) beside *de manière qu'il n'ait pas* (purpose, subjunctive); *Je ne dis pas que la
solution soit*.

## The French school ladder

The picture shows the main stages. *L'école* covers ages about 3 to 11; *le collège* (pupils:
*les collégiens*) runs from *sixième* to *troisième* and ends with *le brevet*; *le lycée* (pupils:
*les lycéens*) runs from *seconde* to *terminale*, where pupils follow a *filière* (general,
technological or vocational) and sit *le bac*. The *programme scolaire* is set nationally.

![A staircase of four steps from bottom to top: école maternelle (about 3 to 6), école élémentaire (about 6 to 11), collège from sixième to troisième ending in the brevet, and lycée from seconde to terminale ending in the bac.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Talking about school, you'll also want: *assidu* (a pupil who attends and works regularly), *la
mixité sociale* (pupils from different backgrounds in the same school), *le savoir* (knowledge),
*l'enseignement* (teaching, education), *pédagogique* (an *équipe pédagogique* is a school's
teaching staff) and *évaluer* (*Les élèves sont évalués en continu*).

**Variants:** in Québec, after secondary school most students go to *le cégep* (two years before
university, or three of technical training); in Belgium, the years of secondary school are still
called *les humanités*; in Switzerland, the school-leaving certificate that gives access to university is *la maturité*
(*la maturité gymnasiale*, informally *la matu*).

## Dialogue: deux parents à la sortie du collège

> **Nadia:** Le conseil de classe propose que Hugo redouble. J'admets qu'il a eu de mauvaises
> notes, mais je ne crois pas qu'un redoublement l'aide.
>
> **Marc:** Je comprends que tu sois déçue. Mais il me semble qu'il a besoin de temps.
>
> **Nadia:** Du temps, oui, avec un soutien pédagogique. Pas une année de plus à s'ennuyer.
>
> **Marc:** Dis-lui surtout qu'il vienne aux cours de soutien. Qu'il soit capable, tout le monde
> le sait.

**Summary.** Nadia's son Hugo may have to repeat the year (*le conseil de classe* is the end-of-term
staff meeting). She admits his marks were bad but doesn't think repeating will help; Marc
understands her disappointment but thinks Hugo needs time. They agree he should go to the support
classes (*les cours de soutien*).

## Common mistakes

- **Using one mood for both meanings.** *Dis-lui qu'il vient* is a statement, not an order. For
  an order: *qu'il vienne*.
- **Indicative in a fronted que-clause.** ~~Qu'il a raison, personne ne le conteste~~ → *Qu'il
  ait raison*.
- **Subjunctive after affirmative *espérer*.** ~~J'espère qu'il vienne~~ → *J'espère qu'il
  viendra*.
- **Reading *de sorte que* without checking the mood.** Indicative = result; subjunctive =
  purpose.
- **Calling *Je ne nie pas qu'il est compétent* wrong.** Both moods are correct after *ne pas
  nier*.

## Key points

- *dire / écrire que*: statement + indicative, order + subjunctive. *admettre, comprendre,
  supposer, expliquer*: the subjunctive changes the meaning.
- *s'attendre à ce que, entendre que* (= require) + subjunctive.
- A negated or questioned declarative verb usually takes the subjunctive in careful style.
- A *que*-clause placed first takes the subjunctive.
- *de sorte que* + indicative = result; + subjunctive = purpose.
- Both moods are correct after *le fait que* and *ne pas nier que*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Quelle que soit la critique: concession at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

To argue at B2 you need to grant a point before you answer it: *The script is weak; even so, the
actors are superb.* That move is **[[concession]]**: admitting a fact or an objection that might work
against your main point, and keeping the point anyway. B1 gave you *bien que, même si, malgré,
avoir beau, pourtant* and previewed *quoi que* and *quel que soit*. This lesson makes the
"whatever" forms productive and adds the constructions of formal writing: *si talentueux qu'il
soit, quand bien même, encore que, il n'empêche que, toujours est-il que, en dépit de*. It ends
with a chart of the whole family and the concession-then-rebuttal paragraph that lesson 21 builds
on. The theme is cinema: making films, reviewing them, the box office.

## Concessive clauses with the subjunctive

A **[[concessive clause]]** is the part of the sentence that carries the conceded fact: *Bien que le
film soit long, …* Most concessive conjunctions take the subjunctive, because the clause is
granted, not asserted as the point.

### quel que soit + noun: whatever (the …)

*Quel* agrees with the noun in gender and number, and *être* agrees in number:

| noun | form |
|---|---|
| *le budget* (m. sg.) | *quel que soit le budget* |
| *la critique* (f. sg.) | *quelle que soit la critique* |
| *les moyens* (m. pl.) | *quels que soient les moyens* |
| *les difficultés* (f. pl.) | *quelles que soient les difficultés* |

- *Quelles que soient ses faiblesses, ce premier film mérite d'être vu.* — Whatever its
  weaknesses, this first film deserves to be seen.
- *Quel que soit le résultat au box-office, la productrice est fière du film.* — Whatever the
  box-office result, the producer is proud of the film.

It is two words, *quel que*. ~~Quelque soit~~ is a frequent spelling mistake.

### quoi que, où que, qui que + clause

- *Quoi qu'en disent les critiques, le public a adoré.* — Whatever the critics say about it, the
  audience loved it.
- *Où que vous alliez, ce film passe en version originale.* — Wherever you go, this film is
  showing in the original language.
- *Qui que vous soyez, le jury vous jugera sur votre travail.* — Whoever you are, the jury will
  judge you on your work.

Don't confuse *quoi que* (two words, whatever) with *quoique* (one word, although: B1).

### si / aussi + adjective + que: however (adjective)

- *Si talentueux qu'il soit, l'acteur ne peut pas sauver ce scénario.* — However talented he
  may be, the actor can't save this script.
- *Aussi spectaculaires que soient les cascades, on s'ennuie.* — However spectacular the stunts
  are, you get bored.

With a noun subject, the subject often comes after the verb (*que soient les cascades*). It also
works with an adverb: *si vite qu'il tourne, …*

### tout + adjective + que: two moods

Traditionally *tout … que* takes the indicative, because it concedes a real fact: *Tout
expérimenté qu'il est, il a eu le trac.* — Experienced as he is, he had stage fright. The
subjunctive is now common too (*tout expérimenté qu'il soit*), and both are correct. *Tout*
agrees before a feminine adjective that begins with a consonant: *toute jeune qu'elle est*.

### Literary forms to recognise

*Pour + adjective + que* and *quelque + adjective + que* (*Pour brillant qu'il soit, …*;
*Quelque habile qu'il soit, …*) mean the same as *si … que*. You'll meet them in older or very
formal writing; you don't need to produce them.

### encore que + subjunctive: although (a reservation)

*Encore que* is formal. It usually comes after the main clause and adds a reservation:

- *Le film est réussi, encore que la fin soit un peu longue.* — The film works, although the
  ending is a bit long.

## Concession with other moods

### quand bien même + conditionnel: even if

*Quand bien même* means *même si* (even if), in a formal register, but it takes the
**[[conditionnel]]**, and the main clause is usually in the conditionnel too:

- *Quand bien même le film ferait un million d'entrées, il ne serait pas rentable.* — Even if
  the film had a million admissions, it wouldn't make a profit.
- *Quand bien même il aurait voulu ce rôle, le producteur ne l'aurait pas choisi.* — Even if he
  had wanted the role, the producer wouldn't have chosen him.

### il n'empêche que, toujours est-il que + indicative

Both start a new sentence or clause after the concession, and both take the indicative, because
what follows is the point you are asserting:

- *Le scénario est faible. Il n'empêche que l'interprétation est remarquable.* — The script is
  weak. Even so, the acting is remarkable.
- *On peut discuter du montage ; toujours est-il que le film a trouvé son public.* — You can argue
  about the editing; the fact remains that the film found its audience.

In speech, *il n'empêche que* is often shortened to *n'empêche* (informal): *N'empêche, j'ai
adoré.* *Toujours est-il que* always keeps its inversion.

### en dépit de + noun

*En dépit de* is a formal *malgré*: *En dépit d'un petit budget, le film a réuni une
distribution prestigieuse.* — Despite a small budget, the film brought together a prestigious
cast.

## The whole family by grammar

![A chart in four columns. Plus subjunctive: bien que, quoique, encore que, quel que soit, quoi que, où que, qui que, si (aussi) … que. Plus conditionnel: quand bien même. Plus indicative: même si, il n'empêche que, toujours est-il que, tout … que (traditional). Plus noun or infinitive: malgré, en dépit de, avoir beau plus infinitive. Each column has one example sentence.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| construction | followed by | register | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *bien que, quoique* | subjunctive | neutral | *Bien que le film soit long, …* |
| *encore que* | subjunctive | formal | *…, encore que la fin soit longue.* |
| *quel que soit, quoi que, où que, qui que* | subjunctive | neutral | *Quels que soient ses défauts, …* |
| *si / aussi* + adjective + *que* | subjunctive | formal | *Si drôle qu'il soit, …* |
| *tout* + adjective + *que* | indicative (subjunctive common) | formal | *Tout drôle qu'il est, …* |
| *même si* | indicative | neutral | *Même si le film est long, …* |
| *quand bien même* | conditionnel | formal | *Quand bien même il serait long, …* |
| *il n'empêche que, toujours est-il que* | indicative | neutral / formal | *Il n'empêche que l'actrice est formidable.* |
| *malgré, en dépit de* | noun | neutral / formal | *Malgré sa longueur, …* |
| *avoir beau* | infinitive | neutral, spoken | *J'ai beau aimer ce réalisateur, …* |

## The concession-then-rebuttal paragraph

In a review or an essay, a common shape is: grant the objection, then turn and assert your view.

1. Concede: *Certes, le film est long* / *Quels que soient ses défauts, …* / *Bien que le
   rythme soit lent, …*
2. Turn: *mais, cependant, il n'empêche que, toujours est-il que*.
3. Assert and support your point, in the indicative.

### Example 1: write the paragraph

*Opinion:* the film is worth seeing. *Objection:* it is a remake.

> Certes, il s'agit d'un remake, et quelle que soit la qualité de l'original, la comparaison
> sera inévitable. Il n'empêche que cette nouvelle version a sa propre personnalité : la
> distribution est plus jeune, le montage plus nerveux, et l'adaptation des dialogues au Paris
> d'aujourd'hui fonctionne.

Notice the order: concession (*certes*, *quelle que soit*), turn (*il n'empêche que*), then the
assertion, with three supporting facts.

### Example 2: choose the construction

*Join "The stunts are impressive" and "the story is empty" four ways.*

- *Bien que les cascades soient impressionnantes, l'histoire est vide.* (subjunctive)
- *Si impressionnantes que soient les cascades, l'histoire est vide.* (subjunctive, formal)
- *Les cascades ont beau être impressionnantes, l'histoire est vide.* (infinitive, spoken)
- *Les cascades sont impressionnantes ; il n'empêche que l'histoire est vide.* (indicative)

### Example 3: correct a draft review

*A learner's draft, with one mistake in each sentence:*

1. ~~Quelque soient les critiques, le film a trouvé son public.~~ The noun is *les critiques*
   (feminine plural), and *quel que* is two words: *Quelles que soient les critiques, …*
2. ~~Même si le montage soit lent, on ne s'ennuie pas.~~ *Même si* takes the indicative: *Même si
   le montage est lent, …*
3. ~~Quand bien même le film est un navet, je le reverrais.~~ *Quand bien même* takes the
   conditionnel: *Quand bien même le film serait un navet, …*
4. ~~Le doublage est raté. Il n'empêche que la version originale soit superbe.~~ *Il n'empêche
   que* introduces your own point, so the indicative: *… la version originale est superbe.*

Check each concession word against the chart above: the mood is part of the construction, not a
choice of style.

## Reading: une critique

> **« Le Dernier Été » : un premier film qui mérite son succès**
>
> On attendait un film modeste, de ceux que le cinéma d'auteur réserve aux salles d'art et
> d'essai. Trois semaines après
> sa sortie en salle, « Le Dernier Été » dépasse pourtant le million d'entrées, et le box-office
> le place devant plusieurs grosses productions américaines.
>
> Le film n'est pas sans défauts, encore que ceux-ci soient vite oubliés. Le scénario, adapté d'un
> roman peu connu, s'égare un peu au milieu, et certaines scènes avec les figurants sentent le
> carton-pâte. Quelles que soient ces faiblesses, l'interprétation emporte tout : Lina Haddad, qui
> interprète une jeune mère dépassée, est d'une justesse rare. Les deux cascades du film, tournées
> sans doublure, sont filmées sobrement, loin du spectacle.
>
> Si modeste que soit son budget, le film soigne aussi la forme : le montage, rapide sans être
> nerveux, laisse respirer les acteurs. On regrettera seulement que les passages en arabe aient été
> doublés pour certaines salles : voyez-le plutôt en version originale.
>
> Les cinéphiles discuteront de la fin, et le producteur parle déjà d'un remake américain.
> Toujours est-il qu'en dépit de ses imperfections, « Le Dernier Été » est tout sauf un navet :
> un premier film juste, sincère et généreux.

**Translation.** **"The Last Summer": a first film that deserves its success.** We were expecting a
modest film, the kind of auteur cinema that stays in art-house cinemas. Yet three weeks after its cinema release, "The Last
Summer" has passed a million admissions, and the box office puts it ahead of several big American
productions.

The film is not without faults, although they are quickly forgotten. The script, adapted from a
little-known novel, loses its way a bit in the middle, and some scenes with the extras look fake (*sentent le carton-pâte*, literally "smell of papier-mâché"). Whatever these weaknesses, the acting carries everything: Lina Haddad, who plays an
overwhelmed young mother, gives a performance of rare truthfulness. The film's two stunts, shot without a double, are
filmed plainly, far from spectacle.

However modest its budget, the film takes care of form too: the editing, fast without being jumpy,
leaves the actors room to breathe. Our only regret is that the passages in Arabic were dubbed for
some cinemas: see it in the original language instead.

Film buffs will argue about the ending, and the producer is already talking about an American
remake. The fact remains that, despite its imperfections, "The Last Summer" is anything but a
turkey: a true, sincere and generous first film.

(The film, the actress and the review are invented.)

**Notice:** *encore que ceux-ci soient*, *Quelles que soient ces faiblesses*, *Si modeste que soit*,
*que les passages … aient été doublés* (subjunctive); *Toujours est-il que … est* (indicative); *en dépit
de ses imperfections* (noun).

In France, most foreign films come out in two versions: *en version originale* (VO, usually
VOSTFR, with French subtitles) and dubbed into French (*le doublage*, the VF). *Les salles d'art
et d'essai* (art-house cinemas) mostly show the VO, and the *cinéphiles* who go there usually
prefer it.

## On the set

The picture shows a film set (*un plateau*): *le réalisateur* (A2) in his chair, the camera,
*les figurants* waiting for their scene, *le cascadeur* falling onto a mattress, and the
clapperboard (*le clap*).

![A film set: a director in a folding chair with a megaphone, a camera on a tripod with its operator, a stuntman falling head first beside a fake building front towards a thick mattress, three extras standing in a row and a clapperboard on a stool.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- **Indicative after concessive *que*-words.** ~~Quoi que tu dis~~ → *Quoi que tu dises*; ~~Si
  bon qu'il est~~ → *Si bon qu'il soit*.
- **Agreement of *quel que soit*.** ~~Quel que soit les risques~~ → *Quels que soient les
  risques*.
- ***Quelque soit*** for *quel que soit*: two words, and *quel* agrees.
- **Subjunctive after *même si*.** ~~Même si le film soit long~~ → *Même si le film est long*.
- **Indicative after *quand bien même*.** ~~Quand bien même il pleut~~ → *Quand bien même il
  pleuvrait*.
- **Subjunctive after *il n'empêche que*.** It introduces your point: indicative.

## Key points

- Concession = grant a point, keep yours. The concessive clause carries what you grant.
- Subjunctive: *bien que, quoique, encore que, quel que soit* (agreeing), *quoi que, où que, qui
  que, si / aussi … que*.
- *Tout … que*: indicative traditionally, subjunctive common: both correct.
- *Quand bien même* + conditionnel; *même si, il n'empêche que, toujours est-il que* +
  indicative; *malgré, en dépit de* + noun; *avoir beau* + infinitive.
- Paragraph: concede (*certes, quel que soit*), turn (*il n'empêche que*), assert.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Malgré que, après que: la norme et l'usage
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 05–08 you met several places where natives say one thing and grammars recommend
another: *après qu'il soit parti* is everywhere, yet you were told to write *après qu'il est
parti*. Who decides? This honors lesson looks at how French separates the **[[norm]]** (what
authorities recommend for careful language) from **[[usage]]** (what speakers actually say and
write), at five classic disputes, and at what you should do in an exam. The aim is not to take
sides: it is to know what each source says, why natives disagree, and which form is safe when you
are being marked.

## Norm and usage

A **[[norm]]** (*la norme*) is a set of rules for "good" language, usually based on careful written
French. A grammar or dictionary that states the norm is *normative* (*normatif*): it tells you
what to write. **[[Usage]]** (*l'usage*) is what people really do; a description of usage records
forms without judging them, or labels them (*familier, critiqué*) and leaves the choice to you.

Most French reference works mix the two, in different proportions:

- **The Académie française** (founded in 1635) writes a dictionary and, on its website, a
  column of advice, *Dire, ne pas dire*. Its line is the most normative: it often *proscribes*
  a usage (*proscrire*, to condemn it), even a common one.
- ***Le Bon Usage***, the grammar begun by the Belgian Maurice Grevisse (first edition 1936,
  updated by André Goosse), describes usage with thousands of quotations from writers, then gives
  advice. It often shows that a "mistake" has a long literary history.
- **The OQLF** (Office québécois de la langue française) publishes the *Banque de dépannage
  linguistique*, free online, with clear explanations of what is standard, accepted or
  criticised.
- **Dictionaries** such as *Le Robert* and *Larousse* record what speakers say and mark
  contested uses with labels.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: From usage to norm
  accDescr: Speakers and writers produce usage. Descriptive works such as dictionaries and Le Bon Usage record it, often with labels such as familiar or criticised. Normative authorities such as the Académie française and style guides judge it and recommend a norm. Schools and exams teach and mark the norm, which in turn shapes careful writing. A usage that spreads widely can, over time, be recorded and then accepted.
  A["Speakers and writers: usage"] --> B["Dictionaries and Le Bon Usage record it, with labels"]
  B --> C["Académie, OQLF, style guides judge it: the norm"]
  C --> D["Schools and exams teach and mark the norm"]
  D --> E["Careful writing follows the norm"]
  A -. "a widespread usage may later be accepted" .-> C
```

Some words you need to talk about mistakes:

- *un barbarisme*: a form that doesn't exist (~~vous disez~~ for *vous dites*, ~~ils
  croivent~~ for *ils croient*);
- *un solécisme*: existing words put together wrongly, a construction error (~~le livre que
  je t'ai parlé~~ for *le livre dont je t'ai parlé*);
- *un abus de langage*: a word used loosely, beyond its meaning (calling a simple delay *une
  catastrophe*);
- *une incorrection*: any incorrect usage, the general word.

*Le purisme* is the attitude that refuses change and borrowing; *un puriste* defends the norm
strictly. A form that authorities let pass without recommending it is *toléré* (tolerated): for
example, French official texts of 1901 and 1976 listed "tolerances" for school exams, such as the
present subjunctive in place of the imperfect subjunctive.

## Five classic disputes

### 1. après que + subjunctive

- **The norm:** *après que* + indicative, because what follows is presented as a fact that has
  happened (or will have happened): *après qu'il est parti, après qu'elle sera rentrée*. The
  Académie and the OQLF both keep this rule; the OQLF calls the subjunctive criticised.
- **Usage:** *après qu'il soit parti* is extremely common in speech, in the press and in many
  writers of the 20th century, probably by analogy with *avant que* + subjunctive.
- **Why natives disagree:** the indicative *après qu'il est parti* sounds odd to many ears, and
  *qu'il ait / qu'il a* sound almost the same, so speakers follow *avant que*.

### 2. malgré que + subjunctive

- **The norm:** use *bien que* or *quoique* for "although". The Académie advises against *malgré
  que* in that sense and accepts it only in the old literary phrase *malgré qu'il en ait*
  ("in spite of himself", with *avoir*).
- **Usage:** *Malgré qu'il pleuve, on sort* is very common in everyday French and appears in
  well-known authors; *Larousse* notes that purists still dislike it and recommends *bien que* in
  careful writing.
- **Why natives disagree:** *malgré* + noun is everyday French, so *malgré que* + clause seems
  natural.

### 3. se rappeler de quelque chose

- **The norm:** *se rappeler* takes a direct object: *Je me rappelle cette soirée*; *se souvenir*
  takes *de*: *Je me souviens de cette soirée*.
- **What is accepted:** the OQLF accepts *de* before a personal pronoun (*Je me rappelle de
  vous*, since *Je me rappelle vous* is impossible), before an infinitive saying what you must
  not forget to do (*Rappelle-toi de fermer la porte*), and when *de* belongs to another
  element (*Je me rappelle de quelle façon il a réagi*).
- **Usage:** *Je me rappelle de cette soirée* has long been common, modelled on *se souvenir
  de*; grammarians note it is widespread but still don't fully endorse it. The related
  *je m'en rappelle* is just as frequent; in careful writing, *je m'en souviens* or *je me le
  rappelle* is safer.

### 4. pallier à

- **The norm:** *pallier* (to make up for, to mitigate) takes a direct object: *pallier un
  manque de personnel*. The Académie condemns *pallier à*.
- **Usage:** *pallier au manque de personnel* is very frequent, even in the press and in some
  well-known writers, by analogy with *remédier à* (to remedy), which does take *à*.
- **Why natives disagree:** two verbs with close meanings and different constructions.

### 5. de façon à ce que, de manière à ce que

- **The norm:** *de façon que, de manière que* + subjunctive for purpose (lesson 07): *Parle fort,
  de façon qu'on t'entende.* The Académie's dictionary says that *de façon à ce que*, though
  common and found "even in good authors", is not to be recommended; most style guides also
  prefer the short forms.
- **Usage:** *de façon à ce que* is very common, built on *de façon à* + infinitive (*de façon à
  être entendu*). Dictionaries record it, often with a warning.
- **Why natives disagree:** the longer form follows the infinitive construction and makes the
  purpose meaning clear.

## What to write in an exam

In the DELF, in an essay or a formal letter, the safe choice is the norm: the marker may not
penalise *après qu'il soit parti*, but nobody will penalise *après qu'il est parti*. Keep the
contested forms for recognition: you'll hear them every day, and you shouldn't "correct" a native
speaker who uses them in conversation.

| contested form | safe form for writing |
|---|---|
| *après qu'il soit parti* | *après qu'il est parti* (or *après son départ*) |
| *malgré qu'il pleuve* | *bien qu'il pleuve* (or *malgré la pluie*) |
| *je me rappelle de cette soirée* | *je me rappelle cette soirée / je me souviens de cette soirée* |
| *pallier au problème* | *pallier le problème* (or *remédier au problème*) |
| *de façon à ce qu'on comprenne* | *de façon qu'on comprenne* |

A noun is often the most elegant way out: *après son départ, malgré la pluie*.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: edit a paragraph for an exam

*A learner's draft:*

> Malgré que la réunion ait commencé tard, nous avons pu pallier au retard. Après que tout le
> monde soit arrivé, j'ai expliqué le projet de façon à ce que chacun comprenne. Je me rappelle
> encore de la réaction du directeur.

1. *Malgré que* → *Bien que la réunion ait commencé tard* (concession, subjunctive kept).
2. *pallier au retard* → *pallier le retard* (direct object).
3. *Après que tout le monde soit arrivé* → *Après que tout le monde est arrivé* (indicative), or
   more simply *Une fois tout le monde arrivé*.
4. *de façon à ce que chacun comprenne* → *de façon que chacun comprenne* (still subjunctive:
   purpose).
5. *Je me rappelle encore de la réaction* → *Je me rappelle encore la réaction* or *Je me
   souviens encore de la réaction*.

None of the original sentences would puzzle a French reader; every change moves the text toward
the norm the exam expects.

### Example 2: name the problem

- *Ils croivent que c'est facile.* A form that doesn't exist (*croient*): *barbarisme*.
- *C'est l'homme que je t'ai parlé.* Words joined wrongly (*dont je t'ai parlé*): *solécisme*.
- *Ce petit retard, c'est une catastrophe !* A word used beyond its meaning: *abus de langage*.
- *Après qu'il soit parti.* Common usage, criticised by the norm: a contested construction,
  not a barbarism. Call it *critiqué* or *non conforme à la norme*.

## Common mistakes

- **Treating every contested form as "wrong".** *Après qu'il soit parti* is common French;
  it is just not the norm. Say "criticised" or "not in careful writing".
- **Over-correcting.** Some learners start writing ~~avant qu'il est parti~~ by analogy with
  *après que*. *Avant que* takes the subjunctive.
- **Dropping de everywhere after *se rappeler*.** *Je me rappelle de vous* and *Rappelle-toi de
  fermer la porte* are accepted.
- **Mixing up *barbarisme* and *solécisme*.** A barbarism is a wrong form; a solecism is a wrong
  construction.

## Key points

- The norm (Académie, style guides, school) says what to write; usage (dictionaries, *Le Bon
  Usage*) records what people say. Many works do both.
- Five disputes: *après que* + indicative (norm), *bien que* not *malgré que*, *se rappeler
  quelque chose*, *pallier quelque chose*, *de façon que*.
- In exams and formal writing, follow the norm or use a noun (*après son départ*).
- Barbarism = wrong form; solecism = wrong construction; abuse of language = loose meaning.
