the lesson.

lessons.title: Les institutions de la Ve République
topics: The institutions of the Fifth Republic
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

French news is full of institutions: *l'Élysée, Matignon, l'Assemblée, le Sénat, le Conseil
constitutionnel*. To follow a debate, read an editorial or write a DELF essay on a public question,
you need to know who does what. This lesson describes the institutions of the Fifth Republic in
the formal style of this module: the passive and the impersonal constructions of lesson 15 and the
**[[nominalisation]]** of lesson 14 (*l'élection du président, la promulgation de la loi*).

It describes how the system works, with dated facts, and takes no side in any political debate. It
names no party and no current politician. The figures are those of the Constitution as it stands in
2026; constitutions change, so check the official texts (Légifrance, the Conseil constitutionnel,
vie-publique.fr) before relying on a detail.

## The Constitution of 1958

The Fifth Republic began with a new constitution, *la Constitution du 4 octobre 1958*. (With a
capital letter, *la Constitution* is the text of a particular country; *une constitution* is any
constitution.) The text was approved by referendum on 28 September 1958, with about 79 % of the
votes cast in metropolitan France, then promulgated on 4 October. It has been revised many times since, by Parliament
meeting in Congress or by referendum.

> La Constitution de 1958 a été rédigée pendant l'été 1958, puis soumise au référendum le
> 28 septembre. Après son adoption par une large majorité, elle a été promulguée le 4 octobre. Il
> a été prévu dès l'origine qu'elle pourrait être révisée.

The Constitution of 1958 was drafted in the summer of 1958, then put to a referendum on
28 September. After its adoption by a large majority, it was promulgated on 4 October. It was
provided from the start that it could be revised.

(Three passives: *a été rédigée, soumise, a été promulguée*; one impersonal passive: *Il a été
prévu*; one nominalisation: *son adoption*.)

## The President of the Republic

- How he or she is elected: At first the president was chosen by a large college of elected
  officials. Since the referendum of 28 October 1962 (about 62 % yes), the president has been
  elected by direct universal suffrage, *au suffrage universel direct*: every voter takes part. The
  first such election was held in December 1965.
- The ballot: *Le scrutin* is two-round: a candidate needs an absolute majority of the votes
  cast; if no one gets it, the two leading candidates face each other in a second round, fourteen
  days later.
- The term: The term of office, *le mandat*, lasted seven years (*le septennat*) until the
  referendum of 24 September 2000 (about 73 % yes), which created the five-year term, *le
  quinquennat*. It was first applied at the 2002 election. Since a revision of 2008, no one may
  serve more than two consecutive terms.
- Some powers: The president appoints the Prime Minister, can dissolve the Assemblée
  nationale, can put certain bills to a referendum, and promulgates the laws: *promulguer une loi*
  is to sign it into force, within fifteen days of the adopted text being sent to the government.

The president lives and works at the Élysée Palace; the Prime Minister, who leads the government,
at the Hôtel de Matignon. The press often uses the buildings for the people: *l'Élysée a annoncé*
= the presidency announced.

## Parliament

*Le Parlement* has two chambers:

| | Assemblée nationale | Sénat |
|---|---|---|
| members | 577 *députés* (*la députée* for a woman) | 348 *sénateurs* (*la sénatrice*) |
| how elected | direct universal suffrage, by constituency, in two rounds | indirect universal suffrage, by colleges of *grands électeurs* in each department, about 95 % of them delegates of municipal councils |
| term | five years, unless the Assemblée is dissolved | six years; half the seats renewed every three years |
| special role | the government is answerable to it and can be brought down by a vote of censure | represents the local authorities (*les collectivités territoriales*) |

*Le député* is the usual translation of "member of parliament" (MP) for the Assemblée nationale; a
senator is not *un député*. *Le scrutin* is the ballot or the vote itself (*le scrutin du
dimanche, un scrutin à deux tours*); *l'élection* is the whole process.

## The Conseil constitutionnel

The Conseil constitutionnel checks that laws respect the Constitution.

- Members: Nine members, appointed for nine years, not renewable. A third of them are renewed
  every three years. The president of the Republic, the president of the Assemblée nationale and
  the president of the Sénat each appoint three. Former presidents of the Republic are members by
  right, for life.
- Referral before promulgation: A law can be referred to it (*le Conseil est saisi*) by the
  president of the Republic, the Prime Minister, the president of either chamber, or sixty
  deputies or sixty senators. It has a month to rule (eight days if the government declares the matter urgent).
- Referral after promulgation: Since 2010 (a reform voted in 2008), a person involved in a
  court case can argue that a law in force violates the rights the Constitution guarantees. This
  is *la question prioritaire de constitutionnalité* (QPC); the Conseil d'État or the Cour de
  cassation decides whether to pass it on.

## How a law is made

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How a law is passed in France (simplified)
  accDescr: A bill is tabled by the government, as a projet de loi, or by members of parliament, as a proposition de loi. It is examined and voted by the Assemblée nationale and the Sénat, going back and forth between them in the navette. If they still disagree, a joint committee of seven deputies and seven senators looks for a compromise; if that fails, the government can ask the Assemblée nationale to have the last word. The law may then be referred to the Conseil constitutionnel. Finally the president promulgates it within fifteen days and it is published in the Journal officiel.
  A["Projet de loi (government) or proposition de loi (MPs)"] --> B["Examined and voted in one chamber, then the other"]
  B --> C["La navette: back and forth until the same text is voted"]
  C -->|"still no agreement"| D["Commission mixte paritaire: 7 deputies, 7 senators"]
  D -->|"no compromise"| E["The government can give the Assemblée the last word"]
  C -->|agreement| F["Possible referral to the Conseil constitutionnel"]
  D -->|compromise voted| F
  E --> F
  F --> G["Promulgation by the president, within 15 days"]
  G --> H["Publication in the Journal officiel"]
```

A government bill is *un projet de loi*; a bill from members of parliament is *une proposition de
loi*. The text travels between the two chambers (*la navette*) until both vote the same version.
If they disagree after two readings in each (one if the government uses the accelerated
procedure), a joint committee may be called, and if it fails, the government can ask the
Assemblée nationale to decide. That's why, in the end, the chamber elected by direct suffrage can prevail.

## The institutions at a glance

![A diagram of the institutions. At the top, the citizens. One arrow, labelled "suffrage universel direct", goes down to the President of the Republic, elected for five years; another goes to the Assemblée nationale, 577 deputies, elected for five years. A third arrow, labelled "suffrage indirect", goes through the grands électeurs to the Sénat, 348 senators, elected for six years. The President appoints the Prime Minister and the government. The Assemblée nationale and the Sénat together form the Parliament, which votes the laws. An arrow marked "loi votée" goes from the Parliament to a box for the law, which the President promulgates; a dashed arrow from the Conseil constitutionnel, nine members, nine years, shows that it checks the law.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Example 1: from news to formal summary

A radio item says it plainly:

> Hier, les députés ont voté la loi. Les sénateurs l'avaient déjà votée en juin. Soixante
> sénateurs ont saisi le Conseil constitutionnel, qui va dire si le texte respecte la
> Constitution.

Yesterday the deputies voted the law. The senators had already voted it in June. Sixty senators
referred it to the Conseil constitutionnel, which will say whether the text respects the
Constitution.

A written summary in the style of this module:

1. Nominalise the main event: *le vote de la loi par les députés* → *Adoptée hier par l'Assemblée
   nationale, …* (a participle opening, lesson 15's passive).
2. Keep the earlier vote as a passive in the pluperfect: *… la loi avait déjà été votée par le
   Sénat en juin.*
3. Put the referral in the passive, the agent kept because it matters: *Le Conseil
   constitutionnel a été saisi par soixante sénateurs.*
4. End with a noun group for what comes next: *Sa décision sur la conformité du texte à la
   Constitution est attendue dans un délai d'un mois.*

Result: *Adoptée hier par l'Assemblée nationale, la loi avait déjà été votée par le Sénat en juin. Le
Conseil constitutionnel a été saisi par soixante sénateurs ; sa décision sur la conformité du
texte à la Constitution est attendue dans un délai d'un mois.*

(*La conformité à*: compliance with. *Saisir*: to refer a matter to a court or council.)

## Example 2: reading the dates right

> Prévu par la Constitution de 1958, le mandat présidentiel de sept ans a été ramené à cinq
> ans à la suite du référendum de 2000. Le quinquennat a été appliqué pour la première fois en
> 2002.

1. *Prévu par* — a passive participle placed first: "Provided for by".
2. *a été ramené à cinq ans* — "was reduced to five years". *Ramener à* + a smaller figure is the
   usual verb for cutting a figure back.
3. *à la suite du référendum de 2000* — "following the 2000 referendum": a compound preposition
   + noun instead of *après que …*.
4. *a été appliqué pour la première fois en 2002* — "was first applied in 2002".

A learner's mistake would be to read 2000 as the first five-year term: the referendum changed the
rule in 2000, and the first president elected for five years was elected in 2002.

## Belgium, Switzerland and Québec

Other French-speaking countries have their own institutions and words:

- In Belgium, the head of a commune is *le bourgmestre* (roughly the mayor), with *les
  échevins* (aldermen).
- In Switzerland, a popular vote on a question is *une votation* (*la votation populaire du
  14 juin*), and votations are frequent at every level.
- In Québec, the provincial parliament is also called *l'Assemblée nationale*, and its members
  are *les députés*. Don't confuse it with the French one.

## Common mistakes

- *Député* for a senator: senators are *sénateurs*; *le Parlement* is both chambers together.
- "Elected by direct suffrage" for the Sénat: senators are elected *au suffrage universel
  indirect*.
- *Le mandat* is a term of office, not an order: *un mandat de cinq ans*. (It also means a
  mandate, as in English, and a money order.)
- Confusing *le scrutin* (the vote, the ballot) with *le sondage* (an opinion poll).
- *Une loi votée* is not yet in force: it must be promulgated and published.
- Capital letters: *la Constitution de 1958, le Parlement, le Sénat, l'Assemblée nationale, le
  Conseil constitutionnel, le président de la République* (a lower-case *p* in standard
  typography).

## Key points

- *La Constitution du 4 octobre 1958*, approved by referendum on 28 September 1958.
- The president: elected *au suffrage universel direct* since the 1962 referendum (first in 1965);
  *le quinquennat* since the 2000 referendum (first applied in 2002); at most two consecutive terms
  since 2008.
- *Le Parlement* = *l'Assemblée nationale* (577 *députés*, five years, direct suffrage) + *le
  Sénat* (348 *sénateurs*, six years, indirect suffrage, half renewed every three years).
- *Le Conseil constitutionnel*: nine members for nine years; referral by the authorities or 60
  deputies or 60 senators; the QPC since 2010.
- A law: *projet* or *proposition*, *la navette*, possibly a joint committee, possibly the
  Conseil constitutionnel, then the president *promulgue* it within fifteen days.
- Write about institutions in the formal style: passives, impersonal constructions, noun groups.

lessons.title: D'autant que, au point que: cause and consequence at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 5 is about the links between ideas: why something happened, what it led to, what it was
for, what stands against it, and who said so. This first lesson takes **[[cause]]** and
**[[consequence]]** beyond B1.

At B1 you met the core set: *parce que, puisque, comme, étant donné que, vu que, sous prétexte
que, en raison de, faute de, à force de* for the cause; *donc, par conséquent, si bien que, d'où,
si / tellement … que* for the result; and the verbs *entraîner* and *provoquer*. They still do
most of the work. B2 adds the words that let you weigh a cause (*d'autant que*), reject
one (*non que*), state a condition that works as a cause (*dès lors que, du moment que*), measure
how far a result went (*au point que, à tel point que*), and write the result in a formal, compact
style (*de là, aussi* + inversion, *il en résulte que*).

The theme is energy and the energy transition: nuclear power, renewables, shortages and the
electricity bill. The lesson presents the arguments on each side without taking one.

## Cause with a clause

All the B2 **[[logical connectors]]** of cause in this section take the indicative, except *non que*,
which rejects a cause.

### D'autant que: one more reason, and a strong one

*D'autant que* + indicative adds a reason that makes the main statement even more true. It comes
after the main clause, usually after a comma:

- *Il faut isoler les vieux logements, d'autant que le prix du chauffage augmente.* — Old housing
  needs insulating, especially as the price of heating is going up.
- *La décision a surpris, d'autant que le ministre avait promis l'inverse.* — The decision came as
  a surprise, all the more so as the minister had promised the opposite.

Don't confuse it with *d'autant plus que* (lesson 12), which you'll often see in the same
places. *D'autant plus* … *que* also measures: *Il est d'autant plus inquiet que sa facture a
doublé* (he is all the more worried because his bill has doubled). *D'autant que* alone simply
adds the reason.

### Non que: the cause you reject

*Non que* + subjunctive gives a reason only to set it aside, and the real reason follows,
usually with *mais*:

- *Je n'ai pas installé de panneaux solaires, non que ce soit trop cher, mais mon toit est mal
  orienté.* — I haven't put in solar panels, not that it's too expensive, but my roof faces the
  wrong way.

The subjunctive shows that this isn't the real reason. *Non pas que* means the same. In speech you'll
hear *ce n'est pas que* + subjunctive: *Ce n'est pas que je sois contre, mais je voudrais des
chiffres.*

### Dès lors que, du moment que: once, given that

*Dès lors que* and *du moment que* + indicative present a fact as a cause that settles the
question, often with a hint of condition:

- *Dès lors que la centrale est à l'arrêt, il faut acheter de l'électricité ailleurs.* — Once the
  power station is shut down, electricity has to be bought elsewhere.
- *Du moment que tu es d'accord, je signe le contrat.* — Since you agree, I'll sign the contract.

*Du moment que* is more spoken, and it often means "as long as": *Du moment que la facture
baisse, je me moque de l'origine de l'électricité* (as long as the bill goes down, I don't care
where the electricity comes from). *Dès lors que* is common in legal and administrative texts.
*Dès lors* on its own, without *que*, is an adverb of time or consequence ("from then on,
therefore"), as in lesson 02.

## Cause with a noun or an infinitive

| connector | use | example |
|---|---|---|
| *compte tenu de* | formal: given, considering | *Compte tenu de la hausse des prix, la commune éteint l'éclairage la nuit.* |
| *à la suite de* | after and because of an event | *À la suite de la tempête, des milliers de foyers ont été privés d'électricité.* |
| *de par* | formal: by its very (nature, position) | *De par sa situation, la région est très ventée.* |
| *pour* + past infinitive | the reason for a reward or a punishment | *Il a été condamné pour avoir fraudé.* |

Notes:

- *Compte tenu de* is close to *étant donné* (B1) and belongs to reports and formal letters.
- *À la suite de* (in the wake of, following) gives an event that came first and caused what
  follows. Everyday French often says *après*, or *suite à*, which some careful writers avoid in formal
  texts.
- *De par* sounds formal and slightly old-fashioned. Use it with a noun of nature, role or place:
  *de par sa fonction, de par sa taille*.
- *Pour* + past infinitive is the usual way to give the reason after verbs of judging:
  *condamner, punir, remercier, féliciter, récompenser*. *Elle a été récompensée pour avoir
  réduit la consommation de l'école de 30 %.*

## Consequence

### Au point que, à tel point que: so far that

These say that something went so far that it led to a result. Both take the indicative:

- *Le vent a soufflé au point que les éoliennes ont dû être arrêtées.* — The wind blew so hard
  that the wind turbines had to be stopped.
- *Les prix ont augmenté, à tel point que certaines familles ne chauffent plus qu'une pièce.* —
  Prices have risen, so much so that some families now heat only one room.

*À tel point que* is a little stronger and usually follows a comma. With the same subject, use
*au point de* + infinitive: *Il a réduit son chauffage au point d'avoir froid chez lui.*

In a question or after a negative, *au point que* can take the subjunctive (*Ce n'est pas grave
au point qu'on doive fermer*). You only need to recognise this.

### De (telle) sorte que, si bien que

*De sorte que* and *de telle sorte que* + indicative give a result: *Le réseau a été renforcé, de
sorte que les coupures sont devenues rares.* With the subjunctive they give a purpose instead
(lessons 07 and 18). *Si bien que* (B1) is the everyday written equivalent of the result
meaning.

### De là: hence

*De là* + noun gives the consequence in a few words, like *d'où* (B1) but more formal:

- *Le gaz a manqué pendant l'hiver ; de là la flambée des prix.* — Gas ran short during the
  winter; hence the surge in prices.
- *De là à dire que le nucléaire est sans risque, il y a un pas.* — But to go from there to saying
  that nuclear power is risk-free is quite a step.

The second pattern, *de là à* + infinitive + *il y a un pas* (or *il n'y a qu'un pas*), is a
common way to refuse a hasty conclusion.

### Aussi + inversion: "and so"

At the start of a sentence in careful writing, *aussi* means "and so, therefore", and the subject
usually comes after the verb:

- *Le budget manquait. Aussi le projet a-t-il été reporté.* — The money wasn't there, and so the
  project was put off.
- *Les réacteurs vieillissent. Aussi faut-il penser dès maintenant à leur remplacement.*

With a noun subject, the noun stays first and a pronoun is added after the verb (*le projet
a-t-il*): this is the **[[complex inversion]]** of lesson 20. Inside a sentence, *aussi* still means
"also": *Le solaire est aussi une option.* In speech, people say *donc* or *du coup* instead.

## Verbs of cause and effect

Verbs let you put the cause as the subject, or put the effect first.

| cause → effect | effect ← cause |
|---|---|
| *entraîner, provoquer* (B1) | *découler de* |
| *susciter* | *résulter de* (*il en résulte que*) |
| *engendrer* | *être dû à* (agrees: *la panne est due à …*) |
| *déclencher* | |

- *Susciter* (to arouse, to give rise to) is for reactions, feelings and debates: *Le projet
  d'éoliennes a suscité la colère de certains riverains* (riverains = local residents) *et
  l'enthousiasme d'autres.*
- *Engendrer* (to generate, to give rise to) is formal and close to *entraîner*: *La hausse du prix
  du gaz a engendré une crise.*
- *Déclencher* (to trigger, to set off) is for something sudden that starts at a point: *Une
  vague de froid peut déclencher une hausse brutale de la consommation.* It's also the word for
  setting off an alarm: *déclencher l'alarme*.
- *Découler de* and *résulter de* turn the link around: the effect is the subject. *Ces difficultés
  découlent d'un choix fait il y a quarante ans.* Both are used mostly in the third person, and
  *résulter* is often impersonal: *Il en résulte que la facture augmente* (as a result, the bill
  goes up).

The chain below runs from an energy shortage to its effects, with a connector on each arrow.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A chain of causes and consequences in an energy shortage
  accDescr: A cold snap triggers a rise in demand. Reactors that are shut down give rise to a shortage of electricity, and the rise in demand makes the shortage worse. The shortage leads to imports and higher prices. Higher prices arouse a public debate, hence a sobriety plan, and from the plan results a fall in consumption.
  A["une vague de froid"] -- "déclenche" --> B["une hausse de la demande"]
  C["des réacteurs à l'arrêt"] -- "engendrent" --> D["une pénurie d'électricité"]
  B -- "aggrave" --> D
  D -- "entraîne" --> E["des importations et des prix plus élevés"]
  E -- "suscitent" --> F["un débat public"]
  F -- "de là" --> G["un plan de sobriété"]
  G -- "il en résulte" --> H["une baisse de la consommation"]
```

## Where the electricity comes from

![A landscape: on a hill on the left, two white wind turbines; in the middle, a power station with two cooling towers giving off white steam; on the right, a house whose roof is covered with dark blue solar panels; pylons and cables run across the picture from the power station to the house and to a small town.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*L'éolienne* (the wind turbine) and *le panneau solaire* (the solar panel) produce renewable
electricity; *la centrale* (here *la centrale nucléaire*) is a power station, and *le réseau
électrique* is the grid that carries the current to homes. Coal, oil and gas are *les combustibles
fossiles* (*fossile* agrees: *les énergies fossiles*). *La transition énergétique* is the shift
from fossil fuels to low-carbon sources; its adjective, *énergétique*, is in *la facture
énergétique, la politique énergétique*. *Le nucléaire* on its own means nuclear power.

## By register

| | spoken | neutral | formal written |
|---|---|---|---|
| cause | *vu que, du moment que, ce n'est pas que* | *comme, puisque, d'autant que, dès lors que* | *étant donné que, compte tenu de, à la suite de, de par, non que* |
| consequence | *du coup, alors* | *donc, si bien que, au point que* | *par conséquent, à tel point que, de là, aussi* + inversion, *il en résulte que* |

The boundaries aren't strict: the table shows where each word sounds most at home.

## Reading: the lesson of the winter of 2022

> *Électricité : la leçon de l'hiver 2022*
>
> À l'automne 2022, la France a vécu une situation inédite. À la suite de la découverte de
> problèmes de corrosion sur plusieurs réacteurs, une partie du parc nucléaire était à l'arrêt, au
> point que le pays a dû acheter de l'électricité à ses voisins pendant de longs mois. Sur
> l'année, la production nucléaire est tombée à 279 térawattheures (TWh). Compte tenu de la guerre
> en Ukraine, qui avait déjà fait flamber le prix du gaz, la crainte d'une pénurie a suscité de
> vifs débats : fallait-il prévoir des coupures ? Le gouvernement a lancé un plan de sobriété, et
> la consommation a nettement baissé cet hiver-là. Aucune coupure générale n'a finalement eu lieu.
>
> Deux ans plus tard, le tableau était tout autre. Selon le bilan publié en janvier 2025 par RTE,
> le gestionnaire du réseau électrique, la production nucléaire est remontée à près de 362 TWh en
> 2024, soit environ 67 % de l'électricité produite. Les énergies renouvelables, surtout les
> barrages, les éoliennes et les panneaux solaires, ont atteint un record de 148 TWh, et moins de
> 5 % de l'électricité est venue de centrales à combustible fossile.
>
> Que faut-il en conclure ? Pour les partisans du nucléaire, la leçon est claire : dès lors que les
> réacteurs fonctionnent, ils fournissent une électricité abondante et peu émettrice de CO2 ; de là
> leur appel à en construire de nouveaux. Leurs adversaires estiment au contraire que l'épisode de
> 2022 montre la fragilité d'un système qui dépend surtout d'une seule source, d'autant que le parc
> vieillit. Non qu'ils refusent toute production nucléaire, précisent certains, mais ils souhaitent
> un mix plus équilibré. Les deux camps s'accordent sur un point : les choix de la transition
> énergétique engagent le pays pour des décennies. Aussi le débat est-il loin d'être clos.

*Electricity: the lesson of the winter of 2022. In the autumn of 2022 France went through an
unprecedented situation. Following the discovery of corrosion problems in several reactors, part
of the nuclear fleet was shut down, to the point that the country had to buy electricity from its
neighbours for many months. Over the year, nuclear output fell to 279 terawatt-hours (TWh). Given
the war in Ukraine, which had already sent the price of gas soaring, the fear of a shortage gave
rise to heated debates: should power cuts be planned? The government launched an energy-saving
plan (plan de sobriété), and consumption fell markedly that winter. In the end there was no
general power cut. Two years later the picture was quite different. According to the review
published in January 2025 by RTE, the grid operator, nuclear output rose again to nearly 362 TWh in
2024, or about 67 % of the electricity produced. Renewable energies, mainly dams, wind turbines
and solar panels, reached a record 148 TWh, and less than 5 % of electricity came from
fossil-fuel power stations. What should we conclude? For supporters of nuclear power, the lesson
is clear: once the reactors are running, they supply plentiful electricity with low CO2 emissions;
hence their call to build new ones. Their opponents believe, on the contrary, that the 2022
episode shows how fragile a system is when it depends mainly on one source, especially as the
fleet is ageing. Not that they reject all nuclear power, some of them make clear, but they want a
more balanced mix. Both camps agree on one point: the choices of the energy transition commit the
country for decades. And so the debate is far from closed.*

Notice the links: *à la suite de, au point
que, compte tenu de, susciter, dès lors que, de là, d'autant que, non que* + subjunctive (*Non
qu'ils refusent*), and *aussi* + inversion in the last line.

## Pronunciation

- *d'autant que* "doh-tahn kuh": the *t* of *autant* is silent.
- *l'éolienne* "lay-oh-lyen"; *le nucléaire* "nü-klay-air".
- *engendrer* "ahn-zhahn-dray"; *susciter* "sü-see-tay" (the *sc* is one *s* sound).
- *compte tenu de* "kohnt tuh-nü duh": the *p* of *compte* is silent.

## Common mistakes

- *Non qu'il est cher* → *non qu'il soit cher*: *non que* rejects the cause, so it takes the
  subjunctive.
- *D'autant que* at the start of a text: it adds to a statement already made, so it follows the
  main clause.
- *Aussi* at the start of a formal sentence read as "also": there it means "and so".
- *Les difficultés résultent la décision* → *résultent de la décision*: *découler* and *résulter*
  need *de* + the cause.
- *Il a été condamné pour frauder* → *pour avoir fraudé*: the reason for a sentence or a reward is
  a past infinitive.
- *Au point que* + subjunctive in a plain statement: use the indicative (*au point que le pays a
  dû importer*).
- *Engendrer, susciter* and *déclencher* aren't interchangeable: interest and debates are
  *suscités*, alarms and crises are *déclenchés*, and *engendrer* is the formal "give rise to".

## Key points

- Cause + indicative: *d'autant que* (an extra, strong reason, after the main clause), *dès lors
  que, du moment que* (once, given that; *du moment que* also "as long as").
- A rejected cause: *non que, non pas que, ce n'est pas que* + subjunctive, then *mais*.
- Cause + noun: *compte tenu de, à la suite de, de par*; *pour* + past infinitive after verbs of
  judging.
- Consequence + indicative: *au point que, à tel point que, de (telle) sorte que, si bien que*;
  *au point de* + infinitive; *de là* + noun; *aussi* + inversion at the start of a formal
  sentence.
- Verbs: *susciter, engendrer, déclencher* (cause → effect); *découler de, résulter de, être dû à*
  (effect ← cause).

the lesson.

lessons.title: De peur de rater le train: purpose and opposition at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 explained why things happen and what they lead to. This lesson covers two more links:
**[[purpose]]** (what an action is for) and **[[opposition]]** (two facts set against each other). At B1
you used *pour, afin de, pour que, afin que* for purpose, and *alors que, tandis que, en revanche,
par contre* for opposition. B2 adds purpose with fear in it (*de peur que*), formal purpose (*en vue
de, dans le but de, de façon à*), and a set of opposition words that argue as much as they contrast
(*loin de, pour autant, quitte à*, the *si* of contrast).

Concession (*bien que, quel que soit, quand bien même*) is lesson 08; here the focus is on aims and
contrasts. The theme is transport and mobility: trains, shared cars, e-scooters, low-emission
zones, and the countryside where the bus doesn't come.

## Purpose: the basic rule

The B1 rule still holds and decides almost everything:

- same subject in both parts: a preposition + infinitive (*pour, afin de, de peur de …*);
- different subjects: a conjunction + subjunctive (*pour que, afin que, de peur que …*).

- *Je prends le train pour lire pendant le trajet.* (I take the train; I read.)
- *Je laisse la voiture à mon fils pour qu'il aille au travail.* (I leave the car; he goes.)

Every pair below follows this rule.

## Purpose with fear: de peur que, de crainte que

*De peur que* and *de crainte que* + subjunctive give a purpose by naming what you want to avoid:
"for fear that, in case". *De crainte que* is more formal.

- *Je pars une heure avant, de peur que le train ne soit supprimé.* — I'm leaving an hour early in
  case the train is cancelled.
- *La mairie a fermé la route, de crainte qu'un camion ne reste bloqué sous le pont.*

The *ne* here isn't a negative. It's the **[[ne explétif]]** of lesson 05: optional, and typical of
careful style. *De peur que le train soit supprimé* means the same and is common in speech. A real
negative needs *ne … pas*: *de peur que le train ne soit pas à l'heure* (in case the train isn't on
time).

With the same subject, use *de peur de / de crainte de* + infinitive: *Elle réserve sa place trois
semaines à l'avance, de peur de voyager debout.* The negative goes before the infinitive: *de peur
de ne pas trouver de place*.

## Formal purpose

### En vue de, dans le but de

*En vue de* (with a view to) takes a noun or an infinitive and points to a goal further ahead:

- *La ligne a été modernisée en vue des Jeux olympiques.*
- *La région achète de nouveaux trains en vue d'améliorer la desserte des petites villes.*

*Dans le but de* (with the aim of) + infinitive is very common in reports and speeches: *La ville
a créé des voies réservées dans le but de réduire les bouchons.* It's a little heavy; in an essay,
*afin de* is often neater.

### De façon à, de manière à + infinitive

*De façon à* and *de manière à* (so as to, in such a way as to) + infinitive stress the way the
action is done to reach the goal:

- *Les horaires ont été revus de façon à mieux relier le bus et le train.*
- *Garez-vous de manière à ne pas gêner la sortie.* — Park so as not to block the exit.

With different subjects, use *de façon que, de manière que* or *de sorte que* + subjunctive: *Les
horaires ont été revus de sorte que les usagers n'aient plus à attendre la correspondance* (so that
passengers no longer have to wait). With the indicative, the same conjunctions give a result, not
a purpose (lesson 07): *Les horaires ont été revus, de sorte que les usagers n'ont plus à attendre*
(and as a result they no longer have to wait). The mood
tells the reader which you mean. (*De façon à ce que* + subjunctive is common but criticised by
some grammarians: see the honors lesson 08h1.)

### Histoire de: informal

In conversation, *histoire de* + infinitive gives a light, casual purpose: *On prend la
trottinette, histoire de gagner dix minutes.* Never in a formal letter or an essay.

## Opposition

### Loin de + infinitive: far from

*Loin de* + infinitive sets what happened against what you might expect:

- *Loin de se plaindre, les usagers ont applaudi la nouvelle ligne.* — Far from complaining, the
  passengers applauded the new line.
- *Loin de réduire le trafic, la nouvelle route l'a augmenté.*

*Loin de là* on its own means "far from it": *Le problème n'est pas réglé, loin de là.*

### The si of contrast

*Si* + indicative at the start of a sentence can contrast two facts, both true. It's not a
condition, so any tense is possible:

- *Si le train est plus lent que l'avion, il est aussi plus confortable.* — While the train is
  slower than the plane, it's also more comfortable.
- *Si la ville a créé des pistes cyclables, la campagne, elle, attend toujours son bus.*

You recognise it by the second clause, which answers the first (*aussi, en revanche, elle, …*).
The conditional *si* (B1) doesn't take the futur or the conditionnel in standard French; this *si*
simply states a fact.

### Pour autant, sans pour autant

*Pour autant* (for all that) says that one fact doesn't lead to the result you'd expect. It's
mostly negative:

- *La ligne est rapide ; elle n'est pas plus fréquentée pour autant.* — The line is fast; it isn't
  any busier for all that.

*Sans pour autant* + infinitive is a favourite of argued writing: *On peut limiter la voiture en
ville sans pour autant isoler ceux qui vivent loin des transports.*

### Quitte à: even if it means

*Quitte à* + infinitive accepts a cost for the sake of a choice:

- *Je prends le train, quitte à arriver plus tard.* — I'm taking the train, even if it means
  arriving later.
- *Quitte à payer un péage, autant prendre l'autoroute.* — If I'm going to pay a toll anyway, I
  might as well take the motorway.

The second pattern, *quitte à …, autant …*, is very common in speech.

### Au contraire, à l'opposé, and autant … autant

*Au contraire* (on the contrary, A2) contradicts; *à l'opposé* (at the other end, by contrast)
compares two ends of a scale: *Les grandes villes sont bien desservies ; à l'opposé, certains
villages n'ont aucun bus.* For *autant … autant* (*Autant il aime le train, autant il déteste
l'avion*), see lesson 12.

## The chart

![A chart with two rows, purpose and opposition, and four columns: plus subjunctive, plus infinitive, plus noun, and adverbs. Purpose: pour que, afin que, de peur que, de crainte que, de façon que, de manière que, de sorte que; pour, afin de, de peur de, de crainte de, de façon à, de manière à, en vue de, dans le but de, histoire de (informal); en vue de, pour; no adverbs. Opposition: no subjunctive in this lesson; loin de, sans pour autant, quitte à; à l'opposé de, contrairement à; pour autant, au contraire, à l'opposé. A note says the si of contrast takes the indicative.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Getting around the countryside

![A rural landscape seen from above: a motorway at the top with a toll barrier across it; a railway running across the middle with a freight train of containers; a small station where a minibus shuttle waits; a village square with an electric car plugged into a charging point; and a person riding a kick scooter on a cycle path beside the road.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La mobilité* is the general word for getting around. In towns, *le trafic* (traffic volume, also
*le trafic aérien, le trafic de drogue*) is dense; in the countryside, the problem is *la
desserte*, how well a place is served. A train line *dessert* (serves) a town; a road *relie*
(links) two villages. *La navette* (the shuttle) runs to and from the station; *le fret* is goods
transport; *la borne de recharge* is where you charge an electric car; *le péage* is the motorway
toll. *L'usager* (the service user) cares above all about *la ponctualité*. *L'autopartage* (a car
club, shared cars you book by the hour) is not *le covoiturage* (A2, sharing a ride in someone's
car). *Le désenclavement* is the opening up of an isolated area.

## Reading: a shuttle for the valley

> *Val-Sauvage : la navette qui change la vie*
>
> Pendant des années, les habitants du Val-Sauvage, une vallée de six villages à quarante
> kilomètres de la ville, ont eu le sentiment d'être oubliés. Le dernier car avait été supprimé en
> 2015, et sans voiture, impossible de se rendre à la gare, au lycée ou à l'hôpital. Dans le but de
> rompre cet isolement, la communauté de communes a lancé il y a un an une navette électrique qui
> dessert les six villages et la gare, de façon à correspondre avec chaque train vers la ville.
>
> Le bilan dépasse les espérances. Loin de rouler à vide, comme le craignaient certains élus, la
> navette transporte en moyenne cent quarante usagers par jour. « Avant, je partais à six heures,
> de peur de rater mon train, raconte Claire, aide-soignante. Aujourd'hui, la navette m'attend à la
> sortie de la gare. » Sa ponctualité est saluée par tous.
>
> Le projet n'a pas fait l'unanimité pour autant. Son coût, financé en partie par la région,
> inquiète certains contribuables. « Si la navette rend service, elle coûte cher pour une si petite
> population », estime un conseiller municipal. Ses défenseurs assument ce choix, quitte à attendre
> plusieurs années avant d'en voir les fruits : selon eux, le désenclavement de la vallée attirera
> de jeunes familles.
>
> En vue de l'hiver, une borne de recharge supplémentaire sera installée près de la gare, de crainte
> que la batterie ne tienne pas par grand froid. Un service d'autopartage est aussi à l'étude, de
> sorte que ceux qui n'ont pas de voiture puissent faire leurs courses le samedi.

*Val-Sauvage: the shuttle that changes lives. For years the people of Val-Sauvage, a valley of six
villages forty kilometres from the city, felt forgotten. The last coach had been cut in 2015, and
without a car it was impossible to get to the station, the secondary school or the hospital. With
the aim of breaking this isolation, the group of local councils (la communauté de communes)
launched an electric shuttle a year ago that serves the six villages and the station, so as to
connect with every train to the city. The results are better than hoped. Far from running empty,
as some councillors feared, the shuttle carries an average of 140 passengers a day. "Before, I left
at six, for fear of missing my train," says Claire, a care assistant. "Now the shuttle is waiting
for me outside the station." Everyone praises its punctuality. Even so, the project hasn't won
everyone over. Its cost, partly paid for by the region, worries some taxpayers. "While the
shuttle is useful, it's expensive for such a small population," says a local councillor. Its
defenders stand by the choice, even if it means waiting several years to see the benefits: in
their view, opening up the valley will attract young families. With the winter in view, an extra charging point will be put in
near the station, for fear that the battery may not last in very cold weather. A car club is also
being studied, so that people without a car can do their shopping on Saturdays.*

Val-Sauvage is invented. Find the purpose words (*dans le but de, de façon à, de peur de, en vue
de, de crainte que … ne, de sorte que* + subjunctive) and the opposition words (*loin de, pour
autant, si, quitte à*).

## Two people disagreeing

Here is the kind of exchange you'll hear about the *zones à faibles
émissions* (ZFE, low-emission zones). Laws of 2019 (on mobility) and 2021 (on climate)
required the largest urban areas to create them, with rules that vary from city to city: where
restrictions apply, the oldest, most polluting vehicles may not enter, and a sticker
(*la vignette Crit'Air*) shows each car's category. Their future has been fiercely debated: Parliament
voted to abolish them within a wider bill, but in May 2026 the Conseil constitutionnel struck that
article out on procedural grounds, so they remain in the law.

> — La ZFE, c'est bien pour l'air, mais moi, je vis à trente kilomètres. Je ne vais pas changer de
> voiture du jour au lendemain.
>
> — Personne ne te demande ça. Tu laisses ta voiture au parking relais et tu prends le tram,
> justement de façon à ne pas entrer en ville en voiture.
>
> — Le tram ? Loin de me faire gagner du temps, il m'en fait perdre.
>
> — Quitte à perdre dix minutes, je préfère respirer un air moins pollué.

The first speaker fears the cost of the ZFE for people who live far out; the second points to the
park-and-ride (*le parking relais*) and accepts a slower trip for cleaner air. *Du jour au
lendemain* = overnight.

## Pronunciation

- *la desserte* "day-sairt": one *s* sound after *de-*, as in *desservir* "day-sair-veer".
- *le fret* "fret" or "fray": both are heard; the *t* is often pronounced.
- *quitte à* "keet-ah", linked.
- *le péage* "pay-ahzh".

## Common mistakes

- *Je pars tôt de peur que je rate le train* → *de peur de rater le train*: same subject, so the
  infinitive.
- Reading the *ne* in *de peur qu'il ne pleuve* as "not": it's the optional *ne explétif*. "In case
  it doesn't rain" is *de peur qu'il ne pleuve pas*.
- *En vue de* + a person: it takes a goal, not a person. *Pour* is the word for "for someone".
- *Pour autant* as "so much": in this lesson it means "for all that", mostly with a negative.
- *Loin de* + noun when you mean an action: *loin de se plaindre*, not *loin de plainte*.
- *Histoire de* in an essay: too casual; write *afin de* or *dans le but de*.
- Mixing up *desservir* (to serve a place) and *servir* (to serve food, to be useful): *Ce train
  dessert Lyon.*

## Key points

- Same subject → preposition + infinitive; different subjects → conjunction + subjunctive.
- Fear: *de peur que, de crainte que* + subjunctive (optional *ne*); *de peur de, de crainte de* +
  infinitive.
- Formal purpose: *en vue de* + noun or infinitive, *dans le but de* + infinitive, *de façon à, de
  manière à* + infinitive; *de façon que, de manière que, de sorte que* + subjunctive (with the
  indicative: a result). Informal: *histoire de* + infinitive.
- Opposition: *loin de* + infinitive, the *si* of contrast + indicative, *pour autant* and *sans
  pour autant* + infinitive, *quitte à* + infinitive, *au contraire, à l'opposé*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Selon le ministre … : reporting and commenting on what others say
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 you learned to report what someone said: the tense shifts after a past verb (*Il a dit
qu'il viendrait*), reported questions (*Elle m'a demandé si …*) and orders (*Il m'a dit de
partir*). That's enough to pass on a message. At B2 you also have to show *how* it was said, and
*what you think* of it: a press review, a summary of a debate or a DELF essay that uses a
document all need it.

This lesson covers:

- orders and wishes reported with the subjunctive;
- **[[reporting verbs]]** that show the speaker's attitude (*insinuer, rétorquer, déplorer, se
  féliciter …*);
- ways to keep your distance from a source (*à en croire, aux dires de*, the conditionnel);
- summing up a long statement in one sentence;
- **[[free indirect speech]]**, a narrative technique to recognise;
- quoting and paraphrasing in an essay.

The theme is public debate: a press review, an interview and a local controversy. The people and
places are invented.

## Orders and wishes with the subjunctive

B1 reported orders with *de* + infinitive: *Il nous a dit de partir.* When the order or wish has
its own subject, or in formal writing, French uses a verb of will + *que* + subjunctive:

- « Partez ! » → *Le directeur a exigé que nous partions.*
- « Que tout le monde se taise ! » → *Elle a demandé que tout le monde se taise.*
- « J'aimerais que la séance soit publique. » → *Il a souhaité que la séance soit publique.*

In modern French the subjunctive stays in the present even after a past verb (*a exigé que
nous partions*). Classical writers shifted it to the imperfect subjunctive (*qu'il partît*):
you'll recognise that in old novels (honors lesson 04h1), but don't write it. For an action that
must be finished first, use the past subjunctive (lesson 05): *Il a exigé que le rapport ait été
remis avant lundi.*

## Reporting verbs that show attitude

*Dire, expliquer, affirmer* (B1) report neutrally. The verbs below add a judgement: they tell the
reader whether the speaker agreed, attacked, gave way or dodged. Choosing one is already a comment.

| verb | construction | what it shows |
|---|---|---|
| *insinuer* | *que* + indicative | suggests something negative without saying it openly |
| *sous-entendre* | *que* + indicative | implies, leaves it unsaid |
| *faire allusion à* | + noun | refers to something indirectly |
| *objecter* | *que* + indicative (*objecter à quelqu'un que*) | raises an objection |
| *rétorquer* | *que* + indicative, or after a quotation | answers back sharply (= *répliquer*, B1) |
| *concéder* | *que* + indicative | admits a point to the other side |
| *déplorer* | + noun, or *que* + subjunctive | regrets publicly, criticises |
| *s'indigner* | *de* + noun or infinitive, or *que* + subjunctive | protests angrily |
| *se féliciter* | *de* + noun or infinitive, or *que* + subjunctive | welcomes, is pleased about |
| *s'interroger* | *sur* + noun, or *si* / question word | wonders, raises a doubt (formal) |
| *garantir* | *que* + indicative; *garantir quelque chose à quelqu'un* | guarantees |
| *mettre en garde* | *contre* + noun; *mettre quelqu'un en garde contre* | warns |
| *éluder* | + noun (*éluder une question*) | dodges, avoids answering |

Watch the mood. Verbs of saying take the indicative (*Il a concédé que le budget était trop
élevé*). Verbs of feeling take the subjunctive (*Elle déplore que la bibliothèque soit fermée le
dimanche; Il s'indigne qu'on ne l'ait pas consulté; Le maire se félicite que le projet ait
abouti*).

Examples from a debate:

- *Le maire a garanti que les horaires seraient étendus avant l'été.*
- *Son adversaire a objecté que le budget ne le permettait pas.*
- *« C'est faux », a rétorqué le maire.*
- *L'opposition a insinué que la décision avait été prise avant la réunion.*
- *Interrogé sur le coût, l'adjoint a éludé la question.*
- *Une association a mis en garde contre une hausse des impôts locaux.*
- *Plusieurs habitants s'interrogent sur l'utilité du projet.*

*Se féliciter* and *s'indigner* are pronominal verbs whose *se* is a direct object, so their
participles agree with the subject: *elle
s'est félicitée, ils se sont indignés*. So does *s'interroger*: *elles se sont interrogées*.

The scale below sorts the verbs by the attitude they show.

![A horizontal scale with five zones from left to right: approving (se féliciter de, garantir), neutral (dire, expliquer, affirmer, préciser), conceding (concéder, reconnaître), critical (objecter, rétorquer, déplorer, s'indigner, insinuer) and evasive (éluder). Above the scale, a smiling face on the left and a frowning face on the right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Keeping your distance from a source

A good report says where each claim comes from, and how far you trust it.

| expression | effect |
|---|---|
| *selon, d'après* + source | neutral attribution |
| *aux dires de* + person | "according to what X says": slight distance |
| *à en croire* + source | "if X is to be believed": clear doubt |
| *soi-disant* (B1) | "so-called": the speaker doesn't believe it |
| the **[[reportive conditional]]** (lesson 10) | the information isn't confirmed |

- *Selon la mairie, le projet coûtera 80 000 euros.* (The paper repeats the figure.)
- *Aux dires de ses voisins, il ne sort jamais.* (That's what they say.)
- *À en croire le maire, tout le monde serait d'accord.* (The writer doubts it.)
- *Le projet coûterait plus de 100 000 euros, selon l'opposition.* (Not confirmed.)

Notice how the conditionnel and *à en croire* often go together.

## From speech bubbles to a report

![Five people at a public meeting, each with a speech bubble. A man in a suit says « Je suis ravi de ce résultat ! » and is labelled se féliciter. A woman with glasses says « Attention, cela risque de coûter très cher. » and is labelled mettre en garde. An older man with grey hair says « Sur ce point, vous avez raison. » and is labelled concéder. A man in a green jacket answers « Le coût ? Parlons plutôt de l'avenir ! », labelled éluder. A young man with raised fists says « C'est scandaleux ! » and is labelled s'indigner.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In a report, each bubble becomes one sentence with the verb that fits: *Le maire s'est félicité
du résultat. Une élue a mis en garde contre le coût. Un habitant a concédé que son adversaire avait
raison sur ce point. Interrogé sur le prix, l'adjoint a éludé la question. Un jeune homme s'est
indigné.*

## Summing up a long statement

A press review can't quote every sentence. Sum up the act of speaking with one verb, or turn the
statement into a noun (**[[nominalisation]]**, lesson 14):

- *Le maire a parlé pendant dix minutes pour dire qu'il regrettait la décision et qu'il ne
  l'approuvait pas.* → *Le maire a déploré la décision.*
- *L'association a dit et répété qu'il fallait faire attention aux coûts.* → *L'association a
  multiplié les mises en garde sur les coûts.*
- *Il a annoncé que la bibliothèque ouvrirait le dimanche.* → *Il a annoncé l'ouverture de la
  bibliothèque le dimanche.*

## Free indirect speech

Novels, and some press articles, use a third way of reporting thoughts and words. Compare:

- Direct: *Elle pensa : « Je partirai demain. Je ne peux plus rester ici ! »*
- Indirect: *Elle pensa qu'elle partirait le lendemain, qu'elle ne pouvait plus rester là.*
- Free indirect: *Elle partirait demain. Elle ne pouvait plus rester ici !*

In **[[free indirect speech]]** (*le style indirect libre*) the character's words or thoughts are
told in the narrative's tenses and in the third person, like indirect speech, but with no
reporting verb, no *que* and no quotation marks. The character's voice stays: exclamations,
questions, spoken words, and time and place words from their point of view (*demain, ici*). The
reader slides into the character's head without being told.

How to spot it:

1. A sentence in the imparfait, the conditionnel or the plus-que-parfait that can't be the
   narrator's own statement (*Elle partirait demain*: a decision, not a fact).
2. Exclamations or questions in the third person: *Comment avait-il pu oublier ?*
3. Words the character would use, not the narrator.

Journalists use it too, to give a politician's view without quoting: *Le ministre ne
démissionnerait pas. Il avait été élu pour cinq ans, et il irait jusqu'au bout.* Here the writer
reports the minister's position without endorsing it.

You only need to recognise free indirect speech and turn it back into direct speech. Honors
lesson 20h1 shows how Flaubert built a novel on it.

## Quoting and paraphrasing

In an essay or a summary, you can use a source in two ways:

- Quote a few striking words, exactly, in « guillemets », with the source: *Comme le souligne
  l'éditorialiste, il s'agit d'un « choix de société ».* Keep quotations short.
- **[[Paraphrase]]**: give the idea in your own words, with a reporting verb: *L'éditorialiste estime
  que la question dépasse le simple budget.*

In the DELF B2, the documents give you ideas, not sentences: reuse their content in your own words,
and quote only a short phrase now and then. Copying whole sentences from a document doesn't show
your French.

## Reading: a press review

> *La revue de presse du jour : la bibliothèque de Belcourt ouvrira-t-elle le dimanche ?*
>
> La polémique enfle à Belcourt. Lundi, le maire, Antoine Ferrand, a annoncé l'ouverture de la
> médiathèque municipale le dimanche après-midi, à partir de septembre. Dans *L'Écho de Belcourt*,
> il se félicite d'une mesure « attendue par les familles » et garantit qu'aucun employé ne sera
> obligé de travailler le dimanche.
>
> Ce n'est pas l'avis du syndicat du personnel. Sa porte-parole, Nadia Bensaïd, s'indigne qu'on
> n'ait pas consulté les agents et déplore « une décision prise dans la précipitation ». Elle
> insinue même que le maire cherche surtout à soigner son image avant les élections. « Ces
> allusions sont indignes », a rétorqué ce dernier.
>
> Plus nuancé, le quotidien régional *Le Courrier* s'interroge sur le coût de la mesure. À en
> croire la mairie, il ne dépasserait pas 40 000 euros par an ; aux dires de l'opposition, il
> serait deux fois plus élevé. Interrogé sur ce point, l'adjoint à la culture a éludé la question,
> se contentant de répéter que « la culture n'a pas de prix ». *Le Courrier* y voit un bel exemple
> de langue de bois.
>
> Enfin, l'éditorialiste de *L'Écho* concède que le projet répond à une vraie demande, mais met en
> garde contre une ouverture « sans moyens supplémentaires ». La controverse ne fait que commencer :
> le conseil municipal votera le 15 juin.

*Today's press review: will the Belcourt library open on Sundays? The row is growing in Belcourt.
On Monday the mayor, Antoine Ferrand, announced that the municipal library would open on Sunday
afternoons from September. In L'Écho de Belcourt he welcomes a measure "that families have been
waiting for" and guarantees that no staff member will be forced to work on Sundays. The staff union
doesn't see it that way. Its spokeswoman, Nadia Bensaïd, protests that the staff weren't
consulted and deplores "a decision taken in haste". She even insinuates that the mayor is mainly
trying to polish his image before the elections. "These hints are shameful," he retorted.
Taking a more balanced view, the regional daily Le Courrier wonders about the cost of the measure.
If the town hall is to be believed, it would not exceed 40,000 euros a year; according to the
opposition, it would be twice as high. Asked about this, the deputy mayor for culture dodged the
question, merely repeating that "culture is priceless". Le Courrier sees this as a fine example of
waffle (la langue de bois). Finally, L'Écho's editorial writer concedes that the project meets a
real demand, but warns against opening "without extra resources". The controversy is only
beginning: the town council will vote on 15 June.*

*Une allusion* is an indirect reference, a hint (*faire allusion à* = to allude to); the mayor
uses the word for hints he finds insulting. *L'indignation* is the noun of *s'indigner*: *La
décision a suscité l'indignation du personnel.* *La polémique* is a public row, often in the media; *la controverse* is
a longer debate of arguments, often among experts, and a *mesure controversée* is one people argue about. A
*sous-entendu* is something implied (*des sous-entendus* = innuendo).

## Pronunciation

- *insinuer* "an-see-nü-ay"; *éluder* "ay-lü-day".
- *la polémique* "poh-lay-meek"; *la controverse* "kohn-troh-vairss".
- *aux dires de* "oh deer duh"; *à en croire* "ah ahn krwahr", linked.
- *rétorquer* "ray-tor-kay".

## Common mistakes

- *Il a exigé que nous partons* → *que nous partions*: a verb of will takes the subjunctive.
- *Elle déplore que la bibliothèque est fermée* → in careful French, *soit fermée*: *déplorer
  que* expresses a feeling, so the subjunctive.
- *Il a concédé que le budget soit trop élevé*: *concéder que* reports a statement, so the
  indicative (*était*).
- *Mettre en garde* + noun takes *contre*: *mettre en garde contre les risques*.
- Using *insinuer* for a neutral suggestion: it implies something unpleasant. For a neutral
  suggestion, use *suggérer*.
- Reading free indirect speech as the narrator's opinion: check whose voice it is.

## Key points

- Orders and wishes: verb of will + *que* + present subjunctive, even after a past verb (*Il a
  exigé que nous partions*).
- Attitude verbs: approving (*se féliciter de, garantir*), conceding (*concéder*), critical
  (*objecter, rétorquer, déplorer, s'indigner, insinuer*), evasive (*éluder*); warning: *mettre
  en garde contre*. Saying → indicative; feeling (*déplorer, s'indigner, se féliciter que*) →
  subjunctive.
- Distance: *selon, d'après* (neutral), *aux dires de* (that's what they say), *à en croire*
  (doubt), the reportive conditional.
- Free indirect speech: narrative tenses, third person, no *que*, the character's voice. Recognise
  it; don't write it.
- Quote a few words exactly; otherwise paraphrase with a reporting verb.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: C'est en 1947 que tout a commencé: emphasis and word order
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English puts emphasis in the voice: "*Vilar* founded the festival", "he founded it in *1947*".
French stress falls on the end of a word group and can't move freely, so French moves the words
instead. This lesson is about that **[[mise en relief]]** (emphasis), and about word order in general:

- *c'est … qui / que* for any part of the sentence;
- *ce qui / ce que … c'est* (B1) reviewed;
- **[[dislocation]]**: a word pushed to the front or the end and picked up by a pronoun (*Ce spectacle,
  je l'ai adoré*);
- presentatives: *il y a … qui, voilà … que*;
- inversion in writing: after *peut-être, sans doute, ainsi, du moins …*, after a quotation, and
  after a relative pronoun.

The first three are everywhere in speech; the last belongs to careful writing. The theme is the
theatre and the performing arts: festivals, a premiere, life backstage.

## C'est … qui, c'est … que

Put the part you want to stress between *c'est* and *qui* or *que*. Use *qui* when the stressed
part is the subject of the verb that follows, and *que* for everything else.

| stressed part | example |
|---|---|
| subject | *C'est Jean Vilar qui a fondé le festival.* |
| direct object | *C'est une tragédie que la troupe a choisie.* |
| time | *C'est en 1947 que tout a commencé.* |
| place | *C'est à Avignon que le festival a lieu.* |
| cause | *C'est grâce à lui que la pièce a été reprise. C'est parce qu'il pleuvait que la représentation a été annulée.* |
| manner | *C'est en répétant chaque jour qu'on apprend son texte.* |
| indirect object | *C'est à toi que je parle. C'est de cette pièce que je te parlais.* |

Notes:

- Keep the preposition with the stressed part and use plain *que*: *C'est de ce rôle que je
  rêve.* Don't add *dont* as well: *C'est de ce rôle dont je rêve* repeats the *de* and is
  criticised in careful French (though you'll hear it).
- The participle agrees as usual: in *C'est une tragédie que la troupe a choisie*, *que* stands
  for *une tragédie*, a direct object placed before *avoir* (lesson 03).
- *C'est* usually stays in the present even for the past: *C'est en 1947 que tout a commencé.*
  *C'était* is also correct, and common in narration.

### Agreement after c'est … qui

The verb after *qui* agrees with the stressed word, not with *c'est*:

- *C'est moi qui ai les billets.* — *C'est nous qui avons gagné.* — *C'est vous qui êtes en
  retard.*
- *C'est toi qui joues ce soir ?*

With a plural noun or *eux, elles*, careful writing uses *ce sont*: *Ce sont les comédiens qui ont
choisi le décor.* Speech often keeps *c'est* (*c'est eux qui ont choisi*), which is accepted in
informal French. With *nous* and *vous*, it's always *c'est*.

### In the negative and in questions

*Ce n'est pas le metteur en scène qui a décidé, c'est le producteur.* Here the contrast is the
point: one person is set aside, another put forward. In a question: *Est-ce que c'est toi qui as
réservé ? C'est qui qui a les clés ?* (the last one is very informal).

## Ce qui …, c'est; ce que …, c'est

B1 lesson 13 taught this frame for stressing a whole idea:

- *Ce qui m'a plu, c'est la mise en scène.* — What I liked was the staging.
- *Ce que je retiens, c'est la dernière tirade.*
- *Ce dont le théâtre a besoin, c'est d'un public jeune.* (*de* is repeated after *c'est* because
  *avoir besoin de*.)

It's very common in essays and at the oral: it announces what matters before saying it.

## Dislocation

In **[[dislocation]]**, a noun or a stressed pronoun is moved out of the sentence, to the front or to
the end, and a pronoun keeps its place in the sentence:

- left: *Ce spectacle, je l'ai adoré.* — *Les places, il en reste ?* — *Moi, je préfère le
  vaudeville.*
- right: *Je l'ai adoré, ce spectacle.* — *Il est génial, ce comédien.* — *Elle est où, la
  billetterie ?*

The pronoun matches the role of the moved word: *le, la, les* for a direct object, *en* for a
quantity, *y* for a place, *lui, leur* for *à* + person (*Le metteur en scène, je lui ai
écrit*). For a whole idea, *ça* or *c'*: *Le théâtre, c'est ma passion. Partir en tournée, ça me
fait peur.*

Dislocation is the normal way to stress something in conversation. In writing, it's natural in
dialogue and in a lively style, but a formal essay prefers *c'est … que* or a plain sentence.

## Presentatives

*Il y a … qui* and *voilà … que* introduce the new information first:

- *Il y a des spectateurs qui partent à l'entracte.* (rather than *Des spectateurs partent …*)
- *Voilà dix ans que la troupe part en tournée chaque été.* (= *La troupe part en tournée depuis
  dix ans.*)

*Il y a … qui* is so common in speech that a plain subject like *Des spectateurs partent …* can
sound bookish.

## The chart

![A chart titled C'est … qui / que. Five rows, each with the stressed part in a coloured box between C'est and qui or que: subject (C'est Vilar qui a fondé le festival), object (C'est Richard II que la troupe a joué), time (C'est en 1947 que tout a commencé), place (C'est à Avignon que le festival a lieu), cause (C'est grâce à lui que la pièce a été reprise). A note at the bottom: qui if the stressed part is the subject, que for everything else.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Inversion in writing

### After an adverb at the start of the sentence

In careful writing, some adverbs and phrases at the start of a sentence are followed by an
inverted subject. With a pronoun subject, the pronoun goes after the verb (simple inversion:
*Peut-être viendra-t-il*). With a noun subject, the noun stays in front and a pronoun is added
after the verb: this is **[[complex inversion]]**.

- *Peut-être la pièce sera-t-elle reprise l'an prochain.*
- *Sans doute le public a-t-il été déçu.* (*sans doute* = probably)
- *À peine le rideau était-il tombé que les applaudissements ont éclaté.* (lesson 02)
- *Aussi la troupe a-t-elle annulé sa tournée.* (and so, lesson 17)
- *Du moins le décor était-il réussi.* (at least)
- *Tout au plus peut-on regretter la longueur du deuxième acte.* (at most)
- *Encore faut-il trouver une salle.* (but you still have to …)

In speech, you avoid the inversion: put the adverb after the verb (*La pièce sera peut-être
reprise*) or add *que* after *peut-être* and *sans doute* (*Peut-être que la pièce sera reprise*;
*sans doute que* is spoken). Don't combine *que* and inversion: *Peut-être que la pièce
sera-t-elle reprise* is a mistake in any register, though you may see it in hasty writing. After *ainsi, du moins, tout au plus*, the inversion is usual in writing
but not compulsory.

### After a quotation

After a quotation, standard writing always inverts the reporting verb and its subject: *« Bravo ! »
s'écria-t-elle* (*s'écrier* = to cry out). *« Rideau ! » a lancé le metteur en scène. « On
recommence », dit-il.* Here the noun subject simply follows the verb: no extra pronoun.

### After a relative pronoun

After *que, où* and other relatives, a noun subject can follow the verb, especially when the
subject is long or nothing comes after the verb:

- *la pièce que joue la troupe* = *la pièce que la troupe joue*
- *la ville où se tient le festival* = *la ville où le festival se tient*

Both orders are correct; the inverted one is more elegant in writing. With a pronoun subject,
there's no inversion: *la pièce qu'elle joue*.

## Backstage and on stage

![A cross-section of a theatre seen from the side of the audience: a red curtain drawn back on both sides of the stage; on the stage, painted scenery showing a garden with a bench and a tree; on the left and right of the stage, the wings, where an actor waits in the shadow; in front, two rows of spectators.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Le rideau* (the curtain) opens on *le décor* (the scenery). Actors wait in *les coulisses* (the
wings, also "behind the scenes" in general). *Le comédien* is an actor, especially on stage (*l'acteur*, A1, is
the general word); *le metteur en scène* (*la metteuse en scène*) directs the play, and *la mise en scène*
is the staging. *Le dramaturge* writes it. A play is divided into *actes*; *la réplique* is one
line of dialogue, *la tirade* a long speech. Before *la première* (the first night) come the
*répétitions* (rehearsals) and *la générale* (the dress rehearsal); after the show come *les
applaudissements*. Between the acts there may be *un entracte* (an interval). *La représentation*
is a performance of a play; *la troupe* is the company; *la tournée* is its tour. A show that's
*à l'affiche* is on now; you buy tickets at *la billetterie*. *La tragédie* ends badly; *le
vaudeville* is a light comedy of mix-ups and lovers in cupboards.

## Reading: the stage, from Molière's company to Avignon

> *Le spectacle vivant en France : quelques repères*
>
> C'est en 1680 que Louis XIV a créé la Comédie-Française, en réunissant deux troupes parisiennes,
> dont celle qu'avait dirigée Molière, mort sept ans plus tôt. Voilà donc plus de trois siècles
> qu'elle existe, et on l'appelle toujours « la maison de Molière ». Ses comédiens jouent la
> tragédie comme la comédie, et les grandes pièces du répertoire y sont toujours à l'affiche.
>
> Le Festival d'Avignon, lui, est beaucoup plus jeune. C'est au comédien et metteur en scène Jean
> Vilar qu'on le doit. En septembre 1947, il présente trois créations, dont *Richard II* de
> Shakespeare, dans la cour d'honneur du Palais des papes. Ce que Vilar voulait, c'était un théâtre
> populaire, ouvert à tous, loin des salles parisiennes. Il y a des spectateurs qui viennent
> aujourd'hui chaque été depuis des décennies : le festival a lieu en juillet, et des centaines de
> compagnies jouent en parallèle dans le « off ».
>
> Derrière le rideau, il y a ceux qu'on ne voit pas : techniciens, costumiers, régisseurs. Beaucoup
> sont des intermittents du spectacle. Leurs contrats sont courts, d'une répétition à une tournée ;
> aussi un régime spécial d'assurance chômage compense-t-il, sous conditions, les périodes sans
> travail. Ce régime, régulièrement réformé, est souvent au cœur des débats sur l'avenir du
> spectacle vivant. Peut-être le public y pense-t-il rarement quand le rideau tombe ; sans les
> coulisses, pourtant, il n'y aurait pas de première.

*The performing arts in France: some landmarks. It was in 1680 that Louis XIV created the
Comédie-Française by merging two Paris companies, one of them the company Molière had led; Molière
had died seven years earlier. So it has existed for more than three centuries, and it is still
called "the house of Molière". Its actors perform tragedy as well as comedy, and the great plays
of the repertoire are still on the bill there. The Festival d'Avignon is much younger. We owe it to the actor and
director Jean Vilar. In September 1947 he presented three new productions, among them
Shakespeare's Richard II, in the main courtyard of the Palais des papes. What Vilar wanted was a
popular theatre, open to everyone, far from the Paris playhouses. There are spectators who now
come every summer and have done for decades: the festival takes place in July, and hundreds of
companies perform alongside it in the "off" (the fringe). Behind the curtain are the people you
don't see: technicians, costume makers, stage managers. Many are intermittents du spectacle
(freelance performing-arts workers). Their contracts are short, from one rehearsal period to one
tour; and so a special unemployment insurance scheme makes up, under certain conditions, for the
periods without work. This scheme, regularly reformed, is often at the heart of debates about the
future of the performing arts. Perhaps the audience rarely thinks of it when the curtain falls;
yet without the wings, there would be no first night.*

Find the emphasis (*C'est en 1680 que, C'est à … qu'on le doit, Ce que Vilar voulait, c'était, Il
y a des spectateurs qui, Voilà … que*), the dislocation (*Le Festival d'Avignon, lui*), the
relative with inversion (*celle qu'avait dirigée Molière*) and the adverbs with complex inversion
(*aussi un régime … compense-t-il, Peut-être le public y pense-t-il*). *Le spectacle vivant* (live
performance) covers theatre, dance, circus, opera and concerts.

## Pronunciation

- *les coulisses* "koo-leess"; *l'entracte* "lahn-trakt".
- *la générale* "zhay-nay-ral"; *la billetterie* "bee-yet-ree".
- *le metteur en scène* "meh-tur ahn sen".
- In *sera-t-elle, a-t-il*, the *-t-* is always pronounced: "suh-ra-tel", "a-teel".

## Common mistakes

- *C'est moi qui a les billets* → *qui ai*: the verb agrees with *moi*.
- *C'est en 1947 où tout a commencé* → *que*: after *c'est* + time or place, standard French uses
  *que* (*où* is heard, but criticised).
- *C'est de ce rôle dont je rêve*: in careful French, use *que* (*C'est de ce rôle que je rêve*).
- *Peut-être que la pièce sera-t-elle reprise*: choose one, *que* or inversion.
- *Peut-être sera la pièce reprise*: a noun subject needs complex inversion (*Peut-être la pièce
  sera-t-elle reprise*).
- *Aussi* at the start of a formal sentence read as "also": there it means "and so".
- Dislocation in a formal essay (*La culture, il faut la financer*): fine in speech; in an essay,
  write *Il faut financer la culture* or *C'est la culture qu'il faut financer*.

## Key points

- *C'est … qui* (subject) / *c'est … que* (everything else); the verb after *qui* agrees with the
  stressed word (*c'est nous qui avons*); keep the preposition (*c'est à toi que*).
- *Ce qui / ce que / ce dont …, c'est* stresses a whole idea.
- Dislocation: *Ce spectacle, je l'ai adoré / Je l'ai adoré, ce spectacle*, with a pronoun that
  matches the role; mostly spoken.
- Presentatives: *il y a … qui, voilà … que*.
- Written inversion: after *peut-être, sans doute, à peine, aussi* (and so), *ainsi, du moins, tout
  au plus, encore*; complex inversion with a noun subject (*la pièce sera-t-elle*); in speech,
  *peut-être que* or the adverb after the verb. After a quotation, invert (standard writing); after a
  relative, you may.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Madame Bovary et le style indirect libre
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 19 introduced **[[free indirect speech]]** (*le style indirect libre*): a character's thoughts
told in the narrative's tenses, with no *que* and no quotation marks. This lesson shows the
novel that made the technique famous in French, Gustave Flaubert's *Madame Bovary* (1857). You'll
read the story retold in original B2 French, see how free indirect speech lets Emma Bovary's
dreams into the narration, and practise recognising it and turning it back into direct speech.

As in lesson 19, free indirect speech is for recognition only: read it, understand it,
convert it, but don't write it in an exam. Nothing here quotes the novel: the passages are
written for this lesson in the manner of a nineteenth-century narrator.

## Flaubert and his novel

Gustave Flaubert was born in Rouen, in Normandy, in 1821, the son of a hospital surgeon, and spent
most of his life at Croisset, near Rouen, where he died in 1880. He wrote slowly and rewrote
endlessly: he searched for the one right word, and read his sentences aloud to test their rhythm.
*Madame Bovary* took him about five years, from 1851 to 1856.

The novel first appeared as a serial in *La Revue de Paris* from 1 October to 15 December 1856,
and the magazine had already cut some passages. In January 1857 Flaubert, the magazine's manager
and its printer were taken to court in Paris for offending public and religious morals. The
prosecutor, Ernest Pinard, argued that the book glorified adultery; the defence lawyer, Jules
Senard, answered that it showed where vice leads. On 7 February 1857 all three were acquitted,
though the judgment criticised the book. The scandal helped sales: the novel came out in two
volumes from the publisher Michel Lévy in April 1857, with the subtitle *Mœurs de province*
(provincial manners). The same year, the same prosecutor attacked Baudelaire's *Les Fleurs du
mal*.

## Realism

**[[Realism]]** (*le réalisme*) is the movement in art and literature that sets out to show ordinary
life as it is, including its dull and ugly sides, instead of heroes and ideals. The word became a
banner in the 1850s, when the painter Gustave Courbet and the critic Champfleury used it for an
art of everyday subjects; Balzac had already painted French society in his novels. *Madame
Bovary* became the model of the realist novel: a country doctor, a small market town, a
pharmacist, a draper, debts.

Three features matter for this lesson:

- an ordinary subject: the *bourgeoisie* (the middle class) of a provincial town, its money
  worries and its *médiocrité*; the adjective is *bourgeois* (*une famille bourgeoise*), neutral
  in sociology, often mocking in literature;
- an impersonal narrator, who rarely comments or judges openly;
- documentation: Flaubert checked medical, legal and farming details.

Flaubert himself disliked being called a realist; he cared above all about style. But the
impersonal narrator is the key to his free indirect speech: since the narrator doesn't judge, the
characters' own words and dreams fill the narration, and the reader must work out whose voice is
speaking.

## The story, retold

> **1. Le mariage.** Charles Bovary, médecin de campagne sans grand talent, soigne un fermier
> normand et tombe amoureux de sa fille, Emma. Veuf, il l'épouse. Emma a été élevée au couvent,
> où elle a lu en cachette des romans pleins de passions et de pays lointains. Elle attend du
> mariage un bonheur romanesque ; elle trouve un mari gentil, mais terne, dans le petit bourg de
> Tostes.
>
> **2. Le bal.** Un marquis invite le couple à un bal dans son château. Pour Emma, c'est une
> révélation : la musique, les robes, les manières de l'aristocratie. De retour chez elle, elle
> ne pense plus qu'à ce monde perdu. La désillusion la rend malade ; Charles, inquiet, décide de
> s'installer dans un autre bourg, Yonville. Emma y met au monde une fille, Berthe.
>
> **3. Deux amants.** À Yonville, Emma rencontre Léon, un jeune clerc de notaire qui partage ses
> rêveries, mais il part pour Paris. Puis Rodolphe, un riche propriétaire, la séduit sans
> difficulté. L'adultère lui donne d'abord l'impression de vivre enfin un roman. Quand elle veut
> s'enfuir avec lui, Rodolphe rompt par une lettre. Plus tard, Emma retrouve Léon à Rouen, et une
> nouvelle liaison commence.
>
> **4. Les dettes.** Pour paraître ce qu'elle rêve d'être, Emma achète à crédit chez Lheureux, un
> marchand qui lui prête de l'argent à des taux énormes. Les dettes s'accumulent, à l'insu de
> Charles. Un jour, les huissiers saisissent les biens du couple. Emma demande de l'aide à Léon,
> puis à Rodolphe : personne ne la sauve.
>
> **5. La fin.** Désespérée, Emma avale de l'arsenic pris chez le pharmacien, Homais, et meurt
> après une longue agonie. Charles découvre ses lettres d'amour et meurt peu après. Leur fille,
> pauvre, finit ouvrière dans une filature de coton. Homais, lui, triomphe : le roman se termine
> sur la décoration du pharmacien.

*1. The marriage. Charles Bovary, a country doctor (strictly an officier de santé, a lower
qualification than a full doctor) of no great talent, treats a Norman farmer and
falls in love with his daughter, Emma. As a widower, he marries her. Emma was brought up in a
convent, where she secretly read novels full of passions and faraway lands. She expects romantic
happiness from marriage; she finds a kind but dull husband in the small market town of Tostes. 2.
The ball. A marquis invites the couple to a ball at his château. For Emma it's a revelation: the
music, the dresses, the manners of the aristocracy. Back home, she can think only of that lost
world. Disillusionment makes her ill; Charles, worried, decides to move to another town, Yonville.
There Emma gives birth to a daughter, Berthe. 3. Two lovers. In Yonville, Emma meets Léon, a young
notary's clerk who shares her daydreams, but he leaves for Paris. Then Rodolphe, a rich landowner,
seduces her with no difficulty. At first adultery gives her the feeling that she is living a novel
at last. When she wants to run away with him, Rodolphe breaks it off in a letter. Later, Emma meets
Léon again in Rouen, and a new affair begins. 4. The debts. To look like what she dreams of being,
Emma buys on credit from Lheureux, a merchant who lends her money at enormous rates. The debts pile
up without Charles knowing. One day the bailiffs (les huissiers) seize the couple's possessions.
Emma asks Léon, then Rodolphe, for help: nobody saves her. 5. The end. In despair, Emma swallows
arsenic taken from the pharmacist, Homais, and dies after a long agony. Charles discovers her love
letters and dies soon after. Their daughter, poor, ends up as a worker in a cotton mill. Homais,
for his part, triumphs: the novel ends with the pharmacist being decorated.*

The retelling is in the present, the usual tense of a French plot summary. Emma is the
*héroïne*, but not a heroine in the old sense: Flaubert shows her dreams and their cost without
admiring or condemning her.

![A timeline, not to scale: 1851 to 1856, Flaubert writes the novel; 1 October to 15 December 1856, it appears as a serial in La Revue de Paris, with cuts; 29 January 1857, the trial opens in Paris; 7 February 1857, acquittal; April 1857, the book is published by Michel Lévy in two volumes. A note gives the subtitle, Mœurs de province.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## How Flaubert uses free indirect speech

Lesson 19 gave three ways to report a thought. Here they are with an original sentence about Emma:

- direct: *Elle se dit : « Je mérite mieux que cette vie ! »*
- indirect: *Elle se disait qu'elle méritait mieux que cette vie.*
- free indirect: *Elle méritait mieux que cette vie !*

The third version keeps Emma's exclamation and her conviction, but in the narrator's imparfait.
Is it Emma who thinks this, or the narrator who states it? The sentence doesn't say, and that
uncertainty is the point. Flaubert uses this in three ways:

1. **To show dreams from inside.** Emma's longings for Paris, for passion, for luxury, pass into
   the narration as if they were the world itself.
2. **To create irony.** Emma's dreams are made of the clichés of the novels she read. When those
   clichés appear in free indirect speech, the reader hears Emma's enthusiasm and, at the same
   time, notices that the words are second-hand. The narrator never says "this is foolish": the
   style shows it.
