3. **To let other voices in.** Homais's pompous opinions and Charles's simple contentment slip
   into the narration in the same way, each in its own vocabulary.

### Example 1: spotting free indirect speech

This passage was written for this lesson:

> *Emma ferma la fenêtre. La pluie tombait toujours sur la place. Encore un dimanche à attendre !
> À Paris, en ce moment, on dansait, on riait, on vivait. Pourquoi le sort l'avait-il jetée dans
> ce bourg où il ne se passait jamais rien ?*

(Emma closed the window. The rain was still falling on the square. Another Sunday spent waiting!
In Paris, at this very moment, people were dancing, laughing, living. Why had fate thrown her
into this town where nothing ever happened?)

- *Emma ferma la fenêtre* and *La pluie tombait toujours* are the narrator: a fact in the passé
  simple, a description in the imparfait.
- *Encore un dimanche à attendre !* has no verb and an exclamation mark: it's Emma's thought.
- *À Paris, en ce moment, on dansait …* keeps *en ce moment* (Emma's "now") and her dream image.
- *Pourquoi le sort l'avait-il jetée …* is a question in the third person and the
  plus-que-parfait: her complaint, in free indirect speech.

### Example 2: turning it back into direct speech

To convert free indirect speech, put back the first person and the present, and add a reporting
verb and quotation marks:

| free indirect | direct |
|---|---|
| *Encore un dimanche à attendre !* | *Elle pensa : « Encore un dimanche à attendre ! »* |
| *À Paris, en ce moment, on dansait.* | *« À Paris, en ce moment, on danse. »* |
| *Pourquoi le sort l'avait-il jetée dans ce bourg ?* | *« Pourquoi le sort m'a-t-il jetée dans ce bourg ? »* |
| *Elle partirait, elle ne resterait pas un jour de plus.* | *« Je partirai, je ne resterai pas un jour de plus. »* |

The tenses move one step towards the present: imparfait → présent, plus-que-parfait → passé composé, conditionnel
→ futur. That's the concordance des temps of B1 in reverse.

### Example 3: whose voice?

> *Le pharmacien, lui, ne doutait de rien. La science avançait à grands pas, et la petite ville
> aurait bientôt, grâce à lui, sa place dans les journaux.*

(The pharmacist, for his part, had no doubts at all. Science was making great strides, and the
little town would soon, thanks to him, have its place in the newspapers.)

The first sentence could be the narrator's. The second is the pharmacist's pride, in his own
grand words (*la science avançait à grands pas*), in the conditionnel of the future in the past.
The narrator doesn't mock him; the reader smiles anyway.

## Bovarysme and romanesque

The novel gave French a word: *le bovarysme*, the habit of dreaming of a more romantic,
glamorous life and seeing yourself as someone else. The philosopher Jules de Gaultier made the
term popular in essays from the 1890s. Today you'll read it in the press: *le bovarysme des
réseaux sociaux*, a life imagined from other people's photos.

*Romanesque* is "as in novels": *une histoire romanesque* (a story full of adventures and
feelings), *une imagination romanesque*. Don't confuse it with *romantique*, which is about
love and feelings in general, and also the name of the earlier literary movement. Emma's
imagination is *romanesque*; her *rêveries* (daydreams) end in *désillusion*.

## Common mistakes

- Taking free indirect speech for the narrator's opinion. Check the clues: exclamations, questions,
  the character's words, *ici, demain, maintenant* in a past narrative.
- Writing free indirect speech in an essay. It belongs to narrative; in an exam essay, report
  with a verb and *que*.
- Forgetting to shift the tenses back when converting: *on dansait* becomes *on danse*, not *on
  dansait*, in direct speech.
- Quoting famous lines from the novel in an essay without being sure of them. A clear description
  in your own words is safer and shows more French.
- Using *romanesque* for "romantic" in the love sense: for love, say *romantique*.

## Key points

- *Madame Bovary*: serialised in *La Revue de Paris* (1 October–15 December 1856, cut), trial in
  January 1857, acquittal on 7 February 1857, book in April 1857 (Michel Lévy), subtitle *Mœurs de
  province*.
- Realism: ordinary middle-class life, an impersonal narrator, documented detail; Flaubert's
  real obsession was style.
- Free indirect speech: narrative tenses and the third person, no *que*, the character's voice.
  Flaubert uses it for dreams, for irony and for other characters' voices.
- To convert it: first person, tenses one step towards the present (imparfait → présent, conditionnel →
  futur), reporting verb and quotation marks.
- *Le bovarysme*: dreaming of a more romantic life; *romanesque*: as in novels.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Les figures de style: saying more, less or otherwise
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 20 showed how word order puts an idea in relief. Writers and speakers have another set of
tools: the **[[figures of speech]]** (*les figures de style*), ways of saying something more strongly,
more softly, or in other words. French schools teach them by name from secondary school on, and a DELF
B2 reading text, an editorial, a speech or an advert will use several. Knowing them helps you in
two ways: you'll spot the tone of a text (is the writer ironic? softening bad news?), and you can
use two or three in your own essay.

This lesson covers ten figures, in six families: comparing, saying less, saying more, opposing,
repeating or replacing, and saying the opposite. All the examples are original or everyday phrases.

## Comparing: la comparaison and la métaphore

A comparison (*la comparaison*) links two things with a comparing word: *comme, tel, pareil
à, semblable à, ressembler à*.

- *Le soir, le quartier est calme comme un village.*
- *Il est têtu comme une mule.* (a fixed comparison: everyone says it)

A **[[metaphor]]** (*la métaphore*) makes the same link with no comparing word: one thing simply *is*
the other.

- *Ce bureau est une ruche.* (une ruche = a beehive: everyone is busy)
- *Le gouvernement doit affronter une tempête sociale.*
- *Les réseaux sociaux sont la vitrine de notre vie.*

Everyday language is full of metaphors nobody notices any more: *le pied de la table, une
avalanche de courriels, le cœur du problème.* In an essay, a fresh metaphor can make an idea
memorable; a worn-out one (*une goutte d'eau dans l'océan*) adds little.

## Saying less: la litote and l'euphémisme

These two are easy to confuse, because both say less than they mean. The difference is the aim.

The **[[litotes]]** (*la litote*) says less in order to mean *more*, often with a negative:

- *Il n'est pas bête.* = he's very clever.
- *Ce n'est pas mauvais du tout !* = it's delicious.
- *Je ne suis pas mécontent du résultat.* = I'm very pleased.

The **[[euphemism]]** (*l'euphémisme*) says less in order to *soften* something unpleasant or
shocking:

- *Il nous a quittés.* = he died.
- *Un plan social* = a round of redundancies.
- *Les demandeurs d'emploi* = the unemployed.
- *Une personne à mobilité réduite* = a person with a disability affecting movement.

Politics, business and administration love euphemisms. A critic may call them *langue de bois*
(lesson 19) when they hide the truth.

## Saying more: l'hyperbole

The **[[hyperbole]]** (*l'hyperbole*) exaggerates on purpose:

- *Je meurs de faim.* — *Je te l'ai dit mille fois !* — *Il y avait un monde fou.*
- In adverts: *Le goût qui va changer votre vie.*

Hyperbole is natural in speech and in advertising. In an argued essay, use it sparingly: an
exaggeration is easy for the reader to refute.

## Opposing: l'antithèse and l'oxymore

An **[[antithesis]]** (*l'antithèse*, B1) sets two opposite ideas side by side, often in parallel
phrases:

- *Les villes se remplissent, les campagnes se vident.*
- *Ce qui était un luxe hier est devenu une nécessité aujourd'hui.*

An **[[oxymoron]]** (*l'oxymore*, masculine) joins two contradictory words in one expression:

- *un silence assourdissant* (a deafening silence: the silence is so striking it "makes noise")
- *une douce violence*, *une croissance négative* (economists' euphemistic oxymoron for a fall)

The antithesis contrasts two parts of a sentence; the oxymoron fuses the contradiction into two
words.

## Repeating and replacing: l'anaphore and la périphrase

An **[[anaphora]]** (*l'anaphore*) repeats the same word or words at the start of several sentences or
phrases. It's the favourite figure of speeches:

- *Nous voulons des écoles ouvertes. Nous voulons des hôpitaux proches. Nous voulons des villages
  vivants.*

A **[[periphrasis]]** (*la périphrase*) replaces a word with a longer description of it:

- *la Ville lumière* = Paris; *l'Hexagone* = France (because of its shape on the map); *le roi
  des animaux* = the lion; *l'or noir* = oil; *la Grande Muette* = the army (it doesn't take
  part in politics).

Journalists use periphrasis constantly to avoid repeating a name: after *la France* twice, they
write *l'Hexagone*.

## Saying the opposite: l'ironie

Irony (*l'ironie*) says the opposite of what you mean, and counts on the listener to
understand:

- *Bravo, quelle organisation !* (the trip was a mess)
- *Génial, encore une grève* (strike) *le jour de mon départ.*

The adjective is *ironique*: *un ton ironique*. In writing, irony depends on the context, so a
reader can miss it: in a formal essay, make sure it's unmistakable, or avoid it.

## The ten figures at a glance

![A chart of ten figures of speech in six coloured boxes: comparing (la comparaison, la métaphore); saying less (la litote, which means more, and l'euphémisme, which softens); saying more (l'hyperbole); opposing (l'antithèse, two ideas, and l'oxymore, two words); repeating or replacing (l'anaphore, la périphrase); saying the opposite (l'ironie). Each figure has a short example.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Worked examples

### Example 1: an advert

> *Votre voiture vous coûte une fortune ? Les bouchons sont votre deuxième maison ? Essayez
> Clémentine, la petite reine électrique. Clémentine, c'est la liberté. Clémentine, c'est le
> silence. Clémentine, c'est la ville rendue aux piétons.*

(Is your car costing you a fortune? Are traffic jams your second home? Try Clémentine, the little
electric queen. Clémentine is freedom. Clémentine is silence. Clémentine is the city given back
to pedestrians.) The brand is invented.

- *une fortune*: hyperbole (it's expensive, not a fortune).
- *Les bouchons sont votre deuxième maison*: metaphor (and hyperbole).
- *la petite reine électrique*: periphrasis. *La petite reine* is an old periphrasis for the
  bicycle; here it suggests an electric bike.
- *Clémentine, c'est … Clémentine, c'est …*: anaphora.
- *la ville rendue aux piétons*: metaphor of a gift.

### Example 2: litotes, euphemism or irony?

1. *Le dîner ? Ce n'était pas désagréable.* — Litotes, if the speaker liked it: saying less to
   mean more.
2. *Après trente ans de service, il a été remercié.* — Euphemism: *remercier* (to thank) here
   means "to dismiss".
3. *Super, il pleut pour notre pique-nique.* — Irony: the opposite is meant.

The same words can change figure with the context and the tone: *Ce n'était pas désagréable*,
said with a sigh about a boring evening, is irony.

### Example 3: two or three figures in an essay

Here is a plain conclusion, then the same one with three figures:

> *Le télétravail présente des avantages et des inconvénients. Il faut l'organiser pour qu'il
> profite à tous.*

> *Le télétravail n'est ni un paradis ni un enfer. Bien organisé, il libère ; mal organisé, il
> isole. À nous d'en faire un outil, et non une prison.*

(Working from home is neither a paradise nor a hell. Well organised, it frees; badly organised,
it isolates. It's up to us to make it a tool, not a prison.) The second version has an antithesis
(*il libère … il isole*), metaphors (*un paradis, un enfer, une prison*) and a parallel structure.
It's more memorable and still argues something precise. Three figures are enough: a whole essay
written like this would sound like an advert.

## Common mistakes

- Calling every negative sentence a litotes. *Ce n'est pas cher* is a litotes only if it means
  "it's a bargain"; if it just means "it's not expensive", it's a plain statement.
- Mixing up litotes and euphemism: litotes strengthens, euphemism softens.
- Mixing up metaphor and comparison: if *comme* or *tel* is there, it's a comparison.
- Using irony or hyperbole in a formal argument where the reader may take it literally.
- *L'oxymore* is masculine (*un oxymore frappant*); *la métaphore, l'hyperbole, l'anaphore* are
  feminine.

## Key points

- Comparing: *la comparaison* (with *comme, tel …*), *la métaphore* (without).
- Saying less: *la litote* (to mean more: *Il n'est pas bête*), *l'euphémisme* (to soften: *Il
  nous a quittés*).
- Saying more: *l'hyperbole* (*Je te l'ai dit mille fois*).
- Opposing: *l'antithèse* (two ideas), *l'oxymore* (two words: *un silence assourdissant*).
- Repeating and replacing: *l'anaphore* (speeches), *la périphrase* (*la Ville lumière, l'Hexagone*).
- Saying the opposite: *l'ironie*, adjective *ironique*.
- In a DELF essay, use two or three figures, clearly and on purpose.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Convaincre: building an argument at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 you learned to give an opinion with two or three reasons, an example each, a concession
(*certes … mais*) and a conclusion. At B2 that is no longer enough. A B2 reader expects you to
say exactly which question you are answering, to take the other side seriously, to answer it
point by point, and to organise the whole text so the reasoning is easy to follow. This lesson
builds that kind of text, the **[[argued essay]]**, on one theme: advertising and the consumer
society. Lesson 22 turns it into the DELF writing task, letters and reviews; lesson 23 does the
same out loud.

The words of B1's essays still apply: *la thèse, l'antithèse, la synthèse, réfuter, l'argument,
convaincre*. Here you add the moves that make an argument *convaincant* (convincing).

## From a topic to a problématique

A topic is not yet a question. "Advertising" is a topic; you can't agree or disagree with it.
The **[[problématique]]** is the precise question your text answers, the one that makes the topic
debatable. Find it before you write a single sentence.

| topic | problématique |
|---|---|
| *la publicité* | *La publicité informe-t-elle le consommateur ou le manipule-t-elle ?* |
| *les enfants et le marketing* | *Faut-il interdire la publicité qui cible les enfants ?* |
| *la société de consommation* | *Consommer moins, est-ce forcément vivre moins bien ?* |

A good problématique has two possible answers (or more), so it creates a tension. It is often
built on a **paradox**, something that seems contradictory: *Tout le monde dit détester la
publicité ; pourtant, elle fonctionne.* That *paradoxe* is a gift: it gives you your opening and
your question. *Il est paradoxal que …* takes the subjunctive (*Il est paradoxal qu'on la
regarde autant*), like other value judgements in *il est* + adjective (*il est normal, étonnant,
regrettable que*); adjectives of certainty (*il est certain, évident, probable que*) take the
indicative.

## The thesis: say where you stand

Your **[[thesis]]** is your answer to the problématique, in one sentence. At B2 it is usually
nuanced: not "advertising is bad" but *La publicité n'est pas nuisible en soi, mais elle le
devient quand elle cible ceux qui n'ont pas encore d'esprit critique.* (Advertising isn't
harmful in itself, but it becomes so when it targets people who don't yet think critically.)

Where you place it depends on the plan (below): in a one-sided essay, in the introduction; in a
dialectical essay, often only in the last part and the conclusion, after you have weighed both
sides. Either way, the reader must never wonder what you think by the end.

## Building an argument: idea, explanation, example

Each argument has three parts. The idea alone is a claim; the explanation shows why it is
true; the example proves it in the real world.

1. **Idea:** *La publicité peut être bénéfique.* (Advertising can be beneficial.)
2. **Explanation:** *Elle informe le public de l'existence d'un produit ou d'un service qu'il
   ne connaissait pas.* (It tells the public about a product or service they didn't know.)
3. **Example:** *Une campagne pour un vaccin ou pour le don du sang sauve des vies.* (A campaign
   for a vaccine or for blood donation saves lives.)

The verb for "back up" is *étayer*: *Étayez chaque argument par un exemple.* An argument that
isn't backed up is the most common weakness of B2 essays. Strong verbs help too: *Cette étude
met en évidence le rôle du marketing* (highlights); *Ce scandale remet en cause la confiance
des consommateurs* (calls into question). *Mettre en évidence* and *remettre en cause* are
conjugated like *mettre*: *L'enquête a mis en évidence …, Cela remettrait en cause …*.

Choose examples that are *pertinents* (relevant): an example about the price of petrol doesn't
support an argument about children's television, however true it is.

## Refutation: answering the other side

**[[Refutation]]** means stating an argument against your view and then showing why it doesn't
hold, or doesn't hold completely. It is the move that separates B2 from B1. There are two
classic shapes.

**1. Concede, then turn it around.** You admit what is true in the other view, then you show
it doesn't change your conclusion.

- *Certes, la publicité finance la presse et la télévision gratuite. Il n'en reste pas moins
  qu'elle envahit notre espace public.* — Admittedly, advertising funds the press and free
  television. It is nonetheless true that it invades our public space.
- *Il n'en reste pas moins que* + indicative is formal and strong. *Toujours est-il que*
  (lesson 08) is close; *mais* is the plain version.

**2. Announce the objection, then refute it.** You introduce the opposing argument with a verb
in the conditionnel (*on pourrait objecter que, certains diraient que*: it is not your view) and
answer it with *or* or *en réalité*.

- *On pourrait objecter que les adultes sont libres de ne pas acheter. Or, les publicitaires
  connaissent mieux nos faiblesses que nous-mêmes.* — One could object that adults are free not
  to buy. But advertisers know our weaknesses better than we do.
- *Or* introduces a new fact that changes the reasoning ("but", "yet", "now"). It is the same
  word as *l'or* (gold), but a different use. It usually opens its sentence or clause and is
  often followed by a comma.

The **contre-argument** you choose matters: refute the strongest one, not an easy one. A
refutation of an argument nobody makes ("some people think advertising is always true") is
a straw man and convinces no one.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The shape of a refutation
  accDescr: A chart of the five steps of a refutation. Step 1, your claim, for example la publicité cible les plus vulnérables. Step 2, the objection, introduced by On pourrait objecter que, in the conditionnel. Step 3, the concession, introduced by Certes, admitting what is true in it. Step 4, the turn, introduced by Or or Il n'en reste pas moins que, giving a new fact. Step 5, your claim again, now stronger.
  A["1. Your claim: la publicité cible les plus vulnérables"] --> B["2. Objection: On pourrait objecter que … (conditionnel)"]
  B --> C["3. Concession: Certes, … (what is true in it)"]
  C --> D["4. Turn: Or … / Il n'en reste pas moins que … (a new fact)"]
  D --> E["5. Your claim again, stronger"]
```

Step 3 is optional: you can go straight from the objection to *Or …*. But conceding first
shows you have understood the other side, and B2 marking rewards that.

## Two plans: dialectical and thematic

The plan is the order of your parts. At B2 you choose it from the problématique.

| plan | when | parts |
|---|---|---|
| **[[dialectical plan]]** (*le plan dialectique*) | a yes-or-no question: *Faut-il …? La publicité est-elle …? Dans quelle mesure …?* | I. *thèse* (arguments for one answer); II. *antithèse* (arguments against, often with refutation); III. *synthèse* (going beyond the opposition: a nuanced answer, conditions, a solution) |
| **[[thematic plan]]** (*le plan thématique*) | a question that asks "what?", "how?" or "what effects?": *Quels sont les effets de la publicité sur les enfants ?* | each part is one aspect: I. economic, II. social, III. psychological (or health, environment …) |

The **[[dialectical plan]]** suits most DELF-style topics, which ask for a position on a debate.
Its third part is the hardest: a *synthèse* isn't "both are right". It goes one step further:
*La publicité n'est ni bonne ni mauvaise en soi ; tout dépend de la cible et des règles.* A
two-part version (for, then against with your answer) is also common in shorter texts.

The **[[thematic plan]]** is clearer when there is no real "for and against", or when you agree
with the statement and want to show it from several angles. Its danger is the list: three
parts with no link. Give each part a role in the answer and end each with a sentence that
leads to the next.

![The plan of a dialectical essay as five stacked boxes, each with a tag on the left. Introduction, tagged problématique: a hook, the question the essay answers, the plan. Part I, tagged thèse: the arguments for, advertising informs. Part II, tagged antithèse: the arguments against, advertising manipulates, with refutation. Part III, tagged synthèse: going beyond the opposition, regulate it and teach critical thinking. Conclusion, tagged ouverture: the answer to the question, then a wider question.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Rhetorical questions

A **[[rhetorical question]]** is asked for effect, not for an answer: it makes the reader think the
answer before you give it. Use one or two, not more.

- *Peut-on vraiment parler de liberté quand un enfant de six ans réclame la marque qu'il a
  vue à la télévision ?* — Can we really talk about freedom when a six-year-old demands the
  brand he saw on television?
- *Faut-il pour autant interdire toute publicité ? Certainement pas.* — Does that mean we
  should ban all advertising? Certainly not.

The second shape (question, then a short answer) makes a good transition between two parts.

## Avoiding repetition

Nothing tires a reader more than *la publicité* in every sentence. Three tools:

- **Pronouns**, including the neutral *le* and *en* (lesson 16): *La publicité ? On la critique,
  mais on en a besoin.*
- **Synonyms and general nouns**: *la publicité → les annonces, les messages publicitaires, ce
  secteur, le marketing* (which is wider: the whole strategy of selling).
- **[[Nominalisation]]** (lesson 14): *Les marques ciblent les enfants. Ce ciblage …* ; *Les promotions
  incitent à acheter. Cette incitation …* (this incentive); *Les ventes ont augmenté de 10 %. Cette
  hausse …*

To reformulate a whole idea, use *en d'autres termes* (formal) or *autrement dit* (neutral):
*Le prix a augmenté, la quantité a baissé ; en d'autres termes, on paie plus pour moins.*

## Connectors by function: a recap

You have all of these already (B1 and lessons 08, 17 and 18; the reference sheet has them by
grammar). What matters at B2 is choosing them by function and varying them.

| function | neutral | formal |
|---|---|---|
| adding a point | *de plus, d'ailleurs, par ailleurs* | *en outre* |
| giving an example | *par exemple, notamment* | *ainsi* |
| cause | *parce que, puisque, comme* | *étant donné que, d'autant que* (17) |
| consequence | *donc, c'est pourquoi, si bien que* | *par conséquent, au point que* (17), *de là* (17) |
| concession | *certes … mais, même si, bien que* | *quand bien même, encore que* (08) |
| opposition | *mais, en revanche, alors que* | *pour autant, loin de* (18) |
| refutation | *en réalité, pourtant* | *or, il n'en reste pas moins que* |
| reformulating | *autrement dit, c'est-à-dire* | *en d'autres termes* |
| concluding | *bref, pour conclure* | *en somme, en définitive* |

Two cautions. *Ainsi* opens an example only when an example follows; it can also mean "thus".
*D'ailleurs* adds support to what you just said ("in fact"), while *par ailleurs* opens a
different point ("besides").

## Reading: an argued text

> **La publicité : information utile ou manipulation ?**
>
> Nous voyons chaque jour des centaines de messages publicitaires, sur nos écrans, dans la rue, jusque sur nos tickets de caisse. Paradoxalement, la plupart d'entre nous affirment ne pas y faire attention. La publicité serait-elle donc inoffensive, ou nous influence-t-elle bien plus que nous ne le croyons ?
>
> Certes, elle a des vertus. Elle informe le public de l'arrivée d'un produit, elle fait vivre les médias et elle peut servir de bonnes causes : une campagne contre le tabac peut inciter des milliers de fumeurs à arrêter. Dans ces cas-là, son effet est sans doute bénéfique.
>
> Il n'en reste pas moins que le marketing moderne ne se contente plus d'informer. Il cible nos émotions et nos habitudes, et il le fait avec une précision croissante grâce à nos données. On pourrait objecter que chacun reste libre de ne pas acheter. Or cette liberté suppose un esprit critique que tout le monde n'a pas. Un enfant qui entend dix fois par jour le slogan d'une boisson sucrée, la marque imaginaire « Pétillo » par exemple, n'est pas un consommateur libre : c'est une cible. En d'autres termes, plus le public est vulnérable, plus la manipulation est facile.
>
> Faut-il pour autant interdire la publicité ? Ce serait remettre en cause le financement de nombreux médias. La solution passe plutôt par des règles strictes pour les publicités destinées aux enfants et par l'éducation : apprendre aux jeunes à décoder une image, c'est leur donner les moyens de résister à la surconsommation.

Translation:

> **Advertising: useful information or manipulation?**
>
> Every day we see hundreds of advertising messages, on our screens, in the street, even on our till receipts. Paradoxically, most of us claim not to pay any attention to them. Is advertising harmless, then, or does it influence us far more than we think?
>
> Admittedly, it has its virtues. It tells the public that a product has arrived, it keeps the media alive, and it can serve good causes: a campaign against smoking can encourage thousands of smokers to stop. In those cases its effect is no doubt beneficial.
>
> It is nonetheless true that modern marketing is no longer content to inform. It targets our emotions and our habits, and it does so with growing precision thanks to our data. One could object that everyone remains free not to buy. Yet that freedom presupposes a critical mind that not everyone has. A child who hears the slogan of a sugary drink ten times a day, the imaginary brand "Pétillo" for example, is not a free consumer: he is a target. In other words, the more vulnerable the public, the easier the manipulation.
>
> Should advertising be banned, then? That would call into question the funding of many media. The solution lies rather in strict rules for advertisements aimed at children, and in education: teaching young people to decode an image is giving them the means to resist overconsumption.

How it is built:

- **Hook and problématique:** a concrete observation, a paradox (*Paradoxalement …*), then the
  question, with the conditionnel of a claim not yet accepted (*serait-elle*, lesson 10).
- **Concession:** *Certes* opens the arguments for, with an example (the anti-smoking campaign).
- **Refutation:** *Il n'en reste pas moins que* turns the text; then a second refutation in two
  steps: *On pourrait objecter que … Or …*. The example (the child and the slogan) backs it up.
- **Reformulation:** *En d'autres termes* + a proportion sentence (*plus … plus*, lesson 12).
- **Synthesis and answer:** a rhetorical question (*Faut-il pour autant …?*), then a nuanced
  answer: rules and education rather than a ban.

Notes: *le ticket de caisse* = till receipt; *inoffensif* = harmless; *la vertu* = virtue;
*se contenter de* = to be content with; *croissant* = growing; *supposer* = to presuppose;
*décoder* = to decode. *Nous ne le croyons*: the *ne* after a comparison (*plus … que nous ne le
croyons*) is the formal *ne explétif* (lesson 05); it adds no negation.

## Pronunciation

- *Paradoxal* [paʁadɔksal], *le paradoxe* [paʁadɔks]: x = [ks].
- *Étayer* [eteje]; *il étaie* [etɛ] and *il étaye* [etɛj] are both heard.
- *Inciter* [ɛ̃site]; *l'incitation* [lɛ̃sitasjɔ̃].
- *Le marketing* [maʁketiŋ]: the English *-ing* sound, stress on the last syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Starting to write before the problématique is clear. A text "about advertising" with no
  question becomes a list of facts.
- Refuting an argument nobody holds. Choose the strongest *contre-argument*.
- *Or* used as "or". "Or" is *ou*; *or* is "but, yet" in an argument.
- *Il n'en reste pas moins que* + subjunctive: it takes the indicative (*il n'en reste pas
  moins qu'elle est utile*).
- *Inciter* with *de*: it is *inciter quelqu'un à faire* (*inciter les clients à acheter*).
- *~~Convainquant~~* as the adjective: the adjective is *convaincant* (*un argument
  convaincant*); *convainquant* is the present participle (*en le convainquant*).
- A third part that only repeats the first two. The *synthèse* must add something.

## Key points

- Turn the topic into a **[[problématique]]**, a precise debatable question; a paradox often
  gives you one.
- The **[[thesis]]** is your answer; in a dialectical essay it is often only fully given at the end.
- Each argument: idea, explanation, example (*étayer*, *mettre en évidence*).
- **Refutation:** *Certes … Il n'en reste pas moins que …* or *On pourrait objecter que … Or …*.
- **[[Dialectical plan]]** for a yes-or-no debate (thèse, antithèse, synthèse); **[[thematic plan]]**
  for "what effects?" or "how?" questions.
- Avoid repetition with pronouns, synonyms and nominalisation; reformulate with *en d'autres
  termes*.

lessons.title: Écrire au niveau B2: the formal letter, the critical review and the essay
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 built the argued essay. This lesson puts it into the forms B2 writers actually use: the
formal letter (here, the letter of complaint), the critical review of a film, book or
show, and the essay's introduction and conclusion. It ends with a checklist for rereading. The
theme is consumer rights and public services; you know *le remboursement, la garantie, le délai,
la réclamation* from A2.

## The DELF B2 writing task in general terms

In the current format the DELF B2 has one writing task, in one hour: an argued text in which
you take a position on a question. FEI's candidate manual names several forms it can take: a
contribution to a debate (a forum, a blog), a formal letter (to a newspaper, a mayor, a
company), a critical article, or a report. The manual asks for **at least 250 words**; you may
write more, never less. Follow the instructions on your paper, which give the form, the reader
and the length, and write your word count at the end, as the manual advises.

Whatever the form, the content is the same as in lesson 21: a clear position, arguments with
examples, a refutation, and a conclusion. What changes is the frame (a letter's layout, a
forum post's tone) and the register. Lesson 24 covers how the text is marked.

## The letter of complaint

A **[[letter of complaint]]** (*la lettre de réclamation*) sets out facts, says what went wrong,
and asks for a remedy, in a firm, polite formal register. Its layout is the formal letter you
know from B1, with one addition at B2: a clear escalation, from request to warning.

![A model letter of complaint laid out on a page: the sender's name and address top left (Julien Marchetti, Lyon); the recipient on the right (Novaro France, service clients, Paris); below it, the place and date (Lyon, le 15 avril 2026); the subject line in bold, Objet : réclamation, commande n° 48213; the opening Madame, Monsieur; the body as three blocks of grey lines tagged 1 les faits, 2 le problème, 3 la demande; the closing formula Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées; and the signature at the bottom right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Stating the facts

Be precise and neutral: dates, order or contract numbers, what you did and what happened. Use
the passé composé and the plus-que-parfait, and keep emotion for later.

- *Le 3 mars, j'ai commandé sur votre site un ordinateur portable (commande n° 48213).* — On 3
  March I ordered a laptop on your website (order no. 48213).
- *L'appareil livré est défectueux : l'écran s'éteint au bout de quelques minutes.* — The
  device delivered is faulty: the screen goes off after a few minutes.
- *Le modèle reçu est, de plus, non conforme à ma commande.* — The model received, what's more,
  isn't what I ordered.

### Saying what went wrong and what it cost you

- *J'ai contacté votre service après-vente à trois reprises, sans résultat.* — I contacted your
  after-sales service three times, without result.
- *Ce retard m'a causé un préjudice important : j'ai dû louer un ordinateur pour travailler.* —
  This delay caused me considerable harm: I had to rent a computer to work.
- *J'ai subi deux semaines de coupures.* — I suffered two weeks of outages. (*Subir* takes a
  direct object: *subir un préjudice, subir des retards*.)

### Asking, then warning

The request comes first; the warning, if any, comes at the end of the letter, never at the
start.

| move | formula | English |
|---|---|---|
| opening | *Je me permets de vous écrire au sujet de …* | I am writing to you about … |
| reluctance | *Je me vois contraint(e) de vous adresser cette réclamation.* (lesson 15) | I find myself obliged to … |
| request | *Je vous saurais gré de bien vouloir procéder au remboursement.* | I should be grateful if you would … |
| request | *Je vous demande donc de me dédommager du préjudice subi.* | I therefore ask you to compensate me for … |
| warning | *À défaut de réponse sous quinze jours, je me verrai dans l'obligation de saisir le médiateur.* | Failing a reply within fifteen days, I shall be obliged to … |
| closing | *Dans l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.* | (formal closing) |

*Je vous saurais gré de* uses the conditionnel of *savoir gré*, "to be grateful": it is polite
and firm. *Sous quinze jours* means "within fifteen days" (*sous huitaine*: within a week).
*Contraint(e)*: add *e* if you are a woman.

### What you can ask for, and where to go next

Know the words of the remedies: *le remboursement* (refund); *le dédommagement* (compensation
for what you lost; *dédommager quelqu'un*); *l'avoir* (a credit note to spend in the same shop;
you can usually refuse it if you are owed a refund); *le geste commercial* (a goodwill gesture,
which the seller offers without admitting fault).

In France, the usual steps of a *litige* (dispute) with a business go from mild to serious:
the customer service; a written complaint; a *lettre recommandée avec accusé de réception*
(registered letter, the receipt proving it arrived); a *mise en demeure* (formal notice to act
by a date); then a *recours* outside the courts, such as the *médiateur de la consommation*
(consumer ombudsman), which takes a case only once you have complained in writing to the business; and,
last, the courts. In the EU, you can normally withdraw from an online purchase within fourteen
days of receiving it (*le délai de rétractation*), and goods carry a legal guarantee of at least
two years. Rules have exceptions and change: check the official consumer sites before you act.

Variants: in Québec, the *Office de la protection du consommateur* informs consumers, and a
*mise en demeure* is also the usual last letter before going to court.

Accusing the other side of *mauvaise foi* (bad faith) is a strong move: keep it for a letter
where the facts prove it.

### A model letter

> Madame, Monsieur,
>
> Le 3 mars dernier, j'ai commandé sur votre site un ordinateur portable Novaro 15 (commande n° 48213), livré le 7 mars. Dès le premier jour, l'appareil s'est révélé défectueux : l'écran s'éteint sans raison au bout de quelques minutes.
>
> Votre service après-vente, que j'ai contacté le 8 mars puis à deux reprises, m'avait promis une réparation sous dix jours. Cinq semaines plus tard, je n'ai reçu ni l'ordinateur réparé ni la moindre explication. À titre de geste commercial, vous m'avez proposé un avoir de 30 euros, que je ne peux accepter : il ne compense en rien le préjudice subi, puisque j'ai dû louer un appareil pour continuer à travailler.
>
> Je vous saurais donc gré de bien vouloir, au choix, remplacer l'ordinateur ou me rembourser intégralement, et de me dédommager des frais de location, dont vous trouverez la facture ci-jointe.
>
> À défaut de réponse sous quinze jours, je me verrai dans l'obligation de saisir le médiateur de la consommation.
>
> Dans l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
>
> Julien Marchetti

Translation:

> Dear Sir or Madam,
>
> On 3 March I ordered a Novaro 15 laptop on your website (order no. 48213), delivered on 7 March. From the first day the device turned out to be faulty: the screen goes off for no reason after a few minutes.
>
> Your after-sales service, which I contacted on 8 March and twice more since, had promised me a repair within ten days. Five weeks later I have received neither the repaired computer nor the slightest explanation. As a goodwill gesture you offered me a credit note of 30 euros, which I cannot accept: it in no way makes up for the harm suffered, since I had to rent a machine to keep working.
>
> I should therefore be grateful if you would either replace the computer or refund me in full, and compensate me for the rental costs, for which you will find the invoice enclosed.
>
> Failing a reply within fifteen days, I shall be obliged to refer the matter to the consumer ombudsman.
>
> I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully,
>
> Julien Marchetti

(Novaro is an invented brand.) Notes: *se révéler* = to turn out (to be); *à deux reprises* =
twice, on two occasions; *ne … en rien* = in no way; *ci-jointe* agrees with *la facture*
because it follows it. The tenses tell the story: the passé composé for the events,
the plus-que-parfait for the earlier promise (*m'avait promis*), the conditionnel for the polite
request, the futur for the warning.

### A formal request

Not every formal letter complains. To a service provider (*le prestataire*) or a public service,
a request uses the same layout with softer moves: *Je souhaiterais savoir si …, Pourriez-vous
m'indiquer …, Je vous remercie par avance de …*. *La prestation* is the service provided
(*la prestation ne correspondait pas au devis*: the work didn't match the estimate); *les
prestations sociales* are welfare benefits.

## The critical review

A **[[critical review]]** (*la critique*, written by *le critique*; *la critique* for a woman) gives
a reasoned judgement of a film, a book, a show or an exhibition. At B2 it is an argued text like
any other: your judgement is the thesis, and each strength or weakness is an argument with an
example from the work.

![The plan of a critical review in four blocks from top to bottom: 1, the title and a short judgement, with the example « Le Dernier Été » : un film sensible; 2, the presentation, the work, its author or director, its genre; 3, the summary, in the present, without revealing the ending; 4, the judgement, with a box for strong points and a box for weak points, each with an example from the work, and a recommendation line: À voir ! or À réserver aux amateurs.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- **Present the work:** title, author or director, genre, where and when. *Dans « Le Dernier
  Été », son deuxième long métrage, Sarah Benali filme …*
- **Summarise briefly** in the present, without giving the ending away.
- **Judge, with nuance.** Praise: *une mise en scène inventive, des acteurs remarquables, un
  scénario d'une grande finesse*. Criticism: *un rythme inégal, une fin décevante, des
  personnages caricaturaux*. Reviews can be *élogieuses* (glowing), *mitigées* (mixed) or
  severe. A mixed review is often the most convincing, because it shows you can tell good from
  less good: *Si le scénario manque de rythme, l'interprétation est remarquable.*
- **Recommend:** *À voir absolument. À réserver aux amateurs du genre.*

Here is an extract from an original review of an invented film:

> Avec *Le Dernier Été*, Sarah Benali signe un film sensible sur trois sœurs qui vident la maison de leur enfance. Le scénario, d'une grande justesse, évite le mélodrame, et les trois actrices sont remarquables. On regrettera cependant une dernière demi-heure trop longue, où le film semble hésiter entre plusieurs fins. Malgré ces faiblesses, l'accueil des critiques a été élogieux, et on comprend pourquoi : c'est un film qui reste en mémoire.

In English: the reviewer calls the film sensitive and its script accurate, praises the three
actresses, regrets a last half hour that is too long and hesitates between endings, and
concludes that, despite these weaknesses, the critics' praise is deserved. Notes: *signer un
film* = to make (literally, sign) a film; *d'une grande justesse* = very accurate, true to life;
*on regrettera* = one may regret (a polite futur of criticism).

## Introductions and conclusions

The **[[hook]]** (*l'amorce*) is the first sentence or two of the introduction: it catches the
reader's interest and leads to the question. It can be a recent fact, a figure (only a real
one, or one your documents give you), a short scene or anecdote, a paradox, or a common saying you will question.
Avoid "Since the dawn of time …" (*Depuis la nuit des temps …*), the most worn-out hook in
French.

An introduction then gives the problématique and announces the plan:

> *Commander un canapé à minuit, depuis son lit, en trois clics : ce geste est devenu banal. Acheter en ligne est si simple que l'on commande parfois sans réfléchir. Le commerce en ligne protège-t-il vraiment le consommateur ? Nous verrons d'abord les droits qu'il lui garantit, puis les limites de cette protection.*

In English: a scene (ordering a sofa at midnight, from bed, in three clicks, has become an
ordinary thing to do), the remark that buying online is so easy that people sometimes order
without thinking, the question (does online shopping really protect the consumer?), and the plan
(first the rights it guarantees, then the limits of that protection). *Si simple que* is a
consequence (B1).

The conclusion answers the problématique in new words (no new argument) and ends with an
*ouverture* (B1): a wider question the debate leads to. *Le consommateur est donc mieux
protégé qu'avant, à condition de connaître ses droits. Reste à savoir si la loi pourra suivre la
vitesse du commerce numérique.*

Your whole case (*l'argumentaire*: the set of arguments you use) should be visible in these two
paragraphs: a reader who reads only the introduction and the conclusion should know your
question, your plan and your answer.

## Register control

At B2 you keep one register from the first line to the last. In a formal letter or an article:
*vous*, no *ça* (use *cela*), no *on* for "we" where *nous* fits better, full negation (*ne …
pas*), no informal words (*super, nul, bosser, du coup*). On a forum the tone can be more
personal (*je*, a rhetorical question, an exclamation), but the grammar stays careful. A mix
(*Madame, Monsieur … ça craint*) reads worse than a text that is consistently neutral, and
register is one of the things examiners look at (lesson 24).

## A final checklist

Keep the last ten minutes for this:

1. **The task:** form, reader, length (count roughly: lines × average words per line).
2. **The plan:** introduction with a question, paragraphs that each do one job, a conclusion.
3. **Agreement** (lesson 03): adjectives and participles, especially after *être* and with a
   preceding direct object (*les lettres que j'ai reçues*).
4. **[[Moods]]** (lessons 05–08): subjunctive after *bien que, pour que, il faut que, il est
   paradoxal que*; indicative after *il n'en reste pas moins que, il est certain que*.
5. **[[Connectors]]** (lesson 21): varied, and each one doing the job it names.
6. **Punctuation:** a space before *; : ? !* and inside *« »* in French typography; a comma
   after a fronted connector (*Certes, …*).
7. **Spelling:** accents, plurals, *-é / -er* (*j'ai commandé, je vais commander*).

## Pronunciation

- *Le litige* [litiʒ]; *le préjudice* [pʁeʒydis].
- *Défectueux* [defɛktɥø]: three syllables, *dé-fec-tueux*, the *u* gliding into *eux*.
- *Le SAV* [ɛsave]; *la mise en demeure* [mizɑ̃dəmœʁ].
- *Élogieux* [elɔʒjø].

## Common mistakes

- Opening a letter with the threat. Facts first, request next, warning last.
- *Le préjudice* as "bias": that is *le préjugé*. *Le préjudice* is harm or loss.
- *Subir de* + noun: *subir* takes a direct object (*subir un préjudice*).
- *Je vous saurais gré ~~pour~~ …*: the construction is *savoir gré de* (*Je vous saurais gré
  de bien vouloir …*). The futur *Je vous saurai gré de …* is also grammatical but less usual;
  it can sound more like an instruction. Keep the conditionnel.
- A review that only summarises. The summary is the shortest part; the judgement is the text.
- Writing less than the minimum, or far more than you can check. Aim a little above it.
- *Le critique* (the person) and *la critique* (the review, or a woman critic): check the
  article.

## Key points

- The DELF B2 writing task is one argued text (a debate contribution, a formal letter, a
  critical article …), at least 250 words in the current format: follow the paper.
- **Letter of complaint:** facts → problem and harm → request → warning; *Je vous saurais gré de
  …, À défaut de réponse sous quinze jours, je me verrai dans l'obligation de …*.
- Remedies and steps: *remboursement, dédommagement, avoir, geste commercial*; *lettre
  recommandée avec accusé de réception, mise en demeure, médiateur*.
- **Critical review:** present, summarise briefly, judge with nuance (*élogieux, mitigé*),
  recommend.
- Introduction: **[[hook]]** (*amorce*), problématique, plan. Conclusion: answer and *ouverture*.
- Keep ten minutes for the checklist: task, plan, agreement, moods, connectors, punctuation.

lessons.title: Parler au niveau B2: presenting a view and debating it
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 21 and 22 built an argument on paper. This lesson does it out loud: a prepared talk in
which you present a short document and defend a view, then a debate in which someone challenges
you. That is the shape of the DELF B2 speaking test, and of many real situations: a meeting, an
interview, a class presentation. You'll learn to structure a talk so a listener can follow it,
to move from one part to the next, to answer objections without losing your thread, and to
sound formal without sounding written. The theme is society debates: working from home,
tourism, screens and children.

## The DELF B2 speaking test in general terms

In the current format, according to FEI's candidate manual, it works like this:

- You draw two subjects, each a short document (often a press extract that raises a debate),
  and choose one.
- You have about **30 minutes of preparation**, alone, with paper for notes.
- The test itself lasts about 20 minutes in all, in two parts: a **[[monologue suivi]]** (the
  manual gives 5 to 7 minutes), in which you present the document's question and defend your
  own point of view; then an **interaction**, a debate in which the examiner challenges what you
  said.

The document is a starting point, not a text to summarise: what is marked is your ability to
find its problem, take a position and defend it. Your examiner will often take the opposite view on
purpose, as a devil's advocate. Lesson 24 has the
other parts of the exam; the honors lesson 24h2 goes through a full model test.

![A timeline of the DELF B2 speaking test. On the left, separate, a block for the preparation, about 30 minutes, alone, with notes. Then the test itself, about 20 minutes in all, bracketed: first the monologue suivi, 5 to 7 minutes, presenting and defending a view; then the debate with the examiner, the rest of the time. A note says the times follow FEI's candidate manual and to check the instructions on the day.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Working from a short document

Here is the kind of short trigger document you might draw (original, about an invented town):

> **Écrans : Saint-Aubin lance « la semaine sans »**
>
> Pendant sept jours, les écoles de Saint-Aubin invitent les familles à éteindre télévisions, tablettes et téléphones après le dîner. Pour la mairie, il s'agit de « rappeler que le temps passé ensemble ne se remplace pas ». Certains parents saluent l'initiative ; d'autres la jugent naïve : « Mes enfants font leurs devoirs sur ordinateur. Je fais comment ? »

In English: for a week, a town's schools invite families to switch off all screens after dinner;
the town hall says time spent together can't be replaced; some parents welcome the idea, others
find it naive because their children do homework on a computer. *Saluer* here means to welcome
(an initiative).

The document gives you a fact, a reason and two reactions. It doesn't give you your view: that
is your job. In your preparation, ask three questions. What is the debate? (Should children's
screen time be limited, and by whom?) What is at stake? (Health, family life, school work.) What
do I think, and why? A possible question for your talk: *Faut-il limiter le temps d'écran des
enfants, et qui doit le faire : l'école, la mairie ou les parents ?*

## The monologue: structure you can hear

A listener can't look back a page, so the structure of an oral presentation must be said out
loud: announce it, follow it, mark each step. A **[[monologue suivi]]** (extended monologue) at B2
has the same parts as an essay, but with signposts.

### 1. Introduce the document and the question

- *Le document que j'ai choisi est un article paru dans un quotidien régional. Il aborde la
  question du temps que les enfants passent devant les écrans.* — The document I chose is an
  article published in a regional daily. It tackles the question of the time children spend
  in front of screens.
- *L'enjeu de ce débat, c'est la santé des plus jeunes, mais aussi le rôle des parents.* — What
  is at stake in this debate is the health of the youngest, but also the role of parents.
- *Cela nous amène à nous demander si …* / *La question qui se pose est la suivante : faut-il
  limiter le nombre de visiteurs dans les sites les plus fréquentés ?* (for a document on tourism)

To **cerner** the problem (pin it down) is the first thing examiners listen for: not "the
document is about screens" but the question it raises. *Aborder* is the verb for taking up a
subject: *J'aborderai d'abord …, puis …*.

### 2. Announce your position and your plan

- *Pour ma part, je pense que les écrans ne sont pas un danger en soi, à condition d'être
  encadrés.* — For my part, I think screens aren't a danger in themselves, as long as they're
  supervised.
- *Je présenterai d'abord les risques, puis les avantages, avant de proposer quelques règles.*

### 3. Move between parts: transitions

A **[[transition]]** closes one part and opens the next. Without them a talk sounds like a list.

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *J'en viens maintenant à mon deuxième point.* | I now come to my second point. |
| *Passons à présent aux avantages.* | Let's now move on to the advantages. |
| *Après avoir vu les risques, voyons ce que les écrans peuvent apporter.* | Having looked at the risks, let's see … |
| *Cela dit, il faut reconnaître que …* | That said, one has to admit that … |

*En venir à* takes *en* in every person: *j'en viens à, nous en venons à*; *Où voulez-vous en
venir ?* means "What are you getting at?" *Après avoir vu* is the past infinitive (B1): same
subject in both halves.

### 4. Conclude

- *Pour récapituler, …* (to sum up) or *En résumé, …* gives the main points again in one or two
  sentences.
- Then your answer and, if you have time, an opening: *Au fond, la vraie question est peut-être
  celle de notre propre usage des écrans.*

*Pour récapituler* is very common in speech; in a written conclusion, *en somme* or *pour
conclure* is more usual.

## Formal spoken connectors

At B2 you are expected to sound more formal than in conversation, without reading out an
essay. These connectors work well in speech:

| connector | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *à mon sens* | in my view (= *à mon avis*) | *À mon sens, le télétravail n'est pas fait pour tout le monde.* |
| *il va de soi que* + indicative | it goes without saying that | *Il va de soi que les enfants ont besoin de règles.* |
| *concrètement* | in practical terms | *Concrètement, cela veut dire deux jours par semaine à la maison.* |
| *en l'occurrence* | in this case | *Certains métiers, en l'occurrence ceux du soin, ne se font pas à distance.* |
| *à cet égard* | in this respect | *À cet égard, l'exemple de Venise est parlant.* |
| *de surcroît* (formal) | moreover | *C'est coûteux et, de surcroît, peu écologique.* |
| *qui plus est* | what is more | *Le trajet est long et, qui plus est, très cher.* |
| *soit dit en passant* | by the way, incidentally | *Ce rapport, soit dit en passant, a dix ans.* |

*Qui plus est* and *de surcroît* add a stronger point after a first one, usually between commas.
*Soit dit en passant* signals a side remark; keep it short and come back at once. *En
l'occurrence* points to the particular case you mean; it doesn't mean "on the occasion".

## The debate: defending, conceding, rebounding

In the second part, the examiner will question, contradict and push you. A good debate answer
does three things: it shows you understood the point, it gives ground where you must, and it
comes back to your position. *Rebondir* (B1), to bounce off what the other person said, is the
key skill.

### Understanding and reformulating

Reformulating the examiner's question gives you a few seconds and shows you understood it:

- *Si je vous comprends bien, vous me demandez si …* — If I understand you correctly, you're
  asking me whether …
- *Vous voulez dire que …, c'est bien ça ?* — You mean that …, is that right?
- *Pourriez-vous reformuler votre question ?* — if you really didn't understand. Asking is
  allowed and better than answering a different question.

### Answering an objection

An **[[objection]]** is an argument against what you said. Acknowledge it, then answer:

- *Je comprends votre objection, mais elle ne tient pas compte du coût.* — I understand your
  objection, but it doesn't take the cost into account.
- *C'est un argument recevable. Cependant, …* — That's a fair argument. However, …
- *Votre contre-exemple est intéressant, mais c'est une exception.* — Your counterexample is
  interesting, but it's an exception.
- *Je ne doute pas de la pertinence de votre remarque ; je dirais simplement que …* — I don't
  doubt the relevance of your remark; I'd simply say that …

A *contre-exemple* is a single case that contradicts a general claim. The best defence is often
to accept it as a case and deny it is the rule.

### Conceding without giving up

Conceding a point is a sign of strength at B2, as long as you keep your **prise de position**
(your stand):

- *Sur ce point, je vous l'accorde.* — On that point, I grant you that.
- *Vous avez raison de le souligner. Il n'en reste pas moins que …* — You're right to point it
  out. It is nonetheless true that …

### Gaining time naturally

Silence is fine for a second or two. Fillers that sound natural: *C'est une bonne question.
Comment dire … Disons que … Voyons …* What sounds bad: a long *euh*, or English.

### Digressions and refocusing

A **digression** wanders from the subject. Notice it and come back:

- *Mais je m'éloigne du sujet. Pour recentrer le débat : …* — But I'm wandering from the subject.
  To bring the debate back to the point: …

The examiner may *relancer* the discussion (keep it going) with a new question or a provocation
(*Et si on interdisait tout simplement les écrans avant six ans ?*). It's an invitation to
develop, not a trap.

## A debate extract

Working from home. The candidate has argued that *le télétravail* (working from home) is good
for both employees and companies; the examiner pushes back.

```dialogue lang=fr-FR
# Le télétravail en débat
Examinatrice: Vous dites que le télétravail améliore la qualité de vie. Mais beaucoup de salariés se sentent isolés chez eux, non ?
= You say working from home improves quality of life. But many employees feel isolated at home, don't they?
Candidat: Je comprends votre objection et, je vous l'accorde, l'isolement est un vrai risque. C'est pourquoi je ne défends pas le télétravail à temps plein.
= I understand your objection, and I grant you that isolation is a real risk. That's why I'm not defending full-time home working.
Examinatrice: Concrètement, vous proposez quoi ?
= In practical terms, what are you proposing?
Candidat: Deux ou trois jours par semaine. Les salariés gagnent du temps de transport et, qui plus est, l'entreprise réduit ses frais de bureaux.
= Two or three days a week. Employees save commuting time and, what is more, the company cuts its office costs.
Examinatrice: Et les métiers qui ne peuvent pas se faire à distance ? Une infirmière ne télétravaille pas.
= And what about jobs that can't be done remotely? A nurse doesn't work from home.
Candidat: C'est un bon contre-exemple. À cet égard, il faut être honnête : le télétravail concerne surtout les emplois de bureau. Il n'en reste pas moins que, pour ces emplois-là, il présente plus d'avantages que d'inconvénients.
= That's a good counterexample. In this respect, one has to be honest: home working mainly concerns office jobs. It is nonetheless true that, for those jobs, it has more advantages than drawbacks.
Examinatrice: Donc vous changez d'avis ?
= So you're changing your mind?
Candidat: Non, je précise ma position. Pour récapituler : le télétravail, oui, mais à temps partiel et seulement là où il est possible.
= No, I'm making my position more precise. To sum up: working from home, yes, but part-time and only where it's possible.
```

What the candidate does: he accepts the objection without giving up his position (*je vous
l'accorde … C'est pourquoi …*), answers *Concrètement* with a precise proposal, adds a point
with *qui plus est*, accepts the counterexample and limits it (*il faut être honnête … Il n'en
reste pas moins que …*), and refuses the trap "so you're changing your mind?" by presenting the
concession as a clarification. He ends with *Pour récapituler*. He never repeats the same
sentence twice and never just says *oui* or *non*.

## Keeping to your speaking time

Your *temps de parole* (speaking time) is part of the task. Too short (two minutes for the
monologue) and you can't show enough; too long and the examiner will stop you, maybe before
your conclusion. Practise with a watch: a plan with three parts of about two minutes each fits
the monologue. Speak to your listeners, your *auditoire*, not to your notes: look up, and use
your notes only for keywords.

## Pronunciation

- *En l'occurrence* [ɑ̃lɔkyʁɑ̃s]; *de surcroît* [də syʁkʁwa] (the *t* is silent).
- *Qui plus est* [ki plyzɛ]: liaison in [z] between *plus* and *est*.
- *L'enjeu* [lɑ̃ʒø], *les enjeux* [lezɑ̃ʒø].
- Intonation: in a list (*d'abord …, ensuite …, enfin …*) the voice rises on each item and
  falls on the last. A falling voice at the end of your conclusion tells the examiner you have
  finished.

## Common mistakes

- Summarising the document for five minutes. One or two sentences on the document; the rest is
  your view.
- Reading full sentences from your notes. Write keywords and your plan, not a script.
- Saying *oui* or *non* and stopping. Every answer in the debate needs a reason and, if
  possible, an example.
- Treating every objection as an attack. Conceding a point is fine if you then come back to
  your position.
- *~~J'en viens maintenant de~~ mon deuxième point*: it is *en venir à*.
- *Qui plus est* as the first thing you say: it adds a second point, so it needs a first one.
- Running over time and losing the conclusion. Keep 30 seconds for it.

## Key points

- The DELF B2 speaking test: two subjects drawn, one chosen; about 30 minutes' preparation;
  about 20 minutes in all: a **[[monologue suivi]]** (5–7 minutes in FEI's manual), then a debate.
- Say the structure: the document and its question (*L'enjeu, c'est …*), your position, your
  plan, **[[transitions]]** (*J'en viens maintenant à …, Passons à …*), a recap.
- Formal spoken connectors: *à mon sens, il va de soi que, concrètement, en l'occurrence, à cet
  égard, de surcroît, qui plus est, soit dit en passant*.
- In the debate: reformulate the question, acknowledge the **[[objection]]**, concede what you must,
  and come back to your position (*Il n'en reste pas moins que …*).
- Notice digressions and refocus (*Pour recentrer le débat …*); keep to your speaking time.
