lessons.title: Le DELF B2: the exam and a course review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson explains what B2 means, describes the **[[DELF]]** B2 and how it is marked,
gives strategies for each part, and reviews the grammar of the course with charts and pointers
to the lessons. You don't need to sit an exam, but FEI's free sample papers are the best way to
check that you have reached the level.

## What B2 means

The six levels A1 to C2 come from the **[[CEFR]]** (Common European Framework of Reference for
Languages), published by the Council of Europe. B1 and B2 are "independent user" levels; B2 is
the upper one. The CEFR describes each level with **[[can-do statements]]**: what a learner is able
to do with the language, not which grammar they know. Summed up in our own words, someone at B2
can:

- follow the main ideas of a demanding text, whether it deals with facts or with ideas, and
  the specialist discussions of their own field;
- hold a conversation with native speakers at a natural pace, without either side having to
  make a special effort;
- write clear, detailed texts on many kinds of subject;
- explain a view on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of the options.

The step up from B1 is from connected speech and writing on familiar topics to argument on
abstract and topical ones, and from getting the message across to choosing *how* to say it:
register, nuance and precision. In French that has meant the subjonctif passé and the fine
choices between the moods, concession and conditions without *si*, every use of the
conditionnel, the nominal and impersonal style of the press, reported speech with attitude, the
passé simple for reading, and the essay, the letter and the debate of this module.

## The DELF B2

*DELF* stands for *Diplôme d'études en langue française*: the official French diplomas for levels
A1 to B2, awarded by the French Ministry of Education and run by France Éducation international
(FEI). Each level is a separate diploma, valid for life; you can take the B2 without having taken
the B1. The adult version is the *DELF tout public*. The figures below follow FEI's candidate
manual and its description of the revised papers; FEI's own pages are the final word, so check
them before you register.

| part | time | what it involves (in the current format) |
|---|---|---|
| *Compréhension de l'oral* (listening) | about 30 minutes | three exercises on five recordings (two longer radio-style documents and three short ones); some are heard twice, the short ones once; multiple choice with three options |
| *Compréhension des écrits* (reading) | 1 hour | three exercises on five texts: two longer informative or argumentative texts, then three short texts by three people, where you say which person holds a given view; multiple choice |
| *Production écrite* (writing) | 1 hour | one argued text giving your position (a contribution to a debate, a formal letter, a critical article …), at least 250 words |
| *Production orale* (speaking) | about 20 minutes, after about 30 minutes of preparation | a prepared monologue presenting and defending a view from a short document, then a debate with the examiner |

![An overview chart of the DELF B2. A box for the written papers, taken together in about 2 hours 30, holds three parts side by side: compréhension de l'oral, listening, about 30 minutes, three exercises, multiple choice, 25 points; compréhension des écrits, reading, 1 hour, three exercises, multiple choice, 25 points; production écrite, writing, 1 hour, one argued text of at least 250 words, 25 points. A separate box for the speaking test, production orale: about 30 minutes of preparation, then about 20 minutes, a monologue and a debate, 25 points. Below: total 100 points; pass with 50, and at least 5 out of 25 in every part; check FEI's pages, as details can change.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each part is marked out of 25. The three written parts are taken together, in about two and a
half hours; the speaking test is separate, often later the same day or on another day. To pass
(*être admis*) you need 50 points out of 100 **and** at least 5 out of 25 in every part. A mark
below 5 in any part fails the diploma (*ajourné*), even with a total above 50: the *seuil* (the
minimum) applies part by part.

### The new format, and older books

FEI revised the listening and reading papers from 2020, phasing the new papers in over a few
years. Its description of the change says that open questions and true/false questions were
removed from the B2 comprehension papers, that each paper now has three exercises on five
documents, and that the reading exercise where you attribute views to three people is new.
Older practice books (and papers from before the transition) have two exercises with one document
each, open answers and true/false questions. If your book looks like that, it still trains
the skills, but practise the format with FEI's own sample papers:

- [DELF B2 tout public: description of the exam](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-b2)
- [DELF B2 sample papers (exemples de sujets)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-b2/exemples-sujets)

Each *centre d'examen* (exam centre) sets its own sessions, fees and deadlines: ask the centre
where you register.

## How the exam is marked

The listening and reading papers are marked by key: one right answer per question.
Preparation guides say wrong answers don't lose points, so never leave a question blank, but
read the instructions on the day.

The writing and speaking parts are marked by a *correcteur* or *correctrice* (for the oral, an
examiner) with a *grille d'évaluation* (marking grid), a list of *critères*. FEI announced new
grids with the revision, so the exact list and point split may change; in general terms, they
look at:

- **the task:** did you do what was asked (form, reader, length)? A *hors-sujet* (an off-topic
  answer) costs a great deal, whatever the quality of the French;
- **register:** is the tone right for the reader (*le registre*: *vous*, formulas, no slang in a
  formal letter)?
- **argument:** do you present facts and defend a position, with examples?
- **coherence and cohesion:** does the text have a plan, and do the sentences link? *La cohésion*
  comes from *connecteurs* (connectives), pronouns and synonyms; *la cohérence* (B1) is the
  logic of the whole;
- **vocabulary:** range and precision (*le lexique* of the topic), and spelling;
- **grammar:** correct forms, and sentences complex enough for B2 (subordinate clauses, the
  subjunctive where it belongs);
- at the oral, also **pronunciation** and how well you interact: answer, nuance, defend.

In the reading and listening papers, the trap is the *contresens*: understanding the opposite
of what the text says, often because of a negation, a concession (*certes … mais*) or a word
such as *éventuellement* ("possibly", not "eventually").

## Strategies for each part

### Listening

- Read the questions and the options before each recording: they tell you what to listen for.
- For the documents heard twice: note the main idea and the speakers' positions the first time;
  check details the second.
- The short documents are heard once: be ready before they start.
- Wrong options often repeat words from the recording; the right one usually says the same
  thing in other words.

### Reading

- Read the questions first, then the text. Find where each answer is; don't rely on memory.
- For the long texts, mark the connectors: *pourtant, or, en revanche, il n'en reste pas moins
  que* tell you where the author really stands.
- For the short opinions: summarise each person's view in three words before reading the
  questions (*pour, contre, pour mais …*).

### Writing

- Spend about ten minutes reading the task and planning (lessons 21–22), about forty writing,
  and ten on *la relecture* (rereading) with the checklist of lesson 22.
- Answer the question asked. The first check is *Suis-je dans le sujet ?*
- Show your B2 grammar where it fits naturally: a concession, a refutation, a subjunctive, a
  conditionnel of hedging. Don't force it.
- Count your words roughly and write the total at the end of your *copie* (answer paper).

### Speaking

- Use the 30 minutes to find the question, your position and a plan, with keywords and an
  example per point (lesson 23; the honors lesson 24h2 goes through a full model test).
- Prepare two objections the examiner is likely to make, and your answer to each.

### Before the day

Do at least one *examen blanc* (mock exam) in real conditions, with a timer, using a sample
paper. Then do an *autoévaluation* (self-assessment): list your *points forts* (strengths) and
*points faibles* (weaknesses), find your *lacunes* (gaps in knowledge), and use the lesson
pointers below to *combler* them (fill them). If one part is far behind the others, work on it
first: every part needs 5/25. Your *progression* (steady progress over time) matters more than
any one result.

## Reading practice: who thinks what?

Three people answer the question *Faut-il supprimer les notes à l'école ?* Read them, then
answer the questions in the lesson quiz.

> **Camille, enseignante :** Les notes découragent les élèves les plus fragiles. Un 6 sur 20 ne dit pas à un enfant ce qu'il doit faire pour progresser. Je préfère des appréciations précises : ce qui est acquis, ce qui ne l'est pas encore.
>
> **Hugo, père de deux enfants :** Je comprends les critiques, mais sans notes, je ne saurais pas où en sont mes enfants. Les appréciations sont souvent vagues. Qu'on améliore les notes, d'accord ; qu'on les supprime, non.
>
> **Inès, lycéenne :** Les notes ne me dérangent pas en soi. Ce qui me gêne, c'est la comparaison permanente avec les autres. Si chacun était évalué par rapport à ses propres progrès, l'école serait moins stressante.

Translation:

> **Camille, teacher:** Marks discourage the most fragile pupils. A 6 out of 20 doesn't tell a child what to do to improve. I prefer precise comments: what has been mastered, what hasn't yet.
>
> **Hugo, father of two:** I understand the criticism, but without marks I wouldn't know where my children stand. Comments are often vague. Improve marks, fine; abolish them, no.
>
> **Inès, secondary-school student:** Marks don't bother me in themselves. What bothers me is the constant comparison with others. If everyone were assessed against their own progress, school would be less stressful.

Notes: *l'appréciation* = teacher's comment; *acquis* = mastered (learnt); *où en sont mes
enfants* = where my children are at; *Qu'on améliore …, qu'on les supprime, non*: a
*que*-clause in the subjunctive at the start of a sentence (lesson 07), here meaning "That we
should improve them, fine". Camille is against marks, Hugo for keeping them, and Inès against
one way of using them: the questions test that kind of nuance.

## Review: the grammar of the course

### Indicative, subjunctive or conditionnel?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the mood after que or a conjunction at B2
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question: is the clause presented as a fact, something known, said or perceived, as after je sais que, il est certain que, il n'en reste pas moins que, parce que? If yes, the indicative. If not, second question: is it wanted, needed, felt, doubted, denied or only possible, or does it follow bien que, pour que, de peur que, quel que soit, à condition que, or a relative after a superlative or a wished-for antecedent? If yes, the subjunctive, with the subjonctif passé if the action comes before the main verb, as in bien qu'elle ait perdu. Third: is it hypothetical, or a claim you report without confirming it? Then the conditionnel, as in selon le ministre, il y aurait eu une erreur. A note says some frames accept two moods: après que, le fait que, a superlative plus relative.
  A["A verb after que or a conjunction"] --> B{"Presented as a fact: known, said, perceived?"}
  B -- yes --> I["Indicative: je sais que, il est certain que, parce que"]
  B -- no --> C{"Wanted, needed, felt, doubted, denied, only possible; or bien que, pour que, de peur que, quel que soit?"}
  C -- yes --> S["Subjunctive (05–08); subjonctif passé if earlier: bien qu'elle ait perdu"]
  C -- no --> D{"Hypothetical, or a claim reported without confirming it?"}
  D -- yes --> K["Conditionnel (09–10): il y aurait eu une erreur"]
  D -- no --> I
  S -.-> N["Two moods accepted in some frames: après que, le fait que, superlative + relative (06, 07)"]
```

Lessons 05–08: the subjonctif passé, the subjunctive in relative clauses (*un appartement qui
soit calme*), verbs whose mood changes their meaning, and concession (*quel que soit, si … que,
quand bien même* + conditionnel). Lessons 09–11: conditions without *si*, the conditionnel in all
its uses, *devoir* and *pouvoir* of probability.

### Connectors by grammar

Lesson 21 groups the connectors by function. Grouped by what follows them:

| followed by | cause, consequence | purpose | opposition, concession |
|---|---|---|---|
| indicative | *d'autant que, dès lors que, au point que, de sorte que* (result) | — | *alors que, tandis que, même si, il n'empêche que, il n'en reste pas moins que* |
| subjunctive | *non que* (a rejected cause) | *pour que, afin que, de peur que, de crainte que* | *bien que, encore que, quel que soit* |
| conditionnel | — | — | *quand bien même* |
| infinitive | *au point de* | *pour, afin de, de peur de, en vue de* | *loin de, quitte à, au lieu de* |
| noun | *compte tenu de, à la suite de, de là* | *en vue de* | *malgré, en dépit de* |

### Tenses: productive and for reading

| tense | example | use | lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| passé composé / imparfait | *il est entré ; il pleuvait* | events / background, in speech and most writing | B1 |
| plus-que-parfait | *il était parti* | a past before the past | B1 |
| futur antérieur | *quand il aura fini ; il aura oublié* | done before a future point; a guess about the past | 04 |
| conditionnel passé | *j'aurais dû ; il aurait menti* | unreal past; a reported claim | 10 |
| subjonctif passé | *bien qu'il soit parti* | a past action after a subjunctive trigger | 05 |
| passé simple (reading) | *il entra, ils firent* | written narrative | 01 |
| passé antérieur (reading) | *dès qu'il eut fini* | the past before a passé simple | 01 |
| imperfect / pluperfect subjunctive (reading) | *qu'il fût, qu'il eût fini* | classical and literary prose | 04h1 (honors) |

You produce the first five; you recognise the last three and can turn them into the passé
composé or the present subjunctive.

### The course at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: French B2 at a glance
  accDescr: A map of the six modules of the course. Module 1, narrating and time, lessons 01 to 04: the passé simple for reading, time relations, participle agreement, the futur antérieur. Module 2, the subjunctive in depth, 05 to 08: subjonctif passé, relatives, mood choices, concession. Module 3, conditions and probability, 09 to 12: conditions without si, the conditionnel, probability, comparison. Module 4, precise and formal French, 13 to 16: relatives, nominalisation, passive alternatives, pronouns. Module 5, logical links and emphasis, 17 to 20: cause and consequence, purpose and opposition, reported speech, emphasis. Each module leads to the next, and the chain ends in module 6, arguing, writing and speaking, 21 to 24: the argued essay, letters and reviews, the oral, the DELF B2.
  M1["1. Narrating and time (01–04): passé simple, agreement, futur antérieur"] --> M2
  M2["2. The subjunctive (05–08): subjonctif passé, mood choices, concession"] --> M3
  M3["3. Conditions and probability (09–12): conditionnel, devoir, comparison"] --> M4
  M4["4. Precise, formal French (13–16): relatives, nominalisation, passive, pronouns"] --> M5
  M5["5. Links and emphasis (17–20): cause, purpose, reported speech, c'est … que"] --> M6
  M6["6. Arguing, writing, speaking (21–24): essay, letter, review, debate, DELF B2"]
```

If you had to keep three things from this course: the mood follows what you mean (fact,
wish, doubt or hypothesis), not the conjunction alone; formal French prefers nouns, impersonal
structures and precise connectors to chains of *et* and *mais*; and a B2 argument answers the
other side instead of ignoring it.

## What comes next

At C1 you will follow long, demanding texts and talks, understand what is implied as well as
what is said, and write and speak with full control of structure and register. The French
diplomas at C1 and C2 are the **[[DALF]]** (*Diplôme approfondi de langue française*); the honors
lesson 24h1 previews its signature task, the synthesis of documents. To *approfondir* (deepen)
your *maîtrise* (command) of French in the meantime: read the press and novels on the reading
list, listen to French radio and podcasts every day, and write something argued every week.

## Pronunciation

- *Le seuil* [sœj]: the *-euil* sound, as in *le fauteuil*.
- *Le critère* [kʁitɛʁ]; *le contresens* [kɔ̃tʁəsɑ̃s] (the final *s* is pronounced).
- *Ajourné* [aʒuʁne]; *admis* [admi] (the *s* is silent; *admise* [admiz]).
- *La cohésion* [kɔezjɔ̃]: two separate vowels, silent *h*.

## Common mistakes

- Giving up on your weakest part: every part needs at least 5/25.
- Practising only with old-format books. Do at least one recent FEI sample paper.
- A *hors-sujet* in the writing paper: rereading the question before you write the conclusion
  takes ten seconds.
- *Éventuellement* as "eventually": it means "possibly, if need be". "Eventually" is *finalement*.
- Learning a speaking answer by heart. Examiners notice, and the debate never follows your
  script.
- *Le critère* as feminine: it is masculine (*un critère important*).

## Key points

- B2: the upper "independent user" level of the **[[CEFR]]**: argue on abstract and topical
  subjects, fluently and with nuance.
- DELF B2 (current format): listening about 30 min, reading 1 h, writing 1 h (one argued text,
  at least 250 words), speaking about 20 min after about 30 min of preparation; each part /25;
  pass with 50/100 and at least 5/25 in every part; written parts together about 2 h 30.
- Comprehension papers: multiple choice with three options in the new format; older books have
  open questions.
- Productions are marked on the task, register, argument, coherence and cohesion, vocabulary,
  grammar (and pronunciation and interaction at the oral).
- Check FEI's pages, practise with its sample papers, and do one mock exam in real conditions.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. Félicitations : you have finished the core of French B2!

lessons.title: Honors: Vers le DALF C1: la synthèse de documents
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is a **C1 preview**: nothing here is needed for B2, and nothing is drilled. Lessons 21 and 22
taught you to defend your own view. The C1 writing task that most surprises B2 learners asks the
opposite: to combine what several documents say, fairly and briefly, **without** giving your
opinion. That exercise is the **[[synthesis of documents]]** (*la synthèse de documents*), and it is
also a real-world skill: briefing notes, literature reviews and press summaries all work this
way. You'll learn the method on an original two-document set and see a model synthesis.

## The DALF C1 in brief

The *DALF* (*Diplôme approfondi de langue française*) is the French diploma for C1 and C2, run by
FEI like the DELF. From what FEI's candidate manual (2022 version) and university descriptions
say, the C1 has the same four parts as the B2, each out of 25, with the same pass rule (50/100,
at least 5/25 in each part), but longer documents and longer tasks:

| part | in general terms |
|---|---|
| listening | about 40 minutes: one long recording and several short ones |
| reading | about 50 minutes: one long text of ideas |
| writing | 2 hours 30: a synthesis of several documents, then an argued essay on the same theme |
| speaking | about 30 minutes, after 1 hour of preparation: a presentation from several documents, then a discussion |

For the writing paper, FEI's 2022 manual gives **200 to 240 words** for the synthesis and **at
least 250 words** for the essay, each marked out of 12.5 (an older sample paper split the 25
points 13 and 12). One university's description gives the documents about
1,000 words in all. Until 2020 candidates chose a field (humanities or sciences) for the
writing and speaking papers; FEI's description of the reform says that choice was removed.
These details have changed before: check FEI's DALF C1 page and its sample papers, and follow
the instructions on your paper.

## What a synthesis is, and what it isn't

A synthesis is a new, short, organised text that gives the reader the content of a set of
documents, *le corpus*, as if they hadn't read them. Four rules make it different from
everything you have written so far:

1. **No personal view.** No *je pense*, no *à mon sens*, no judgement such as *l'auteur a tort*.
   Your opinion goes in the essay that follows, not here.
2. **Nothing from outside.** Only what the documents say: no extra example, no fact you know.
3. **Your own words.** You reformulate; copying sentences is penalised. Key technical terms can
   stay.
4. **Organised by ideas, not by documents.** "Document 1 says …, document 2 says …" is a
   summary of each, not a synthesis. A synthesis is built around the questions the documents
   answer, and shows where they agree and disagree.

The skill is to *condenser* (condense) about a thousand words into about two hundred without
losing what matters, and to *confronter* the documents (set them side by side) so the reader sees
the debate.

## The method

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The method for a synthesis of documents
  accDescr: Seven steps from top to bottom. 1, read the whole corpus once, for the common theme. 2, find the shared question the documents answer, the problématique. 3, reread and note each document's main ideas in a few words. 4, compare them in a grid, idea by idea, marking where they converge and where they diverge, and cross-check the facts. 5, rank the ideas by importance and drop the details. 6, build a neutral plan of two or three parts, each part an idea, not a document. 7, write, then count the words and reread.
  A["1. Read the whole corpus: what is the common theme?"] --> B["2. Find the shared question (problématique)"]
  B --> C["3. Note each document's main ideas in a few words"]
  C --> D["4. Compare in a grid: convergent or divergent? Cross-check the facts"]
  D --> E["5. Rank the ideas; drop details and examples"]
  E --> F["6. A neutral plan: 2 or 3 parts, each an idea"]
  F --> G["7. Write, count the words, reread"]
```

Steps 4 and 5 are the heart of it. In step 4, *la confrontation des documents* (comparing them
side by side), you look for convergences (points where the
documents agree: *des analyses convergentes*) and divergences (points where they disagree:
*des avis divergents*). You also *recouper* the facts: if two documents give the same figure or
the same event, it is solid; if they give different figures, the synthesis says so neutrally. In
step 5 you *hiérarchiser* (rank) the ideas: the main ones get a sentence; secondary ones a few
words; examples usually disappear. The *hiérarchie* of ideas then becomes your plan.

Useful neutral language:

| to … | French |
|---|---|
| attribute a view | *selon l'auteur du premier document, …; d'après une économiste, …* |
| report with a verb | *X souligne, estime, rappelle, met en garde contre, reconnaît que …* |
| show agreement | *Les deux documents s'accordent sur …; Tous deux constatent que …* |
| show disagreement | *En revanche, …; Les avis divergent sur …; Là où l'un voit …, l'autre …* |
| sum up the debate | *Le débat porte donc moins sur … que sur …* |

Nominalisation (lesson 14) is your best tool for condensing: *Les tarifs ont été supprimés, ce
qui a fait augmenter le nombre de voyageurs* becomes *la suppression des tarifs a entraîné une
hausse de la fréquentation*.

## Example 1: two documents and a grid

The corpus below is original and short (two documents of about 90 words each; a real C1 corpus
is much longer and usually has three). The theme: free public transport. The town is invented.

> **Document 1. « La gratuité, une mesure de justice » (tribune du maire de Valmont)**
>
> Depuis que nos bus sont gratuits, il y a deux ans, la fréquentation a presque doublé. Ce chiffre dit l'essentiel : la gratuité rend la ville à ceux qui en étaient exclus, les jeunes, les retraités, les familles modestes. Bien sûr, la mesure a un coût, car il a fallu renoncer aux recettes des billets. Mais ces recettes ne couvraient qu'une petite partie du budget du réseau, et le centre-ville, plus accessible, a retrouvé des commerces. La gratuité n'est pas un cadeau : c'est un investissement dans la cohésion sociale et dans la qualité de l'air.
>
> **Document 2. « Gratuité des transports : une fausse bonne idée ? » (article d'une économiste)**
>
> Les villes qui rendent leurs bus gratuits annoncent toutes une hausse spectaculaire de la fréquentation. Encore faut-il savoir d'où viennent ces nouveaux voyageurs. Les études disponibles montrent qu'une partie importante d'entre eux marchaient ou se déplaçaient à vélo auparavant : les automobilistes, eux, changent peu leurs habitudes. Par ailleurs, le manque à gagner doit être compensé par l'impôt, au risque de freiner les investissements dans un réseau plus fréquent et plus rapide. Or, pour convaincre les automobilistes de laisser leur voiture, la qualité du service compte davantage que le prix.

In English: the mayor says ridership almost doubled in two years, that free buses give access to
the city to young, retired and low-income people, that ticket income covered only a small share
of costs, that the town centre regained shops, and calls free transport an investment in social
cohesion and clean air. The economist says the new passengers are often former walkers and
cyclists, that drivers change little, that the lost income must come from taxes and may slow
investment, and that quality of service matters more than price for getting people out of their
cars. Glosses: *la fréquentation* = ridership, number of users; *la tribune* = opinion piece;
*les recettes* = income (takings); *le manque à gagner* = lost income; *encore faut-il* + infinitive
= one still has to (formal inversion after *encore*, lesson 20).

The grid (step 4):

| idea | Document 1 (mayor) | Document 2 (economist) | relation |
|---|---|---|---|
| ridership | almost doubled | rises sharply everywhere | **convergent** (the fact) |
| who the new passengers are | young, retired, low-income people | often former walkers and cyclists; few drivers | **divergent** (the reading of the fact) |
| cost | real but limited (tickets covered little) | must be paid by taxes; may slow investment | **divergent** |
| what matters most | access and social cohesion; air quality | quality of service, more than price | **divergent** |

Cross-checking (*recouper*): both documents agree that ridership rises. They disagree on what the
rise means. That is the problématique: *La gratuité des transports en commun est-elle un moyen
efficace de changer les habitudes de déplacement ?* Ranking: the main ideas are ridership, the
profile of the new users and the cost; the town centre's shops are a secondary example and can
go.

## Example 2: the model synthesis

A neutral plan in two parts: (I) an observed success, (II) a contested effectiveness.

> **La gratuité des transports en commun : succès ou illusion ?**
>
> Rendre les bus gratuits suffit-il à changer nos façons de nous déplacer ? Les deux documents, la tribune d'un maire et l'article d'une économiste, s'accordent sur un constat mais divergent sur sa portée.
>
> Tous deux reconnaissent que la gratuité fait nettement augmenter la fréquentation des réseaux. Pour le maire, cette hausse prouve que la mesure ouvre la ville aux publics qui en étaient exclus, faute de moyens, et qu'elle profite à la vie du centre comme à la qualité de l'air.
>
> L'économiste nuance toutefois ce bilan. Selon elle, les nouveaux voyageurs sont souvent d'anciens piétons ou cyclistes, tandis que les automobilistes changent peu leurs habitudes. Le coût de la mesure fait lui aussi débat : jugé modeste par le maire, puisque les billets ne finançaient qu'une faible part du réseau, il pèserait selon l'économiste sur les impôts et sur les investissements futurs. Elle estime enfin que la qualité du service compte davantage que son prix.
>
> La gratuité apparaît donc comme une mesure sociale reconnue, mais dont l'efficacité contre l'usage de la voiture reste discutée.

(About 180 words with the title. That is as long as the two short documents together, only
because this corpus is tiny: with a real corpus of about 1,000 words, the range on the paper
means keeping about a fifth.)

Translation:

> **Free public transport: success or illusion?**
>
> Is making buses free enough to change the way we get around? The two documents, an opinion piece by a mayor and an article by an economist, agree on an observation but differ on how far it goes.
>
> Both acknowledge that free transport clearly increases the number of passengers. For the mayor, this rise proves that the measure opens the city to people who were excluded from it for lack of means, and that it benefits the life of the town centre as well as air quality.
>
> The economist, however, qualifies this assessment. According to her, the new passengers are often former pedestrians or cyclists, while drivers change their habits little. The cost of the measure is also debated: considered modest by the mayor, since tickets funded only a small share of the network, it would, according to the economist, weigh on taxes and on future investment. Finally, she considers that the quality of the service matters more than its price.
>
> Free transport therefore appears as a recognised social measure, but one whose effectiveness against car use remains disputed.

What makes it a synthesis:

- **Organised by ideas:** part one is the point of agreement, part two the points of
  disagreement; the documents appear inside each part, never one after the other as blocks.
- **Neutral:** every view is attributed (*pour le maire, selon elle*); no *je*, no judgement. The
  conditionnel *pèserait* reports the economist's claim without endorsing it (lesson 10).
- **Condensed:** the shops of the town centre became *la vie du centre*; the figures and the
  examples are gone; *faute de moyens* sums up "young, retired and low-income people".
- **Readable alone:** someone who hasn't seen the documents understands the debate.
- **Reformulated:** *la fréquentation a presque doublé* became *fait nettement augmenter la
  fréquentation*; *le manque à gagner doit être compensé par l'impôt* became *pèserait sur les
  impôts*.

## Common mistakes

- Giving your opinion, even in the last line (*À mon avis, la gratuité est une bonne idée*). The
  conclusion of a synthesis sums up the debate; it doesn't settle it.
- Summarising document 1, then document 2. Build the parts around ideas.
- Adding an example you know (Dunkirk, Tallinn …) that isn't in the documents.
- Copying whole phrases. Reformulate, keep only key terms.
- Keeping every detail. *Hiérarchiser* means deciding what to drop.
- Confusing a synthesis with the B2 essay: the essay that follows is where you argue.
- Ignoring the word range. Count, and write the number at the end if the instructions ask.

## Key points

- C1 preview: the DALF C1 writing paper (2 h 30) has a **synthesis** (200–240 words in FEI's
  2022 manual) and an argued essay (at least 250 words); check FEI's current pages.
- A synthesis combines a corpus for a reader who hasn't read it: no opinion, nothing from
  outside, your own words, organised by ideas.
- Method: read, find the shared question, note, *confronter* in a grid (*convergences,
  divergences*), *recouper*, *hiérarchiser*, plan, write, count.
- Neutral tools: *selon, d'après*, reporting verbs, *s'accorder sur, en revanche*, the reportive
  conditionnel, and nominalisation to condense.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: L'oral du DELF B2 en pratique
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 23 gave you the language of a talk and a debate. This honors lesson puts it to work on a
full model test: two short trigger documents, the 30 minutes of preparation minute by minute, a
model **[[monologue suivi]]** with commentary, and a model debate in which the candidate contradicts
himself and recovers. It ends with the mistakes examiners hear most. The times follow FEI's
candidate manual (about 30 minutes of preparation, a monologue of 5 to 7 minutes, about 20
minutes in all); check the instructions on the day.

## The two documents

You draw two subjects and choose one. Each *support* (prompt document) is short: it raises a
debate but doesn't settle it. Here are two original ones, about invented places.

> **Sujet A. Lorvan limite le nombre de visiteurs**
>
> Dès l'été prochain, la petite ville côtière de Lorvan n'accueillera plus que 5 000 visiteurs par jour sur son île, contre près de 12 000 aujourd'hui. Réservation obligatoire, accès payant : la mairie veut « protéger les habitants et la nature ». Les commerçants, eux, craignent une baisse de leur chiffre d'affaires.
>
> **Sujet B. Fini les devoirs à la maison à l'école Jean-Moulin**
>
> L'école primaire Jean-Moulin a décidé de supprimer les devoirs écrits à la maison. « Les enfants qui ont des parents disponibles sont avantagés », explique la directrice. Certains parents approuvent ; d'autres s'inquiètent de ne plus savoir ce que leurs enfants apprennent.

In English: in A, a small coastal town will cap visitors to its island at 5,000 a day (against
nearly 12,000 now), with compulsory booking and a fee, to protect residents and nature; shop
owners fear lower takings. In B, a primary school drops written homework, because children with
available parents have an advantage; some parents approve, others worry they won't know what
their children are learning. *Le chiffre d'affaires* = turnover, takings.

Which to choose? The one where you can find **two or three arguments and an example for each**
fastest, not the one whose theme you like best. Here the candidate chooses A: he has visited
crowded tourist towns and can give concrete examples.

## Example 1: thirty minutes of preparation

A plan for the 30 minutes (adapt it, but decide it before the day):

| minutes | what you do |
|---|---|
| 0–3 | read both documents, choose |
| 3–8 | *cerner* the problem: what is the debate, what is at stake? Write the question |
| 8–23 | the *plan détaillé* (detailed outline): position, two or three parts, an argument and an example in each, in keywords |
| 23–27 | write out your first two sentences and your conclusion in full |
| 27–30 | list two objections the examiner may raise, and your answer to each |

The *prise de notes* (note-taking) is the skill here. Write *mots-clés* (keywords) and arrows,
not sentences: if you write full sentences, you will read them, and reading sounds flat. The two
exceptions are your opening and your conclusion, which you may write out, because the first and
last seconds are the ones a nervous speaker loses.

Find a *fil conducteur* (common thread): one idea that links all your parts and that you can
come back to. Here: *Un lieu touristique appartient d'abord à ceux qui y vivent.*

![A candidate's preparation sheet for subject A, written as notes. At the top, the question: limiter les visiteurs, protéger ou exclure? Under it, the position: oui, mais quota juste et temporaire, and the common thread: un lieu appartient d'abord à ses habitants. Then three parts with keywords and arrows. Part 1, pourquoi limiter: habitants, logements, loyers; nature, sentiers abîmés. Part 2, les risques: commerçants, chiffre d'affaires; tourisme réservé aux riches si accès payant. Part 3, ma proposition: quota oui, tarif réduit jeunes et familles, bilan après deux ans. In a box at the bottom: objections, emplois perdus and la liberté de circuler, each with a short answer.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Example 2: a model monologue

This model is shorter than a real monologue: spoken at a calm pace, it takes about three
minutes. In the exam, a second example in each part, or a third argument, would bring it to the
five to seven minutes the task expects.

> Le document que j'ai choisi est un article sur la ville de Lorvan, qui va limiter à 5 000 par jour le nombre de visiteurs sur son île. La question qu'il pose est la suivante : faut-il limiter l'accès aux lieux touristiques pour les protéger, au risque d'en exclure une partie du public ? À mon sens, oui, à condition que la limite soit juste et temporaire. J'aborderai d'abord les raisons de limiter, puis les risques de cette mesure, avant de proposer une solution.
>
> Tout d'abord, pourquoi limiter ? Parce qu'un lieu touristique appartient d'abord à ceux qui y vivent. Quand une île reçoit douze mille visiteurs par jour, les logements deviennent des locations de vacances, les loyers montent, et les habitants partent. De surcroît, la nature souffre : j'ai vu moi-même, dans une région très fréquentée, des sentiers complètement abîmés en un seul été.
>
> J'en viens maintenant aux risques. Il va de soi que les commerçants vont perdre une partie de leur chiffre d'affaires, et des emplois sont en jeu. Qui plus est, si l'accès devient payant, le tourisme risque d'être réservé à ceux qui en ont les moyens. Ce serait un paradoxe : protéger un lieu en le rendant inaccessible aux familles modestes.
>
> Que proposer, alors ? Concrètement, je garderais le quota, mais avec un tarif réduit pour les jeunes et les familles, et un bilan au bout de deux ans, pour vérifier que la mesure protège vraiment l'île sans la vider.
>
> Pour récapituler : limiter, oui, parce qu'un lieu appartient d'abord à ses habitants ; mais limiter de façon juste. Au fond, la vraie question est peut-être de savoir quel tourisme nous voulons.

Translation:

> The document I chose is an article about the town of Lorvan, which is going to limit the number of visitors to its island to 5,000 a day. The question it raises is this: should access to tourist sites be limited to protect them, at the risk of excluding part of the public? In my view, yes, provided the limit is fair and temporary. I'll first tackle the reasons for limiting, then the risks of the measure, before proposing a solution.
>
> First of all, why limit? Because a tourist site belongs first and foremost to the people who live there. When an island receives twelve thousand visitors a day, homes become holiday lets, rents go up and residents leave. Moreover, nature suffers: I myself have seen, in a very busy region, paths completely damaged in a single summer.
>
> I now come to the risks. It goes without saying that shop owners will lose part of their takings, and jobs are at stake. What is more, if access becomes paid, tourism risks being reserved for those who can afford it. That would be a paradox: protecting a place by making it inaccessible to low-income families.
>
> So what should we propose? In practical terms, I would keep the quota, but with a reduced rate for young people and families, and a review after two years, to check that the measure really protects the island without emptying it.
>
> To sum up: limiting, yes, because a place belongs first and foremost to its residents; but limiting fairly. In the end, the real question may be what kind of tourism we want.

Commentary:

- **The opening** presents the document in one sentence, then the question, then the position
  and the plan: about 30 seconds, no summary of the article beyond that.
- **The thread** (*un lieu appartient d'abord à ceux qui y vivent*) appears in part one and again
  in the recap: the listener hears the same idea twice and remembers it.
- **[[Transitions]]** are said: *Tout d'abord …, J'en viens maintenant aux risques, Que proposer,
  alors ?* (a rhetorical question as a transition).
- **The concession is real:** part two gives the other side its best arguments (jobs, fairness)
  before part three answers them with a proposal.
- **The grammar shows B2 without effort:** *à condition que* + subjunctive, *au risque de*, *il va
  de soi que* + indicative, the conditionnel of a proposal (*je garderais*), *de façon juste*.
- **A personal example** (*j'ai vu moi-même …*) is allowed and useful at B2, as long as it backs
  up an argument.

## Example 3: a model debate

The examiner's job is to push. Here she takes the opposite view on purpose and catches the
candidate in a contradiction.

```dialogue lang=fr-FR
# Débat : Lorvan et ses visiteurs
Examinatrice: Vous parlez des habitants. Mais beaucoup d'entre eux vivent du tourisme. Les priver de visiteurs, c'est les priver de travail, non ?
= You talk about the residents. But many of them live off tourism. Depriving them of visitors means depriving them of work, doesn't it?
Candidat: C'est vrai pour une partie d'entre eux, je vous l'accorde. Mais 5 000 visiteurs par jour, c'est encore beaucoup pour une petite île. Le quota ne supprime pas le tourisme, il le limite.
= That's true for some of them, I grant you. But 5,000 visitors a day is still a lot for a small island. The quota doesn't abolish tourism, it limits it.
Examinatrice: Tout à l'heure, pourtant, vous disiez que l'accès payant était injuste. Et maintenant vous défendez un quota qui sera forcément payant.
= Earlier, though, you were saying paid access was unfair. And now you're defending a quota that will necessarily be paid.
Candidat: Vous avez raison de le relever : je me suis mal exprimé. Ce que je voulais dire, c'est que le prix ne doit pas exclure les familles modestes. Un accès payant avec un tarif réduit, ce n'est pas une contradiction.
= You're right to point that out: I put it badly. What I meant was that the price mustn't exclude low-income families. Paid access with a reduced rate isn't a contradiction.
Examinatrice: Et la liberté de circuler ? On ne peut pas interdire à quelqu'un d'aller sur une île.
= And freedom of movement? You can't forbid someone to go to an island.
Candidat: Justement, c'est un point intéressant. D'ailleurs, quand j'étais étudiant, j'ai travaillé un été dans un camping, et… pardon, je digresse. Pour revenir à votre question : on limite déjà l'accès à certains musées ou à certains parcs naturels, et personne ne parle d'atteinte à la liberté.
= Precisely, that's an interesting point. Actually, when I was a student, I worked one summer at a campsite, and… sorry, I'm digressing. To come back to your question: access to some museums or nature parks is already limited, and nobody calls it an attack on freedom.
Examinatrice: Donc, pour vous, une île est un musée ?
= So, for you, an island is a museum?
Candidat: Non, bien sûr. C'est un lieu de vie, et c'est justement pour ça qu'il faut le protéger. On en revient à mon idée de départ : un lieu appartient d'abord à ceux qui y vivent.
= No, of course not. It's a place where people live, and that's exactly why it must be protected. We come back to my starting point: a place belongs first and foremost to those who live there.
```

Commentary: the candidate concedes the first objection only partly (*pour une partie d'entre
eux*); when caught out, he doesn't deny it or panic but reformulates (*je me suis mal exprimé.
Ce que je voulais dire, c'est que …*) and shows the two ideas fit together; he notices his
digression and stops it himself (*pardon, je digresse. Pour revenir à votre question …*); he
answers a provocation calmly and returns to his *fil conducteur*. *Relever* here means to point
out (a mistake, a detail).

## Contradicting yourself and recovering

Everyone *se contredit* (contradicts himself or herself) sometimes under pressure, and examiners
sometimes *prennent le contre-pied* (take the opposite view) just to see how you react. What
counts is how you handle the *contradiction*:

- Admit and correct: *Je me suis mal exprimé(e). Ce que je voulais dire, c'est que …* / *Je me
  corrige : …*
- Show the two ideas are compatible: *Il n'y a pas de contradiction : …* (only if it's true).
- Change your mind openly, with a reason: *Votre argument me fait nuancer ma position : …*. That
  is not a failure; it shows you are listening.

What doesn't work: denying you said it, or abandoning your position completely at the first
objection.

*Se contredire* is conjugated like *contredire* (B1), with *vous vous contredisez* (not
*~~contredites~~*, unlike *vous dites*); its *se* is a direct object, so the participle agrees:
*elle s'est contredite*.

## Timing yourself

At home, practise with a *chronomètre* (stopwatch) or your phone's timer:

1. Choose a short article, give yourself 30 minutes, and prepare as in Example 1.
2. Record your monologue and time it. Under 5 minutes: add an example per part. Over 7: cut
   the introduction and any *digression*.
3. Listen back. Note every *euh*, every English word, every sentence you read from your notes.
4. Ask someone to play the examiner, or record five objections yourself and answer each in
   one minute.

You don't need to *digresser* to fill time; another example does it better.

## Common mistakes at the oral

- Spending three minutes summarising the document. One or two sentences, then the question.
- Notes in full sentences, read aloud with your eyes down.
- No position, or a position that disappears at the first objection.
- *Oui.* / *Non.* with nothing after it in the debate.
- Pretending you understood a question you didn't. Ask: *Pourriez-vous reformuler ?*
- Learning a monologue by heart for a topic you hope to get. The examiner notices, and the
  document will be different.
- Forgetting to greet and thank the examiner. It costs nothing (FEI's manual mentions it too).

## Key points

- Choose the subject where you find arguments and examples fastest.
- Plan the 30 minutes: read and choose, *cerner* the question, a *plan détaillé* in *mots-clés*,
  opening and conclusion in full, two objections ready.
- A *fil conducteur* makes a talk memorable: say it in part one and again in the recap.
- In the debate, concede part of an objection and come back to your thread; when you
  contradict yourself, reformulate (*Ce que je voulais dire, c'est que …*).
- Time yourself with a *chronomètre*: 5 to 7 minutes for the monologue in the current format.

lessons.title: Voltaire, Candide (1759)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors module opens with one of the most read French books of the eighteenth century,
Voltaire's *Candide*. You follow the story in French written for this lesson: the first half in the
**[[passé simple]]** (lesson 01), which you read but don't write, and the second half in the passé
composé, as you would tell it. Then you see how Voltaire's irony works and practise decoding it.
Nothing in this lesson is Voltaire's own text: the retelling and every example are original.
Lesson 92 covers the Enlightenment as a movement.

## Voltaire and the philosophical tale

Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie Arouet (Paris, 1694 – Paris, 1778): poet,
playwright, historian and, above all, a polemicist. He wrote *Candide* in 1758 while living near Geneva.
The book appeared early in 1759, printed by Gabriel Cramer in Geneva and almost at once in Paris
and other cities, without the author's name: the title page presented it as a translation from
the German of a certain "Doctor Ralph". The authorities banned it in several places, which
only helped it sell; about twenty editions came out in 1759 alone.

*Candide* is a **[[philosophical tale]]** (*un conte philosophique*): a short, fast story with
the look of a fairy tale whose real purpose is to test an idea. The characters are simple, almost
puppets; what matters is the argument the plot makes. The subtitle names the idea under test: *ou l'Optimisme*.

In Voltaire's day *l'optimisme* was not a cheerful mood but a philosophical system. The German
philosopher Leibniz had argued (in his *Essais de théodicée*, 1710) that God, being perfect, must
have created the best world that was possible, so that every evil serves some greater good;
the English poet Alexander Pope had put a similar view into verse. Voltaire's tutor-philosopher,
Pangloss, turns this into a formula he applies to everything. The opposite system, *le
pessimisme*, is defended later in the book by a character called Martin.

What made Voltaire impatient with the system was history. On 1 November 1755 an earthquake,
followed by a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of Lisbon and killed tens of thousands of people.
Voltaire answered with a poem on the disaster (1756), then with *Candide*, which sends its hero to
Lisbon on the very day of the earthquake. From 1756 Europe was also at war (the Seven Years' War,
1756–1763), and the book's battle scenes reflect it.

![A simplified map in two panels. Left, South America: a route from Buenos Aires up to Paraguay, across to a star marking the imaginary Eldorado in the Andes, then up to Surinam on the north coast, with dashed sea crossings to and from Europe. Right, Europe: a route from Westphalia to Holland, by sea to Lisbon, overland to Cadiz, then from Bordeaux to Paris, by sea from the Channel via Portsmouth round Spain to Venice, and by sea from Venice to Constantinople. A key shows solid lines for land and dashed lines for sea.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The story, part 1 (passé simple)

> Candide était un jeune homme d'une grande naïveté. Il vivait dans le château d'un baron, en Westphalie, où son précepteur, le docteur Pangloss, lui enseignait que le monde était parfaitement réglé et que chaque malheur servait un bien plus grand. Candide le croyait sans la moindre hésitation. Un jour, le baron le surprit en train d'embrasser sa fille, Cunégonde, et le chassa du château.
>
> Seul et sans un sou, Candide fut enrôlé de force dans l'armée des Bulgares. Il vit une bataille où les deux camps détruisirent des villages entiers, puis il s'enfuit en Hollande. Là, un homme généreux, Jacques, le recueillit. Peu après, Candide retrouva Pangloss, devenu un mendiant malade : des soldats avaient ravagé le château, et Cunégonde, disait-on, était morte. Jacques fit soigner Pangloss, puis les emmena vers Lisbonne.
>
> Près du port, une tempête fit couler le navire, et Jacques se noya. À peine Candide et Pangloss eurent-ils atteint la ville que la terre trembla et que la moitié de Lisbonne s'écroula. Pour éviter un nouveau désastre, les autorités religieuses décidèrent de brûler quelques « coupables » en public. Pangloss fut pendu et Candide fouetté. Une vieille femme le soigna, puis le conduisit auprès de Cunégonde, qui avait survécu.

*Candide was a very naive young man. He lived in a baron's castle in Westphalia, where his tutor,
Doctor Pangloss, taught him that the world was perfectly ordered and that every misfortune served
a greater good. Candide believed it without the slightest hesitation. One day the baron caught him
kissing his daughter, Cunégonde, and drove him out of the castle.*

*Alone and penniless, Candide was forced to join the army of the Bulgars. He saw a battle in which
both sides destroyed whole villages, then he fled to Holland. There a generous man, Jacques, took him in. Soon after, Candide found
Pangloss again, now a sick beggar: soldiers had laid waste to the castle and Cunégonde, people said,
was dead. Jacques had Pangloss treated, then set off with them for Lisbon.*

*Near the port a storm sank the ship and Jacques drowned. No sooner had Candide and Pangloss reached
the city than the earth shook and half of Lisbon collapsed. To prevent another disaster, the
religious authorities decided to burn a few "culprits" in public. Pangloss was hanged and Candide
flogged. An old woman tended his wounds, then took him to Cunégonde, who had survived.*

In the book the "Bulgars" and their enemies the "Abars" are invented peoples; many readers
see in them the armies of the Seven Years' War. The public burning is an *auto-da-fé*, a ceremony
of the Inquisition. Pangloss turns up again later: the hanging failed.

### Reading the tenses

The events are in the passé simple: *-er* verbs in *-a / -èrent* (*chassa, retrouva, emmena,
trembla, décidèrent, soigna*), *-i-* forms (*surprit, vit, détruisirent, s'enfuit, recueillit,
fit, conduisit*), and *fut* + participle for passives (*fut enrôlé, fut pendu*). The background is
in the imparfait (*était, vivait, enseignait, croyait*), and what happened before in the
plus-que-parfait (*avaient ravagé, avait survécu*). *À peine … eurent-ils atteint … que* is the
**[[passé antérieur]]** after *à peine … que*, with the inversion of written French (lessons 01 and
02): one event immediately before the next.

### Example 1: From the passé simple to the passé composé

Retell four sentences as you would say them.

1. *Le baron le surprit et le chassa.* Two *avoir* verbs, object pronoun *le* = Candide (masculine,
   so no visible agreement): *Le baron l'a surpris et l'a chassé.*
2. *Il s'enfuit en Hollande.* Pronominal, so *être*: *Il s'est enfui en Hollande.* For Cunégonde:
   *elle s'est enfuie*.
3. *Une tempête fit couler le navire.* *Faire* + infinitive: *Une tempête a fait couler le
   navire.* (*Fait* before an infinitive never agrees.)
4. *À peine eurent-ils atteint la ville que la terre trembla.* Speech avoids the passé antérieur:
   *Ils venaient d'arriver en ville quand la terre a tremblé* (they had just arrived when …).

## The story, part 2 (passé composé)

> Pour sauver Cunégonde, Candide a tué deux hommes, puis il s'est enfui avec elle et la vieille jusqu'à Cadix, d'où ils ont embarqué pour Buenos Aires. Recherché par la justice, il a dû repartir sans Cunégonde, avec son valet Cacambo. Au Paraguay, il a blessé le frère de Cunégonde, qui refusait leur mariage, et a cru l'avoir tué. Après bien des aventures, les deux voyageurs se sont perdus et sont arrivés par hasard dans l'Eldorado, un pays caché où l'or n'a aucune valeur, où personne ne persécute personne et où il n'y a ni procès ni prisons. Mais Candide voulait retrouver Cunégonde : ils sont repartis avec des moutons chargés d'or, et ils en ont perdu la plupart en chemin.
>
> Au Surinam, ils ont rencontré un esclave mutilé : il avait perdu une main au travail, et on lui avait coupé une jambe parce qu'il avait tenté de fuir. Candide a douté plus que jamais de la philosophie de Pangloss. Il a envoyé Cacambo racheter Cunégonde et il est rentré en Europe avec Martin, un savant pour qui le mal domine le monde. Ils sont passés par Paris, par un port anglais et par Venise, et partout ils ont vu la même misère, les mêmes vices.
>
> À Constantinople, enfin, Candide a retrouvé Cunégonde, devenue laide et esclave, et il a racheté tous ses anciens compagnons, Pangloss compris. Ils se sont installés dans une petite ferme, où ils se sont vite ennuyés.

In short: Candide flees from Europe to South America and back. Eldorado, hidden, peaceful and
fabulously rich, is the book's utopia (*l'utopie*), but Candide leaves it for love. An enslaved man in Surinam makes him doubt optimism more than ever, and
Martin, his pessimistic companion, finds evil everywhere in Europe. At the end the whole group is
reunited on a small farm near Constantinople, safe but bored.

Glosses: *mutilé* = maimed; *racheter* = to buy back (here, to free someone by paying); *s'ennuyer* = to be bored. Agreement check: *elle s'est enfuie*, *ils se sont perdus*,
*ils se sont installés* (pronominal verbs whose *se* is a direct object); *ils en ont perdu la
plupart* (no agreement with *en*, lesson 03); *devenue laide* (past participle used as an
adjective, agreeing with Cunégonde).

## The ending

In the last chapter the group meets an old farmer who lives contentedly by working a small plot of
land with his children and doesn't care about the news from the capital. Pangloss launches into
one more demonstration that everything has led to the best possible result. Candide answers him
with a short piece of practical advice, the most famous sentence in the book: the friends should
stop arguing and tend their own garden.

What the garden means has been argued over ever since. Most readers see in it a rejection of
grand systems in favour of modest, useful work; others read it as withdrawal from public life.
Voltaire himself went on campaigning very publicly after 1759 (lesson 92).

## Irony and satire

**[[Satire]]** (*la satire*) attacks people, institutions or ideas by making them ridiculous.
*Candide* is a satirical tale (*un conte satirique*) with many targets: the optimistic
philosophers, war and the princes who wage it, fanaticism (*le fanatisme*) and
intolerance (*l'intolérance*) in religion, slavery, the vanity of the nobility, the greed of
colonists. Pangloss is the satire of a philosopher who sees the hand of providence (*la
providence*, God's plan for the world) in every catastrophe.

Voltaire's main weapon is **[[irony]]**: saying something different from, often the opposite of, what
you mean, and trusting the reader to see the gap. In *Candide* it comes in a few recognisable
forms:

- **A naive viewpoint.** The story is told close to Candide, who believes what he is told; the
  reader sees what he doesn't.
- **A calm tone for horrors.** Massacres and tortures are reported in short, neutral sentences, as
  if they were normal.
- **Mock logic.** *Donc, par conséquent, c'est pourquoi* link ideas that don't follow from each
  other, imitating a philosopher's proof.
- **Mock praise.** An adjective of admiration (*admirable, sage, glorieux*) is attached to
  something absurd or cruel.

### Example 2: Decoding irony

These three sentences are pastiches written for this lesson, not quotations. Say what each one
claims and what it really means.

1. *Grâce à la guerre, les paysans n'eurent plus à s'inquiéter de leurs récoltes : il n'y en avait
   plus.* Literally war is presented as a benefit (*grâce à*); in fact the soldiers have destroyed
   the harvests. The connector *grâce à*, used for good causes, is the ironic signal.
2. *Le docteur démontra, par trois arguments irréfutables, que la maison avait brûlé pour le bien
   de ses habitants.* Mock logic: the solemn word *irréfutables* exposes the absurd conclusion. This
   is the satire of the optimist philosopher.
3. *Le ministre fut si satisfait de sa réforme qu'il décida sagement de ne jamais en mesurer les
   effets.* Mock praise: *sagement* (wisely) sits next to an irresponsible decision. The real
   message: he avoids facts that might contradict him.

## Common mistakes

- Taking *l'optimisme* in *Candide* for everyday optimism. Voltaire mocks a philosophical system
  that explains away suffering, not the habit of hoping for the best.
- Calling *Candide* a novel (*un roman*) in a French essay. It is usually called *un conte* (*un
  conte philosophique*); it is short (thirty brief chapters) and its characters are types.
- Reading ironic sentences literally: when praise sits next to cruelty, the praise is the target.
- Writing the passé simple in your own essay: summarise a story in the present (*Candide quitte
  le château …*) or the passé composé.
- Quoting the famous last sentence from memory in an exam and getting it wrong. Paraphrase it:
  *Candide conseille à ses amis de se consacrer à un travail utile et modeste.*

## Key points

- *Candide, ou l'Optimisme*: Voltaire (1694–1778), printed by Cramer in Geneva early in 1759,
  without the author's name, as a "translation" from the German; banned in several places and a
  best-seller at once.
- A **[[philosophical tale]]**: a short story that tests an idea, here the optimism of Leibniz and
  Pope, through a naive hero (*la naïveté*), his tutor (*le précepteur* Pangloss) and a pessimist
  (Martin).
- Real events behind the fiction: the Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755 and the Seven Years'
  War (1756–1763).
- Targets of the **[[satire]]**: optimism, war, fanaticism, intolerance, slavery, greed. Eldorado is
  a utopia (*l'utopie*).
- **[[Irony]]**: naive viewpoint, calm tone for horrors, mock logic, mock praise.
- The ending's advice to tend one's own garden is described and debated, not quoted.

lessons.title: Voix de la francophonie
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

French B1 (lesson 91) showed you the French-speaking world in numbers: official languages,
speakers, regional words. This lesson turns to its literature. French has been a language of
literature on every continent, often in places where it arrived with colonisation (*la
colonisation*). You meet some of the writers and movements every educated French speaker has
heard of, through facts and dates, not quotations. You also practise presenting a debate
neutrally, a DELF B2 skill, with the concession language of lesson 08 and the argument language of
lesson 21.

![A simplified map of the North Atlantic with seven points: Québec (Gabrielle Roy), Martinique (Aimé Césaire), Senegal (Léopold Sédar Senghor), Mali (griots and the epic of Sundiata), Belgium (Georges Simenon), Switzerland (C. F. Ramuz) and Algeria (Kateb Yacine and Assia Djebar).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Negritude: three students in Paris

In the early 1930s three students from France's colonies met in Paris: Aimé Césaire (1913–2008)
from Martinique, Léopold Sédar Senghor (1906–2001) from Senegal and Léon-Gontran Damas
(1912–1978) from French Guiana. Far from home, in a kind of voluntary exile (*l'exil*), they
found that the colonial school had taught them the history of "our ancestors the Gauls" and little
about Africa. Together they founded a movement that turned an insult into a source of pride:
**[[Negritude]]** (*la négritude*), the affirmation of Black identity and of African cultures, written
in French. They launched a student journal, *L'Étudiant noir*, in the mid-1930s, and Césaire is
usually credited with coining the word.

- Césaire's long poem *Cahier d'un retour au pays natal* (Notebook of a Return to My Native
  Land) first appeared in a Paris review in 1939. Back in Martinique, he was mayor of
  Fort-de-France for more than half a century (1945–2001) and a deputy in the French parliament.
- Senghor published in 1948 an anthology of new Black and Malagasy poetry in French, prefaced
  by Jean-Paul Sartre. A poet and a politician, he became the first president of independent
  Senegal (1960–1980), and in 1983 the first African elected to the Académie française. He
  defended *le métissage*, the mixing of cultures: in his view African and European
  cultures would enrich each other.

The movement was never one doctrine. Later African writers criticised Negritude as too focused on
an idealised past; others saw it as a necessary first step before decolonisation (*la
décolonisation*), which in French-ruled Africa came mostly around 1960.

## Before writing: the griots and oral tradition

Long before books, West Africa had its literature in speech. The griot (*le griot*), in
Mandinka *jeli*, is a hereditary keeper of memory: genealogies, the history of a family or a
kingdom, songs and epics, performed with music (often the *kora*). The griot is at once
historian, storyteller (*le conteur*, *la conteuse*), musician and adviser. The best-known epic is
that of Sundiata (*Soundiata*), founder of the Mali empire in the thirteenth century; the
historian Djibril Tamsir Niane published a French prose version in 1960, from the telling of a
Guinean griot.

This **[[oral tradition]]** gives francophone African literature a strong *oralité*: proverbs,
repetition, a narrator who addresses the audience, stories within stories. Birago Diop's *Les
Contes d'Amadou Koumba* (1947) are tales he heard from a family griot and rewrote in French.

## Québec, Belgium, Switzerland

- Québec: Gabrielle Roy (1909–1983), born in Manitoba, set her first novel, *Bonheur
  d'occasion* (1945), in Saint-Henri, a poor working-class district of Montréal during the war. In
  1947 it won the prix Femina, the first Canadian book to win it; in English it is *The Tin
  Flute*.
- Belgium: Georges Simenon (Liège, 1903 – Lausanne, 1989) wrote, under his own name and many
  pen names, several hundred novels and stories, among them the Maigret detective novels. Many
  readers in France think he was French.
- Switzerland: Charles Ferdinand Ramuz (1878–1947), from the canton of Vaud, wrote about
  peasants, mountain villages and the shores of Lake Geneva in a French close to the spoken
  language. His portrait appeared on the Swiss 200-franc note of the 1990s series.

## The Maghreb: writing in the colonial language

In Algeria, under French rule from 1830 to independence in 1962, French was the language of the
school and the administration, and many writers of the independence generation wrote in it.

- Kateb Yacine (1929–1989) published *Nedjma* in 1956, during the Algerian war: a novel with a
  broken chronology, four young men and the mysterious woman of the title, often read as an image
  of Algeria itself. In the 1970s he turned to popular theatre in Algerian Arabic.
- Assia Djebar (1936–2015, the pen name of Fatima-Zohra Imalayen), novelist, historian and
  film-maker, wrote about the lives and voices of Algerian women (*Femmes d'Alger dans leur
  appartement*, 1980; *L'Amour, la fantasia*, 1985). In 2005 she became the first writer from the
  Maghreb elected to the Académie française.

For writers like these, French raised a question of belonging (*l'appartenance*): can you
express one culture in the language of another? Many francophone writers have also written from abroad, some of them *exilés* (in exile) after
wars or dictatorships at home. The question has several defensible answers, which is exactly what
makes it a good DELF B2 topic.

## Reading: Écrire dans la langue de l'autre

> Pourquoi tant d'écrivains africains, antillais ou maghrébins ont-ils écrit en français, la langue de l'ancienne puissance coloniale ? D'abord, parce que c'était souvent la seule langue écrite qu'on leur avait enseignée : l'école coloniale ignorait les langues locales. Ensuite, parce que le français leur permettait d'être lus bien au-delà de leur pays, à Paris comme à Dakar ou à Montréal.
>
> Certains critiques y voient pourtant une contradiction : comment dénoncer la domination coloniale dans la langue de cette domination ? Quelques auteurs ont d'ailleurs fini par écrire aussi dans leur langue maternelle.
>
> D'autres répondent que ces écrivains n'ont pas simplement emprunté le français : ils l'ont transformé. Ils y ont fait entrer les rythmes de la parole, les proverbes, des mots venus d'autres langues. Si bien qu'aujourd'hui, le français n'appartient plus seulement à la France. Qu'on approuve ou non ce choix, il a profondément enrichi la littérature de langue française.

*Why have so many African, Caribbean or North African writers written in French, the language of
the former colonial power? First, because it was often the only written language they had been
taught: the colonial school ignored local languages. Next, because French allowed them to be read
far beyond their own country, in Paris as in Dakar or Montréal.*

*Some critics, however, see a contradiction in this: how can you denounce colonial domination in
the language of that domination? Some authors did in fact end up writing in their mother tongue as
well.*

*Others answer that these writers did not simply borrow French: they transformed it. They brought
into it the rhythms of speech, proverbs, words from other languages. So much so that today French
no longer belongs to France alone. Whether one approves of this choice or not, it has deeply
enriched literature in French.*

Notice the structure: two reasons (*D'abord … Ensuite*), an objection (*Certains critiques y
voient pourtant …*), a reply (*D'autres répondent que …*), and a conclusion that respects both
sides (*Qu'on approuve ou non …*, concession with *que* + subjunctive, lesson 08). *Y voient* uses
*y* for an idea; in *ils l'ont transformé* the participle agrees with *l'* (= *le français*),
masculine singular, so the agreement doesn't show.

### Example 1: A biographical notice in nominal style

Reference books and exam documents give lives in noun phrases (lesson 14). Turn the facts into a
notice.

Facts: *Senghor est né en 1906 au Sénégal. Il a été élu président en 1960. Il est entré à
l'Académie française en 1983.*

Notice: *Léopold Sédar Senghor (1906–2001). Naissance au Sénégal ; élection à la présidence du
pays en 1960 ; entrée à l'Académie française en 1983, une première pour un Africain.*

*Est né → naissance, a été élu → élection, est entré → entrée*: the noun takes the place of the
verb, and the dates carry the story.

### Example 2: Presenting a debate neutrally

Topic: *Un écrivain doit-il écrire dans sa langue maternelle ?* A neutral paragraph gives each side
its best argument and lets the reader judge.

*Certes, écrire dans sa langue maternelle permet de rester fidèle à sa culture et de la faire
vivre. Il n'en reste pas moins que le français ouvre l'accès à un public international. Si
certains y voient une forme de dépendance, d'autres y voient un outil de liberté.*

*Certes … il n'en reste pas moins que* (lesson 21) concedes and then balances; *si* of contrast
(lesson 18) sets two views side by side. No *je pense*: the paragraph presents, it doesn't take
sides.

## Common mistakes

- Treating *francophone* as "French". Simenon, Roy, Djebar or Senghor are not called French
  writers but writers in French: say *un écrivain francophone* or *de langue française*.
- Taking Negritude for a political party. It was a literary and cultural movement, though its
  founders also went into politics.
- Thinking a griot is only a singer. The griot is also a historian and a keeper of family and
  royal memory.
- *Colonial* has its masculine plural in *-aux*: *les empires coloniaux*, *les écoles coloniales*.
- Quoting a famous line you half remember. In an exam, give the author, the work, the date and
  the idea in your own words.

## Key points

- **[[Negritude]]**: Césaire, Senghor and Damas, students in Paris in the 1930s; *Cahier d'un retour
  au pays natal* (1939); Senghor, president of Senegal (1960–1980), Académie française (1983).
- **[[Oral tradition]]**: the griot, historian, storyteller and musician; the epic of Sundiata (Niane's
  French version, 1960); Birago Diop's *Contes d'Amadou Koumba* (1947).
- Québec: Gabrielle Roy, *Bonheur d'occasion* (1945, prix Femina 1947). Belgium: Simenon (Liège,
  1903). Switzerland: Ramuz (1878–1947).
- The Maghreb: Kateb Yacine, *Nedjma* (1956); Assia Djebar, Académie française (2005).
- Writing in French after colonisation raises questions of belonging and freedom: present the
  sides with *certes … il n'en reste pas moins que*, and keep your own view for the conclusion.
