lessons.title: Les Lumières et l'Encyclopédie
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 90 read one book of the eighteenth century. This lesson looks at the movement behind it:
**[[the Enlightenment]]** (*les Lumières*), the writers and thinkers who, roughly between the end of
Louis XIV's reign (1715) and the Revolution (1789), set out to examine every belief, law and
institution in the light of reason. You meet four authors and one collective work, see how ideas
travelled under censorship, and read about the Declaration of 1789 that turned some of these
ideas into law. Then you use the argument language of lesson 21 to present an idea and an
objection to it. The lesson presents ideas; it doesn't ask you to agree with them.

![A timeline from 1745 to 1790 with six dated events: 1748, De l'esprit des lois by Montesquieu; 1751, the first volume of the Encyclopédie; 1759, Candide by Voltaire; 1762, Du contrat social by Rousseau; 1763, Traité sur la tolérance by Voltaire; 1789, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. A shaded band from 1751 to 1772 marks the publication of the Encyclopédie.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Montesquieu and the separation of powers

Charles-Louis de Secondat, baron de Montesquieu (1689–1755), was a magistrate in Bordeaux before he
became a writer. His *Lettres persanes* (1721) look at Paris through the eyes of two invented
Persian travellers, a clever way of criticising French society from the outside. His great work,
*De l'esprit des lois* (1748), first published anonymously in Geneva, compares the laws and
governments of many peoples. Montesquieu distinguishes three kinds of government: the republic,
the monarchy and despotism (*le despotisme*), where one person rules by fear and without laws.

To protect freedom, he argues, power must not sit in one pair of hands. The power to make laws,
the power to carry them out and the power to judge should belong to different bodies, so that each
can check the others. This is the **[[separation of powers]]** (*la séparation des pouvoirs*). He took
part of the idea from what he had seen of England's institutions. It later influenced the authors
of the United States Constitution (1787) and the French Declaration of 1789.

## The *Encyclopédie*

The *Encyclopédie, ou Dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers*, directed by
Denis Diderot (1713–1784) with the mathematician Jean Le Rond d'Alembert (1717–1783), was the great
collective project of the age: 17 volumes of articles (1751–1765) and 11 volumes of plates
(1762–1772), written by more than a hundred contributors, among them Voltaire and Rousseau.

### Reading: Une encyclopédie contre les préjugés

> Au départ, l'éditeur Le Breton voulait simplement faire traduire une encyclopédie anglaise. Sous la direction de Diderot et de d'Alembert, le projet est devenu tout autre chose : un inventaire de toutes les connaissances de l'époque, des mathématiques à la fabrication du papier. Les planches, d'une grande précision, montrent les outils et les gestes de ces artisans que les savants avaient longtemps méprisés.
>
> Mais l'*Encyclopédie* ne se contente pas de décrire. Certains articles, en apparence inoffensifs, critiquent l'intolérance religieuse ou l'absolutisme ; des renvois d'un article à l'autre conduisent le lecteur attentif vers des idées plus audacieuses. Les autorités ne s'y sont pas trompées : en 1752, les deux premiers volumes ont été interdits, et en 1759, l'autorisation de publier a été retirée. D'Alembert, découragé, avait déjà quitté l'entreprise. Diderot, lui, a continué presque seul, en secret, pendant des années.
>
> Le succès a pourtant été considérable. Bien qu'elle ait coûté très cher, l'*Encyclopédie* a trouvé des milliers de souscripteurs dans toute l'Europe.

*At first the publisher Le Breton simply wanted to have an English encyclopedia translated. Under
the direction of Diderot and d'Alembert, the project became something quite different: an
inventory of all the knowledge of the age, from mathematics to the making of paper. The plates,
very precise, show the tools and movements of those craftsmen whom scholars had long despised.*

*But the Encyclopédie does not merely describe. Some articles, harmless on the surface, criticise
religious intolerance or absolutism; cross-references from one article to another lead the
attentive reader towards bolder ideas. The authorities were not fooled: in 1752 the first two
volumes were banned, and in 1759 permission to publish was withdrawn. D'Alembert, discouraged,
had already left the enterprise. Diderot carried on almost alone, in secret, for years.*

*Its success was nevertheless considerable. Although it was very expensive, the Encyclopédie
found thousands of subscribers all over Europe.*

Grammar to notice: *faire traduire* (*faire* + infinitive: to have something translated); *que les
savants avaient longtemps méprisés* (the participle agrees with *que* = *ces artisans*, masculine
plural, lesson 03); *Bien qu'elle ait coûté* is a subjonctif passé after
*bien que* (lesson 05). *L'absolutisme* is the system in which the king holds all powers, as Louis
XIV did.

## Voltaire and tolerance

In 1761 Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant of Toulouse, was accused of having killed his son to stop
him from becoming a Catholic. On flimsy evidence he was tortured and executed in March 1762. Voltaire, then
living at Ferney near the Swiss border, became convinced of his innocence and led a long public
campaign; his *Traité sur la tolérance* (1763) grew out of it. In 1765 Calas was declared innocent
after his death. Tolerance (*la tolérance*) here means accepting that others hold beliefs you
don't share, and refusing to persecute them for it.

A sentence about defending to the death the right of someone you disagree with to speak is often
attributed to Voltaire. He never wrote it: it comes from a 1906 book about him by the English
writer Evelyn Beatrice Hall, who later explained that the words were her own summary of his
attitude. It is a good reminder to check a quotation before using it.

## Rousseau and the social contract

Jean-Jacques Rousseau (Geneva, 1712 – Ermenonville, 1778) was often in conflict with the other
*philosophes*. In *Du contrat social* (1762) he asks what can make political power legitimate. His
answer: an agreement, the social contract (*le contrat social*), by which people join together
into one body and obey the laws they make together, the expression of the "general will". On this
view, sovereignty (*la souveraineté*), the supreme power in a state, belongs to the people. In
1762 Geneva condemned it together with his treatise on education, *Émile*, which was also
condemned in Paris, and Rousseau had to flee.

## Salons, cafés and censorship

Ideas circulated in literary salons (*un salon littéraire*, plural *des salons littéraires*): regular gatherings in private
houses, often hosted by women such as Madame Geoffrin or Julie de Lespinasse, where writers,
scientists and aristocrats discussed new books. They also circulated in cafés, academies and
letters. Censorship was real: a book needed royal permission, and bold works were printed abroad
(in Amsterdam or Geneva), published without the author's name and sold under the counter. Freedom
of expression (*la liberté d'expression*) was a demand, not yet a right.

## The Declaration of 1789

On 26 August 1789, a few weeks after the storming of the Bastille, the National Constituent
Assembly adopted the *Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen*: seventeen short articles
setting out human rights (*les droits de l'homme*) that the authors considered natural and
universal. In summary, and in our words: equality in rights from birth; sovereignty belonging to
the nation; the law as the expression of the general will, the same for everyone; the presumption
of innocence; freedom of opinion, including religious opinion, and the free communication of ideas
within the limits set by law; and the separation of powers, without which, says one article, a
society has no constitution. You can hear Montesquieu, Rousseau and Voltaire in it.

The Declaration still has legal force in France: the Constitution of 1958 refers to it in its
preamble, and since 1971 the Conseil constitutionnel has treated it as part of constitutional
law. Its limits were debated from the start. It said nothing about women's rights: in 1791 Olympe
de Gouges answered with her own declaration for women. And it did not end slavery in the colonies,
which France abolished in 1794, restored in 1802 and abolished for good in 1848.

## Presenting an idea and an objection

A B2 essay often has to present an idea fairly, then test it (lesson 21). The pattern: state the
idea, give its reason, introduce an objection, then answer or weigh it.

### Example 1: One idea, one objection

Idea: the separation of powers protects freedom.

*Selon Montesquieu, la séparation des pouvoirs protège la liberté : si un même homme fait la loi,
l'applique et juge, rien ne l'empêche d'abuser de son pouvoir. On pourrait objecter qu'un pouvoir
trop divisé devient lent, voire paralysé. Certes, la séparation ralentit parfois les décisions.
Il n'en reste pas moins qu'elle évite le despotisme, ce qui justifie, pour beaucoup, ce prix.*

The **[[refutation]]** (lesson 21) concedes the objection's truth (*Certes …*) and then weighs it
(*Il n'en reste pas moins que …*). *Voire* (= or even) strengthens a point; *ce qui justifie*
sums up the previous clause.

### Example 2: Presenting a work in one sentence

Facts: *Montesquieu publie De l'esprit des lois en 1748. Il le publie sans son nom, à Genève. Le
livre défend la séparation des pouvoirs.*

One sentence with a participle at the front: *Publié anonymement à Genève en 1748, De l'esprit des
lois défend la séparation des pouvoirs.* The participle agrees with the subject it describes
(*publié*, masculine, for the book; for *la Déclaration*: *Adoptée le 26 août 1789, la Déclaration
…*). Check that the participle and the subject really match: *Publié à Genève, Montesquieu défend …*
would mean that Montesquieu himself was published.

## Common mistakes

- Writing *les lumières* for the movement. The movement takes a capital: *les Lumières*, *le
  siècle des Lumières*. With a small letter, *les lumières* are lights.
- Treating *les droits de l'homme* as only men's rights. In this phrase *l'homme* means the human
  being; many people today prefer *les droits humains*, and both are common.
- Confusing the *contrat social* (a theory of legitimate power) with *un contrat* (A1) between two
  parties.
- Quoting the famous "defend to the death" sentence as Voltaire's.
- Giving every Enlightenment writer the same views: Rousseau quarrelled with Voltaire and with
  Diderot, and Montesquieu was a nobleman who admired a limited monarchy.

## Key points

- **[[The Enlightenment]]** (*les Lumières*): reason applied to laws, beliefs and institutions,
  roughly 1715–1789.
- Montesquieu, *De l'esprit des lois* (1748): the **[[separation of powers]]** against despotism.
- Diderot and d'Alembert's *Encyclopédie*: 17 volumes of text (1751–1765) and 11 of plates
  (1762–1772); banned in 1752 and 1759, finished anyway.
- Voltaire and the Calas affair (1761–1765); *Traité sur la tolérance* (1763).
- Rousseau, *Du contrat social* (1762): popular sovereignty and the general will.
- The *Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen*, 26 August 1789: seventeen articles,
  still part of French constitutional law.
- To argue: idea, reason, objection (*On pourrait objecter que …*), refutation (*Certes … Il n'en
  reste pas moins que …*).

lessons.title: Dossier de presse: le train ou l'avion ?
topics: Writing and speaking from a dossier
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the course's last lesson: a capstone in the format you will meet at B2 and beyond. You get
a short press dossier on one real debate, France's limit on short domestic flights, then two
tasks: a 250-word argued text and a five-minute talk, each with a model. All four documents were
written for this lesson; the people quoted are invented, but the facts about the law are real and
dated. Read each document twice: once for the facts and the positions, once for the language.

## The facts in brief

- In June 2020 the *Convention citoyenne pour le climat*, a panel of 150 citizens drawn by lot,
  proposed ending domestic flights where a low-carbon alternative of under four hours exists.
- The *Climat et résilience* law of 22 August 2021 (article 145) kept a narrower version: scheduled
  domestic passenger flights are banned on routes that the train covers in **under 2 h 30**, without
  a change of train.
- The European Commission accepted the measure on 1 December 2022, on the basis of a decree that
  would apply for three years and be reviewed along the way.
- The application decree of 22 May 2023 added conditions: several direct trains a day, at times
  that allow more than eight hours at the destination. In 2023 that meant three routes from
  Paris-Orly: Bordeaux, Nantes and Lyon, where flights had in fact already stopped. Flights from
  Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle to the same cities, often taken as connections, were not affected.
- The Conseil d'État, France's highest administrative court, upheld the decree on 2 February 2024.
- The same law (article 147) requires airlines to offset (*compenser*) the emissions of most
  domestic flights: half in 2022, 70 % in 2023, all of them from 2024.

Rules like this change. The decree's three years ran to May 2026, after which the measure was to
be evaluated and any new version notified to the Commission; yet in April 2026 the ministry's list
for the summer season (to 30 October 2026) named eight routes from Paris airports where flights
could be banned. This lesson can't tell you what was decided after that: check the environment
ministry's page (ecologie.gouv.fr) before quoting the current situation.

New senses of words you know: *l'émission* (A2: a programme) is also an emission (*les émissions
de CO₂*); *le bilan* (A2: taking stock) appears in *le bilan carbone*, a carbon audit. *Ferroviaire*
and *la grande vitesse* are B1 words; *la desserte* (rail service to a place) is lesson 18's.

## Document 1: la brève

> **Vols courts : le décret enfin publié**
>
> Le décret d'application de la loi Climat et résilience est paru le 23 mai 2023 au *Journal officiel*. Il interdit les liaisons aériennes intérieures lorsqu'il existe une alternative en train de moins de 2 h 30, sans correspondance. Trois lignes au départ d'Orly sont concernées. Selon une estimation de la Commission européenne, la mesure éviterait environ 55 000 tonnes de CO₂ par an.

A news item (*une brève*): title in nominal style (lesson 14), facts first, a number with its
source, and a reportive conditional (*éviterait*, lesson 10) for an estimate the paper doesn't
vouch for itself.

## Document 2: l'éditorial

> **Un premier pas, trop timide**
>
> Il aura fallu près de deux ans pour qu'une loi votée en 2021 trouve son décret d'application, et le résultat déçoit. Trois lignes, déjà abandonnées par les compagnies aériennes : la mesure est surtout symbolique. Pourtant, le symbole compte. Pour la première fois, l'État admet qu'un vol intérieur n'est pas un service comme un autre lorsqu'il existe une solution moins polluante.
>
> Car les chiffres parlent d'eux-mêmes : sur un trajet moyen, un passager en avion émet bien plus de CO₂ qu'en train. Réduire l'empreinte carbone des transports sans toucher à l'avion relève de l'illusion. Quant à compenser les émissions en plantant des arbres, c'est utile, mais cela ne remplace pas la décarbonation.
>
> Encore faut-il que le train soit à la hauteur. Des billets trop chers, des retards, des trains de nuit qu'on relance trop lentement : voilà ce qui pousse les voyageurs vers l'aéroport. Interdire sans investir, c'est punir. Investir sans jamais interdire, c'est attendre. Il faudra faire les deux.

*It took nearly two years for a law passed in 2021 to get its implementing decree, and the result is
disappointing. Three routes, already abandoned by the airlines: the measure is mostly symbolic.
And yet the symbol matters. For the first time, the State accepts that a domestic flight is not a
service like any other when a less polluting option exists.*

*For the figures speak for themselves: on an average journey, a passenger emits far more CO₂ by
plane than by train. Reducing the carbon footprint of transport without touching air travel is an
illusion. As for offsetting emissions by planting trees, it is useful, but it does not replace
decarbonisation.*

*The train still has to be up to the job. Tickets that are too expensive, delays, night trains
that are being relaunched too slowly: that is what pushes travellers towards the airport. Banning
without investing is punishing. Investing without ever banning is waiting. Both will be needed.*

Language to notice: *Il aura fallu* (futur antérieur of a past assessment, lesson 04); *pour
qu'une loi … trouve* (subjunctive after *pour que*); *Encore faut-il que* + subjunctive, with
inversion after *encore* (lesson 20); *Quant à* introduces a new point; the parallel sentences
*Interdire sans investir … Investir sans jamais interdire …* form an antithesis, a typical
editorial ending.

## Document 3: l'interview

```dialogue
# « On déplace le problème »
Journaliste: Vous critiquez cette interdiction. Pourquoi ?
= You criticise this ban. Why?
Claire Morand: Parce qu'elle vise les mauvais vols. Les lignes concernées représentaient une part infime du trafic aérien. Le vrai enjeu, ce sont les vols long-courriers.
= Because it targets the wrong flights. The routes concerned were a tiny share of air traffic. The real issue is long-haul flights.
Journaliste: Le symbole n'a-t-il pas son importance ?
= Doesn't the symbol matter?
Claire Morand: Si, à condition qu'il ne serve pas d'alibi. Une mesure symbolique peut donner l'impression qu'on a agi, alors que le bilan carbone du secteur change à peine.
= It does, provided it isn't used as an alibi. A symbolic measure can give the impression that something has been done, while the sector's carbon audit hardly changes.
Journaliste: Et les régions ?
= And the regions?
Claire Morand: Pour certaines villes mal desservies par le train, l'avion reste vital. Si on étendait la règle sans dérogation, on risquerait de les isoler davantage.
= For some towns poorly served by rail, the plane is still vital. If the rule were extended without exemptions, we would risk isolating them further.
Journaliste: Que proposez-vous ?
= What do you propose?
Claire Morand: De taxer davantage les vols les plus émetteurs et d'investir cet argent dans le rail. Interdire est facile ; rendre le train attractif, c'est plus difficile.
= Taxing the most polluting flights more and investing that money in rail. Banning is easy; making the train attractive is harder.
```

In short: an invented transport economist accepts the symbol but says the ban targets a tiny
share of traffic, may serve as an alibi, and could isolate poorly served regions if it were
extended without exemptions (*sans dérogation*). She prefers taxing the most polluting flights
and investing in rail. Note *Si* (not *oui*) to contradict a negative question; *à condition
que* + subjunctive (lesson 09); *Si on étendait …, on risquerait* (si + imparfait, conditionnel);
*alors que* of contrast.

## Document 4: le graphique

![A bar chart titled "Un trajet de 450 km entre deux villes françaises", marked "chiffres inventés pour l'exercice". Left panel, emissions per passenger in kilograms of CO2: train 3 kg, plane 80 kg. Right panel, door-to-door journey time in hours: train 3 h 15, plane 3 h 00. A note says the train runs centre to centre without a change, and the plane times include getting to and from the airport, security and boarding.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

These figures are **invented** for practice, in a plausible range: for real ones, use the
calculator of ADEME, the French environment agency (impactco2.fr), and give the date. To describe
a chart (lesson 12h1 covers it in depth): *L'avion émet plus de vingt-cinq fois plus que le train*;
*le train ne met qu'un quart d'heure de plus*; *l'écart de durée est faible, alors que l'écart
d'émissions est considérable.* Note that the 2021 rule looks at the train journey between stations, not
at the door-to-door time: a useful nuance for the debate.

## From the dossier to your text

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Planning an argued text from a press dossier
  accDescr: Six steps from top to bottom. Read the documents and note each position. Find the problématique, the question the text will answer. Choose a plan, for example arguments for, then objections and a refutation. Write the introduction with a hook, the problématique and the plan. Write the body, one argument per paragraph with an example from the dossier. Conclude with an answer and an opening.
  A["Lire les documents : qui dit quoi ?"] --> B["Trouver la problématique"]
  B --> C["Choisir un plan : pour, puis objections et réfutation"]
  C --> D["Introduction : amorce, problématique, plan"]
  D --> E["Développement : un argument et un exemple par paragraphe"]
  E --> F["Conclusion : réponse et ouverture"]
```

The **[[problématique]]** (lesson 21) is the real question under the topic. Here, not "train or
plane?" but, for example: *Faut-il interdire pour changer les comportements, ou rendre le train
plus attractif ?*

### Example 1: Using a document without copying it

Document 3 says: *Les lignes concernées représentaient une part infime du trafic aérien.* In your
text, report it with a reporting verb and your own words (lesson 19): *Comme le souligne une
économiste interrogée par la presse, la mesure ne concerne qu'une très faible part des vols.*
*Souligner* shows you agree; *prétendre* would show doubt.

### Example 2: Conceding and answering

Objection from document 3: *the measure is symbolic.* Answer: *Certes, la mesure ne touche que
trois lignes. Il n'en reste pas moins qu'elle fixe un principe : lorsqu'une alternative existe,
l'avion n'est plus un choix neutre.* *Certes* concedes, *il n'en reste pas moins que* (+
indicative) keeps the argument standing.

## Task 1: a 250-word argued text

*Le magazine d'une association de voyageurs ouvre un débat : « Faut-il interdire les vols
intérieurs lorsque le train fait le même trajet en moins de 2 h 30 ? » Vous donnez votre avis
dans un texte argumenté d'au moins 250 mots.*

### Model text (269 words)

> **Interdire, oui, mais pas seulement**
>
> Prendre l'avion pour un trajet que le train fait en deux heures : il y a quelques années encore, ce choix paraissait banal. Depuis la loi Climat et résilience de 2021, il est interdit sur les lignes où le train permet de faire le trajet en moins de deux heures et demie, sans correspondance. Cette mesure est-elle une avancée réelle ou un simple symbole ?
>
> Il faut d'abord reconnaître qu'elle repose sur un constat solide. Sur une distance moyenne, un passager émet beaucoup plus de CO₂ en avion qu'en train, alors que la durée totale du voyage est souvent comparable. Interdire ces vols, c'est donc réduire l'empreinte carbone des transports sans priver personne de la possibilité de voyager.
>
> On pourrait objecter que la mesure ne concerne qu'une poignée de lignes, et que l'essentiel des émissions de l'aviation vient des longs trajets. C'est vrai. Il n'en reste pas moins qu'elle fixe un principe : lorsqu'une solution moins polluante existe, l'avion n'est plus un choix neutre. Encore faut-il que cette solution soit réelle. Si les billets de train restent chers et les retards fréquents, les voyageurs se sentiront punis plutôt que convaincus.
>
> C'est pourquoi l'interdiction ne peut être qu'une partie de la réponse. Elle doit s'accompagner d'investissements dans le rail, de prix plus justes et du retour des trains de nuit pour les trajets plus longs. Les régions mal desservies, quant à elles, doivent pouvoir bénéficier de dérogations.
>
> En somme, interdire certains vols courts est utile, à condition de ne pas s'arrêter là. La vraie question n'est peut-être pas de savoir s'il faut limiter l'avion, mais comment rendre le train évident.

In short: the writer accepts the ban as a sound principle, concedes that it covers few routes,
and argues that it only works with investment in rail, fairer prices, night trains and exemptions
for poorly served regions. Spot in it: a hook and a **[[problématique]]** in the introduction; *Il
faut d'abord reconnaître*; *On pourrait objecter que … C'est vrai. Il n'en reste pas moins que*;
*Encore faut-il que* + subjunctive; a si-clause; *ne … que*; *quant à elles*; *à condition de*;
a conclusion with an opening question.

## Task 2: a five-minute talk

Prepare a talk on the same question, with the dossier as your trigger document. A plan that fits
five minutes:

1. About 30 seconds. Introduce the documents and the topic: *Le dossier porte sur …*.
2. About 30 seconds. The problématique and your plan: *Je me demanderai si … D'abord …,
   ensuite …*.
3. About 1 minute 30. Your first part, with one figure and one example from the dossier.
4. About 1 minute 30. The objection and your answer: *On m'objectera sans doute que …*.
5. About 1 minute. Conclusion and an opening question for the discussion.

Speak from keywords, not sentences; use spoken connectors (*à mon sens, en l'occurrence, qui plus
est*, lesson 23); say *deux heures et demie*, not *deux h trente*. Time yourself.

## Checklist for the whole course

| Check | Lessons |
|---|---|
| Past participle agreement (*que* + avoir, pronominal verbs, *en*) | 03, 05 |
| Mood after conjunctions and verbs (*pour que, bien que, encore faut-il que*) | 05–08 |
| Conditions and the conditionnel (*à condition que, si on étendait*) | 09–10 |
| Probability and nuance (*sans doute, il se peut que*) | 11 |
| Relatives and nominal style (*dont, ce qui; la publication du décret*) | 13–14 |
| Pronouns for ideas (*le, en, y*) | 16 |
| Connectors of cause, consequence, purpose, opposition | 17–18 |
| Reporting verbs and distance from a source | 19 |
| Emphasis and inversion (*c'est … que, encore faut-il*) | 20 |
| Problématique, refutation, plan | 21–22 |
| Speaking: structure, transitions, timing | 23–24 |

## Common mistakes

- Copying sentences from the documents. Report them with a reporting verb, in your own words.
- Presenting an estimate as a fact. Give the source and use the conditionnel or *selon*.
- Mixing up *émettre* (to emit) and *émission* in the A2 sense: *une émission de télévision* is
  a programme, *les émissions de CO₂* are emissions.
- Writing *2h30* in a text. Write *2 h 30* or *deux heures et demie*.
- Forgetting the opposing view. A B2 text that never concedes anything reads as a tract.

## Key points

- *Climat et résilience* (22 August 2021, article 145): no scheduled domestic flight where the
  train takes under 2 h 30 without a change; decree of 22 May 2023, made for three years; three Orly routes in 2023;
  upheld by the Conseil d'État on 2 February 2024. Check the current list before quoting it.
- A press dossier mixes genres: the news item (facts, sources), the editorial (opinion, rhetoric),
  the interview (a named view), the chart (figures to describe with care).
- From dossier to text: positions, **[[problématique]]**, plan, concession and refutation, conclusion
  with an opening.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: Narrating and placing events in time
Logical links, reported speech and emphasis
Arguing, writing, speaking and the DELF B2
Honors: Littérature, idées et société (literature, ideas and society)

questions.stem: How did Candide first appear in 1759?
choices: Under Voltaire's name, published by the Académie française in Paris
Printed by Cramer in Geneva without the author's name, presented as a translation from German
As a serial in a Paris newspaper, signed by Voltaire
As a play performed at the Comédie-Française
questions.explanation: Candide was printed by Gabriel Cramer in Geneva early in 1759, with editions in Paris and elsewhere almost at once. The title page gave no author and claimed the book was translated from the German of a "Doctor Ralph". It was banned in several places and sold all the better for it.

questions.stem: The subtitle of Candide is "ou l'Optimisme". What does "l'optimisme" mean here?
choices: The philosophical system, after Leibniz, holding that this world is the best possible and that every evil serves a greater good
The belief that kings rule by divine right
questions.explanation: In the eighteenth century "l'optimisme" named a system: Leibniz (Essais de théodicée, 1710) argued that a perfect God created the best possible world, so every evil has its purpose. Pangloss applies this to every catastrophe; the tale tests it against war, an earthquake and slavery. It is not the everyday sense of hoping for the best.

questions.stem: Which real event does Candide witness on his arrival in Lisbon?
choices: The start of the Seven Years' War in 1756
questions.explanation: Candide and Pangloss reach Lisbon just as the earthquake of 1 November 1755 strikes, a disaster that killed tens of thousands of people and shook the optimists' arguments. The Seven Years' War (1756–1763) is behind the battle scenes, not the Lisbon chapter; the Bastille fell in 1789, eleven years after Voltaire's death.

questions.stem: Name the numbered stages of Candide's journey.

image.alt: The map of Candide's journey without place names: a South America panel and a Europe panel, with dots joined by land routes and dashed sea routes, and a star in the Andes. Six stages are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 Westphalia, where the baron's castle stands (just east of Holland). 2 Lisbon, on the Atlantic coast, where the earthquake strikes. 3 Venice, at the top of the Adriatic. 4 Constantinople, the last stage, where the friends settle on a small farm. 5 Eldorado, the imaginary country, marked with a star in the Andes. 6 Buenos Aires, where Candide lands from Cadiz. Candide never goes to Madrid or London (his ship only stops at an English port, Portsmouth).

questions.stem: Put these episodes of Candide in order.
choices: The baron drives Candide out of the castle.
Candide is forced into the army of the Bulgars.
In Surinam they meet an enslaved man who has been mutilated.
The friends settle on a small farm near Constantinople.
questions.explanation: The expulsion from the castle, the Bulgar army, the Lisbon earthquake (part 1, Europe); Eldorado and Surinam (part 2, South America); and the farm near Constantinople at the end. Surinam comes after Eldorado: it is where Candide arrives with the little gold he has left.

questions.stem: Match each sentence of the passé simple retelling to the same sentence in the passé composé.
left: Les deux camps détruisirent des villages.
Une tempête fit couler le navire.
Une vieille femme le conduisit auprès de Cunégonde.
choices: Les deux camps ont détruit des villages.
Une tempête a fait couler le navire.
Une vieille femme l'a conduit auprès de Cunégonde.
Une vieille femme l'a conduite auprès de Cunégonde.
questions.explanation: Détruisirent → ont détruit; trembla → a tremblé; fit couler → a fait couler (fait + infinitive); fut pendu → a été pendu (a passive: être goes into the passé composé); conduisit → a conduit, with le = Candide, so the participle stays masculine. "Pangloss était pendu" is a state in the imparfait, not the event, and "l'a conduite" would mean the woman took a female person.

questions.stem: The retelling says "Puis il s'enfuit en Hollande." Retell it in the passé composé: Puis il ___ en Hollande.
questions.explanation: S'enfuir is pronominal, so it takes être, and the participle (enfui) agrees with the subject: il s'est enfui, elle s'est enfuie. In the story, s'enfuit is the passé simple, between other passé simple events.

questions.stem: In "À peine Candide et Pangloss eurent-ils atteint la ville que la terre trembla", what is "eurent atteint"?
questions.explanation: Eurent (passé simple of avoir) + atteint is the passé antérieur, used in passé simple narration for an event just before the next one, here after à peine … que, with inversion. The plus-que-parfait would be avaient atteint. In speech: "Ils venaient d'arriver quand la terre a tremblé."

questions.stem: What makes Candide a "conte philosophique"?
choices: It is a long novel about the inner life of realistic characters.
It is a short tale whose simple characters and fast plot serve to test an idea.
It is a treatise of philosophy written in the form of a dialogue.
It is a traditional folk tale collected from oral sources.
questions.explanation: A philosophical tale looks like a fairy tale (a castle, a beautiful young woman, journeys, reversals of fortune), but its purpose is to test an idea: here, philosophical optimism. Its characters are types rather than realistic people, so "novel about inner life" doesn't fit.

questions.stem: Which of these are targets of the satire in Candide? Select all that apply.
choices: War and the princes who wage it
questions.explanation: Voltaire mocks the optimists (Pangloss), war (the Bulgar battle), fanaticism (the Lisbon auto-da-fé) and slavery (the man in Surinam). Tolerance is what he defends, notably in the Traité sur la tolérance (1763), and modest work is what the ending recommends.

questions.stem: A pastiche sentence reads: "Grâce à la guerre, les paysans n'eurent plus à s'inquiéter de leurs récoltes : il n'y en avait plus." What does it really mean?
choices: The war protected the farmers' harvests.
The peasants stopped farming because they were no longer worried.
The war ended in time for the harvest.
The soldiers destroyed the harvests, and the writer is mocking anyone who calls war a benefit.
questions.explanation: "Grâce à" normally introduces a good cause; here it introduces a destruction. The gap between the grateful wording and the fact (there were no harvests left) is the irony: the sentence condemns war by pretending to praise it.

questions.stem: "Le docteur démontra, par trois arguments irréfutables, que la maison avait brûlé pour le bien de ses habitants." Which ironic device is this?
choices: Mock logic: the solemn proof leads to an absurd conclusion
A calm tone for a happy event
A naive narrator who misunderstands a word
An understatement about a minor accident
questions.explanation: The words of a learned proof (démontra, trois arguments irréfutables) lead to a conclusion nobody could accept: a fire for the good of its victims. This is the satire of the optimist philosopher, who explains every disaster away.

questions.stem: How does Candide end?
choices: Candide goes back to Eldorado with Cunégonde.
Pangloss admits that he was wrong all along.
After one more speech by Pangloss, Candide advises his friends to tend their own garden.
Candide inherits the baron's castle in Westphalia.
questions.explanation: The friends live on a small farm near Constantinople. Pangloss offers one more demonstration that all has turned out for the best; Candide answers with practical advice to tend their garden, which readers still interpret in different ways. Pangloss never gives up his system.

questions.stem: In the tale, Eldorado is a hidden country where gold has no value and there are no trials and no prisons. What is it?
choices: A real kingdom of eighteenth-century Peru
The place where Candide was born
questions.explanation: Eldorado is the book's utopia (l'utopie): an ideal society, peaceful and rich, that shows by contrast what is wrong with the real world. It is imaginary, though Voltaire places it in the mountains of South America. Candide leaves it to find Cunégonde.

questions.stem: You are summarising the story in a B2 essay. Which sentence uses the tense the lesson recommends for a summary?
choices: Candide quitta le château et rencontra Pangloss en Hollande.
Candide quitte le château et retrouve Pangloss en Hollande.
Candide quittait le château et retrouvait Pangloss en Hollande.
Candide quittera le château et retrouvera Pangloss en Hollande.
questions.explanation: A summary of a story is usually written in the present (or the passé composé). The passé simple (quitta) is the narrative tense of the book itself: read it, don't write it. The imparfait would make the events sound like habits or background, and the futur makes no sense for a story already told.

questions.stem: Who founded the Negritude movement in Paris in the 1930s?
choices: Victor Hugo, Émile Zola and Gustave Flaubert
Gabrielle Roy, Georges Simenon and C. F. Ramuz
Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas
Kateb Yacine, Assia Djebar and Birago Diop
questions.explanation: Césaire (Martinique), Senghor (Senegal) and Damas (French Guiana) met as students in Paris and launched the movement, with a student journal, L'Étudiant noir, in the mid-1930s. Roy, Simenon and Ramuz are Québec, Belgian and Swiss writers; Kateb and Djebar belong to a later Algerian generation, and Birago Diop, though close to the movement, was not one of its founders.

questions.stem: Which work first appeared in a Paris review in 1939?
choices: Aimé Césaire's Cahier d'un retour au pays natal
Birago Diop's Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba
questions.explanation: Césaire's long poem, the founding text of Negritude, appeared in 1939. Bonheur d'occasion is from 1945, Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba from 1947 and Nedjma from 1956.

questions.stem: Which statement about Léopold Sédar Senghor is true?
choices: He was mayor of Fort-de-France for more than fifty years.
He wrote the Maigret detective novels.
He refused to write in French after independence.
He was the first president of independent Senegal (1960–1980) and, in 1983, the first African elected to the Académie française.
questions.explanation: Senghor, poet and politician, led Senegal from 1960 to 1980 and was elected to the Académie française in 1983. Césaire was the mayor of Fort-de-France (1945–2001); Simenon wrote Maigret; Senghor wrote in French all his life and defended the mixing of cultures (le métissage).

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on the map of francophone literature.

image.alt: A map of the North Atlantic with no names: North America, the Caribbean, Western Europe and West Africa, with seven dots, six of them numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 Québec (Gabrielle Roy), in North America; 2 Martinique (Aimé Césaire), in the Caribbean; 3 Senegal (Senghor), on the westernmost tip of Africa; 4 Belgium (Simenon), the northern of the two European dots; 5 Switzerland (Ramuz), just south of it; 6 Algeria (Kateb Yacine, Assia Djebar), on the Mediterranean coast of Africa. The unnumbered dot inland in West Africa is Mali.

questions.stem: Match each writer to one of their works.
choices: Cahier d'un retour au pays natal
questions.explanation: Roy: Bonheur d'occasion (1945), set in Montréal. Kateb: Nedjma (1956). Césaire: Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (1939). Diop: tales heard from a family griot (1947). Djebar: L'Amour, la fantasia (1985). Candide is Voltaire's and De l'esprit des lois Montesquieu's.

questions.stem: What is a griot in West Africa?
choices: A village chief who settles disputes
A travelling merchant who sells books
A religious teacher of the Koran
A keeper of memory: historian, storyteller and musician, often from a family of griots
questions.explanation: The griot (Mandinka jeli) preserves genealogies, history, epics and songs, and performs them, often with the kora. The role is usually hereditary. Thinking of the griot as "only a singer" leaves out the historian and adviser.

questions.stem: Which features show the "oralité" of a written francophone text? Select all that apply.
choices: A narrator who addresses the audience
A strictly chronological plot with no digressions
questions.explanation: Proverbs, repetition, a narrator who speaks to the listeners and stories within stories all come from oral performance. Footnotes and bibliographies belong to scholarly writing, and oral storytelling is full of digressions.

questions.stem: Georges Simenon, the author of the Maigret novels, was born in…
questions.explanation: Simenon was born in Liège in 1903 and died in Lausanne in 1989. Many readers in France take him for a French writer. Ramuz was born in 1878 in the canton of Vaud, and Gabrielle Roy in 1909, in Manitoba.

questions.stem: Complete with the plural of "colonial": Au XIXe siècle, la France et le Royaume-Uni avaient les plus grands empires ___.
questions.explanation: Adjectives in -al usually take -aux in the masculine plural: un empire colonial, des empires coloniaux. The feminine is regular: une école coloniale, des écoles coloniales.

questions.stem: In the reading "Écrire dans la langue de l'autre", what is the critics' objection to writing in French?
choices: French is too difficult for African readers.
It seems contradictory to denounce colonial domination in the language of that domination.
French has no words for African realities.
questions.explanation: The text gives two reasons for writing in French (it was often the only written language taught, and it reached readers far away), then the critics' objection: a contradiction in using the coloniser's language against colonialism. The reply is that these writers transformed French.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in the order of a balanced argument, as in the lesson's reading.
choices: D'abord, c'était souvent la seule langue écrite qu'on leur avait enseignée.
Ensuite, le français leur permettait d'être lus bien au-delà de leur pays.
Certains critiques y voient pourtant une contradiction.
D'autres répondent que ces écrivains ont transformé le français.
Qu'on approuve ou non ce choix, il a enrichi la littérature de langue française.
questions.explanation: D'abord and Ensuite give the reasons; pourtant introduces the objection; D'autres répondent answers "Certains critiques"; and the concessive "Qu'on approuve ou non" sums up both sides in a conclusion.

questions.stem: In "ces écrivains n'ont pas simplement emprunté le français : ils l'ont transformé", why is the participle "transformé" written without -e or -s?
choices: It agrees with l', which stands for "le français", masculine singular.
Transformer is an exception to the agreement rule.
questions.explanation: With avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object placed before it. Here the object is l' = le français, masculine singular, so the agreement adds nothing. Compare: la langue, ils l'ont transformée. It never agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is avoir.

questions.stem: Who became, in 2005, the first writer from the Maghreb elected to the Académie française?
questions.explanation: Assia Djebar (1936–2015), the Algerian novelist, historian and film-maker, was elected in 2005. Kateb Yacine (1929–1989) wrote Nedjma; Césaire and Roy were never members.

questions.stem: What does "un écrivain francophone" mean?
choices: A writer who writes in French, whatever his or her country
A French writer who lives abroad
A writer who translates from French
questions.explanation: Francophone means French-speaking: Senghor, Simenon, Roy and Djebar are called francophone writers, writers in French. Un écrivain français is a writer from France.

questions.stem: A biographical notice turns verbs into nouns. Which noun replaces "est né" in "Senghor est né en 1906 au Sénégal"?
questions.explanation: Naître → la naissance: "Naissance au Sénégal en 1906". La natalité is the birth rate, and la nation has nothing to do with being born, despite the shared Latin root.

questions.stem: Which thinker and which work are linked with the separation of powers?
questions.explanation: In De l'esprit des lois Montesquieu argues that making laws, carrying them out and judging should belong to different bodies so that power checks power. Rousseau's Contrat social is about the legitimacy of power and popular sovereignty.

questions.stem: Name the work or text that matches each numbered date on the timeline.

image.alt: A timeline from 1745 to 1790 with six dated points, 1748, 1751, 1759, 1762, 1763 and 1789, each numbered, and a shaded band from 1751 to 1772.

choices: Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen
questions.explanation: 1748 De l'esprit des lois (Montesquieu); 1751 the first volume of the Encyclopédie; 1759 Candide; 1762 Du contrat social (Rousseau); 1763 Traité sur la tolérance (Voltaire, after the Calas affair); 1789 the Declaration, adopted on 26 August. The Lettres persanes date from 1721, and Bonheur d'occasion is a 1945 Québec novel.

questions.stem: Which description of the Encyclopédie is accurate?
choices: A single volume written by Voltaire alone in 1764
An official dictionary of the Académie française, published with the king's support
17 volumes of articles (1751–1765) and 11 volumes of plates (1762–1772), directed by Diderot and d'Alembert
A translation of an English encyclopedia, finished in 1751
questions.explanation: The Encyclopédie had 17 volumes of text and 11 of plates, by more than a hundred contributors. It began as a plan to translate an English encyclopedia but became something much larger. It was never the Académie's dictionary, and the authorities banned it in 1752 and 1759.

questions.stem: What happened to the Encyclopédie in 1759?
choices: Permission to publish it was withdrawn, but Diderot carried on in secret.
It was finished and presented to the king.
questions.explanation: In 1759 the authorities withdrew the permission to publish. D'Alembert had already left (1758); Diderot went on almost alone, and the remaining volumes of text came out in 1765, the plates by 1772.

questions.stem: What led Voltaire to write the Traité sur la tolérance (1763)?
choices: The execution of Jean Calas, a Protestant of Toulouse wrongly accused of killing his son
The banning of Candide in Geneva
questions.explanation: Jean Calas was executed in 1762 after an unfair trial. Voltaire campaigned for his innocence, wrote the Traité sur la tolérance, and Calas was declared innocent in 1765. The Lisbon earthquake lies behind Candide, not the Traité.

questions.stem: The famous sentence about defending to the death someone's right to say what you disapprove of is often credited to Voltaire. Who actually wrote it?
choices: Rousseau, in a letter to Voltaire
Voltaire, in the Traité sur la tolérance
Evelyn Beatrice Hall, in a 1906 book about Voltaire
questions.explanation: The English writer Evelyn Beatrice Hall wrote it in a 1906 book about Voltaire and his friends, as her own summary of his attitude; she later said the words were hers. A good reason to check any quotation before using it.

questions.stem: According to Rousseau's Du contrat social, to whom does sovereignty belong?
choices: To the king, by divine right
questions.explanation: For Rousseau, legitimate power comes from an agreement by which people form one body and obey the laws they make together, the "general will": sovereignty (la souveraineté) belongs to the people. Divine-right monarchy is the absolutism he rejects.

questions.stem: Match each idea or work to the thinker most associated with it.
questions.explanation: Montesquieu: De l'esprit des lois (1748). Rousseau: Du contrat social (1762). Voltaire: the Traité sur la tolérance (1763). Diderot directed the Encyclopédie, with d'Alembert. Leibniz is the philosopher of optimism mocked in Candide; Senghor is a twentieth-century poet.

questions.stem: Which of these does the Declaration of 26 August 1789 contain? Select all that apply.
choices: The idea that sovereignty belongs to the nation
Freedom of opinion, including religious opinion
The abolition of slavery in the colonies
questions.explanation: The Declaration states the presumption of innocence, national sovereignty, freedom of opinion and the separation of powers. It said nothing about slavery, which France abolished in 1794, restored in 1802 and abolished for good in 1848, and nothing about women's rights: Olympe de Gouges answered with her own declaration in 1791.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen is true today?
choices: It was replaced by the Constitution of 1958.
It still has legal force: the 1958 Constitution refers to it in its preamble.
It was never adopted, only proposed.
questions.explanation: The 1958 Constitution's preamble refers to the Declaration, and since 1971 the Conseil constitutionnel has treated it as part of constitutional law. "L'homme" in its title means the human being.

questions.stem: Use the past participle of "adopter" at the front of the sentence: ___ le 26 août 1789, la Déclaration compte dix-sept articles.
questions.explanation: A participle at the front of a sentence describes the subject that follows and agrees with it: la Déclaration is feminine singular, so adoptée. Check that the subject really is what was adopted.

questions.stem: In the reading, "les gestes de ces artisans que les savants avaient longtemps méprisés": why "méprisés"?
choices: It agrees with "les savants", the subject.
It agrees with "que", which stands for "ces artisans", a direct object placed before the verb.
It agrees with "les planches", the subject of the main clause.
questions.explanation: With avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object that comes before it. Que stands for ces artisans, masculine plural, so méprisés. The subject never triggers agreement with avoir, and les planches (feminine) would give méprisées.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of this argued paragraph in order: idea, reason, objection, concession, conclusion.
choices: Selon Montesquieu, la séparation des pouvoirs protège la liberté.
En effet, si un même homme fait la loi et juge, rien ne l'empêche d'abuser de son pouvoir.
On pourrait objecter qu'un pouvoir trop divisé devient lent.
Certes, la séparation ralentit parfois les décisions.
Il n'en reste pas moins qu'elle évite le despotisme.
questions.explanation: The idea comes first; En effet gives its reason; On pourrait objecter que introduces the objection; Certes concedes its truth; Il n'en reste pas moins que weighs it and keeps the idea standing. This is the refutation pattern of lesson 21.

questions.stem: How do you write "the Age of Enlightenment" in French?
questions.explanation: The movement takes a capital and the plural: les Lumières, le siècle des Lumières. With a small letter, les lumières are lights; l'éclairage is lighting.

questions.stem: How did bold books usually reach readers under eighteenth-century French censorship?
choices: They were printed abroad, often without the author's name, and sold under the counter.
They were published by the Académie française.
They were read aloud in churches.
They were sent free to every household by the king.
questions.explanation: A book needed royal permission, so daring works were printed in Amsterdam or Geneva, often anonymously, and sold discreetly. Ideas also circulated in literary salons, cafés and letters. De l'esprit des lois and Candide both appeared without their authors' names.

questions.stem: Under the Climat et résilience law of 22 August 2021, when is a scheduled domestic flight banned?
choices: When the train makes the same trip in under four hours
When the train makes the same trip in under 2 h 30 without a change
When the flight lasts less than one hour
When the flight leaves from Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle
questions.explanation: Article 145 bans scheduled domestic passenger flights where the train covers the trip in under 2 h 30 without a change; a 2023 decree added conditions on frequency and timetables. Four hours was the citizens' convention's proposal (2020). Flights from Charles-de-Gaulle to Bordeaux, Nantes and Lyon were not affected in 2023.

questions.stem: What did the Convention citoyenne pour le climat propose in 2020?
choices: Banning all domestic flights at once
Ending domestic flights where a low-carbon alternative of under four hours exists
questions.explanation: The 150 citizens drawn by lot proposed a four-hour threshold. Parliament kept a narrower version: 2 h 30, without a change of train.

questions.stem: Which routes did the decree of 22 May 2023 cover when it came into force?
choices: Paris-Orly to Bordeaux, Nantes and Lyon
All flights between Paris and Marseille
Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle to Bordeaux, Nantes and Lyon
questions.explanation: Three routes from Orly, where flights had in fact already stopped. Flights from Charles-de-Gaulle to the same cities, often taken as connections, were left out. The decree was made for three years; in April 2026 the ministry listed eight routes for the summer season where flights could be banned.

questions.stem: The news item says: "Selon une estimation de la Commission européenne, la mesure éviterait environ 55 000 tonnes de CO₂ par an." Why "éviterait"?
choices: It is a si-clause with the si left out.
It expresses a wish of the journalist.
It is the reportive conditional: an estimate from a source that the paper does not vouch for itself.
questions.explanation: The press uses the conditionnel to report information it attributes to someone else (lesson 10), here with "selon". It distances the paper from the figure without contradicting it.

questions.stem: According to the invented figures in this chart, which sentence is accurate?

image.alt: A bar chart of invented figures for a 450 km trip: emissions per passenger, train 3 kg and plane 80 kg of CO2; door-to-door time, train 3 h 15 and plane 3 h 00.

choices: Le train est deux fois plus rapide que l'avion.
L'avion émet plus de vingt-cinq fois plus que le train, pour un gain de temps d'un quart d'heure.
Les deux modes émettent à peu près autant.
L'avion est plus lent d'un quart d'heure.
questions.explanation: 80 kg against 3 kg is more than 25 times as much, and the plane saves only 15 minutes door to door (3 h 00 against 3 h 15). The train is slightly slower, not faster. These figures are invented for practice; real ones vary by route and year.

questions.stem: Which of these positions does the editorial "Un premier pas, trop timide" defend? Select all that apply.
choices: Offsetting emissions does not replace decarbonisation.
The train must improve if people are to use it.
Planes now emit less than trains.
questions.explanation: The editorial calls the measure symbolic but says the symbol matters, that offsetting is useful but no substitute for decarbonisation, and that banning without investing in the train is punishing. It never asks for the ban to be abolished, and it says the opposite about emissions.

questions.stem: Match each document type in the dossier to what it does.
choices: gives short facts with their source
gives one named person's view in questions and answers
shows figures to be described with care
questions.explanation: A brève is a short news item (facts, a source); the éditorial is the paper's opinion, with rhetoric; the interview gives a named view; the chart gives figures. Asking a company for compensation is a letter of complaint (lesson 22), not a press document.

questions.stem: Complete with "émettre" in the present: Un passager en avion ___ bien plus de CO₂ qu'en train.
questions.explanation: Émettre is conjugated like mettre: j'émets, tu émets, il émet, nous émettons, vous émettez, ils émettent. The noun is l'émission (here an emission, not a programme).

questions.stem: Listen to the radio item. What did the Conseil d'État decide?

audio.text: Le Conseil d'État a validé ce vendredi le décret qui interdit certains vols intérieurs lorsque le train permet de faire le trajet en moins de deux heures et demie. Ceux qui contestaient le texte ont donc perdu.

choices: It upheld the decree, so the challenge failed.
It extended the ban to every domestic route.
questions.explanation: "A validé le décret" means it upheld it; those who challenged it lost. This happened on 2 February 2024 (a Friday). Annuler would be to cancel; reporter to postpone.

questions.stem: Listen to two people disagreeing. What does the second speaker think of the ban?

audio.text: Interdire ces vols, c'est enfin agir pour le climat ! — Agir ? Trois lignes où plus personne ne volait ! C'est de la communication, rien de plus.

choices: It goes too far and will ruin the airlines.
It is a real step for the climate.
It is mostly communication, because it affects only routes with no flights left.
It should be extended to night trains.
questions.explanation: The first speaker welcomes the ban; the second answers with an ironic question ("Agir ?") and calls it mere communication, since the three routes had no flights left. This is the "symbolic measure" criticism of the dossier.

questions.stem: In the editorial, what does "Encore faut-il que le train soit à la hauteur" mean?
choices: The train is already good enough.
The train must once again be improved.
There is still a condition: the train has to be up to the job.
The train will never be as good as the plane.
questions.explanation: "Encore faut-il que" + subjunctive adds a condition to what was just said ("still, … has to …"), with the inversion of written French after "encore". "Encore" here is not "again".

questions.stem: The journalist asks "Le symbole n'a-t-il pas son importance ?" and the economist answers "Si, à condition qu'il ne serve pas d'alibi." Why "si" and not "oui"?
choices: Si answers yes to a negative question.
Si means "if" and starts a condition.
Si is more polite than oui in interviews.
Si shows that she disagrees completely.
questions.explanation: After a negative question, French answers "yes" with si: she agrees that the symbol matters, then adds a condition with "à condition que" + subjunctive. Oui would sound wrong here.

questions.topic: Writing and speaking from a dossier
questions.stem: Put the parts of a five-minute talk on the dossier in order.
choices: Present the documents and the topic.
Give the problématique and announce the plan.
Develop the first part, with a figure and an example from the dossier.
Present the objection and answer it.
Conclude and open the discussion with a question.
questions.explanation: Introduction (documents, topic), problématique and plan, then the two parts (argument, then objection and answer), then the conclusion with an opening. About 30 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute 30, 1 minute 30 and 1 minute.

questions.topic: Writing and speaking from a dossier
questions.stem: You want to use the economist's point in your essay and show that you agree with it. Which sentence does that?
choices: Comme le souligne une économiste, la mesure ne concerne qu'une très faible part des vols.
Une économiste prétend que la mesure ne concerne qu'une très faible part des vols.
Une économiste insinue que la mesure ne concerne qu'une très faible part des vols.
Les lignes concernées représentaient une part infime du trafic aérien.
questions.explanation: Souligner presents the point as true and important. Prétendre shows doubt and insinuer suggests a hidden intention (lesson 19). Copying the document's sentence word for word, without quotation marks or a source, is exactly what the lesson warns against.

questions.stem: The economist says: "Si on étendait la règle sans dérogation, on risquerait de les isoler davantage." What is "une dérogation"?
questions.explanation: Une dérogation is an exemption: permission not to apply a rule in a particular case. She wants poorly served towns to keep their flights. A carbon audit is un bilan carbone.

questions.stem: In a novel you read: "Ils firent le tour de la maison." What is the infinitive of "firent"?
questions.explanation: "Ils firent" is the passé simple of faire (il fit, ils firent). Finir gives "ils finirent", fuir gives "ils fuirent", and fixer, an -er verb, gives "ils fixèrent".

questions.stem: What does "Elle vit le cadavre" mean?
questions.explanation: "Vit" here is the passé simple of voir (il vit, ils virent). It looks like the present of vivre, but vivre's passé simple is "vécut", and "vivre le cadavre" makes no sense. In speech: "Elle a vu le cadavre."

questions.stem: "Le suspect fut arrêté le lendemain." Which verb is "fut" a form of?
questions.explanation: "Fut" is the passé simple of être, here in a passive: "fut arrêté" = was arrested (spoken: "a été arrêté"). Faire gives "fit", falloir gives "fallut", fuir gives "fuit".

questions.stem: The story opens: "Ce soir-là, une pluie fine tombait sur Honfleur. Vers minuit, la cuisinière découvrit le cadavre." Why is "tombait" in the imparfait?
choices: It is an event that moves the story on.
It happened before the discovery and was over.
It sets the scene: background going on at the time.
The passé simple of tomber is never used.
questions.explanation: The rain is background, already going on when the event happens, so it is in the imparfait, exactly as in speech. "Découvrit" is the event. The passé simple of tomber ("il tomba") is very common in novels.

questions.stem: You are telling a friend the story you read. Which sentence retells "Ils s'enfuirent par le jardin" in the passé composé?
choices: Ils se sont enfuis par le jardin.
Ils s'étaient enfuis par le jardin.
Ils ont enfui par le jardin.
questions.explanation: S'enfuir is pronominal, so it takes être, and the participle agrees with the subject: "ils se sont enfuis". "S'enfuyaient" is the imparfait, "s'étaient enfuis" the plus-que-parfait, and "ont enfui" uses the wrong auxiliary and drops se.

questions.stem: "Dès qu'elle eut terminé, elle fit venir les suspects." What does "eut terminé" tell you?
choices: She was in the middle of finishing when she called them.
She had finished just before she sent for them.
She finished every day before calling them.
questions.explanation: "Eut terminé" is a passé antérieur: in passé simple narration, after dès que, it marks an action finished just before the next event. In speech: "Dès qu'elle a terminé, elle a fait venir les suspects."

questions.stem: "Le voleur ouvrit la fenêtre et s'enfuit." What is "s'enfuit" here?
questions.explanation: "Il s'enfuit" is both present and passé simple. Here it follows "ouvrit", a passé simple, in a chain of events, so it is the passé simple too. The imparfait would be "s'enfuyait", the subjunctive "s'enfuie".

questions.stem: Which form is the passé simple of commencer (il)?
questions.explanation: -cer verbs keep a soft c before a with a cedilla: "il commença". Without the cedilla it would sound [k]. "Commençait" is the imparfait; "commencea" mixes up the -ger rule (il mangea).

questions.stem: In "Le mystère de la villa des Tilleuls", why did the case look impossible at first?
choices: The library door was locked from the inside.
All the witnesses had run away.
questions.explanation: "La porte était fermée à clé de l'intérieur ; on dut la forcer. Personne, semblait-il, n'avait pu entrer ni sortir." Everyone, in fact, had a motive.

questions.stem: In the story, what was Dr Fabre's motive?
choices: He was waiting for an inheritance.
He was about to lose his job.
Ledru had insulted him at dinner.
He owed Ledru twenty thousand francs.
questions.explanation: "Le docteur devait vingt mille francs à Ledru." The inheritance was Julien's motive and the job was the secretary's. The torn diary page recorded the date by which Fabre had to pay him back.

questions.stem: How did the inspector explain the locked room?
choices: The murderer climbed in through the window.
The poison was already in the decanter before Ledru locked himself in.
The cook had a second key.
Ledru had locked the murderer in with him.
questions.explanation: The doctor refilled the decanter at about ten, while the library was still open; Ledru shut himself in at half past eleven and drank, as every evening. The window was the false lead.

questions.stem: Which word means the reason someone commits a crime?
questions.explanation: Le mobile is the motive. L'alibi is proof you were elsewhere, l'indice a clue, and la piste a lead the investigators follow.

questions.stem: Where would you most expect to read "Le roi mourut en 1715"?
choices: In a text message to a friend
In a transcript of a casual conversation
In an e-mail to a colleague
questions.explanation: The passé simple belongs to written narrative cut off from the present: novels, tales and history books. In messages, e-mails and conversation, the passé composé does the job ("Le roi est mort en 1715").

questions.stem: "Elle naquit à Rouen et vécut à Paris." What does it mean?
choices: She was born in Rouen and lived in Paris.
She lived in Rouen and died in Paris.
She was born in Rouen and saw Paris.
She grew up in Rouen and came to Paris.
questions.explanation: "Naquit" is the passé simple of naître (to be born) and "vécut" of vivre (to live). Don't confuse "vécut" (vivre) with "vit" (voir).

questions.stem: "Le complice est passé aux aveux." What did the accomplice do?
questions.explanation: Passer aux aveux means to confess (les aveux = a confession). To run away is s'enfuir; to be arrested, être arrêté.

questions.stem: Retell in the passé composé: "Elle entra dans la pièce." → Elle ___ dans la pièce.
questions.explanation: Entrer takes être, and the participle agrees with elle: "Elle est entrée dans la pièce."

questions.stem: Retell in the passé composé: "Les gendarmes prirent la route de Caen." → Les gendarmes ___ la route de Caen.
questions.explanation: "Prirent" is the passé simple of prendre (ils prirent). In the passé composé: avoir + pris, "ils ont pris".

questions.stem: Match each passé simple form to its infinitive.
questions.explanation: The classic traps are fut (être) / fit (faire) and vit (voir) / vécut (vivre). Naître has the stem naqu-: il naquit. Falloir gives il fallut and venir il vint.

questions.stem: Which of these are passé simple forms? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Il parla" (-er set), "ils finirent" (-i- set) and "il voulut" (-u- set) are passé simple. "Il parlait" is the imparfait and "ils ont fini" the passé composé.

questions.stem: Put these events of the story in the order in which they happened.
choices: Mme Aubry s'enfuit vers le jardin.
questions.explanation: The doctor filled the decanter at about ten; Ledru locked himself in at half past eleven; the cook found the body at about midnight; the inspector arrived at dawn; and the secretary ran off when the inspector explained the poison.

questions.stem: Name the numbered items on the inspector's evidence board.

image.alt: A cork board with four pinned items joined by red strings to a central photo marked Dr F.: a photo of a decanter under a magnifying glass, a card with a clock and playing cards, a card with banknotes, and a photo of a woman marked Mme A. Four items are numbered.

questions.explanation: The decanter under the magnifying glass is the clue (l'indice); the card with cards and times is the doctor's alibi; the debt is the motive (le mobile); Mme Aubry, who kept watch, is the accomplice (la complice).

questions.stem: Listen to the inspector telling the end of the story. What happened at the gate?

audio.text: Alors voilà : la secrétaire s'est levée d'un coup et elle s'est enfuie vers le jardin. On l'a rattrapée au portail, et elle est passée aux aveux tout de suite.

choices: The secretary was caught and confessed at once.
questions.explanation: "On l'a rattrapée au portail, et elle est passée aux aveux tout de suite": she was caught at the gate and confessed straight away. Notice the spoken passé composé, where the novel had "On la rattrapa … Elle passa aussitôt aux aveux."

questions.stem: Complete in careful written French: "À peine ___ arrivée qu'on l'appela."
questions.explanation: When à peine opens a written sentence, the subject pronoun usually goes after the verb (stylistic inversion), and the first event is in the plus-que-parfait here: "À peine était-elle arrivée". "Elle soit" is a subjunctive, which à peine doesn't take; "est-elle" is the wrong tense for a past story; "avait arrivée" uses the wrong auxiliary.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the usual spoken version of "À peine était-il rentré qu'il repartit"?
choices: Il avait à peine rentré qu'il est reparti.
Il était à peine rentré qu'il soit reparti.
Il était à peine rentré qu'il est reparti.
Il était rentré à peine, qu'il repartit.
questions.explanation: In speech, à peine follows the auxiliary, there is no inversion, and the second event is in the passé composé: "Il était à peine rentré qu'il est reparti." Rentrer takes être, not avoir, and the clause after que is indicative.

questions.stem: "En attendant que l'historienne ___, nous avons lu les registres."
questions.explanation: En attendant que takes the subjunctive: the historian's arrival is still to come when the main action happens. "Vienne" is the present subjunctive of venir.

questions.stem: "Le temps que je ___ prête, le taxi sera là."
questions.explanation: Le temps que (in the time it takes for) takes the subjunctive: "le temps que je sois prête". Even though the sentence is about the future, the clause stays in the present subjunctive.

questions.stem: Paul moved to Verdun three years ago and still lives there. "Ça fait trois ans qu'il ___ à Verdun."
questions.explanation: For a situation that is still going on, ça fait … que (like depuis and il y a … que) takes the present: "Ça fait trois ans qu'il habite à Verdun" = he has lived there for three years. English "has lived" pulls learners towards the passé composé.

questions.stem: "I haven't seen him for a long time." → "Il y a longtemps que je ne l'___ vu."
questions.explanation: With a negative, il y a … que often takes the passé composé: the last meeting is a completed event whose result (not seeing him) lasts until now. "Avais" would place it in a past story; "aie" is subjunctive; "aurai" is future.

questions.stem: Which sentence means the same as "Il est parti il y a trois ans"?
choices: Il est parti pendant trois ans.
Ça fait trois ans qu'il est parti.
questions.explanation: Il y a + time = ago. "Ça fait trois ans qu'il est parti" says the same thing from the present: he left three years ago (and is still away). "Pendant trois ans" would mean he was away for three years.

questions.stem: Which word means "long ago" in a literary style?
questions.explanation: Jadis is the literary "long ago" (everyday autrefois). Désormais and dorénavant mean "from now on"; entre-temps means "in the meantime".

questions.stem: What does "Sitôt arrivée aux archives, elle a demandé le registre" mean?
choices: As soon as she got to the archives, she asked for the register.
Although she arrived at the archives, she asked for the register.
She arrived at the archives after asking for the register.
While she was going to the archives, she asked for the register.
questions.explanation: Sitôt + past participle = as soon as … had. Here the participle stands alone, so it refers to the subject of the main verb and agrees with it (arrivée: she).

questions.stem: In "Restez jusqu'à ce que le maire arrive", when does the mayor's arrival happen compared with the staying?
choices: At the end of it, later (posteriority)
questions.explanation: Jusqu'à ce que marks the end point of the main action: the arrival comes later, so this is posteriority, and the clause is in the subjunctive (arrive).

questions.stem: In "Le carnet de Lucien", how did the writer find her great-grandfather's notebook?
choices: A historian sent it to her.
She found it in an old tin box in her grandmother's attic.
She bought it on the internet.
It was displayed on the war memorial.
questions.explanation: "Tout a commencé dans le grenier de ma grand-mère … À peine l'avais-je ouverte que je suis tombée sur son carnet de guerre." The historian later taught her to read a service record.

questions.stem: According to the text, since when has 11 November been a public holiday in France?
questions.explanation: "Le 11 Novembre est férié depuis 1922." 1918 is the armistice itself, 2008 the death of the last poilu, and since 2012 the day has honoured everyone who died for France.

questions.stem: Why were there no First World War veterans at the ceremony?
choices: The ceremony was for another war.
Veterans no longer attend the ceremony.
questions.explanation: "Le dernier poilu, Lazare Ponticelli, est mort en 2008." Veterans of other wars were there.

questions.stem: "Pour consulter les registres, inscrivez-vous au préalable." What does "au préalable" mean?
questions.explanation: Au préalable (formal) = beforehand, first. Later is ultérieurement, in the meantime entre-temps, from now on désormais or dorénavant.

questions.stem: Someone says: "D'ici à ce que la mairie répare ce toit, on aura le temps de vieillir !" What do they mean?
choices: The repair will take a very long time.
The town hall has just repaired the roof.
The repair will be done before they get old.
They are too old to wait.
questions.explanation: D'ici à ce que (+ subjunctive) = by the time that; here, with a touch of irony, it says the repair is a long way off: by then, we'll have grown old.

questions.stem: Complete with revenir: "Lis le journal en attendant que je ___."
questions.explanation: En attendant que takes the subjunctive: "que je revienne" (revenir, like venir: ils reviennent → que je revienne).

questions.stem: Spoken French: "She had hardly arrived when they called her." → "Elle était ___ ___ arrivée qu'on l'a appelée."
questions.explanation: In speech, à peine goes after the auxiliary, with no inversion: "Elle était à peine arrivée qu'on l'a appelée."

questions.stem: Put the words in order (written style): "Hardly had the train left when the storm broke."
questions.explanation: "À peine le train était-il parti que l'orage éclata." With a noun subject, the noun stays first and a pronoun (il) is inverted after the auxiliary; que introduces the second event, in the passé simple.

questions.stem: Match each conjunction to the time relation it expresses: does the time-clause event come before the main event, at the same time, or after it?
questions.explanation: Dès que and une fois que place the time-clause event first; pendant que and au moment où at the same time; en attendant que looks at an event still to come, which is why it takes the subjunctive.

questions.stem: Which of these take the subjunctive? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: En attendant que, le temps que and d'ici à ce que look at an event that hasn't happened yet: subjunctive. Dès que and pendant que take the indicative.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this 11 November scene.

image.alt: A village square: a stone memorial with a plaque of names and a soldier statue on top, a wreath at its foot; an old man in a beret with medals holding a French flag; a man wearing a blue, white and red sash; two children; the town hall behind. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The statue on top shows a poilu, a First World War soldier; the stone with the names is le monument aux morts; the old man with medals is l'ancien combattant; the man with the tricolour sash is le maire.

questions.stem: "Les médicaments que le médecin m'a ___ sont efficaces." (prescrire)
questions.explanation: Avoir + a direct object placed before: que = les médicaments (masculine plural), so "prescrits". M' is the indirect object (to me) and doesn't count.

questions.stem: "La chirurgienne ? Je l'ai ___ ce matin." (voir)
questions.explanation: L' stands for la chirurgienne, a feminine singular direct object placed before avoir: "vue".

questions.stem: "La généraliste a ___ des antibiotiques." (prescrire)
questions.explanation: With avoir, the participle agrees only with a direct object placed before it. Here the object (des antibiotiques) comes after, and the subject never counts with avoir: "prescrit".

questions.stem: "Les trois semaines de soins qu'il a ___ m'ont paru longues." (falloir)
questions.explanation: Falloir is impersonal (il = it), and impersonal verbs never agree, even after que: "qu'il a fallu".

questions.stem: "Elle s'est ___ dans la salle d'attente." (s'évanouir)
questions.explanation: S'évanouir is essentially pronominal (there is no "évanouir quelqu'un"), so the participle agrees with the subject: "elle s'est évanouie".

questions.stem: In careful written French: "Avant l'opération, la chirurgienne s'est ___ les mains."
questions.explanation: She washed what? Her hands: les mains is the direct object, and it comes after. Se means "for herself", an indirect object, so no agreement: "s'est lavé les mains". Compare "les mains qu'elle s'est lavées", where the object comes first.

questions.stem: "Les infirmières se sont ___ toute la nuit au chevet du malade." (se succéder)
questions.explanation: Succéder à quelqu'un: se is an indirect object, so there is no agreement: "se sont succédé".

questions.stem: "Ma tante s'est ___ opérer du genou."
questions.explanation: Fait followed by an infinitive never agrees: "elle s'est fait opérer".

questions.stem: "Les deux heures qu'a ___ l'opération ont semblé interminables." (durer)
questions.explanation: Durer never has a direct object: "deux heures" is a measure of time, not an object. No agreement: "qu'a duré l'opération".

questions.stem: "Les nouveau-nés que l'infirmière a ___ ce matin vont bien." (peser)
questions.explanation: Here peser has a real direct object: the nurse put the babies on the scales. Que = les nouveau-nés, masculine plural, placed before: "pesés". With a measure ("les trois kilos qu'il a pesé"), there would be no agreement.

questions.stem: In careful written French: "Les infirmières que j'ai ___ rire dans le couloir étaient de bonne humeur." (entendre)
questions.explanation: The nurses do the laughing, so que (= les infirmières, feminine plural) is the object of entendre: "entendues". Compare "les chansons que j'ai entendu chanter", where the songs are the object of chanter.

questions.stem: "Elle a fait tous les efforts qu'elle a ___."
questions.explanation: An infinitive is left out: "qu'elle a pu (faire)". Que is the object of faire, not of pouvoir, so pu doesn't agree.

questions.stem: "La patiente s'est ___ compte qu'elle avait trop attendu."
questions.explanation: Se rendre compte never agrees: compte is the direct object, and se is indirect. "Elle s'est rendu compte."

questions.stem: In Inès's letter, why is it "nous nous sommes beaucoup parlé" but "nous nous sommes bien entendues"?
choices: Parler takes avoir and entendre takes être.
Parler à quelqu'un has an indirect object; entendre quelqu'un has a direct one.
The second verb is in the future.
Inès made a mistake in the first one.
questions.explanation: Both are reciprocal. With se parler, se means "to each other" (indirect): no agreement. With s'entendre, se means "each other" (direct): agreement with the two women, "entendues".

questions.stem: What advice does Inès give her friend at the end of the letter?
choices: To do the screening test she was sent
questions.explanation: "Le test de dépistage que l'Assurance maladie t'a envoyé, fais-le !" Inès realised she had waited too long before seeing a doctor.

questions.stem: Write the participle of prescrire with the right agreement: "Quelles analyses vous a-t-il ___ ?"
questions.explanation: After quel(le)s, the direct object (quelles analyses, feminine plural) comes before the verb: "prescrites".

questions.stem: Write the participle of parler with the right agreement: "Ma sœur et moi, nous nous sommes ___ hier soir."
questions.explanation: Parler à quelqu'un: se (here nous) is an indirect object, so no agreement, even with two women: "nous nous sommes parlé".

questions.stem: Match each sentence to the reason for its participle ending.
