audio.text: — Monsieur le maire, combien coûtera l'ouverture de la médiathèque le dimanche ? — Écoutez, l'essentiel, c'est que les familles soient contentes. Parlons plutôt de l'avenir de la culture dans notre ville.

choices: He admits the cost is too high.
questions.explanation: Asked how much Sunday opening will cost, the mayor talks about families being happy and suggests talking "plutôt de l'avenir de la culture": he avoids the question politely. In a press review: "Le maire a éludé la question."

questions.stem: Listen to the press review. What does L'Écho criticise?

audio.text: Dans la presse ce matin : Le Courrier se félicite de l'ouverture du nouveau pont sur la Loire, tandis que L'Écho déplore son coût, qui aurait doublé en trois ans, selon l'opposition.

choices: The cost of the new bridge.
questions.explanation: "L'Écho déplore son coût, qui aurait doublé en trois ans, selon l'opposition": the paper criticises the cost. The conditionnel "aurait doublé" shows that the doubling is the opposition's claim, not a confirmed fact. Le Courrier, by contrast, welcomes the opening.

questions.stem: « Que tout le monde se taise ! » Complete the report with the right form of "se taire": "Elle a demandé que tout le monde se ___."
questions.explanation: "Demander que" + subjunctive reports an order: que tout le monde se taise. The present subjunctive stays even after the past verb "a demandé".

questions.stem: Complete with the right preposition: "Plusieurs habitants s'interrogent ___ l'utilité du projet."
questions.explanation: "S'interroger sur" + noun = to wonder about, to raise doubts about. It's the formal equivalent of "se demander".

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "The mayor guaranteed that the opening hours would be extended."
questions.explanation: Le maire a garanti que les horaires seraient étendus. "Garantir que" + indicative; after the past verb, the future becomes the conditionnel (seraient), and "étendus" agrees with "les horaires".

questions.stem: Match each verb with the attitude it shows.
questions.explanation: "Se féliciter de" welcomes something; "concéder" gives a point to the other side; "s'indigner" protests angrily; "éluder" dodges. Neutral verbs are "dire, expliquer, affirmer".

questions.stem: In careful French, which of these take the subjunctive in a que-clause? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Verbs of feeling (déplorer, s'indigner) and of will (exiger) take the subjunctive. "Garantir que" and "insinuer que" report a statement, so they take the indicative.

questions.stem: Which reporting verb fits each speaker? Name the numbered speakers.

image.alt: Five people at a public meeting, each numbered and each with a speech bubble: « Je suis ravi de ce résultat ! », « Attention, cela risque de coûter très cher. », « Sur ce point, vous avez raison. », « Le coût ? Parlons plutôt de l'avenir ! » and « C'est scandaleux ! »

questions.explanation: 1 se féliciter (he's delighted with the result), 2 mettre en garde (she warns about the cost), 3 concéder (he admits the other side is right on one point), 4 éluder (he answers a question about cost by changing the subject), 5 s'indigner (he's outraged). Nobody guarantees anything or hints at something unpleasant.

questions.stem: In standard written French: "C'est moi qui ___ les billets."
questions.explanation: After "c'est … qui", the verb agrees with the stressed word: moi → "ai" (c'est moi qui ai). "C'est moi qui a" is heard in casual speech but isn't standard; "avons" would go with "nous".

questions.stem: In standard French: "C'est en 1947 ___ le festival a été créé."
questions.explanation: After "c'est" + a time or a place, use "que": C'est en 1947 que … "Qui" is only for the subject, and "où" here is a common mistake in careful French.

questions.stem: In careful French: "C'est de ce rôle ___ je rêve depuis toujours."
questions.explanation: Keep the preposition with the stressed part (de ce rôle) and use plain "que". "C'est de ce rôle dont …" repeats the "de" and is criticised in careful French; "qui" is for the subject.

questions.stem: Complete: "C'est nous qui ___ gagné le prix du public."
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with "nous": c'est nous qui avons gagné. "Gagner" takes "avoir", so "sommes" is wrong too.

questions.stem: Which sentence stresses the place in "Le festival a lieu à Avignon"?
choices: C'est à Avignon qui le festival a lieu.
C'est Avignon que le festival a lieu.
C'est à Avignon que le festival a lieu.
C'est à Avignon dont le festival a lieu.
questions.explanation: Keep the preposition "à" with the place and use "que": C'est à Avignon que … "Qui" is for subjects, "C'est Avignon que" drops the preposition, and "dont" replaces "de", not "à".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ce spectacle, je lui ai adoré.
questions.explanation: In a dislocation, the pronoun matches the role of the moved word. "Adorer" takes a direct object, so the pronoun is "le" (l'): je l'ai adoré. "Lui" is for à + person, "en" for de or a quantity, "y" for à + thing or a place.

questions.stem: Which is the careful written version of "La pièce sera peut-être reprise"?
choices: Peut-être que la pièce sera-t-elle reprise.
questions.explanation: With "peut-être" first and a noun subject, careful writing uses complex inversion: the noun stays in front and "elle" follows the verb: la pièce sera-t-elle. "Peut-être que" is followed by normal order, never by inversion as well.

questions.stem: Complete the inversion after the quotation: "« Bravo ! » ___"
questions.explanation: After a quotation the verb comes before the subject, and when the verb ends in a vowel, a hyphenated -t- is added: s'écria-t-elle. The "t" is not an apostrophe and isn't part of the verb.

questions.stem: What does "Tout au plus peut-on regretter la longueur du deuxième acte" mean?
choices: Above all, everyone regretted the second act.
The second act was far too long for everyone.
At most, one might regret that the second act is long.
The second act was too short, unfortunately.
questions.explanation: "Tout au plus" (at most) limits the criticism: the only reservation is the length of the second act. The inversion (peut-on) is the usual written order after this phrase.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ce ___ le théâtre a besoin, c'est d'un public jeune."
questions.explanation: "Avoir besoin de" takes "de", so the relative is "ce dont" (B1); the "de" comes back after "c'est": c'est d'un public jeune.

questions.stem: What is the last full rehearsal before the first night called?
questions.explanation: La générale (la répétition générale) is the last full rehearsal. La première is the first public performance, l'entracte the interval, la tournée a tour.

questions.stem: Why does careful writing say "Ce sont les comédiens qui ont choisi le décor" rather than "C'est les comédiens …"?
choices: Ce sont is required whenever qui follows.
Careful writing uses ce sont before a plural noun.
The verb is in the passé composé.
questions.explanation: Before a plural noun (or eux, elles), careful writing uses "ce sont". In speech "c'est les comédiens qui …" is common and accepted informally. With "nous" and "vous", it's always "c'est".

questions.stem: Listen to the announcement. When is the interval?

audio.text: Mesdames et messieurs, la représentation va commencer dans cinq minutes. Nous vous rappelons qu'il y aura un entracte de vingt minutes après le deuxième acte. La billetterie restera ouverte pendant l'entracte.

choices: After the first act, for ten minutes.
After the second act, for twenty minutes.
At the end, before the applause.
questions.explanation: "Il y aura un entracte de vingt minutes après le deuxième acte": a twenty-minute interval after the second act. The ticket office stays open during it.

questions.stem: Listen to the conversation. What disappointed the speaker most?

audio.text: — Alors, cette pièce ? — La pièce, je l'ai trouvée un peu longue. Mais les comédiens, eux, étaient formidables. C'est surtout la mise en scène qui m'a déçue.

questions.explanation: "C'est surtout la mise en scène qui m'a déçue": the "c'est … qui" frame stresses the staging. She found the play a bit long, but that isn't what she stresses, and the actors, she says, were wonderful.

questions.stem: Stress the date: "___ en 1680 que Louis XIV a créé la Comédie-Française." (Type the first words.)
questions.explanation: "C'est … que" stresses the date: C'est en 1680 que … "C'était" is also correct, especially in a narrative, and "ce fut" is the literary form you may meet in older texts.

questions.stem: Complete with the present of "avoir": "C'est vous qui ___ raison."
questions.explanation: After "c'est … qui", the verb agrees with the stressed pronoun: vous → avez.

questions.stem: Put the words in order, in careful written French: "Perhaps the play will be revived."
questions.explanation: Peut-être la pièce sera-t-elle reprise. After "peut-être" at the start, careful writing uses complex inversion: noun subject, verb, then the pronoun "elle".

questions.stem: Match each device with its example.
choices: C'est à Avignon que le festival a lieu.
Voilà dix ans que la troupe part en tournée.
Sans doute le public a-t-il été déçu.
questions.explanation: "C'est … que" puts the place forward; the dislocation moves "ce spectacle" to the front and picks it up with "l'"; "voilà … que" presents a duration; "le public a-t-il" is complex inversion after "sans doute". "Il a dit qu'il viendrait" is reported speech.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct standard French? Select all that apply.
choices: Ce spectacle, je lui ai adoré.
questions.explanation: Complex inversion after "peut-être" (la pièce sera-t-elle) and the adverb after the verb (sera peut-être) are both correct. "Peut-être sera la pièce reprise" puts a noun subject after the verb without the pronoun; "je lui ai adoré" uses an indirect pronoun with a verb that takes a direct object.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the theatre.

image.alt: A theatre seen from the audience with four numbered markers: on the red curtain drawn back at the side, on the painted tree of the scenery, on the dark area beside the stage where an actor waits, and on the wooden stage floor.

questions.explanation: 1 le rideau (the curtain), 2 le décor (the scenery), 3 les coulisses (the wings, where the actor waits), 4 la scène (the stage). L'entracte is the interval, a time, and the ticket office (la billetterie) isn't shown.

questions.stem: How did Madame Bovary first appear?
choices: As a serial in La Revue de Paris, from October to December 1856.
As a book, published by Michel Lévy in 1851.
As a serial in a Rouen newspaper in 1860.
As a book printed in Belgium to avoid the censors.
questions.explanation: Flaubert wrote the novel from 1851 to 1856; it ran as a serial in La Revue de Paris from 1 October to 15 December 1856, with cuts. The book edition (Michel Lévy) followed in April 1857, after the trial.

questions.stem: What was the outcome of the 1857 trial?
choices: Flaubert was found guilty and fined.
Flaubert, the magazine's manager and the printer were acquitted on 7 February 1857.
Flaubert was sent to prison for a month.
questions.explanation: The three men were tried in Paris for offending public and religious morals. On 7 February 1857 all three were acquitted, though the judgment criticised the book. The scandal helped sales.

questions.stem: What does realism (le réalisme) set out to do?
choices: Show ideal heroes and noble feelings.
Show ordinary life as it is, including its dull and ugly sides.
questions.explanation: Realism shows everyday life without idealising it: ordinary subjects, an impersonal narrator, documented detail. Madame Bovary became its model, though Flaubert disliked the label.

questions.stem: Read this original passage: "Charles rentra tard. Quelle journée ! Trois malades, un accouchement, et cette jument qui boitait encore." Which part is Charles's thought in free indirect speech?
choices: All of it, including « Charles rentra tard ».
None: the whole passage is the narrator's.
Quelle journée ! Trois malades, un accouchement, et cette jument qui boitait encore.
questions.explanation: "Charles rentra tard" is the narrator's fact in the passé simple. The exclamation and the list without a main verb are Charles's tired thoughts, given without a reporting verb or quotation marks: free indirect speech.

questions.stem: Turn this free indirect speech into direct speech: "Pourquoi le sort l'avait-il jetée dans ce bourg ?"
choices: « Pourquoi le sort m'a-t-il jetée dans ce bourg ? »
« Pourquoi le sort l'avait-il jetée dans ce bourg ? »
« Pourquoi le sort me jettera-t-il dans ce bourg ? »
« Pourquoi le sort l'a-t-il jeté dans ce bourg ? »
questions.explanation: Back to the first person (l' → m') and one tense towards the present (plus-que-parfait → passé composé): m'a-t-il jetée. The participle keeps its agreement with "me" (Emma, a woman). The future would change the meaning, and "l'a-t-il jeté" keeps the third person.

questions.stem: What is le bovarysme?
choices: A legal term for adultery in the 19th century.
Dreaming of a more romantic life and imagining yourself as someone else.
questions.explanation: The word comes from Emma Bovary: the habit of dreaming of a more glamorous life and seeing yourself as someone else. The philosopher Jules de Gaultier made it popular from the 1890s.

questions.stem: Why does free indirect speech create irony in Madame Bovary?
choices: The narrator openly mocks Emma in every chapter.
Emma herself is an ironic character who jokes about her dreams.
We hear Emma's enthusiasm in clichés from her novels, so we see the gap without the narrator commenting.
The novel is written in the present tense.
questions.explanation: The narrator rarely judges. When Emma's borrowed, novel-fed phrases appear in free indirect speech, the reader hears both her sincerity and the second-hand words: the style creates the irony.

questions.stem: In the novel, who is Lheureux?
choices: A young notary's clerk who shares her daydreams.
A merchant who sells to Emma on credit and lends her money at high rates.
questions.explanation: Lheureux sells and lends at enormous rates, and Emma's debts to him lead to the seizure. The pharmacist is Homais, the clerk is Léon, and her first lover is Rodolphe.

questions.stem: How does the novel end?
choices: Emma poisons herself, Charles dies soon after, and Homais is decorated.
Emma runs away to Paris with Rodolphe.
Charles discovers nothing and lives happily with Berthe.
Emma pays her debts and returns to her father's farm.
questions.explanation: Emma swallows arsenic and dies; Charles discovers her letters and dies soon after; their daughter ends up working in a cotton mill; the pharmacist Homais triumphs and is decorated.

questions.stem: What does "Emma a une imagination romanesque" mean?
choices: She is fond of Rome and Italy.
Her imagination is shaped by novels, full of adventures and feelings.
She has no imagination at all.
questions.explanation: "Romanesque" = as in novels. Emma's daydreams come from the novels she read at the convent. For love and feelings in general, French says "romantique".

questions.stem: In "Elle partirait demain", what tense is "partirait"? Type its French name.
questions.explanation: "Partirait" is the conditionnel présent, here the future in the past: in direct speech Emma thinks « Je partirai demain ».

questions.stem: Match each character with their role in the novel.
choices: a rich landowner who seduces Emma
questions.explanation: Charles Bovary is the dull but kind country doctor; Rodolphe the landowner who breaks off their affair by letter; Léon the clerk she meets in Yonville and again in Rouen; Homais the self-satisfied pharmacist.

questions.stem: Put these events of the novel in order.
choices: The ball at the marquis's château
The seizure of the couple's possessions
questions.explanation: After the ball, Emma's disillusion makes her ill and the couple move to Yonville, where Berthe is born. Rodolphe seduces her there; later her debts lead to the seizure, and she poisons herself.

questions.stem: Which are clues that a sentence is free indirect speech? Select all that apply.
choices: Exclamations or questions in the third person
No reporting verb and no que
Words like demain or ici seen from the character's point of view, in a past narrative
A verb of saying followed by que
questions.explanation: Free indirect speech has no quotation marks (that's direct speech) and no "dit que" (that's indirect speech). Its clues are the character's voice inside the narration: exclamations and questions, and the character's own time and place words.

questions.stem: Someone says "Il n'est pas bête" to mean that a person is very clever. Which figure is this?
questions.explanation: Litotes says less in order to mean more, often with a negative. A euphemism softens something unpleasant; hyperbole exaggerates; an oxymoron joins two contradictory words.

questions.stem: "Il nous a quittés la semaine dernière" (he died last week). Which figure is this?
questions.explanation: "Il nous a quittés" softens the word "mourir": a euphemism. It doesn't say less to mean more (litotes) or the opposite (irony), and nothing is repeated (anaphora).

questions.stem: Which figure is "un silence assourdissant" (a deafening silence)?
questions.explanation: Two contradictory words joined in one expression: an oxymoron. An antithesis contrasts two ideas across a sentence; a periphrasis replaces a word with a description.

questions.stem: A journalist writes "l'Hexagone" instead of "la France". Which figure is this?
questions.explanation: A periphrasis replaces a word with a longer description of it (France is roughly six-sided on the map). Journalists use it to avoid repeating a name.

questions.stem: Which figure is "Ce bureau est une ruche"?
questions.explanation: The office is called a beehive with no comparing word: a metaphor. With "comme" (Ce bureau est comme une ruche) it would be a comparison.

questions.stem: Which figure is "Les villes se remplissent, les campagnes se vident"?
questions.explanation: Two opposite ideas side by side in parallel phrases: an antithesis. An oxymoron would fuse the contradiction into two words.

questions.stem: "Super, il pleut pour notre pique-nique !" Which figure is this?
questions.explanation: The speaker says "super" but means the opposite: irony. Nothing is exaggerated, softened or replaced by a description.

questions.stem: A speech says: "Nous voulons des écoles ouvertes. Nous voulons des hôpitaux proches. Nous voulons des villages vivants." Which figure is used?
questions.explanation: "Nous voulons" is repeated at the start of each sentence: an anaphora, a favourite figure of speeches.

questions.stem: Which figure is "Je te l'ai dit mille fois !"?
questions.explanation: "Mille fois" is a deliberate exaggeration: hyperbole. Litotes and euphemism say less, not more.

questions.stem: After a delicious dinner, a guest says with obvious delight: "Ce n'était pas désagréable du tout !" Which figure is this?
questions.explanation: Said with delight, it says less to mean more (it was excellent): litotes. Said with a sigh about a dull evening, the same words would be irony; context decides.

questions.stem: Type the French name of the figure, with its article: "Le soir, le quartier est calme comme un village."
questions.explanation: The comparing word "comme" makes it a comparison (la comparaison). Without "comme", it would be a metaphor.

questions.stem: Type the adjective that goes with l'ironie: "un ton ___"
questions.explanation: L'ironie → ironique: un ton ironique, une remarque ironique (same form for both genders).

questions.stem: Match each example with its figure.
questions.explanation: Saying less to mean more is litotes; "la Ville lumière" describes Paris instead of naming it (periphrasis); "je meurs de faim" exaggerates (hyperbole); "assourdissant" contradicts "silence" (oxymoron).

questions.stem: Which of these are euphemisms? Select all that apply.
choices: Il nous a quittés (for he died)
questions.explanation: The first three soften something unpleasant: euphemisms. "Je meurs de faim" exaggerates (hyperbole), and "un silence assourdissant" is an oxymoron.

questions.stem: Which of these is a problématique for the topic "la publicité et les enfants"?
choices: Faut-il interdire la publicité qui cible les enfants ?
La publicité et les enfants : un sujet important.
Les enfants regardent beaucoup la télévision.
Il existe des publicités pour enfants depuis longtemps.
questions.explanation: A problématique is a precise question with more than one possible answer, so it creates a debate: "Faut-il interdire …?" can be answered yes, no or "yes, but". The other three are a title and two facts: you can't agree or disagree with them.

questions.stem: Complete: "Certes, la publicité finance les médias. Il n'en reste pas moins qu'elle ___ notre espace public."
questions.explanation: "Il n'en reste pas moins que" (it is nonetheless true that) presents a fact, so it takes the indicative: "elle envahit". "Envahisse" is the subjunctive, "envahir" the infinitive and "envahissant" a participle or adjective.

questions.stem: What does "Or" do in "On pourrait objecter que chacun est libre de ne pas acheter. Or, cette liberté suppose un esprit critique."?
choices: It offers an alternative, like English "or".
It introduces a fact that changes the reasoning ("but", "yet").
questions.explanation: In an argument, "or" brings in a new fact that turns the reasoning against the objection: "Yet that freedom presupposes critical thinking." English "or" is "ou" in French. The noun "l'or" (gold) is the same word in a different use, and "donc" would conclude, not object.

questions.stem: According to the lesson, which plan usually suits the question "Quels sont les effets de la publicité sur les enfants ?"
choices: a dialectical plan: for, against, synthesis
one part per source you have read
no plan: a list of examples
a thematic plan, one aspect per part (economic, social, psychological)
questions.explanation: A "what effects?" question has no real for and against, so the lesson suggests a thematic plan, each part one aspect of the answer. The dialectical plan suits yes-or-no questions such as "Faut-il …?". A list of examples isn't a plan, and a synthesis by source is what the lesson warns against in the C1 preview.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses "inciter" correctly?
choices: Les promotions incitent les clients d'acheter.
Les promotions incitent aux clients d'acheter.
Les promotions incitent les clients à acheter.
Les promotions incitent les clients pour acheter.
questions.explanation: The construction is "inciter quelqu'un à faire quelque chose": a direct object for the person and "à" before the infinitive. "De" and "pour" are wrong here, and the person isn't introduced by "à".

questions.stem: Complete: "Son exemple est concret et très ___."
questions.explanation: The adjective is "convaincant" (convincing). "Convainquant" is the present participle (en le convainquant), "convaincu" means convinced (a person is convaincu, an argument is convaincant), and "convaincre" is the infinitive.

questions.stem: Why is the objection usually in the conditionnel in "On pourrait objecter que les adultes sont libres"?
choices: "Objecter" can only be used in the conditionnel.
It places the objection in the past.
It is a polite way of agreeing with the objection.
It marks a view the writer reports but doesn't hold.
questions.explanation: The conditionnel keeps the objection at a distance: it is something "one could" say, not the writer's own view, and the refutation (Or …) follows. "Objecter" exists in every tense, the conditionnel doesn't make it past, and the writer is about to disagree, not agree.

questions.stem: Which example best backs up the argument "La publicité peut être bénéfique"?
choices: Le prix de l'essence a beaucoup augmenté cette année.
Une campagne contre le tabac peut inciter des fumeurs à arrêter.
Les enfants regardent souvent la télévision le soir.
La publicité existe depuis plus d'un siècle.
questions.explanation: A pertinent example proves the argument it follows: an anti-smoking campaign shows advertising doing good. The price of petrol is off the subject, children watching television says nothing about benefit, and the age of advertising proves nothing either way.

questions.stem: To avoid repeating the verb, complete: "Les marques ciblent les enfants. ___ est de plus en plus précis."
questions.explanation: "Le ciblage" is the noun of the action (targeting), and it is masculine, so "précis" agrees. "Cette cible" would be the children themselves (and would need "précise"); "ce cibler" and "ce ciblé" aren't nouns.

questions.stem: What does "en d'autres termes" do in "Le prix a augmenté et la quantité a baissé ; en d'autres termes, on paie plus pour moins."?
choices: It concedes a point to the other side.
It reformulates the idea in other words.
It opens a wider question at the end.
questions.explanation: "En d'autres termes" (formal) and "autrement dit" (neutral) restate what has just been said more clearly. Adding a point is "de plus", conceding is "certes", and a wider question at the end is an "ouverture".

questions.stem: In the lesson's reading text, what does the author propose?
choices: strict rules for advertisements aimed at children, and education
no change, because adults are free to choose
a tax on advertising to fund the media
questions.explanation: The text rejects a total ban because it would call into question the funding of many media ("Ce serait remettre en cause le financement …"), and argues for "des règles strictes pour les publicités destinées aux enfants" and education. It refutes the "adults are free" objection, and no tax is mentioned.

questions.stem: In the reading text, why does the author mention a child who hears a slogan ten times a day?
choices: to prove that the brand "Pétillo" really exists
to give an official statistic about children
to show that slogans are easy to forget
to show that freedom to choose depends on a critical mind the child doesn't have yet
questions.explanation: The child is the example that backs up the refutation: the objection says everyone is free not to buy, and the author answers that this freedom "suppose un esprit critique que tout le monde n'a pas". Pétillo is presented as an imaginary brand, there is no statistic, and the point is that slogans stick.

questions.stem: What makes a good third part (synthèse) in a dialectical essay?
choices: It repeats the arguments of the first two parts.
It says that both sides are equally right.
It goes beyond the opposition with a nuanced answer, conditions or a solution.
It opens a new topic unrelated to the question.
questions.explanation: The synthèse moves the debate one step further, for example: "advertising is neither good nor bad in itself; it depends on the target and the rules". Repeating, or simply saying both sides are right, adds nothing; a new topic belongs at most in the ouverture of the conclusion.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il est paradoxal que la publicité ___ si efficace alors que tout le monde dit la détester."
questions.explanation: Value judgements with "il est" + adjective + "que" (il est paradoxal, étonnant, normal que) take the subjunctive: "qu'elle soit" (adjectives of certainty such as "il est certain que" take the indicative). "Est" and "sera" are indicative, and the infinitive can't follow "que" with a subject.

questions.stem: Type the formal three-word phrase meaning "in other words": "Le produit n'a pas changé ; ___, on paie l'emballage."
questions.explanation: "En d'autres termes" is the formal way to reformulate; "en d'autres mots" is also accepted (less formal). "Autrement dit" (A2) is the everyday equivalent but has two words.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of this refutation in order.
choices: La publicité cible les plus vulnérables.
On pourrait objecter que chacun est libre de ne pas acheter.
Certes, cette liberté existe en principe.
Or, elle suppose un esprit critique qu'un enfant n'a pas encore.
La publicité destinée aux enfants doit donc être encadrée.
questions.explanation: The claim comes first; the objection follows in the conditionnel; "Certes, cette liberté" concedes the point just raised (it needs "liberté" from the objection); "Or, elle suppose …" turns it around; "donc" brings back the claim, stronger.

questions.stem: Match each connector with its job in an argument.
choices: brings in a fact that challenges the objection
adds support to what was just said
questions.explanation: "Certes" concedes; "or" turns the reasoning; "en d'autres termes" restates; "d'ailleurs" (in fact) supports the last point, while "par ailleurs" (besides) moves to another one. Cause is "puisque, étant donné que".

questions.stem: Which are signs of a good refutation? Select all that apply.
choices: It admits what is true in the other view before answering it.
It attacks an argument nobody really holds.
It ends by coming back to the writer's claim, made stronger.
It avoids mentioning the other side at all.
questions.explanation: A refutation takes the best opposing argument, concedes what is true in it (certes) and turns it (or, il n'en reste pas moins que) to come back to the claim. Attacking a view nobody holds convinces no one, and ignoring the other side isn't a refutation at all.

questions.stem: Name the numbered tags of this dialectical essay plan.

image.alt: The plan of a dialectical essay as five stacked boxes, each with an empty numbered tag on the left: 1 Introduction, a hook, the question asked and the plan; 2 Part I, the arguments for, advertising informs and funds the media; 3 Part II, the arguments against, it manipulates, with a refutation; 4 Part III, going beyond the opposition, regulate advertising and teach critical thinking; 5 Conclusion, the answer to the question, then a wider question to finish.

questions.explanation: The introduction sets out the problématique (the question); part I is the thèse (arguments for), part II the antithèse (arguments against, with refutation), part III the synthèse (going beyond the opposition); the conclusion answers and ends with an ouverture, a wider question.

questions.stem: Listen to the radio item. What do the manufacturers reply?

audio.text: Une association de consommateurs demande l'interdiction des publicités pour les boissons sucrées avant vingt et une heures. Selon elle, ces messages incitent les enfants à consommer trop de sucre. Les fabricants répondent que les parents restent responsables de ce que boivent leurs enfants.

choices: that the ads will stop before 9 p.m.
that parents remain responsible for what their children drink
that their drinks contain less sugar than before
that children don't watch television in the evening
questions.explanation: "Les fabricants répondent que les parents restent responsables de ce que boivent leurs enfants." The ban before 9 p.m. is what the consumer association asks for; sugar content and viewing habits aren't mentioned.

questions.stem: Listen to two friends. What is the second speaker suggesting?

audio.text: Franchement, la publicité, je ne la vois même plus. — Tu crois ça ? Pourtant, tu as acheté la même crème que dans le spot d'hier soir ! — C'est un hasard. — Un hasard, vraiment ? Moi, j'appelle ça du marketing réussi.

choices: that the cream was cheaper than in the advert
that advertising never works on adults
that advertising influences the first speaker without them noticing
that the first speaker should complain about the advert
questions.explanation: The first speaker claims not to notice advertising any more; the second points out that this person bought the cream from last night's advert and calls it "du marketing réussi" (successful marketing), not chance. Nothing is said about price or complaints.

questions.stem: In a letter of complaint, where does a warning such as "À défaut de réponse sous quinze jours, je me verrai dans l'obligation de saisir le médiateur" usually go?
choices: at the end, after the facts and the request
in the first sentence, to set the tone
before the facts, in the subject line
in place of the closing formula
questions.explanation: The order is facts, problem, request, and only then the warning: a letter that starts with a threat sounds aggressive and is less convincing. The closing formula still ends the letter.

questions.stem: Complete the formal request: "Je vous saurais gré ___ bien vouloir procéder au remboursement."
questions.explanation: The construction is "savoir gré à quelqu'un de quelque chose", so "Je vous saurais gré de bien vouloir …". "Pour", "à" and "que" don't fit this verb.

questions.stem: What does "le préjudice" mean in "Cette panne m'a causé un préjudice important"?
questions.explanation: "Le préjudice" is the harm or loss you suffer (subir un préjudice). A bias is "le préjugé"; a formal notice is "la mise en demeure"; a refund is "le remboursement".

questions.stem: Complete: "… dont vous trouverez la facture ___."
questions.explanation: "Ci-joint" agrees with the noun when it comes after it, like an adjective: "la facture ci-jointe". It stays invariable at the start of a sentence (Ci-joint la facture) or before a noun without a determiner (Vous trouverez ci-joint copie de la facture). One invoice, feminine singular: "ci-jointe".

questions.stem: A shop offers you a document worth 50 euros to spend in the same shop instead of a refund. What is it?
questions.explanation: "L'avoir" is a credit note (store credit). "Le dédommagement" is compensation for a loss, "la mise en demeure" a formal notice, and "l'accusé de réception" the proof that a letter arrived.

questions.stem: What is "un geste commercial"?
choices: a goodwill gesture the seller offers without admitting fault
a legal obligation to refund within fourteen days
a complaint sent by registered letter
questions.explanation: A "geste commercial" (free delivery, a discount, a small credit note) is offered to keep a customer happy; it doesn't mean the seller accepts it was at fault. A sales pitch is "un argumentaire de vente".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Les usagers ont subi de trois semaines de retards.
Les usagers ont subis trois semaines de retards.
Les usagers se sont subi trois semaines de retards.
Les usagers ont subi trois semaines de retards.
questions.explanation: "Subir" takes a direct object (subir des retards, subir un préjudice), and with "avoir" the participle doesn't agree with the subject: "ils ont subi". It isn't pronominal, and it takes no "de".

questions.stem: Which sentence fits the register of a formal letter of complaint?
choices: Je me vois contraint de vous adresser cette réclamation.
Du coup, je veux être remboursé tout de suite.
questions.explanation: "Je me vois contraint de …" is formal and firm (lesson 15). "Ça craint", "du coup" and "bon, ben" are informal speech and break the register of the letter.

questions.stem: A newspaper writes: "Le film a reçu des critiques mitigées." What were the reviews like?
questions.explanation: "Mitigé" means mixed, partly positive and partly negative. Glowing is "élogieux"; unanimously negative would be "des critiques très sévères" or "désastreuses".

questions.stem: What should the summary in a critical review avoid?
questions.explanation: The summary is short, in the present, and doesn't give the ending away. The title, the author and the genre belong in the presentation.

questions.stem: Which opening does the lesson advise against?
choices: Commander un canapé à minuit, depuis son lit, est devenu banal.
Depuis la nuit des temps, l'homme achète des objets.
Tout le monde dit détester la publicité ; pourtant, elle fonctionne.
« Le client est roi », dit-on. Est-ce toujours vrai en ligne ?
questions.explanation: "Depuis la nuit des temps" (since the dawn of time) is the most worn-out hook in French and leads nowhere. A concrete scene, a paradox or a saying to question all catch the reader and lead to the problématique.

questions.stem: According to FEI's candidate manual, as the lesson describes it, how long must the DELF B2 written text be in the current format?
questions.explanation: The manual asks for at least 250 words: you may write more, never less. 160 is the minimum usually given at B1. Follow the number on your paper.

questions.stem: In the model letter, why does Julien refuse the 30-euro credit note?
choices: He wants a different brand of computer.
The shop sent it too late.
It doesn't make up for the harm, since he had to rent a computer to keep working.
questions.explanation: "Il ne compense en rien le préjudice subi, puisque j'ai dû louer un appareil pour continuer à travailler." He asks for a replacement or a full refund plus the rental costs; nothing is said about another brand or a late credit note.

questions.stem: Complete with "dédommager" in the present: "Nous vous ___ pour le retard."
questions.explanation: Like "manger", "dédommager" keeps the e before -ons to keep the soft g sound: "nous dédommageons". "Dédommagions" is the imparfait or subjunctive, and the other two forms don't exist.

questions.stem: Why is "m'avait promis" in the plus-que-parfait in "Votre service après-vente m'avait promis une réparation sous dix jours. Cinq semaines plus tard, je n'ai reçu ni l'ordinateur ni la moindre explication."?
choices: It is a polite form, like the conditionnel.
It describes a habit in the past.
It reports a claim the writer doesn't believe.
The promise came before the other past events in the letter.
questions.explanation: The plus-que-parfait is the past before the past: the promise was made before the five weeks went by. Politeness is the conditionnel's job, a habit the imparfait's, and a reported claim uses the conditionnel.

questions.stem: Type the French term, with its article: the formal notice to pay or act by a date, often the last letter before legal action.
questions.explanation: "La mise en demeure" (plural "les mises en demeure"): "mettre quelqu'un en demeure de payer" is to give formal notice to pay.

questions.stem: Put the parts of this letter of complaint in order.
choices: Le 3 mars, j'ai commandé un ordinateur portable sur votre site.
Je vous saurais gré de bien vouloir me rembourser.
À défaut de réponse sous quinze jours, je saisirai le médiateur.
Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
questions.explanation: Subject line, then the opening; the facts come first in the body, then the request, then the warning; the closing formula ends the letter.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this formal letter.

image.alt: A formal letter on a page, with every line shown as a grey bar and six numbered markers: 1 on three short lines at the top left; 2 on three short lines on the right, lower down; 3 on one line on the right under them; 4 on one longer line on the left; 5 on the three blocks of long lines in the middle of the page; 6 on two lines near the bottom, above a short line at the bottom right.

questions.explanation: In a French formal letter the sender is at the top left, the recipient on the right, then the place and date; the subject line (Objet :) comes before the opening and the body; the closing formula comes just before the signature.

questions.stem: Match each term with its meaning.
choices: a formal notice to act by a date
someone who helps settle a dispute out of court
the period in which you can cancel a purchase
a credit note to spend in the same shop
questions.explanation: A credit note is "l'avoir". The registered letter with "accusé de réception" proves the date your complaint arrived; the "médiateur de la consommation" comes after a written complaint, before the courts.

questions.stem: Which belong in a critical review? Select all that apply.
choices: a short summary in the present, without the ending
a judgement backed up by examples from the work
a recommendation for a type of reader or viewer
a detailed account of how the story ends
the closing formula "Je vous prie d'agréer …"
questions.explanation: A review presents the work, summarises it briefly without spoiling it, judges it with examples and recommends it or not. Giving away the ending spoils it for the reader, and the closing formula belongs to formal letters.

questions.stem: Listen to the voicemail. What will the company do?

audio.text: Bonjour, ici le service après-vente de Novaro. Nous avons bien reçu votre réclamation. Votre ordinateur sera remplacé, et, à titre de geste commercial, nous vous rembourserons les frais de livraison. Vous recevrez un courriel de confirmation sous quarante-huit heures.

choices: repair the computer within forty-eight hours
replace the computer and refund the delivery costs
send a credit note for the delivery costs
questions.explanation: "Votre ordinateur sera remplacé" and, as a goodwill gesture, "nous vous rembourserons les frais de livraison". Forty-eight hours is when the confirmation e-mail arrives; no repair, full refund or credit note is mentioned.

questions.stem: Listen to the radio item. From when does the period for changing your mind run?

audio.text: Vous avez acheté un produit en ligne et vous changez d'avis ? Dans l'Union européenne, vous disposez en général de quatorze jours pour vous rétracter, à compter de la réception du produit. Attention : certains achats, comme les billets de concert, sont exclus.

choices: from the day you receive the product
from the day of the concert
questions.explanation: "À compter de la réception du produit": from receipt of the goods. Concert tickets are mentioned as an exception, not as a starting point.

questions.stem: In the DELF B2 speaking test as the lesson describes it, what comes straight after the preparation?
choices: a monologue presenting and defending your view
questions.explanation: After about 30 minutes of preparation you give your monologue suivi (5 to 7 minutes in FEI's manual), and only then the debate. You don't read the document aloud, and the unprepared role play belongs to the B1 exam.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'en viens maintenant ___ mon deuxième argument."
questions.explanation: The phrase is "en venir à" + noun or infinitive: "j'en viens à mon deuxième argument". The "en" stays in every person (nous en venons à).

questions.stem: Which sentence is a transition between two parts of a talk?
choices: Le document que j'ai choisi est un article de presse.
Après avoir vu les risques, voyons ce que les écrans peuvent apporter.
À mon sens, les écrans ne sont pas un danger en soi.
Bonjour, je vous remercie de m'écouter.
questions.explanation: A transition closes one part (the risks) and opens the next (what screens can bring). The other sentences introduce the document, state a position and greet the examiner.

questions.stem: What does "qui plus est" mean in "Le trajet est long et, qui plus est, très cher"?
questions.explanation: "Qui plus est" adds a stronger point after a first one, like "de plus" or "de surcroît". It has nothing to do with a person, it doesn't contrast (however = cependant), and "in my view" is "à mon sens".

questions.stem: What does "en l'occurrence" mean in "Certains métiers, en l'occurrence ceux du soin, ne se font pas à distance"?
questions.explanation: "En l'occurrence" points to the particular case in question. "On this occasion" is "à cette occasion", "by accident" is "par hasard", "in the end" is "finalement".

questions.stem: The examiner raises an objection. Which answer works best at B2?
choices: Je comprends votre objection, mais elle ne tient pas compte du coût.
Non, je ne suis pas d'accord.
questions.explanation: A good answer acknowledges the objection and then answers it with a reason. A bare "non", "vous avez tort" or "je ne sais pas" gives the examiner nothing to assess.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il va de soi que les enfants ___ besoin de règles."
questions.explanation: "Il va de soi que" (it goes without saying that) presents something as obvious, so it takes the indicative: "ils ont besoin". "Aient" is the subjunctive.

questions.stem: What is "un contre-exemple"?
choices: an example that supports your own argument
a single case that contradicts a general claim
a summary of the opposing side
a question you ask to gain time
questions.explanation: A counterexample is one case against a general statement ("a nurse can't work from home" against "home working suits everyone"). The lesson's advice: accept it as a case, and deny that it is the rule.

questions.stem: Why does the lesson suggest reformulating the examiner's question ("Si je vous comprends bien, vous me demandez si …")?
choices: It shows you understood and gives you a few seconds to think.
It is required by the exam rules.
It lets you change the subject.
questions.explanation: Reformulating proves you understood and buys a little time naturally. It isn't a rule, it must lead to an answer, and it should keep you on the subject, not take you off it.

questions.stem: Which verb completes "Pour ___ le débat : revenons aux enfants" (to bring the debate back to the point)?
questions.explanation: "Recentrer le débat" is to bring it back to the point after a digression. "Récapituler" sums up, "aborder" takes up a subject, "cerner" pins down a problem.

questions.stem: What should you do with the short document in the DELF B2 speaking test?
choices: summarise it in detail for the whole monologue
present its question briefly, then defend your own view
read it aloud to the examiner
questions.explanation: The document is a starting point: one or two sentences on it, then the debate it raises and your position with arguments and examples. A long summary is one of the commonest mistakes.

questions.stem: In the lesson's debate extract, the examiner asks "Donc vous changez d'avis ?". What does the candidate do?
choices: He admits he was wrong and takes the opposite view.
He refuses to answer the question.
He changes the subject to tourism.
He presents his concession as a clarification of his position.
questions.explanation: "Non, je précise ma position": he keeps his position (working from home, yes) and adds the limits he conceded (part-time, where it is possible). Conceding a point isn't changing sides.

questions.stem: Which is the most natural way to gain a few seconds before answering?
choices: C'est une bonne question. Disons que …
questions.explanation: Short French fillers (C'est une bonne question, Disons que, Voyons) sound natural and keep you speaking French. A long "euh", English words and a long silence all count against fluency.

questions.stem: What does "soit dit en passant" signal?
choices: a new part of the plan
questions.explanation: "Soit dit en passant" (by the way, incidentally) adds a remark in passing: keep it short and come back at once. It doesn't conclude, concede or open a new part.

questions.stem: Complete with a verb meaning "to sum up": "Pour ___ : deux avantages, un inconvénient majeur."
questions.explanation: "Pour récapituler" is the oral recap phrase this lesson teaches; "pour résumer" is also correct.

questions.stem: Put the parts of this monologue in order.
choices: Le document que j'ai choisi aborde la question du télétravail.
L'enjeu de ce débat, c'est l'équilibre entre vie privée et travail.
À mon sens, le télétravail est utile, à condition d'être limité.
J'aborderai d'abord ses avantages, puis ses limites.
J'en viens maintenant à ses limites.
Pour récapituler : oui au télétravail, mais à temps partiel.
questions.explanation: Document, then what is at stake, then your position and the announced plan; the first part (the advantages) follows the plan, and "J'en viens maintenant à ses limites" opens the second; "Pour récapituler" concludes.

questions.stem: Match each connector with its meaning.
questions.explanation: "Therefore" is "donc" or "par conséquent". "À mon sens" = "à mon avis"; "de surcroît" is formal, like "qui plus est".

questions.stem: Which are good moves in the debate part? Select all that apply.
choices: Reformulating the examiner's question before answering.
Conceding part of an objection, then coming back to your position.
Asking the examiner to rephrase a question you didn't understand.
Reading out an answer you prepared word for word.
questions.explanation: Reformulating, conceding then rebounding, and asking for a question to be rephrased are all good debate skills. A bare yes or no says nothing, and reading a prepared answer stops you interacting.

questions.stem: Name the numbered stages of the DELF B2 speaking test.

image.alt: A timeline with three numbered blocks and an arrow from the first to the second. 1, separate on the left: about 30 minutes, alone, with notes. Then a bracket over the other two, in front of the examiner, about 20 minutes in all: 2, 5 to 7 minutes, present and defend; 3, the rest of the time, answer and nuance. A note says the times follow FEI's candidate manual.

choices: la lecture du document à voix haute
questions.explanation: About 30 minutes of preparation alone, then about 20 minutes with the examiner: the monologue suivi (5 to 7 minutes in FEI's manual) and the debate for the rest. There is no reading aloud, and the synthesis of documents is a C1 written task.

questions.stem: Listen to the examiner. What is her objection?

audio.text: Vous dites que les écrans isolent les enfants. Pourtant, beaucoup d'adolescents se parlent surtout en ligne. Ils ne sont pas isolés, ils communiquent autrement, non ?

choices: that teenagers spend too much time online
that teenagers who talk online are not isolated, they communicate differently
that screens are bad for children's eyes
that parents should control screen time
questions.explanation: "Ils ne sont pas isolés, ils communiquent autrement": she objects to the claim that screens isolate children. She doesn't say they spend too much time online, and eyesight and parental control aren't mentioned.

questions.stem: Listen to the candidate's answer. What does he do?

audio.text: Je comprends votre objection et, je vous l'accorde, ils communiquent beaucoup. Mais parler en ligne ne remplace pas complètement les rencontres réelles. Concrètement, je proposerais une soirée sans écran par semaine.

choices: He concedes a point, keeps his position and makes a practical proposal.
He asks the examiner to repeat the question.
He refuses the objection without giving a reason.
questions.explanation: "Je vous l'accorde" concedes that teenagers communicate a lot; "Mais … ne remplace pas" keeps his position; "Concrètement, je proposerais …" adds a practical proposal.

questions.stem: What do you need to pass the DELF B2?
choices: 50 points out of 100, with at least 5 out of 25 in every part
50 points out of 100, whatever the marks in each part
at least 12.5 out of 25 in every part
questions.explanation: The pass mark is 50/100, and every part also needs at least 5/25: a lower mark in any part fails the diploma even with 50 or more in total.

questions.stem: A candidate has 62/100 in total but 4/25 in listening. What is the result?
choices: admis, but only for the written parts
admis if the speaking mark is above 15
questions.explanation: Below 5/25 in any part, the candidate fails ("ajourné"), whatever the total. There is no partial pass.

questions.stem: How long is the DELF B2 reading paper (compréhension des écrits) in the current format?
questions.explanation: Reading takes 1 hour; listening about 30 minutes; writing 1 hour; together the written parts take about 2 h 30. 35 and 45 minutes are figures from the B1 exam.

questions.stem: Which can-do statement best describes B2, in the lesson's words?
choices: can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases
can describe experiences and events and briefly give reasons for opinions
can express ideas fluently and precisely, with full control of complex texts
can explain a view on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of the options
questions.explanation: Explaining a view on a topical issue with pros and cons is a B2 statement. Familiar everyday expressions are A1, briefly giving reasons is B1, and full control of complex texts is C1 or beyond.

questions.stem: What is "un contresens"?
choices: an answer that is off the topic
understanding the opposite of what a text says
questions.explanation: A "contresens" is a misreading, often caused by a negation, a concession or a false friend. An off-topic answer is "un hors-sujet".

questions.stem: In a reading text, "Le projet sera éventuellement reporté" means:
choices: The project may possibly be postponed.
The project will eventually be postponed.
The project has finally been postponed.
The project will obviously be postponed.
questions.explanation: "Éventuellement" means possibly, if need be. "Eventually" is "finalement" or "à terme". Reading it the English way is a classic contresens.

questions.stem: In the new format, what kind of questions do the DELF B2 listening and reading papers use?
choices: true/false with a quotation to justify
a short essay on each document
questions.explanation: FEI's description of the revised papers says open and true/false questions were removed from the B2 comprehension papers; older practice books still have them.

questions.stem: What gives a text "cohésion", in the sense the lesson uses?
choices: the links between sentences: connectives, pronouns, synonyms
the logic of the whole plan only
questions.explanation: "La cohésion" is the way sentences link (connecteurs, pronouns, synonyms); "la cohérence" is the logic of the whole text. Grids look at both.

questions.stem: In careful written French, complete: "Bien qu'elle ___ le premier match, elle a gagné le tournoi."
questions.explanation: "Bien que" takes the subjunctive, and the loss came before the win, so the subjonctif passé: "bien qu'elle ait perdu" (lesson 05). "Perde" would put the loss at the same time; "a perdu" and "avait perdu" are indicative.

questions.stem: Which sentence reports a claim with the reportive conditionnel, without the journalist confirming it?
choices: Le ministre a reconnu une erreur de calcul.
Il y a eu une erreur de calcul, c'est certain.
Selon le ministre, il y aurait eu une erreur de calcul.
Le ministre savait qu'il y avait une erreur de calcul.
questions.explanation: "Il y aurait eu" is the conditionnel passé used to report information that isn't confirmed (lesson 10). The other sentences present the error as a fact.

questions.stem: Which of these is taught in this course for reading only, not for writing?
choices: the passé simple (il entra, ils firent)
questions.explanation: The passé simple, the passé antérieur and the literary subjunctives are for recognition: you read them and can turn them into the passé composé. The other three are productive at B2.

questions.stem: In the reading practice, who wants to keep marks but improve them?
questions.explanation: Hugo: "Qu'on améliore les notes, d'accord ; qu'on les supprime, non." Camille prefers comments to marks, and Inès doesn't mind marks but objects to constant comparison.

questions.stem: In the reading practice, what bothers Inès?
choices: the constant comparison with other pupils
questions.explanation: "Les notes ne me dérangent pas en soi. Ce qui me gêne, c'est la comparaison permanente avec les autres." Vague comments are Hugo's complaint; homework isn't mentioned.

questions.stem: In the listening paper, what should you do before each recording?
choices: read the questions and the three options
write a summary of what you expect to hear
questions.explanation: The questions and options tell you what to listen for. There is no transcript, and a guessed summary wastes time.

questions.stem: Which connector takes the subjunctive?
questions.explanation: "Encore que" (even though, formal) takes the subjunctive like "bien que" (lesson 08). "D'autant que", "dès lors que" and "au point que" introduce facts and usually take the indicative (lesson 17).

questions.stem: Type the French term, with its article, for a mock exam done in real conditions.
questions.explanation: "L'examen blanc" (masculine; plural les examens blancs). Do at least one with a sample paper and a timer.

questions.stem: Match each exam word with its meaning.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment is "l'autoévaluation". "Ajourné" is the official word on results; "admis" is also a noun (la liste des admis).

questions.stem: Which statements about the DELF B2 tout public are true, as the lesson describes it? Select all that apply.
choices: Each of the four parts is marked out of 25.
The three written parts are taken together.
The writing task asks for at least 250 words.
You must have passed the DELF B1 before taking the B2.
The speaking test has no preparation time.
questions.explanation: Four parts of 25 points; listening, reading and writing in one sitting; at least 250 words. Each level is a separate diploma, so you can take the B2 without the B1, and the speaking test has about 30 minutes of preparation.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this DELF B2 overview.

image.alt: An overview of the DELF B2 with the names of the parts left out. A box for the written papers, about 2 h 30 in all, holds three numbered blocks: 1, about 30 minutes, 3 exercises, multiple choice, 25 points; 2, 1 hour, 3 exercises, multiple choice, 25 points; 3, 1 hour, one argued text, 250 words minimum, 25 points. A separate box for the individual test holds block 4: preparation about 30 minutes, then about 20 minutes, monologue suivi and debate, 25 points.

questions.explanation: Listening (compréhension de l'oral) is the 30-minute paper; reading (compréhension des écrits) the 1-hour multiple-choice paper; writing (production écrite) the argued text; speaking (production orale) the separate test. The synthesis of documents is a C1 task.

questions.stem: Listen to the message from the exam centre. Why should the candidate arrive thirty minutes early?

audio.text: Bonjour, ici le centre d'examen. Votre épreuve orale aura lieu le jeudi 12 juin à quatorze heures. Merci d'arriver trente minutes avant, pour la préparation, avec une pièce d'identité.

choices: to fill in the registration form
questions.explanation: "Merci d'arriver trente minutes avant, pour la préparation": the 30 minutes are the preparation time. The message also asks for an identity document; no form, fee or other paper is mentioned.

questions.stem: Listen to a learner's self-assessment. What is her weak point, and what will she do?

audio.text: Mon point fort, c'est l'écrit : j'ai eu dix-huit sur vingt-cinq à l'examen blanc. Mais en compréhension orale, je n'ai eu que six. Il me reste deux mois pour combler mes lacunes, alors je vais écouter la radio tous les jours.

choices: writing; she will write an essay every week
listening; she will listen to the radio every day
speaking; she will take a course
reading; she will read a newspaper every day
questions.explanation: Her strong point is writing (18/25); her weak point is listening ("je n'ai eu que six"), and to fill her gaps she will listen to the radio every day. With 6/25 she is just above the 5/25 minimum, so that part is the one to work on.

questions.stem: What must a synthesis of documents never contain?
choices: a plan in two or three parts
questions.explanation: A synthesis reports what the documents say, neutrally: no "je pense", no judgement. Reformulating, attributing views (selon l'auteur …) and having a plan are exactly what it needs.

questions.stem: How should a synthesis be organised?
choices: one paragraph per document, in order
by the date of the documents
by ideas, showing where the documents agree and disagree
from the shortest document to the longest
questions.explanation: A synthesis is built around the questions the documents answer; document-by-document paragraphs make a series of summaries, not a synthesis.

questions.stem: What does "confronter deux documents" mean in this lesson?
choices: to set them side by side and compare them
to summarise only the first one
questions.explanation: "Confronter" here is to compare documents point by point, to see what converges and what diverges. Être confronté à means to be faced with.

questions.stem: In the lesson's two documents on free public transport, on which point do they converge?
choices: Most new passengers are former drivers.
The cost of the measure is small.
Price matters more than quality of service.
Ridership rises sharply when buses become free.
questions.explanation: Both say the number of passengers rises. They diverge on who the new passengers are, on the cost, and on what matters most (the economist says quality of service matters more than price).

questions.stem: What does "recouper les faits" mean?
questions.explanation: "Recouper" is to check one source against another: if two documents give the same fact, it is solid; if not, the synthesis says so neutrally. "Les témoignages se recoupent": the accounts tally.

questions.stem: Why does the model synthesis say "il pèserait, selon l'économiste, sur les impôts"?
choices: The conditionnel reports her claim without endorsing it.
It is a polite form addressed to the reader.
questions.explanation: This is the reportive conditionnel (lesson 10): the writer of a synthesis reports a view without taking it on. "Selon" alone doesn't require the conditionnel; here it reinforces the distance.

questions.stem: Which sentence could appear in a synthesis of the two documents?
choices: À mon avis, la gratuité des transports est une erreur.
À Tallinn, les transports publics sont gratuits depuis des années.
Le maire a tort de croire que la gratuité est un investissement.
Selon l'économiste, les nouveaux voyageurs sont souvent d'anciens piétons.
questions.explanation: Attributed, neutral and taken from the documents. The other sentences give the writer's opinion, add an example from outside the corpus, or judge an author.

questions.stem: According to FEI's 2022 candidate manual, as the lesson reports it, how long should the DALF C1 synthesis be?
questions.explanation: The manual gives 200 to 240 words for the synthesis and at least 250 for the essay that follows. Check the instructions on the paper.

questions.stem: What does "hiérarchiser les idées" mean?
choices: to rank the ideas by importance
to put the ideas in alphabetical order
to give each idea the same space
questions.explanation: Ranking decides what gets a sentence, what gets a few words and what goes: examples and details usually disappear. The hierarchy of ideas becomes the plan.

questions.stem: Which version condenses "Les tarifs ont été supprimés, ce qui a fait augmenter le nombre de voyageurs" with nominalisation?
choices: On a supprimé les tarifs et il y a eu plus de voyageurs.
Les tarifs, ils ont été supprimés, donc plus de voyageurs.
La suppression des tarifs a entraîné une hausse de la fréquentation.
Comme les tarifs ont été supprimés, le nombre de voyageurs a augmenté.
questions.explanation: Nouns (la suppression, la hausse, la fréquentation) pack two clauses into one shorter, more formal sentence (lesson 14). The others keep two verbs, and one is informal speech.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning.
choices: in agreement, pointing the same way
to shorten while keeping the essentials
questions.explanation: "To cross-check" is "recouper". "Des analyses convergentes" agree; "des avis divergents" differ.

questions.stem: Put these steps of the method in the order the lesson gives.
choices: Note each document's main ideas in a few words.
Compare the documents in a grid, idea by idea.
Rank the ideas and drop the details.
Build a neutral plan around ideas.
Write, count the words and reread.
questions.explanation: You can only compare ideas you have noted, rank them after comparing, plan once you know which ideas matter, and write last.

questions.stem: Which are rules of the synthesis of documents? Select all that apply.
choices: Use only what the documents say.
Add a well-known example to make it livelier.
questions.explanation: No opinion, nothing from outside, your own words. Paragraphs are built around ideas, not documents, and an outside example breaks the second rule.

questions.stem: Type the French verb (infinitive) meaning "to cross-check" (sources, facts).
questions.explanation: "Recouper": un journaliste recoupe ses sources. Pronominal: les témoignages se recoupent (the accounts tally).

questions.stem: You have drawn two subjects. Which should you choose, according to the lesson?
choices: the one where you can find arguments and examples fastest
the one whose theme you like best
the one the examiner seems to prefer
questions.explanation: What is marked is your argument, so pick the subject where two or three arguments with examples come quickly, even if the other theme appeals more.

questions.stem: How should you take notes during the preparation?
choices: every sentence of the monologue in full
keywords and arrows, with only the opening and the conclusion written out
questions.explanation: Full sentences get read aloud and sound flat; keywords keep you speaking. The opening and conclusion can be written out, because those are the seconds nerves take away.

questions.stem: What is "le fil conducteur" of a talk?
choices: the common thread that links the parts
questions.explanation: In the model, the thread is "un lieu appartient d'abord à ceux qui y vivent": said in part one, again in the recap, and used to answer the last question.

questions.stem: Complete with "se contredire" in the present: "Vous vous ___ !"
questions.explanation: Unlike "vous dites" (and "vous redites"), contredire takes -disez, like interdire, prédire and médire: "vous vous contredisez". "Contredisiez" is the imparfait or subjunctive.

questions.stem: Complete: "Pendant le débat, elle s'est ___ deux fois."
questions.explanation: With "se contredire" the "se" is the direct object (she contradicted herself), so the participle agrees with the subject: "elle s'est contredite".

questions.stem: The examiner points out that you have contradicted yourself. Which answer does the lesson recommend?
choices: Je me suis mal exprimé : ce que je voulais dire, c'est que …
Vous avez raison, j'abandonne ma position.
(say nothing and wait for the next question)
questions.explanation: Admit it and reformulate, or show that the two ideas fit together. Denying what you said, giving up your whole position or freezing all make it worse.

questions.stem: The model monologue takes about three minutes. How should a candidate bring a real one to five to seven minutes?
choices: by summarising the document at length
by adding a second example to each part, or a third argument
questions.explanation: More substance fills time usefully. A digression, a long summary of the document or an unnaturally slow delivery all count against you.

questions.stem: What does "prendre le contre-pied de" mean in "L'examinatrice a pris le contre-pied de ma thèse"?
choices: to take the opposite view of
to ask for a summary of
questions.explanation: Examiners often take the opposite view on purpose to see how you defend your position.

questions.stem: In the model debate, how does the candidate deal with his digression about working at a campsite?
choices: He notices it, stops himself and comes back to the question.
He finishes the story in detail.
He waits for the examiner to stop him.
He uses it as his main argument.
questions.explanation: "Pardon, je digresse. Pour revenir à votre question …": noticing and refocusing yourself is the best way to handle a digression.

questions.stem: In this lesson, what is "le support"?
choices: the short document that prompts the discussion
questions.explanation: "Le support" is the prompt document; it also means a medium (un support numérique). Notes are "la prise de notes", the timer "le chronomètre".

questions.stem: Put the stages of the 30-minute preparation in the order the lesson suggests.
choices: Read both documents and choose one.
Pin down the question and what is at stake.
Write a detailed outline in keywords.
Write out your opening and conclusion in full.
List two likely objections and your answers.
questions.explanation: Choosing comes first; the question shapes the outline; the opening and conclusion come from the finished outline; the last minutes prepare for the debate.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning.
questions.explanation: "To contradict yourself" is "se contredire". "Le mot-clé" (also written "le mot clé"), plural "les mots-clés".

questions.stem: Which are common mistakes at the oral, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
choices: Spending three minutes summarising the document.
Reading full sentences from your notes.
Asking the examiner to rephrase a question.
Learning a monologue by heart for a topic you hope to get.
questions.explanation: A long summary, reading notes aloud and a learned-by-heart monologue are the mistakes. Asking for a question to be rephrased and conceding part of an objection are good moves.

questions.stem: Type the French word for "keyword", with its article.
questions.explanation: "Le mot-clé" (plural les mots-clés); "le mot clé" without a hyphen is also accepted.

cards.back: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet, 1694–1778). Printed by Gabriel Cramer in Geneva early in 1759, without the author's name, as a "translation" from the German of a "Doctor Ralph"; banned in several places and a best-seller at once.

Driven out of a Westphalian castle, the naive Candide meets war, the Lisbon earthquake and the Inquisition, finds Eldorado in South America and loses most of its gold, sees slavery in Surinam, and settles with his friends on a small farm near Constantinople.
Pangloss: Candide's tutor (le précepteur), the optimist philosopher. Martin: the pessimist. Cunégonde: the baron's daughter Candide loves. Cacambo: his loyal valet.

Not a cheerful mood but a philosophical system: after Leibniz (Essais de théodicée, 1710), this world is the best possible and every evil serves a greater good. Its opposite in the tale: le pessimisme (Martin).
The Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755 (Candide arrives that day) and the Seven Years' War (1756–1763), behind the battle scenes.
A short tale with simple characters, journeys and reversals of fortune, written to test an idea. Candide tests optimism.
Optimism, war, fanaticism (le fanatisme) and intolerance (l'intolérance) in religion, slavery, greed, the vanity of nobles.
A naive viewpoint; a calm tone for horrors; mock logic (donc, par conséquent between ideas that don't follow); mock praise (an admiring word next to something cruel or absurd).
The tale's utopia (l'utopie): a hidden, peaceful country where gold has no value and there are no trials or prisons. Candide leaves it to find Cunégonde.
After one more demonstration by Pangloss, Candide advises his friends to tend their own garden: modest, useful work rather than grand systems (one reading among several). Describe it; don't quote it.
Literary and cultural movement founded in Paris in the 1930s by Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas: the affirmation of Black identity and African cultures, written in French.
Martinique. Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (1939); usually credited with the word négritude; mayor of Fort-de-France 1945–2001.

Senegal. Poet; anthology of new Black and Malagasy poetry (1948, preface by Sartre); first president of Senegal (1960–1980); first African in the Académie française (1983); defended le métissage of cultures.
West African keeper of memory, often hereditary: historian, storyteller (le conteur) and musician (often with the kora). The epic of Sundiata, founder of the Mali empire, is the best-known example.
Proverbs, repetition, a narrator who speaks to the audience, stories within stories. Birago Diop, Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba (1947): tales heard from a griot, rewritten in French.
Québec (1909–1983, born in Manitoba). Bonheur d'occasion (1945), set in Saint-Henri, Montréal; prix Femina 1947, the first Canadian book to win it.
Georges Simenon: Belgian, born in Liège in 1903, author of the Maigret novels. C. F. Ramuz (1878–1947): Swiss, from the canton of Vaud, peasants and mountains in a French close to speech.
Algeria. Kateb Yacine (1929–1989): Nedjma (1956). Assia Djebar (1936–2015): L'Amour, la fantasia (1985); in 2005 the first writer from the Maghreb elected to the Académie française.
Un écrivain francophone writes in French, whatever his or her country: Senghor, Simenon, Roy and Djebar are francophone writers. Un écrivain français is a writer from France.
Reason applied to beliefs, laws and institutions; in France roughly 1715–1789. Capital L: le siècle des Lumières.
Published anonymously in Geneva. Three governments (republic, monarchy, despotism). The separation of powers: making laws, carrying them out and judging belong to different bodies.
Directed by Diderot and d'Alembert: 17 volumes of text (1751–1765) and 11 of plates (1762–1772); banned in 1752 and 1759; d'Alembert left in 1758; Diderot finished it.
Jean Calas, a Protestant of Toulouse, executed in 1762 for a murder he didn't commit; Voltaire's campaign and Traité sur la tolérance (1763); declared innocent in 1765.
Not Voltaire's: written by Evelyn Beatrice Hall in a 1906 book about him, as her summary of his attitude.

Legitimate power rests on an agreement by which people form one body and obey the laws they make together (the general will): sovereignty (la souveraineté) belongs to the people. Condemned in Geneva in 1762.
Ideas circulated in literary salons (Mme Geoffrin, Julie de Lespinasse), cafés and letters. Bold books were printed abroad (Amsterdam, Geneva), often anonymous, sold under the counter.

cards.front: Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen
cards.back: 26 August 1789, 17 articles: equal rights from birth, national sovereignty, law as the general will, presumption of innocence, freedom of opinion and expression within the law, separation of powers. Still in force via the 1958 Constitution's preamble.
Women's rights (Olympe de Gouges's declaration, 1791) and slavery (abolished 1794, restored 1802, abolished for good 1848).
Idea → En effet (reason) → On pourrait objecter que … → Certes … → Il n'en reste pas moins que …

Loi Climat et résilience, 22 August 2021, article 145: no scheduled domestic flight where the train makes the trip in under 2 h 30 without a change. The citizens' convention (2020) had proposed four hours.

Made for three years (to May 2026). Conditions: several direct trains a day, more than eight hours at the destination. In 2023: Orly–Bordeaux, Orly–Nantes, Orly–Lyon. Upheld by the Conseil d'État, 2 February 2024. Check the current list.
Airlines must offset (compenser) the emissions of most domestic flights: 50 % in 2022, 70 % in 2023, all from 2024.
Like mettre: j'émets, nous émettons, ils émettent; j'ai émis. L'émission = emission (and, A2, a programme).
La brève: short facts with a source. L'éditorial: the paper's opinion. L'interview: one named view. Le graphique: figures to describe with care (and a date and source).
Never copy: use a reporting verb and your own words. Souligner (agree), rappeler (neutral), prétendre (doubt), insinuer (suspicion). Estimates: selon + conditionnel.
cards.topic: Writing and speaking from a dossier

cards.back: Documents and topic (30 s) → problématique and plan (30 s) → part 1 (1 min 30) → objection and answer (1 min 30) → conclusion and opening (1 min).
